problems.title: A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test)
problems.summary: Decide whether two conversion rates differ by more than chance with a pooled two-proportion z-test, and plan how many users each arm needs before the experiment starts.
problems.bruteForce: Small counts (use Fisher's exact test), continuous metrics (use a t-test or bootstrap), repeated peeking at results without a sequential method, or users that are not independent (clustering, network effects).
problems.intuition: Under the null hypothesis both arms share one true rate, so the observed gap is just sampling noise whose size is known from the binomial variance. Dividing the gap by that noise gives a $z$-score that says how many standard errors apart the arms are. Sample size works the other way round: the smaller the effect you want to detect, the more users you need, growing with the inverse square of that effect.
problems.whyItWorks: For large samples the sample proportions are approximately normal by the central limit theorem, so the standardised difference is approximately standard normal under the null. The pooled rate estimates the common variance under that null. The sample-size formula comes from requiring the gap to clear the critical value under the null while still being detected with the desired power under the alternative.
approach: Compute each arm's observed rate and the pooled rate — the pooled rate is the estimate under the null
Form the standard error with the pooled variance — the noise expected if there is no true difference
Divide the observed difference by it to get $z$ — how many standard errors apart the arms are
Convert $z$ to a two-sided $p$-value with the normal tail — evidence against the null
Report a confidence interval with unpooled variance — shows the plausible size of the effect, not just significance
Before the test, size each arm from the minimum detectable effect, significance and power — avoids underpowered experiments
problems.time: O(1) for the test and the sample-size formula
dryRun: $\delta = p_2 - p_1$ is the minimum detectable effect
problems.description: Comparing binary outcomes such as clicks or conversions between a control and a treatment with independent users, enough successes and failures in each arm, and a fixed analysis time decided in advance.

examples.input: What does a $p$-value mean in an A/B test?
examples.output: It is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two arms truly had the same rate; it is not the probability that the treatment is better.

examples.input: Why pool the rates for the test statistic?
examples.output: The null hypothesis says there is one common rate, so the pooled estimate is the best variance estimate under that null; the confidence interval uses unpooled variances because it describes the actual difference.

examples.input: What happens if you peek at the results every day?
examples.output: Each look is another chance for a spurious significant result, so the overall false-positive rate rises well above $\alpha$; use a fixed horizon or a sequential or alpha-spending design.

examples.input: How does sample size scale with effect size?
examples.output: Inversely with the square of the minimum detectable effect, so detecting half the effect needs about four times as many users.

constraints: Significance level $\alpha$ — false-positive rate allowed (two-sided here)
Power $1-\beta$ — chance of detecting the minimum effect
Minimum detectable effect $\delta$ — smallest change worth detecting
Baseline rate $p$ — needed for the variance
edgeCases: Peeking and stopping when $p$ dips below $\alpha$ inflates false positives; fix the sample size or use sequential tests
The normal approximation needs enough successes and failures in each arm
Testing many metrics or variants without correction raises the chance of a false win

The constants 1.96 and 0.84 are rounded critical values for $\alpha=0.05$ two-sided and 80% power; pass other values for other settings, and check the interval for practical size, not just significance

problems.title: Activation Functions
problems.summary: Element-wise non-linear functions applied between linear layers so a network can represent more than a single linear map.
problems.bruteForce: Avoid sigmoid or tanh deep in a stack because they saturate. Avoid plain ReLU if many units die (use a leaky variant), and do not put an activation on a regression output that must be unbounded.
problems.intuition: Without a non-linearity, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear layer, so depth buys nothing. The choice of activation also decides how gradients flow: saturating curves squash them toward zero, while piecewise-linear ones like ReLU pass them through unchanged wherever they are active.
problems.whyItWorks: A non-linear activation lets a sum of simple units approximate complicated functions. ReLU keeps a derivative of one on its active side, which avoids the repeated shrinking that sigmoid and tanh cause, so deep networks train much more easily. GELU is a smooth variant that weights its input by how likely it is to be positive.
approach: Pick the function by role — hidden layers want cheap non-saturating curves, outputs want a specific range
Apply it element-wise to the pre-activation z — it adds the non-linearity without mixing units
Keep its derivative for backprop — the gradient is the upstream error times f′(z)
Check the saturation regions — tiny derivatives there are what stall learning
problems.time: O(n) for n elements, forward and backward
problems.space: O(n) to keep the input or output for the derivative
problems.description: ReLU or GELU for hidden layers by default, sigmoid for binary outputs and gates, tanh for bounded zero-centred values, softmax for multi-class outputs.

examples.input: Why do we need non-linear activations?
examples.output: Composing linear maps gives another linear map, so without them extra layers add no expressive power.

examples.input: Why did ReLU replace sigmoid in hidden layers?
examples.output: Its gradient does not shrink on the active side, it is cheap, and it yields sparse activations, which eases training of deep networks.

examples.input: What is the dying ReLU problem?
examples.output: If a unit's input stays negative its output and gradient are zero, so its weights never update; leaky variants keep a small slope.

constraints: Choice of function (ReLU, GELU, tanh, sigmoid, ...)
Leaky slope (negative-side slope of LeakyReLU, so units cannot die)
Approximation mode for GELU (exact erf or the tanh form)
edgeCases: Dying ReLU: a unit that always sees negative input gets zero gradient forever
Plain exp in sigmoid overflows for large negative inputs; use a stable form in production
Do not apply softmax before a loss that already applies it
ReLU is not differentiable at 0; frameworks pick a convention for that single point

problems.title: AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps)
problems.summary: Build a strong classifier as a weighted vote of weak ones, training each new stump on the data re-weighted to emphasise earlier mistakes.
problems.bruteForce: With noisy or mislabelled data, since the exponential loss keeps raising the weight of bad points and the ensemble chases them. Also when you need calibrated probabilities or very large datasets (gradient boosting libraries are faster and more flexible).
problems.intuition: A stump alone is barely better than guessing, but different stumps can be wrong on different points. AdaBoost keeps a weight on every sample and, after each round, raises the weight of the points just misclassified so the next weak learner is forced to fix them. Stumps that do well get a larger say in the final vote.
problems.whyItWorks: AdaBoost is stagewise minimisation of the exponential loss over additive models. Given the current ensemble, the best new weak learner minimises the weighted error, and the optimal vote weight for it has the closed form of half the log odds of that error. The training error of the ensemble falls exponentially as long as every learner beats chance on the reweighted data.
approach: Start with uniform sample weights — every point matters equally at first
Search every feature, threshold and sign for the stump with the smallest weighted error — the best weak learner for the current weights
Set the vote weight $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}$ — accurate stumps get larger votes, chance-level ones get none
Multiply each weight by $\exp(-\alpha\, y\, h(x))$ and renormalise — mistakes grow, hits shrink
Repeat for $T$ rounds and store $(\alpha, \mathrm{stump})$ pairs — the ensemble
Predict the sign of the $\alpha$-weighted sum of stump outputs — a weighted majority vote
problems.time: O(T·d·n²) as written (O(T·d·n log n) with sorted splits)
problems.space: O(n + T) for the weights and the stored stumps
problems.description: Tabular classification with clean labels where a simple weak learner is available, as a fast strong baseline, and to learn boosting before moving to gradient boosting.

examples.input: How does AdaBoost reweight samples?
examples.output: It multiplies the weight of each sample by $\exp(-\alpha\, y\, h(x))$: misclassified points are scaled up, correct ones scaled down, then all weights are renormalised.

examples.input: Why is a weak learner enough?
examples.output: The training error bound shrinks multiplicatively each round whenever the learner is even slightly better than chance on the current weights.

examples.input: Why is AdaBoost sensitive to noise?
examples.output: The exponential loss grows quickly for misclassified points, so mislabelled samples receive ever larger weights and the ensemble bends to fit them.

examples.input: How is AdaBoost related to gradient boosting?
examples.output: It is gradient boosting with the exponential loss; gradient boosting generalises the idea to arbitrary differentiable losses.

constraints: Number of rounds $T$ — more rounds fit more; use early stopping on validation data
Weak learner depth — stumps here, shallow trees are common
Learning rate — shrinks each vote to slow overfitting (fixed at one here)
edgeCases: Labels must be $-1$ and $+1$ in this code; sklearn takes any labels
Label noise and outliers get exponentially up-weighted and degrade the model
An error of exactly zero would give an infinite vote weight, so the code clips the error
The stump search here is the slow quadratic version; sort once per feature in practice

problems.title: Adam Optimizer
problems.summary: Gradient descent that keeps running averages of the gradient and its square, and scales each parameter's step by the inverse of the gradient's recent size.
problems.bruteForce: Plain SGD with momentum can generalise better on some vision tasks, and when weight decay is wanted, prefer AdamW, which decouples decay from the adaptive step.
problems.intuition: The first moment smooths noisy gradients like momentum, while the second moment gives each parameter its own step size, so weights with small gradients take larger steps and volatile ones take smaller steps. Bias correction fixes the zero start of the averages so the first steps are not artificially small.
problems.whyItWorks: Dividing by the root of the second moment makes the update roughly scale-invariant to the gradient magnitude, so one learning rate works across layers with very different gradient sizes. The averages start at zero and are therefore biased low early on; dividing by $(1-\beta^t)$ removes that bias.
approach: Keep $m$, $v$ (zeros) and a step counter $t$ per parameter — the state that makes steps adaptive
Update $m$ as a moving average of the gradient — smooths direction like momentum
Update $v$ as a moving average of the squared gradient — tracks per-parameter scale
Bias-correct both with $1-\beta^t$ — undoes the zero initialisation
Step by $\eta\,\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)$ — a normalised step whose size is roughly η
problems.time: O(d) per step for d parameters
problems.space: O(d) extra, two moment buffers the size of the parameters
problems.description: Default optimiser for deep networks, transformers and problems with sparse or noisy gradients, where it needs little tuning.

examples.input: What do $m$ and $v$ represent?
examples.output: $m$ is an exponential average of gradients (momentum) and $v$ is an exponential average of squared gradients (per-parameter scale).

examples.input: Why bias correction?
examples.output: m and v start at zero, so early averages are biased toward zero; dividing by $1-\beta^t$ rescales them.

examples.input: How does AdamW differ from Adam with L2?
examples.output: AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding it to the gradient, so the decay is not rescaled by the adaptive denominator.

constraints: Learning rate $\eta$
$\beta_1$ (decay of the gradient average)
$\beta_2$ (decay of the squared-gradient average)
$\epsilon$ (numerical floor in the denominator)
edgeCases: Skipping bias correction makes early steps too small
L2 regularisation inside Adam is not true weight decay; use AdamW
Adam can generalise worse than tuned SGD on some tasks
Near-zero gradients with a tiny ε can still produce large steps

problems.title: AdamW Decoupled Weight Decay
problems.summary: Adam with L2 puts the decay term inside the gradient, where the adaptive denominator rescales it. AdamW subtracts the decay from the weights directly, so every weight shrinks at the same rate.
problems.bruteForce: With plain SGD, where L2 regularisation and weight decay are equivalent and no change is needed. Decay is also usually skipped for biases and normalisation parameters.
problems.intuition: With L2 regularisation the penalty gradient $\lambda w$ is added to $g$ and then divided by $\sqrt{\hat{v}}$ like everything else, so a weight with a large gradient history is decayed less, and one with a small history is decayed more. That is not what weight decay means. AdamW takes the decay out of the gradient and applies it as a separate shrink $-\eta\lambda w$, so the regularisation strength no longer depends on the gradient scale and is easier to tune. Flow: gradient + history → adaptive step → separate decay → update.
problems.whyItWorks: For SGD, adding $\lambda w$ to the gradient gives the update $-\eta\lambda w$, so L2 and weight decay coincide. In Adam the added term is divided by $\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon$, so the effective decay is $\eta\lambda w/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)$, which differs per weight and is entangled with the gradient scale. AdamW restores the fixed decay $\eta\lambda w$, which also makes the best $\lambda$ less dependent on the learning rate, as reported in the paper.
approach: Form the gradient $g$ of the loss alone — in AdamW the penalty is not added to it
Update $m$ and $v$ with bias correction as in Adam — the adaptive part is unchanged
Compute the adaptive step $\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)$ — scaled per parameter
Add $\lambda w$ outside the adaptive ratio — the decay bypasses the denominator
Update $w \leftarrow w - \eta(\ldots)$ — decay and step share only the learning rate
problems.time: O(d) per step for d parameters
problems.space: O(d) extra, two moment buffers
dryRun: Adam+L2: $g^{\prime} = g + \lambda w$, then the Adam step
problems.description: Training transformers and most modern networks with Adam-style optimisers when weight decay is wanted; it is the standard choice.

examples.input: Why is L2 regularisation not the same as weight decay in Adam?
examples.output: The L2 term enters the gradient and is divided by the adaptive denominator, so weights with large gradient history are decayed less. Weight decay should shrink all weights by the same factor.

examples.input: What does AdamW change in the update?
examples.output: It adds $\lambda w$ to the final step, outside the ratio $\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)$, instead of to the gradient.

examples.input: What happens to AdamW weights when the gradient is zero?
examples.output: The moments decay but the decay term still applies, so the weight keeps shrinking by about $\eta\lambda w$ each step.

constraints: Learning rate $\eta$
Weight decay $\lambda$
$\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$
$\epsilon$
edgeCases: Passing the L2 coefficient to Adam and calling it weight decay; the behaviour differs from AdamW
Applying the decay to biases and normalisation scales, which usually should not be decayed
Assuming $\lambda$ is comparable across libraries; some scale the decay by the learning rate and some do not

problems.title: Bottleneck Adapter Layers
problems.summary: Insert a small bottleneck module with a residual connection after a frozen sublayer and train only the module, a few percent of the weights.
problems.bruteForce: Latency-critical inference, since adapters add sequential layers that cannot be folded into the weights. LoRA is preferred when merging for zero extra latency matters.
problems.intuition: A pretrained network already computes useful features, so a task only needs a small correction on top of them. A narrow down-then-up projection with a skip connection is exactly that: it can pass features through unchanged, or add a learned low-dimensional edit. Initialising the up-projection at zero makes the module the identity, so training starts from the pretrained function. Unlike LoRA, the module is a new sequential layer and cannot be merged away. Flow: sublayer output → down-project → nonlinearity → up-project → add back.
problems.whyItWorks: With the up-projection at zero, $y = x + W_u\,\sigma(W_d x + b_d) + b_u$ reduces to $y = x$ when $W_u = 0$ and $b_u = 0$, so the adapted model equals the pretrained one at step zero. Gradients flow through the skip and the bottleneck to the adapter, while the frozen weights get none. The bottleneck restricts the correction to an $r$-dimensional space, which is enough for many tasks and keeps the parameter count near $2dr$ instead of $d^2$ per layer.
approach: Freeze every pretrained weight — only adapters and task heads will train
Down-project $d \rightarrow r$ with $r \ll d$ — the bottleneck keeps the parameter count small
Apply a nonlinearity — lets the adapter learn more than a linear map
Up-project $r \rightarrow d$ and add the input back — the skip makes the adapter a residual correction
Zero-initialise the up-projection — the adapter starts as the identity
problems.time: O(n·d·r) extra per adapter and token, paid at inference too
problems.space: $2dr + r + d$ trainable parameters per adapter
dryRun: $W_d: d \rightarrow r,\;\; W_u: r \rightarrow d,\;\; r \ll d$
problems.description: Serving many tasks from one frozen base, where each task stores only small adapter weights, and when adding a task must not disturb earlier ones.

examples.input: Why is the adapter initialised near the identity?
examples.output: So the model starts exactly as the pretrained one. A random adapter would perturb every layer and destroy the pretrained features before training could help.

examples.input: How many parameters does one adapter add?
examples.output: $2dr + r + d$ with hidden size $d$ and bottleneck $r$: two weight matrices plus two bias vectors. For $r \ll d$ this is far less than $d^2$.

examples.input: Adapters versus LoRA: what is the trade-off?
examples.output: LoRA's low-rank update is parallel and merges into $W$, so inference is unchanged. Adapters add sequential layers and extra latency, but they are simple, modular and can use a nonlinearity.

examples.input: Where are adapters placed in a transformer layer?
examples.output: In the original design, after the attention sublayer's output projection and after the feed-forward sublayer, before the residual addition and layer norm.

constraints: Bottleneck size $r$
Nonlinearity (ReLU, GELU)
Placement: after attention, after feed-forward, or both
Initial scale of the weights
edgeCases: Exactly zero initialisation of both $W_u$ and $W_d$ would give zero gradients; zero only the up-projection and keep $W_d$ random
Adapters cannot be merged into the base weights, so inference latency grows with depth
Remember to unfreeze layer norms or task heads if the recipe trains them; this code covers only the adapter

problems.title: Approximate Nearest-Neighbour Vector Index (IVF)
problems.summary: Exact search scans every vector for each query. An IVF index clusters the vectors with k-means, stores each one in its nearest cell, and at query time scans only the $n_{probe}$ cells closest to the query, trading a little recall for a large speed-up.
problems.bruteForce: Small corpora, where exact search is one matrix product and has no recall loss. Also data that changes constantly with no retraining, since stale centroids hurt recall, and cases that need guaranteed exact results.
problems.intuition: Nearby vectors tend to fall in the same cluster, so most of the corpus is provably irrelevant to a query that lands far from it. The index pays once to learn the clusters, then each query compares against $n_{list}$ centroids and scans only a few cells instead of all $N$ vectors. The cost is that a true neighbour sitting just across a cell boundary is missed unless a neighbouring cell is probed as well, which is why $n_{probe}$ is the recall-versus-speed dial. Graph indexes such as HNSW take a different route: a layered proximity graph where search greedily walks to closer nodes, from a sparse top layer down to the dense bottom layer, keeping a candidate list of size $ef$. Product quantisation instead compresses each vector into a few small codes so more of the index fits in memory. Flow: query → nearest cells → scan candidates → top-k.
problems.whyItWorks: If the clustering respects the geometry, the nearest neighbours of a query are concentrated in the few cells whose centroids are closest to it. Scanning those cells gives the exact top-$k$ of that subset, and probing all cells scans everything, so the method degrades smoothly to exact search. The cost is about $n_{list} d + \frac{n_{probe}}{n_{list}} N d$, minimised near $n_{list} \approx \sqrt{N}$ for small $n_{probe}$.
approach: Run k-means on the vectors to get nlist centroids — the cells that partition the space
Assign every vector to its nearest centroid — an inverted list per cell, each vector stored once
At query time rank the centroids by distance to the query — cheap, only nlist comparisons
Take the nprobe nearest cells and scan their vectors — the only exact distance work
Return the k closest scanned vectors — approximate top-k
Measure recall@k against brute force — tells how much accuracy the speed-up cost
problems.time: O(nlist·d + (nprobe/nlist)·N·d) per query versus O(N·d) exact; build is k-means
problems.space: O(N·d) for the vectors plus O(nlist·d) for centroids
dryRun: Exact search per query: cost $= N d$
Lloyd step: $c_j \leftarrow$ mean of cell $j$ vectors
problems.description: Corpora of millions of vectors where brute force per query is too slow or too costly, and a small recall loss is acceptable because the generator or a re-ranker tolerates it.

examples.input: Why does IVF raise recall when nprobe grows?
examples.output: More cells are scanned, so more of the corpus is searched exactly. At $n_{probe} = n_{list}$ every vector is scanned and the result equals brute force.

examples.input: How does HNSW differ from IVF?
examples.output: HNSW is a layered proximity graph. Search enters at the sparse top layer, greedily moves to closer neighbours, then descends, keeping $ef$ candidates at the bottom. It usually gives high recall at low latency but uses more memory and has no training step.

examples.input: What does product quantisation do?
examples.output: It splits each vector into sub-vectors and replaces each with the index of its nearest codebook entry, compressing a vector to a few bytes. Distances are approximated from the codes, trading accuracy for memory.

examples.input: How do you choose nlist and nprobe?
examples.output: Pick $n_{list}$ near $\sqrt{N}$, then raise $n_{probe}$ until recall@k on held-out queries meets the target, accepting the latency that results.

constraints: nlist, the number of cells, often about $\sqrt{N}$
nprobe, the number of cells scanned per query
k-means iterations and seed
HNSW alternative: graph degree $M$ and search width $ef$
edgeCases: Recall is not guaranteed: a true neighbour in an unprobed cell is lost, so always measure recall@k against brute force on real queries
Cells are rarely balanced, so the real cost depends on the sizes of the probed cells, not just the formula
Centroids go stale when the data distribution drifts; re-train the quantiser periodically
Euclidean cells assume the metric matches the one used to cluster; normalise vectors if you search by cosine

problems.title: ARIMA Forecasting
problems.summary: Difference the series until it is roughly stationary, regress it on its own recent values, forecast the differenced series forward, and sum the forecasts back to the original scale. This card implements the AR part with d differences, ARIMA(p, d, 0).
problems.bruteForce: Skip it for series with strong seasonality unless you add seasonal terms, for many exogenous drivers, for nonlinear dynamics, and for long horizons where forecasts collapse to a constant or a line.
problems.intuition: Many series wander, so their level is unpredictable, but the changes between steps are stable and depend on recent changes. Differencing turns the wandering series into a steadier one that a plain regression on lagged values can model, and summing the predicted changes brings the forecast back to the original level.
problems.whyItWorks: Stationarity makes the dependence on lags constant over time, so coefficients estimated on the past still apply to the future. Fitting an AR(p) by least squares is conditional maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise, and integrating the differenced forecast is exact because differencing is an invertible linear operation given the starting values.
approach: Difference the series d times — removes stochastic trend so the dependence structure is stable
Build a lag matrix of the last p values plus a constant column — each row predicts the next difference
Solve least squares for the constant and AR coefficients — conditional maximum likelihood for Gaussian noise
Forecast the differenced series recursively, feeding each forecast back in — future lags are not yet observed
Undo differencing by cumulative sums from the last observed values — returns forecasts to the original scale
problems.time: O(n·p²) for least squares plus O(h·p) for forecasting
problems.space: O(n·p) for the lag matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def fit_ar(z, p):
    n = len(z)
    cols = [z[p - j - 1:n - j - 1] for j in range(p)]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n - p)] + cols)
    return np.linalg.lstsq(X, z[p:], rcond=None)[0]

def forecast(y, p, d, h):
    z = y
    for _ in range(d):
        z = np.diff(z)
    beta = fit_ar(z, p)
    hist = list(z[-p:])
    for _ in range(h):
        lags = hist[::-1][:p]
        hist.append(beta[0] + beta[1:] @ lags)
    dz = np.array(hist[p:])
    for lvl in reversed(range(d)):
        last = np.diff(y, n=lvl)[-1]
        dz = last + np.cumsum(dz)
    return dz, beta
dryRun: Difference: $\nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$, apply $d$ times to get $z_t$
problems.description: Univariate forecasting of autocorrelated series with trend that differencing removes, a transparent baseline to beat with machine learning models, and when ACF and PACF plots suggest low orders.

examples.input: What do p, d and q stand for?
examples.output: p is the number of lagged values in the autoregression, d the number of differences to make the series stationary, q the number of lagged forecast errors in the moving-average part.

examples.input: How do you choose d?
examples.output: Difference until a plot and the ACF look stationary, typically once or twice; stationarity tests such as ADF help, but over-differencing hurts.

examples.input: Why do ARIMA forecasts get flat at long horizons?
examples.output: Future values are fed back as inputs, so shocks average out and the forecast converges to the mean of the differenced series, which becomes a straight drift line once integrated.

constraints: p autoregressive order — read from the PACF or chosen by AIC
d differencing order — usually 0, 1 or 2, enough to look stationary
q moving-average order — not in this code, which fits ARIMA(p, d, 0)
Constant — include for a drift after differencing, drop it if the series has none
edgeCases: Over-differencing adds negative autocorrelation and inflates forecast variance
This is conditional least squares; libraries that fit exact likelihood or MA terms give slightly different estimates
Point forecasts of a stationary part revert to the mean, so long horizons look flat
Judge models on a rolling-origin hold-out, never on in-sample fit

problems.title: Autocorrelation (ACF and PACF)
problems.summary: The ACF is the correlation of a series with a lagged copy of itself. The PACF is the correlation at each lag after removing the effect of the shorter lags, computed from the ACF with the Durbin-Levinson recursion.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it on non-stationary data without differencing first, for strongly nonlinear dependence that correlation misses, and for very short series where lag estimates are too noisy.
problems.intuition: If today resembles yesterday, the lag-1 correlation is high, but it also makes today resemble two days ago through yesterday. The ACF mixes direct and relayed dependence; the PACF strips the relayed part, so an AR($p$) process shows a PACF that cuts off after lag $p$ while its ACF decays.
problems.whyItWorks: For an autoregression the Yule-Walker equations link the ACF to the coefficients through a Toeplitz system. The PACF at lag $k$ is the last coefficient $\phi_{kk}$ of the best order-$k$ autoregression, and the Durbin-Levinson recursion builds order $k$ from order $k-1$ in O(k) work instead of solving a fresh system.
approach: Centre the series — correlation is about deviations from the mean
Compute autocovariances with a divisor of $n$ at every lag — keeps the covariance matrix positive semi-definite
Divide by lag zero to get the ACF — makes it scale free in $[-1, 1]$
Run Durbin-Levinson on the ACF — gives each order's last coefficient without solving a linear system per lag
Compare each lag with the band of about two over root $n$ — spikes outside are unlikely to be noise
problems.time: O(n·K) for the ACF directly, O(K²) for Durbin-Levinson
problems.space: O(K) for the recursion state
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def acf(x, K):
    x = x - x.mean()
    c = np.array([x[: len(x) - k] @ x[k:] for k in range(K + 1)])
    return c / c[0]

def pacf(r, K):
    phi, out = np.zeros(0), [1.0]
    for k in range(1, K + 1):
        num = r[k] - phi @ r[k - 1:0:-1]
        den = 1 - phi @ r[1:k]
        c = num / den
        phi = np.append(phi - c * phi[::-1], c)
        out.append(c)
    return np.array(out)
dryRun: PACF: $\alpha_k = \phi_{kk}$ (last coefficient of the order-$k$ fit)
problems.description: Choosing AR and MA orders for ARIMA, spotting seasonality and trend from slowly decaying or periodic spikes, and checking that model residuals look like white noise.

examples.input: How do ACF and PACF identify an AR or MA model?
examples.output: An AR($p$) has a PACF that cuts off after lag $p$ and an ACF that decays; an MA($q$) has an ACF that cuts off after lag $q$ and a PACF that decays.

examples.input: What does the PACF at lag $k$ measure?
examples.output: The correlation between $y_t$ and $y_{t-k}$ after linearly removing the effect of the lags in between, equal to the last coefficient of an order-$k$ autoregression.

examples.input: Why divide by $n$ and not $n-k$ in the autocovariance?
examples.output: Dividing by $n$ guarantees the estimated autocovariance sequence is positive semi-definite, which the Yule-Walker system needs; $n-k$ is less biased but can give invalid values.

constraints: max lag $K$ — a common rule is a fraction of $n$, such as $n/4$
Divisor $n$ versus $n-k$ — $n$ keeps a valid covariance sequence and is the usual default
Differencing order — applied before computing so the series is near stationary
edgeCases: Trending series give an ACF that decays very slowly and hides the real structure; difference first
Many lags are tested at once, so a few spikes outside the band are expected by chance
Seasonal data needs a lag at the season length, not just short lags
Different libraries estimate the PACF differently (Yule-Walker, OLS, Burg), so small numeric differences are normal

problems.title: Autoencoder
problems.summary: Train a network to reproduce its input after squeezing it through a narrow bottleneck, so the bottleneck holds a compressed code.
problems.bruteForce: If a linear projection is enough, PCA is exact and needs no training. A bottleneck-free autoencoder can learn the identity and nothing useful, and it is not a proper generative model.
problems.intuition: The target is the input itself, so the only way to get low error through a small code is to keep the directions that carry the most information about the data. With linear layers this is exactly principal component analysis in disguise; nonlinear layers let the code follow curved structure that PCA cannot.
problems.whyItWorks: Minimising squared reconstruction error through a $k$-dimensional code forces the encoder-decoder pair to span the best $k$-dimensional subspace. For a linear autoencoder the optimum spans the top principal subspace, though the learned axes are an arbitrary rotation of the principal components.
approach: Encode the batch through a layer with fewer units than inputs — the bottleneck forces compression
Decode back to input size with a second layer — produces the reconstruction
Compute the reconstruction error against the input itself — no labels needed
Backpropagate the error through decoder then encoder — chain rule layer by layer
Take gradient steps until the error stops improving — the code now summarises the data
problems.time: O(steps · n·d·k) for full-batch training
problems.space: O(n·(d+k)) for activations and O(d·k) for the weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def train_ae(X, k, f, df, lr=0.01, steps=20000, seed=0):
    n, d = X.shape
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W1 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (d, k))
    b1 = np.zeros(k)
    W2 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (k, d))
    b2 = np.zeros(d)
    for _ in range(steps):
        H = f(X @ W1 + b1)
        E = (H @ W2 + b2 - X) / n
        dH = (E @ W2.T) * df(H)
        W2 -= lr * H.T @ E
        b2 -= lr * E.sum(0)
        W1 -= lr * X.T @ dH
        b1 -= lr * dH.sum(0)
    return W1, b1, W2, b2

def reconstruct(P, X, f):
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = P
    return f(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2
dryRun: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2} = h^{\top}E,\;\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial b_2} = \sum E$
Linear $f$: min error = dropped PCA variances
problems.description: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection by reconstruction error, and pretraining representations without labels.

examples.input: How is a linear autoencoder related to PCA?
examples.output: With linear layers and squared error, the best code spans the same subspace as the top principal components. The reconstruction error is the same, but the axes may be rotated.

examples.input: How can an autoencoder detect anomalies?
examples.output: Train on normal data only. Anomalies reconstruct poorly, so a large reconstruction error is the anomaly score.

examples.input: What is a denoising autoencoder?
examples.output: It corrupts the input with noise and trains to reconstruct the clean version, which prevents the identity solution and learns robust features.

constraints: Bottleneck size $k$
Activation function $f$ (identity here gives the PCA-like case)
Learning rate and number of steps
Regularisation: weight decay, sparsity penalty or input noise
edgeCases: Too large a bottleneck lets the network copy the input
df takes the activation output (tanh: $1-h^2$); identity is the constant 1
Inputs should be centred; the linear-to-PCA match here assumes centred data
Full-batch gradient descent here is for clarity; real training uses minibatches and Adam

problems.title: Autoregressive Decoding Loop
problems.summary: Generate text one token at a time. Read the next-token logits at the last position, pick a token, append it, and repeat until an end token or the length limit.
problems.bruteForce: Greedy picking on long open-ended text, where it tends to repeat itself. Use sampling or beam search there. Training and scoring use teacher forcing with one parallel pass, not this loop.
problems.intuition: A language model only ever answers one question: given everything so far, what comes next? Generation is that question asked in a loop, with each answer fed back as input. Token $t+1$ needs token $t$, so the decode steps cannot run in parallel, unlike the prompt, which is processed in one pass (prefill). The loop is therefore latency-bound. Flow: prompt → logits → pick token → append → repeat until EOS.
problems.whyItWorks: The model factorises the sequence probability as $p(x_{1:T}) = \prod_t p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, so sampling or picking one token at a time from each conditional is a valid way to generate a whole sequence. A causal model's logits at position $t$ do not depend on later positions, so a cached run gives the same logits as a full recompute.
approach: Run the prompt through the model once (prefill) — gives logits at every position
Take the logits at the last position only — they define the next-token distribution
Pick a token, greedy argmax here — any sampling rule plugs in at this step
Append it to the sequence — the output becomes part of the next input
Stop at the EOS token or after $n_{\max}$ new tokens — otherwise the loop may never end
problems.time: O(T) sequential model calls for T new tokens; each call costs one forward pass (cheaper with a KV cache)
problems.space: O(T) for the token list, plus any cache the model keeps
dryRun: Stop at EOS or after $n_{\max}$ new tokens
problems.description: Any decoder-only language model producing text, from a chat reply to code completion. Swap the argmax for a sampling rule to get varied outputs.

examples.input: Why is generation sequential even though training is parallel?
examples.output: Training knows all the target tokens, so it can score every position at once with a causal mask. At inference the next token is not known until the previous one is chosen, so each step waits for the last.

examples.input: What are the prefill and decode phases?
examples.output: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and is compute-bound. Decode generates one token per step, reads the model weights and cache each time, and is usually memory-bandwidth-bound.

examples.input: How does the loop know when to stop?
examples.output: It stops when the model emits an end-of-sequence token or when a maximum number of new tokens is reached, whichever comes first.

examples.input: Why does a KV cache not change the output?
examples.output: It only stores values that a causal model would recompute identically, so the logits match up to floating-point rounding.

constraints: Maximum number of new tokens $n_{\max}$
EOS token id (and any extra stop tokens)
Token selection rule (greedy, temperature, top-$k$, top-$p$)
Batch size when decoding many sequences together
edgeCases: Feeding the whole sequence again every step is correct but costs $O(T^2)$ forward work without a cache
Using logits from any position other than the last gives the wrong next token
Without a max length, a model that never emits EOS loops forever
Greedy decoding can fall into repeating loops, as the repeated token in the example shows

problems.title: Backpropagation
problems.summary: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards, layer by layer, reusing values saved during the forward pass.
problems.bruteForce: Not for non-differentiable operations (hard thresholds, sampling) without a surrogate or estimator, and not when you only need a handful of derivatives of a tiny function, where finite differences or forward mode can be simpler.
problems.intuition: Each layer only needs to know how the loss changes with its output; it multiplies that by its own local derivative and hands the result to the layer below. Because the forward activations are cached, one backward sweep costs about the same as one forward pass, instead of one pass per weight.
problems.whyItWorks: The network is a composition of differentiable functions, so the chain rule factors the total derivative into a product of local Jacobians. Evaluating that product from the loss backwards turns every step into a matrix-vector product, which is far cheaper than forming full Jacobians.
approach: Run the forward pass and keep the hidden activations — the backward pass needs them
Differentiate the loss with respect to the output — this seeds the backward sweep
Get the last layer's weight gradient as activations$^{\top}$ times the error — each weight's blame is input times error
Push the error through $W^{\top}$ and multiply by the activation derivative — this is the chain rule across a layer
Repeat down to the first layer, summing rows for biases — every parameter receives its gradient
problems.time: O(parameters × batch size), about the cost of the forward pass
problems.space: O(activations) to cache layer outputs for the backward pass
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def forward(p, X):
    h = np.tanh(X @ p["W1"] + p["b1"])
    return h, h @ p["W2"] + p["b2"]

def loss_and_grads(p, X, y):
    h, out = forward(p, X)
    loss = ((out - y) ** 2).mean()
    d_out = 2 * (out - y) / out.size
    g = {"W2": h.T @ d_out, "b2": d_out.sum(axis=0)}
    d_h = d_out @ p["W2"].T
    d_pre = d_h * (1 - h ** 2)
    g["W1"] = X.T @ d_pre
    g["b1"] = d_pre.sum(axis=0)
    return loss, g
dryRun: Loss: $L = \mathrm{mean}$ over all entries of $(\hat{y} - y)^2$
problems.description: Training any differentiable model with gradient-based optimisers; it is what autograd frameworks implement for you.

examples.input: Why go backwards instead of forwards?
examples.output: Reverse mode gets the gradient of one scalar loss with respect to all parameters in one sweep; forward mode would need one sweep per parameter.

examples.input: Why must the forward activations be stored?
examples.output: Local derivatives such as $a^{\top}\delta$ and $1-a^2$ depend on forward values, so they are cached, trading memory for compute.

examples.input: How do you check a backprop implementation?
examples.output: Compare against a finite-difference gradient or an autograd framework on a small random problem.

constraints: Loss function (sets the starting error signal $\delta$)
Activation function (its derivative scales every backward step)
Weight initialisation (controls gradient size at the start)
Gradient clipping threshold (guards against exploding gradients)
edgeCases: Saturating activations (sigmoid, tanh) shrink gradients layer by layer and cause vanishing gradients
Forgetting to divide by batch size (or to sum bias gradients over the batch) scales updates wrongly
Shape mistakes in transposes still run when dimensions coincide; verify against a numerical gradient check
Gradients accumulate in frameworks unless zeroed each step

problems.title: Bag of Words and the N-gram Language Model
problems.summary: Bag of words counts each word per document and ignores order. A bigram language model counts adjacent word pairs and turns them into smoothed next-word probabilities.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks that depend on word order, long-range context or meaning, where one-hot counts treat "good" and "great" as unrelated. Large $n$ makes the count table huge and mostly empty.
problems.intuition: Bag of words keeps what words appear and throws away where, which is enough for topic-like tasks. A language model needs order, and the Markov trick makes it tractable: assume the next word depends only on the previous one, so a table of pair counts is the whole model. Unseen pairs would get probability zero and wreck any sentence that contains one, so add-$k$ smoothing moves a little mass to every pair. Flow: tokens → counts → smoothed probabilities → sentence log-prob.
problems.whyItWorks: The chain rule writes $P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)$ as a product of conditional probabilities, and the bigram assumption cuts each condition down to the previous word. The smoothed ratio is a proper distribution because the numerators over all $V$ next words sum to $c(\mathrm{prev})+kV$, exactly the denominator.
approach: Build a vocabulary from the corpus — fixes a column for every word
Bag of words: count each word per document — gives one count vector per text
Pad sentences with start and end markers — lets the model score the first and last word
Count adjacent pairs $c(w_{t-1}, w_t)$ — these are the sufficient statistics
Divide by the smoothed context total, $\frac{c+k}{c(\mathrm{prev})+kV}$ — each row becomes a distribution
Sum $\log P$ over the pairs of a sentence — avoids underflow from multiplying small numbers
problems.time: O(N) to count N tokens; O(V²) to build the table; O(T) to score T tokens
problems.space: O(V²) for the dense bigram table (sparse in practice)
dryRun: BoW: $X_{d,w}$ = count of word $w$ in doc $d$
problems.description: Strong, cheap baselines: bag of words for classification and retrieval features, and n-gram models for quick language scoring, spelling correction and as a comparison for neural models.

examples.input: Why do n-gram models need smoothing?
examples.output: A pair never seen in training gets probability zero, which makes any sentence containing it impossible and perplexity infinite. Smoothing reserves some mass for unseen events.

examples.input: What is the downside of add-one smoothing?
examples.output: With a large vocabulary it takes too much mass from seen events. Using a small $k$, or better methods such as backoff and Kneser-Ney, works better in practice.

examples.input: Why use log probabilities for sentences?
examples.output: Multiplying many small probabilities underflows, while adding their logs is stable and gives the quantity used to compute perplexity.

examples.input: What does bag of words lose?
examples.output: Word order and context, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vector.

constraints: Smoothing constant $k$ (1 is add-one; smaller is usually better)
N-gram order $n$
Vocabulary size and handling of unknown words
Whether to count words or use binary presence
edgeCases: The row for the end marker has no observed successors, so smoothing makes it uniform; it is never used as a context when scoring
Words not in the vocabulary raise a KeyError here; real systems map them to an unknown token
Log-probabilities of sentences of different length are not comparable without normalising by length

problems.title: Additive (Bahdanau) Attention
problems.summary: Score each encoder state against the current decoder state with a small one-hidden-layer network, softmax the scores, and return the weighted sum of encoder states as the context vector.
problems.bruteForce: Large transformer-style models where scaled dot-product attention is faster because it is a single matrix multiplication and parallelises well over positions.
problems.intuition: A sequence-to-sequence decoder that sees only one fixed summary of the source must squeeze a whole sentence into one vector. Additive attention lets the decoder look back at every encoder state at each step and decide which ones matter now. The relevance score comes from a learned tanh network over both vectors, so the two sides need not have the same size.
problems.whyItWorks: The tanh network can represent a learned relevance function between a query and each key, rather than just a dot product, and sees both vectors jointly. Softmax weighting is differentiable, so the model learns an alignment end to end from translation loss alone, and the decoder gets direct access to any source position instead of one compressed summary.
approach: Project the decoder state with $W_s$ and every encoder state with $W_h$ — maps both into a shared scoring space
Add them (broadcast over positions) and apply tanh — lets query and key interact nonlinearly
Dot with a learned vector $v$ — reduces each position to one scalar score
Softmax over source positions — turns scores into weights that sum to one
Weighted sum of the encoder states — the context vector fed to the decoder
problems.time: O(T·(d_s + d_h)·d_a) per decoder step for T source positions
problems.space: O(T) for the weights
problems.description: RNN encoder-decoder models for translation, summarisation or speech, and whenever query and key have different dimensions or you need a small, parametrised scorer.

examples.input: Why is it called additive attention?
examples.output: The query and key projections are added before the tanh and scoring vector, unlike the multiplicative dot-product form.

examples.input: What problem does attention solve in seq2seq?
examples.output: It removes the fixed-size bottleneck by letting the decoder read all encoder states with a different weighting at each output step.

examples.input: How does it differ from scaled dot-product attention?
examples.output: It uses a learned one-hidden-layer scorer and works with different query and key sizes; dot-product is cheaper and parallelises but needs matching dimensions or a projection.

examples.input: What are the shapes of the attention weights and context?
examples.output: One weight per source position $(T,)$ and a context vector of the encoder width $d_h$.

constraints: Attention hidden width $d_a$
Encoder and decoder state sizes
Whether encoder states are bidirectional
Attention dropout
edgeCases: Padded source positions need masking before the softmax
Original Bahdanau attention uses the previous decoder state; some variants use the current one
Costs more than dot-product attention since scoring has its own hidden layer
This sketch is one query and has no mask, bias or batching

problems.title: Batch Normalization
problems.summary: Normalise each feature to zero mean and unit variance across the mini-batch, then let the network rescale and shift it with learned parameters.
problems.bruteForce: Avoid with very small batches (noisy statistics) and for sequence models with variable lengths, where layer normalisation is the usual choice.
problems.intuition: Layers keep seeing inputs whose scale drifts as earlier weights change, which forces small learning rates. Re-centering and re-scaling every feature per batch keeps those inputs in a steady range, and the learned $\gamma$ and $\beta$ let the layer undo the normalisation if that is what helps.
problems.whyItWorks: Stable input statistics make the loss surface better behaved, so larger learning rates train reliably, and the noise from batch statistics acts as a mild regulariser. At inference the batch is not available, so running averages collected during training replace the batch mean and variance.
approach: Compute the per-feature mean and variance over the batch axis — these are the statistics to remove
Divide the centred input by $\sqrt{\mathrm{var}+\epsilon}$ — $\epsilon$ avoids division by zero
Apply $\gamma$ and $\beta$ — restores representational freedom
Update running mean and variance with momentum — they will be used at inference
In eval mode use the running statistics instead — outputs must not depend on other samples
problems.time: O(n·d) for n samples and d features
problems.space: O(d) for γ, β and the running statistics
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def bn_train(x, gamma, beta, run, mom=0.1, eps=1e-5):
    mu, var = x.mean(axis=0), x.var(axis=0)
    xhat = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
    n = len(x)
    run["mean"] = (1 - mom) * run["mean"] + mom * mu
    unbiased = var * n / (n - 1)
    run["var"] = (1 - mom) * run["var"] + mom * unbiased
    return gamma * xhat + beta

def bn_eval(x, gamma, beta, run, eps=1e-5):
    xhat = (x - run["mean"]) / np.sqrt(run["var"] + eps)
    return gamma * xhat + beta
dryRun: Running var uses the unbiased variance $\sigma^2 \cdot \frac{n}{n-1}$
problems.description: Deep feed-forward and convolutional networks with reasonably large batches, where it speeds up and stabilises training.

examples.input: How does batch norm behave differently in training and inference?
examples.output: Training uses statistics of the current batch and updates running averages; inference uses those running averages so each sample is processed independently.

examples.input: Why learn $\gamma$ and $\beta$?
examples.output: Forcing zero mean and unit variance would limit what a layer can represent; $\gamma$ and $\beta$ let the network restore any scale and shift.

examples.input: When is layer norm preferred?
examples.output: When batch statistics are unreliable or undefined, as in small batches or variable-length sequences, since layer norm normalises per sample.

constraints: Momentum of the running averages
$\epsilon$ (numerical floor added to the variance)
Batch size (small batches give noisy statistics)
edgeCases: Forgetting model.eval() at inference uses batch statistics and makes predictions depend on the batch
Tiny batches make the statistics unreliable
Normalisation uses the biased variance but the running variance stores the unbiased one
Placing it relative to the activation (before or after) changes behaviour; be consistent

problems.title: Bayes' Theorem
problems.summary: Update a prior belief about a hypothesis into a posterior after seeing evidence, by weighting each hypothesis by how well it predicted the data.
problems.bruteForce: Be careful when the prior is unknown or contested, when the evidence items are not conditionally independent, or when the hypothesis space is too large to normalise exactly (use sampling or variational methods).
problems.intuition: The posterior is the prior reweighted by the likelihood and then renormalised. A rare condition stays unlikely after a positive test unless the test is very specific, because most positives still come from the large healthy group. Think in terms of odds: each piece of evidence multiplies the odds by its likelihood ratio.
problems.whyItWorks: It is just the definition of conditional probability written both ways: $P(H,E) = P(E\,|\,H)\,P(H) = P(H\,|\,E)\,P(E)$. Dividing by $P(E)$, which is the sum of the joint over all hypotheses, makes the posteriors add up to one.
approach: List the hypotheses with their priors — the starting belief
Multiply each prior by the likelihood of the evidence — joint probability per hypothesis
Sum the joints to get the evidence $P(E)$ — the normalising constant
Divide each joint by the sum — posteriors now add to one
Feed the posterior in as the next prior — handles independent evidence in sequence
problems.time: O(h) per update for h hypotheses
problems.space: O(h)
dryRun: Sequential: posterior after $E_1$ is the prior for $E_2$
problems.description: Combining prior knowledge with data: diagnostic tests, spam filters, Naive Bayes classifiers, and any sequential belief update.

examples.input: A test is accurate, so why can a positive result still mean you probably do not have the disease?
examples.output: If the disease is rare, the healthy group is so large that its false positives outnumber the true positives; the base rate drives the posterior.

examples.input: How is Naive Bayes related?
examples.output: It applies Bayes' theorem with the assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class, so the likelihood is a product.

examples.input: What is the evidence term for?
examples.output: It normalises the numerator so the posterior is a proper distribution; it is often only needed up to a constant.

constraints: Prior distribution over hypotheses (flat, informative or empirical)
Likelihood model for the evidence
edgeCases: Ignoring the base rate (prior) and reading the likelihood as the posterior
Zero prior or zero likelihood permanently rules a hypothesis out
Sequential updating assumes the evidence items are conditionally independent given the hypothesis

problems.title: Beam Search Decoding
problems.summary: Generate a sequence by keeping the $B$ highest-scoring partial sequences at every step instead of committing to a single best token.
problems.bruteForce: Open-ended generation, where beam search tends to give repetitive, generic text; sampling is preferred there. It also gives no guarantee of finding the true best sequence.
problems.intuition: Greedy decoding can take a locally best token that leads to a poor continuation, while checking every sequence is exponential. Beam search is the compromise: a small frontier of the best prefixes is extended and pruned each step, so a good path that starts with a second-best token can still survive.
problems.whyItWorks: The score of a sequence is the sum of per-token log-probabilities, so extending a prefix only adds terms. Keeping the top $B$ prefixes is exact whenever $B$ is at least the number of prefixes at that depth, which makes beam width a smooth dial between greedy search and exhaustive search. For smaller $B$ it is only a heuristic.
approach: Start with one beam holding only the start token and score zero — the initial frontier
Ask the model for next-token log-probabilities of each beam — gives all one-token extensions
Add each log-probability to its beam's score — scores of sequences are additive
Sort all $B\cdot|V|$ candidates and keep the best $B$ — prunes the exponential tree
Repeat for the target length and return the top beam — highest total log-probability found
problems.time: O(L · B · |V| · log(B·|V|)) plus L·B model calls
problems.space: O(B · L) for the stored beams
dryRun: Beams at step $t$: top $B$ of $(y, y{+}w)$ pairs
problems.description: Machine translation, summarisation and speech recognition, where the single most probable output is wanted and the model is well calibrated.

examples.input: Is beam search optimal?
examples.output: No. It only keeps $B$ prefixes, so the best full sequence can be pruned early. It is exact only when $B$ covers all prefixes.

examples.input: What are greedy and exhaustive search as special cases?
examples.output: Beam width one is greedy. A width that never prunes is exhaustive search over all sequences.

examples.input: Why use log-probabilities?
examples.output: Products of many probabilities underflow, and sums of logs are numerically stable and additive over steps.

constraints: Beam width $B$ (larger is closer to exact search but slower)
Length penalty (sum of log-probs favours short outputs)
Maximum length and end-of-sequence handling
n-gram repetition blocking
edgeCases: Raw summed log-probability prefers short sequences; normalise or add a length penalty
This sketch decodes a fixed length and has no end-of-sequence token, which real decoders need
Beams often collapse to near-identical outputs; diverse beam search addresses this
A wider beam can lower quality in generation even though it raises model probability

problems.title: Benchmark Contamination - N-gram Overlap and Memorisation Test
problems.summary: Check whether benchmark items leaked into training data. Flag verbatim overlap with long n-grams, compare the model's loss on an item against paraphrases of it, and report accuracy on contaminated and clean subsets separately.
problems.bruteForce: As a proof of cleanliness: no flag only means no verbatim overlap was found. Items that are short, paraphrased or translated escape n-gram matching, and the loss test is only a signal when good perturbations exist.
problems.intuition: A benchmark score only measures generalisation if the model has not seen the answers. Long n-grams almost never repeat by chance, so a shared 13-gram between a test item and the training text is strong evidence of a leak, but it misses paraphrases and cannot be run when the training data is hidden. For those cases ask the model itself: if the original item gets a much lower loss than equivalent rewordings, it has probably seen that exact wording. Finally, split results by flag, since the gap between the two subsets is the inflation. Flow: benchmark items → n-gram overlap and loss test → contaminated flag → clean vs contaminated accuracy.
problems.whyItWorks: The chance that a specific long word sequence appears by accident in unrelated text falls quickly with its length, so a shared 13-gram is almost always a copy rather than coincidence. The loss ratio compares the model on the exact wording with the same content in new wording: a model that generalises treats them alike, so a ratio far below $1$ points to memorised surface form. The subset accuracy gap estimates the inflation, assuming contaminated and clean items are of similar difficulty.
approach: Tokenise and build the set of $n$-grams of the training text — a fast membership table
Flag a benchmark item if any of its $n$-grams appears in that set — verbatim leaks share long spans
Compute the contamination rate, the flagged fraction of items — the size of the problem
When training data is unavailable, make paraphrases or perturbations of an item — equivalent text the model could not have memorised
Compute $\rho = L(\mathrm{item}) / \overline{L(\mathrm{perturbed})}$ — values well below $1$ suggest memorisation
Compute accuracy on contaminated and clean subsets and their gap — shows how much the score is inflated
Prefer private or regularly refreshed held-out sets for new claims — unseen items cannot have leaked
problems.time: O(T) to index $T$ training tokens, then O(L) per item of length $L$; the memorisation test costs one model pass per variant
problems.space: O(T) for the training n-gram set, which is why real pipelines use hashing or suffix arrays
problems.description: Before trusting or publishing a benchmark number for a model trained on web-scale or unknown data, and when building a new evaluation from public text.

examples.input: Why use long n-grams such as 13 for decontamination?
examples.output: Short n-grams match common phrases and give false alarms. A long shared span almost never happens by chance, so a match is strong evidence of a copy, though paraphrases still slip through.

examples.input: How do you test contamination without the training data?
examples.output: Compare the model's loss on the original item with its loss on paraphrases or perturbations. A ratio $\rho$ much below $1$ means the exact wording is unusually easy, which suggests memorisation. A canary string planted in the data gives a similar check.

examples.input: What do you report once you find contamination?
examples.output: Accuracy on the clean and contaminated subsets separately and their gap, plus the contamination rate. A large positive gap means the headline score is inflated.

examples.input: How can future benchmarks avoid this?
examples.output: Keep test items private, refresh them dynamically, or build them from text newer than the training cutoff, so the items cannot be in the training corpus.

constraints: N-gram length $n$ and the tokeniser or normalisation used
Minimum overlap needed to flag an item
Number and type of perturbations, such as paraphrase or option shuffling
Threshold on the loss ratio $\rho$
edgeCases: An item shorter than $n$ tokens has no n-grams and can never be flagged; lower $n$ or match whole items
Tokenise training and benchmark text identically, or the n-gram sets will not line up
Contaminated items may be easier or harder than clean ones, so the accuracy gap is suggestive, not exact
A low loss ratio can also come from an item that is simply easy or common; compare against several paraphrases

problems.title: BERT Masked Language Modelling
problems.summary: Pre-train a bidirectional encoder by hiding a random subset of input tokens and training it to predict the originals from the surrounding context on both sides.
problems.bruteForce: Open-ended text generation, where a left-to-right decoder is the natural fit. Masked models also learn from only a fraction of positions per pass, so they are less sample-efficient per token than causal models.
problems.intuition: A left-to-right language model cannot see the future, but an encoder that sees the whole sentence would trivially copy its input. Masking breaks the copy: the model must reconstruct hidden words from context on both sides. Not every selected token becomes a mask symbol, though. Since the mask never appears at fine-tuning time, some selected tokens are swapped for random words or left unchanged, so the model cannot assume that only masked-looking positions need attention.
problems.whyItWorks: Predicting a missing token from both directions forces the encoder to build contextual representations that capture syntax and meaning. The loss is computed only on the selected positions, so the learning signal is a clean cross-entropy over the vocabulary where the targets are unambiguous. Random and unchanged replacements reduce the mismatch between pre-training inputs, which contain mask symbols, and downstream inputs, which do not.
approach: Draw a uniform number per token and select those below 0.15 — random positions to hide
Set labels to the original id at selected positions and −100 elsewhere — only selected positions contribute to the loss
Draw a second uniform number for the selected tokens: below 0.8 become [MASK] — the main corruption
Replace the next tenth with a random vocabulary token and leave the last tenth as is — reduces the pre-train/fine-tune mismatch
Run the encoder, take the logits at selected positions and average the cross-entropy — predict the originals
problems.time: O(T) for masking; the loss is O(M·V) for M masked positions and vocabulary V, plus the encoder cost
problems.space: O(M·V) for the logits at masked positions (a full-sequence output layer would be O(T·V))
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def mask_tokens(ids, vocab, mask_id, rng, p=0.15):
    ids = ids.copy()
    labels = np.full(ids.shape, -100)
    sel = rng.random(ids.shape) < p
    labels[sel] = ids[sel]
    u = rng.random(ids.shape)
    ids[sel & (u < 0.8)] = mask_id
    rand = sel & (u >= 0.8) & (u < 0.9)
    ids[rand] = rng.integers(0, vocab, rand.sum())
    return ids, labels      # last 10% of selected stay unchanged

def mlm_loss(logits, labels):
    m = labels != -100
    z = logits[m]
    z = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logp = z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return -logp[np.arange(len(z)), labels[m]].mean()
dryRun: Labels: original id if selected, $-100$ elsewhere
$z_i$: logits at position $i$;  $y_i$: original token id
problems.description: Pre-training encoder models for classification, tagging, retrieval and other tasks that need rich bidirectional context rather than text generation.

examples.input: Why not replace every selected token with [MASK]?
examples.output: The mask symbol never appears at fine-tuning time, creating a train-test mismatch. Leaving some selected tokens unchanged or random forces the model to produce good representations for all tokens.

examples.input: Why does the loss ignore unmasked positions?
examples.output: At unmasked positions the input equals the target, so predicting it is trivial and would dilute the signal. Labels of −100 are skipped by the cross-entropy so only hidden tokens train the model.

examples.input: What is the downside of masked language modelling compared with causal modelling?
examples.output: Only the selected fraction of tokens gives a training signal per sequence, and the model is not a natural generator, since it predicts tokens independently given the corrupted context.

constraints: Masking probability (0.15 in the original paper)
Split between mask, random and unchanged (80/10/10)
Dynamic masking (new mask each epoch) versus static
Vocabulary and sequence length
edgeCases: This code treats every token as maskable; real pipelines never select special tokens such as [CLS], [SEP] and padding
Random replacement here may draw any vocabulary id, including the mask id or the original token
Averaging over masked positions means batches with few masks give noisy loss; an empty selection gives NaN here
WordPiece pieces of one word are masked independently here; whole-word masking is a common variant

problems.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
problems.summary: Split a model's expected squared error into bias (systematic miss), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise.
problems.bruteForce: The clean decomposition is for squared loss. For 0-1 loss or very large over-parameterised networks the classical U-curve can break down (double descent), so treat it as intuition rather than a law.
problems.intuition: Imagine retraining the same model on many fresh datasets. Bias is how far the average prediction sits from the truth; variance is how much single predictions scatter around that average. Flexible models shrink the first and inflate the second, so test error is U-shaped in complexity.
problems.whyItWorks: For a fixed input, expand the squared error around the mean prediction $E[\hat{y}]$. The cross terms vanish because the noise is independent of the fit and the deviation $\hat{y}-E[\hat{y}]$ has zero mean, leaving exactly $\mathrm{bias}^2$, variance and noise as three non-negative pieces. Only the first two can be traded against each other by changing model complexity.
approach: Pick a known true function $f$ and a test point $x_0$ — so bias can be measured exactly
Draw many independent noisy training sets — they play the role of 'retraining'
Fit the model on each and predict at $x_0$ — gives a distribution of predictions
$\mathrm{bias}^2$ from the mean prediction versus $f(x_0)$ — the systematic part
variance as the spread of predictions — the instability part
Sweep model complexity and compare — bias falls while variance rises
problems.time: O(runs · n · degree²) for the polynomial fits
problems.space: O(runs + n)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def bias_variance(f, x0, degree, sigma=0.3, n=30, runs=500, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    preds = np.empty(runs)
    for r in range(runs):
        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)
        y = f(x) + sigma * rng.normal(size=n)
        coef = np.polyfit(x, y, degree)
        preds[r] = np.polyval(coef, x0)
    bias2 = (preds.mean() - f(x0)) ** 2
    var = preds.var()
    return bias2, var, sigma ** 2
dryRun: $\sigma^2$ = noise variance, a floor no model can beat
Expectation over training sets $D$ and noise in $y$
problems.description: Use it to diagnose whether a model underfits (high bias, both errors high) or overfits (high variance, big train-test gap), and to decide between more data, regularisation or a simpler or richer model.

examples.input: How do you recognise high bias versus high variance from learning curves?
examples.output: High bias: train and validation error are both high and close. High variance: train error is low and validation error is much higher, with a large gap.

examples.input: How does regularisation move you along the tradeoff?
examples.output: Stronger regularisation constrains the model, which raises bias and lowers variance.

examples.input: Does more training data fix high bias?
examples.output: No. It reduces variance; a model that is too simple stays wrong however much data it sees.

examples.input: Why can test error never reach zero in this decomposition?
examples.output: The irreducible noise term $\sigma^2$ is part of every noisy target and no model can predict it.

constraints: Model complexity (polynomial degree, tree depth, $k$ in k-NN)
Regularisation strength (more shrinkage means more bias, less variance)
Training set size (more data lowers variance, not bias)
Number of simulation runs (more runs make the estimates less noisy)
edgeCases: Bias and variance cannot be computed on real data because the true $f$ is unknown; only simulation or proxies work
Too few simulation runs give a noisy variance estimate
Measured at one $x_0$ only; the trade-off differs across the input space

problems.title: Bidirectional RNN
problems.summary: Run one recurrent network left to right and another right to left over the same sequence, then concatenate their states at every position.
problems.bruteForce: Autoregressive language modelling, streaming or real-time prediction, where future tokens do not exist at prediction time. Use causal models there.
problems.intuition: A forward RNN at position t has only seen the past, but many tasks such as tagging or reading comprehension also need the words that come later. Running a second RNN backwards gives each position a summary of its future, and concatenating both gives full-sentence context at every step. The price is that it cannot be used when the future is not available, such as in autoregressive generation.
problems.whyItWorks: The two directions have separate weights and each one is a valid summary of one side of the position. Concatenating them gives the downstream layer both left and right context without any change to the recurrent cell itself, so it works with plain RNN, GRU or LSTM cells alike.
approach: Run the forward RNN from t = 1 to T — each state summarises the prefix up to t
Reverse the sequence and run a separate backward RNN — each state summarises the suffix from t onward
Reverse the backward outputs back into time order — so both states line up at position t
Concatenate forward and backward states on the feature axis — output width becomes 2H
problems.time: O(T·(I·H + H²)) per direction, so about twice a unidirectional RNN
problems.space: O(T·2H) for the concatenated states
problems.description: Tasks where the whole input is available at once: tagging, named entity recognition, speech recognition with offline audio, and encoders in sequence-to-sequence models.

examples.input: Why can't a bidirectional RNN do language generation?
examples.output: The backward pass needs future tokens, which do not exist while generating, so generation must use a causal (unidirectional) model.

examples.input: What are the output and final-state shapes?
examples.output: Per-step outputs have width 2H (forward and backward concatenated); the final states are the forward state at T and the backward state at the first position.

examples.input: Do the two directions share weights?
examples.output: No, each direction has its own parameters, so the parameter count doubles.

examples.input: How do you use it for sentence classification?
examples.output: Concatenate the last forward state and the first backward state, since each has read the entire sentence, then feed that to a classifier.

constraints: Hidden size H per direction
Cell type (RNN, GRU, LSTM)
Number of stacked layers
How to merge directions (concatenate, sum, average)
edgeCases: The backward outputs must be flipped back, otherwise states are misaligned in time
Padded batches need packing or masks, or the backward pass starts on padding
Not usable for causal or streaming prediction
This sketch is a plain tanh RNN for one sequence; real models use GRU or LSTM cells

problems.title: Measuring Big-O Empirically
problems.summary: Count the operations an algorithm performs at growing input sizes and fit a straight line to the log-log plot: the slope is the exponent of the growth, so Big-O becomes something you can measure.
problems.bruteForce: Predicting wall-clock time, which also depends on caches, memory layout and constants. A fitted slope only says how cost grows over the sizes you tried, so it cannot prove an asymptotic bound.
problems.intuition: If cost grows like $c \cdot n^{k}$, taking logs gives $\log \text{cost} = \log c + k \log n$, a straight line whose slope is the exponent $k$. Counting comparisons instead of seconds removes machine noise, so linear search shows slope 1, insertion sort 2, merge sort a little above 1, and binary search nearly 0 because its cost is $\log n$, which a log-log fit cannot tell from a tiny power. Flow: input size n → operation count → log-log points → fitted slope → complexity class.
problems.whyItWorks: For a cost of the form $c \cdot n^{k}$ the log-log plot is exactly a line of slope $k$, and least squares recovers it. For $n \log n$ the local slope is $1 + 1/\ln n$, which stays slightly above 1 and slowly falls toward it, and for $\log n$ the slope is $1/\ln n$, near 0 and shrinking.
approach: Instrument each algorithm to return (result, op_count) — the count is deterministic, unlike wall time
Generate seeded random inputs at doubling sizes — the same data on every run
Take logs of sizes and costs — power laws become straight lines
Fit a line with least squares and read the slope — the empirical exponent
For logarithmic growth, divide the cost by $\log_2 n$ — a flat ratio confirms it
problems.time: O(n), O(log n), O(n²), O(n log n) for the four algorithms measured
problems.space: O(1) extra for the searches and insertion sort, O(n) for merge sort
dryRun: Attention $T^2 d$ vs KV-cache step $T d$
problems.description: Checking that code scales the way you claim, comparing two implementations, and building intuition for costs such as quadratic self-attention before running anything on a GPU.

examples.input: Why count operations instead of timing the code?
examples.output: Wall time is noisy and depends on the machine, caches and the interpreter. An operation count is deterministic and reflects the algorithm itself.

examples.input: What slope do you expect for O(n log n)?
examples.output: Slightly above 1, for example about 1.1 to 1.2 at moderate sizes, falling toward 1 as n grows, because the extra factor log n adds a small exponent.

examples.input: How does Big-O relate to transformers?
examples.output: Self-attention compares every token with every other, so cost is quadratic in sequence length. With a KV cache, each new token attends once over the stored rows, which is linear.

examples.input: Does a measured slope prove the complexity?
examples.output: No. It only describes the sizes tested. Worst cases, small-n effects and different input distributions can all change the exponent.

constraints: Input sizes (use doubling, for example 256 to 4096)
Random seed and input distribution
Which operation to count (comparisons or swaps)
edgeCases: Random input shows the average case; sorted input makes insertion sort linear, so choose the case deliberately
Very small sizes are dominated by constants and distort the fit; use a wide range of n
Python slicing in merge_sort copies data, so its time is higher than its comparison count suggests
A flat cost-versus-$\log n$ ratio, not a slope near 0, is the evidence for logarithmic growth

problems.title: BLEU Score
problems.summary: Score a generated text against a reference by how many of its n-grams also appear in the reference, with a penalty for being too short.
problems.bruteForce: Single sentences (any missing n-gram order gives zero without smoothing), paraphrase-heavy tasks, open-ended generation, and comparisons across different tokenisations. It ignores meaning, so fluent paraphrases score poorly.
problems.intuition: Precision alone rewards a one-word output that happens to be correct, so BLEU does two things to stop that. It clips each n-gram's credit to the number of times it occurs in the reference, so repeating a word earns nothing extra, and it multiplies by a brevity penalty so short outputs cannot win by being safe. Combining 1- to 4-gram precisions with a geometric mean checks both word choice and local fluency.
