problems.whyItWorks: Matching n-grams of several orders is a cheap proxy for adequacy (unigrams) and fluency (longer n-grams) that correlates with human judgement when averaged over a whole corpus. Counts are summed over the corpus before taking ratios, which keeps one short sentence from producing a zero that wipes out the score. The geometric mean means a single order with no matches drives the score to zero.
approach: Count hypothesis n-grams for n = 1 to 4 — the units being matched
Clip each count to the reference count — repeated words cannot be rewarded twice
Sum matches and totals over the whole corpus, then divide for each pₙ — corpus-level precision is more stable than per-sentence
Compute the brevity penalty from total hypothesis and reference lengths — precision cannot see missing content
Take BP times the geometric mean of the pₙ — one number that needs every order to match
problems.time: O(total tokens · N) for N-gram orders, using hash-based counting
problems.space: O(distinct n-grams in one sentence)
dryRun: $\mathrm{BP} = 1$ if $c > r$, else $\exp(1 - r/c)$ ($c, r$: lengths)
problems.description: Comparing machine translation systems on the same test set, using a standard tool such as sacreBLEU so that tokenisation is identical.

examples.input: Why does BLEU clip n-gram counts?
examples.output: Without clipping, a hypothesis repeating a reference word many times would get full precision. Clipping caps credit at the number of times the n-gram appears in the reference.

examples.input: What does the brevity penalty do and why is there no recall term?
examples.output: BLEU is precision-based, so very short outputs could score high. The brevity penalty multiplies the score down when total hypothesis length is below the reference length. It is a length-based stand-in for recall.

examples.input: Why compute BLEU at corpus level rather than averaging sentence BLEU?
examples.output: Summing n-gram counts over the corpus avoids zero precisions on short sentences and gives a more stable statistic. Averaging sentence scores treats a three-word sentence like a long one.

constraints: Maximum n-gram order N (4 is the standard BLEU-4)
Tokenisation (scores are only comparable under the same tokeniser)
Smoothing method for short texts (this code uses none)
Number of references (this code uses one)
edgeCases: Scores from different tokenisers or casing are not comparable; report the sacreBLEU signature
Without smoothing, a corpus with no matching 4-gram scores exactly zero
This code takes one reference per sentence and tokens already split; real BLEU allows several references and picks the closest length
BLEU measures overlap, not meaning, and is not reliable for single sentences

problems.title: Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization
problems.summary: Build a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in a corpus, starting from single characters.
problems.bruteForce: Not ideal for languages without clear whitespace unless pre-tokenised appropriately, and merges chosen by frequency need not match morphology. Unigram or byte-level variants are alternatives.
problems.intuition: Frequent character sequences become single tokens, so common words are short in token count while rare words fall back to smaller pieces and never become unknown. The vocabulary size is simply the number of merges you choose to run, a direct knob between characters and words.
problems.whyItWorks: Each merge replaces the most common pair by one symbol, which is a greedy step toward the shortest encoding of the training corpus. The ordered merge list is the whole model: encoding replays the merges in order on a new word, so training and encoding agree exactly.
approach: Split every word into characters — the initial symbols
Count all adjacent symbol pairs over the corpus — pair frequencies
Pick the most frequent pair, breaking ties deterministically — a reproducible merge order
Rewrite every word with that pair fused into one symbol — new symbol joins the vocabulary
Repeat for k merges, then encode new words by replaying merges in order — same procedure at train and test time
problems.time: O(k · corpus length) for training, O(k · word length) per encoded word
problems.space: O(corpus length) for the working symbol sequences
dryRun: Start: each word is a sequence of characters
Repeat $k$ times; the merge list is the model
Encode a word: apply the merges in learned order
problems.description: Tokenising text for language models and translation when you need a fixed-size vocabulary that handles rare and unseen words.

examples.input: How does BPE avoid unknown tokens?
examples.output: Its base alphabet is single characters, or bytes in byte-level BPE, so any word can be spelled out even if no merge applies.

examples.input: How do you encode a new word?
examples.output: Start from characters and apply the learned merges in the order they were learned, not by frequency in the new text.

examples.input: How is BPE different from WordPiece?
examples.output: BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece picks the merge that most increases the likelihood of the training data under a language model.

constraints: Number of merges k (sets vocabulary size)
Tie-breaking rule for equally frequent pairs
Pre-tokenisation (whitespace or regex split before BPE)
Byte-level versus character-level base alphabet
edgeCases: Recounting all pairs each merge is slow for big corpora; real code updates counts incrementally
Without word-boundary markers a merge can cross word edges or lose where words end
This sketch ignores word frequencies by taking a plain list of words, so repeats are counted by listing them
Different tie-breaking gives different but equally valid vocabularies

problems.title: Causal Masking in Attention
problems.summary: Set the attention scores for future positions to minus infinity before the softmax, so each token mixes only itself and earlier tokens.
problems.bruteForce: Bidirectional encoders such as BERT, where each token should see the whole sequence. For padding, use a separate key-padding mask instead.
problems.intuition: A language model is trained to predict token $t+1$ from tokens up to $t$, so if position $t$ could see later tokens it would simply copy the answer. Masking the upper triangle of the score matrix makes every row a distribution over the past only, which lets one forward pass train all next-token predictions in parallel without leaking the future.
problems.whyItWorks: After the softmax a $-\infty$ score becomes a weight of exactly zero, so the output at position $t$ is a function of $Q[t]$ and of $K$, $V$ rows up to $t$ only. The diagonal is kept, so every row has at least one finite score and the softmax is well defined. Because future tokens contribute nothing, changing them cannot change earlier outputs.
approach: Compute raw scores $Q K^{\top} / \sqrt{d}$ — the usual scaled dot-product similarities
Build a boolean matrix that is true above the diagonal — marks every (query, future key) pair
Replace those scores with $-\infty$ — $\exp(-\infty)$ is exactly 0 after the softmax
Apply the softmax along each row — each row sums to 1 over visible keys only
Multiply by $V$ — each output is a mix of past and current values
problems.time: O(T²·d) for length T and width d
problems.space: O(T²) for the score matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(s):
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    future = np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=1)
    scores = np.where(future, -np.inf, scores)
    A = softmax(scores)
    return A @ V, A
problems.description: Decoder-only language models, the decoder of encoder-decoder models, and any autoregressive generator, during both training and prefill.

examples.input: Why mask before the softmax rather than zero the weights after?
examples.output: Zeroing after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to 1 and still lets the future affect the normaliser. Masking scores with $-\infty$ gives exact zeros and a correct normalisation.

examples.input: How does one forward pass train every position at once?
examples.output: With the mask, row $t$ only uses tokens up to $t$, so the loss on every next token can be computed together without the model seeing its own targets.

examples.input: How is a causal mask different from a padding mask?
examples.output: The causal mask hides future positions and is the same for every sequence; a padding mask hides pad tokens and depends on each sequence's length. They are usually combined.

constraints: Mask diagonal offset ($k=1$ keeps the token itself visible)
Sliding-window size, if attention is also limited to recent tokens
Mask value ($-\infty$ or a large negative number)
edgeCases: A row that is fully masked gives NaN from the softmax; always keep the diagonal
Using a large negative number in half precision can overflow; $-\infty$ or the dtype minimum is safer
This code builds the full $T \times T$ matrix; efficient kernels skip the masked blocks entirely

problems.title: Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
problems.summary: Ask the model to write its reasoning steps before the answer, then sample $n$ such reasoning paths at temperature above zero, parse each final answer and return the most common one.
problems.bruteForce: Open-ended generation with no single answer to vote on, latency or cost sensitive paths, and easy questions where one direct answer is already reliable.
problems.intuition: Intermediate steps give the model room to compute, because each generated token adds work before the answer is committed. A single path can go wrong anywhere, but wrong paths tend to disagree with each other while correct paths converge on the same result, so a vote over several paths filters out much of the random error. Flow: question → $n$ sampled reasoning paths → parse answers → vote.
problems.whyItWorks: If each independent sample is correct with probability $p > 0.5$, the number of correct votes is binomial and the chance that more than half are correct is $\sum_{k > n/2}\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, which rises towards 1 as $n$ grows. When $p < 0.5$ it falls towards 0, so voting amplifies whichever side is more likely. Wrong answers that are spread over many values need even fewer correct votes to win a plurality, so this majority figure is a conservative bound.
approach: Prompt for step-by-step reasoning and a fixed last line such as Answer: X — makes the final answer easy to parse
Sample $n$ completions at temperature above 0 — greedy decoding would give the same path every time
Extract the final answer from each completion with a regex — only the answer is compared, never the reasoning text
Drop completions with no parsable answer — they carry no vote
Return the most frequent answer, ties broken by first seen — a deterministic majority vote
problems.time: $n$ model calls (parallelisable), so about $n$ times the cost and tokens of one answer; voting itself is O(n)
problems.space: O(n) stored answers, plus the text of each reasoning path if kept
problems.description: Multi-step problems with a short checkable final answer, such as arithmetic, logic or multiple choice, when accuracy matters more than cost and latency.

examples.input: Why does self-consistency need temperature above zero?
examples.output: At temperature zero every sample is the same greedy path, so voting adds nothing. Sampling makes the paths differ and the vote averages their errors.

examples.input: Why is majority-vote accuracy higher than single-sample accuracy?
examples.output: For $p > 0.5$ the binomial tail above $n/2$ exceeds $p$ and grows with $n$, because independent errors rarely line up on the same wrong answer.

examples.input: When does self-consistency fail?
examples.output: When samples are correlated or the model is systematically wrong, since the same wrong answer repeats and wins the vote, and when $p < 0.5$ the vote makes things worse.

examples.input: How is it different from chain-of-thought alone?
examples.output: Chain-of-thought is one reasoning path, usually greedy. Self-consistency samples many paths and votes only on the final answers.

constraints: Number of samples $n$ (odd avoids ties; returns diminish)
Sampling temperature and top-$p$
Answer-extraction pattern and normalisation
Tie-break rule
edgeCases: Samples from one model are not independent; shared blind spots make the same wrong answer repeat, so the binomial formula is optimistic
Wrong answers can agree on a popular mistake and win the vote; more samples then make the wrong answer more certain
Unnormalised answers split votes (such as 1,200 and 1200); normalise before counting
Cost grows linearly with $n$ in tokens and calls, and a shown reasoning chain need not be the real cause of the answer

problems.title: Class Imbalance
problems.summary: When one class is rare, plain training optimises mostly for the common class. Fix it by weighting the loss inversely to class frequency or by resampling the training set, and judge the result with metrics that ignore the base rate.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you need calibrated probabilities (reweighting distorts them unless you correct afterwards), or when a threshold change on an unweighted model already gives the trade-off you need.
problems.intuition: A loss that sums over examples is dominated by the majority class, so a model can look excellent by ignoring the minority. Reweighting says one rare example should count as much as many common ones, and resampling achieves the same by showing the rare ones more often. Neither adds information; they only change what the optimiser cares about.
problems.whyItWorks: With weight $w^c$ on class $c$, the weighted loss is the expected loss under a re-balanced class prior, so errors on the minority are no longer drowned out. Random oversampling duplicates minority rows, which matches integer weights in the loss on average. The decision threshold, not only the weights, then sets the precision-recall trade-off.
approach: Split first, then look only at the training class counts — resampling must not touch validation or test rows
Compute balanced weights $\frac{n}{K\,n^c}$ — each class then carries equal total weight
Weight the per-example loss and normalise by the weight sum — rare-class errors count more and the scale stays comparable
Alternatively oversample minority rows with replacement up to the majority count — the same effect through the data instead of the loss
Evaluate with precision-recall, F1 or PR-AUC on untouched data and tune the threshold — accuracy hides minority failures
problems.time: O(n) for weights and for the weighted loss; oversampling grows n to K·n_max
problems.space: O(K) for weights; oversampling stores the enlarged dataset
dryRun: Oversample: draw $(n_{max} - n^c)$ extra rows of $c$
Do it on the training split only, never before splitting
problems.description: Fraud, defects, rare diseases and other skewed targets, when recall on the rare class matters and plain accuracy is misleading.

examples.input: A fraud model has high accuracy but catches no fraud. Why?
examples.output: With a rare positive class, predicting all negatives scores high accuracy; use precision, recall, PR-AUC and a tuned threshold instead.

examples.input: Class weights or resampling?
examples.output: Weights are cheaper and add no duplicates; resampling works with any learner and can be paired with weights or ensembling. Compare them on validation data.

examples.input: How do you evaluate fairly after resampling?
examples.output: Keep validation and test sets at the natural class ratio and resample only the training fold, inside cross-validation.

examples.input: Does rebalancing fix probabilities?
examples.output: No, it distorts them; recalibrate or correct for the prior shift if you need real probabilities.

constraints: class_weight — balanced, custom ratios, or none
Resampling strategy — random over/under-sampling or synthetic (SMOTE)
Decision threshold — tuned on validation data for the metric you care about
edgeCases: Oversampling before the split puts duplicates of the same row in train and test, inflating scores
Reweighting or resampling shifts predicted probabilities away from true rates
Duplicated minority rows make flexible models memorise them and overfit
Accuracy and ROC-AUC can both look fine while minority precision is poor

problems.title: CLIP Contrastive Loss
problems.summary: Embed a batch of images and their captions, score every image against every caption, and train each image to pick its own caption and each caption to pick its own image.
problems.bruteForce: Small batches, where there are too few negatives, or data with many near-duplicate captions in a batch, which creates false negatives.
problems.intuition: Within a batch the true pair sits on the diagonal of a similarity matrix and every other entry is a free negative. Treating each row as a classification over captions, and each column as a classification over images, pulls matching pairs together and pushes the rest apart without any labels beyond the pairing. The temperature controls how sharply the softmax separates near and far, so it matters a lot.
problems.whyItWorks: The loss is an InfoNCE bound on the mutual information between the two modalities: it rewards scoring the true partner above all $N-1$ other candidates. Larger batches provide more negatives and a tighter bound. Normalising and using a temperature keeps the similarities bounded while still letting the softmax become sharp.
approach: L2-normalise image and text embeddings — dot products become cosine similarities
Form logits = $I T^{\top} / \tau$, an $N \times N$ matrix — every image against every caption, $\tau$ sharpens the softmax
Use labels $0 \ldots N-1$ as targets — the matching pair is the diagonal entry
Cross-entropy along rows — image-to-text, each image must pick its caption
Cross-entropy along columns (logits transposed) and average both — text-to-image, symmetric training
problems.time: O(N²·D) for the N × N similarity matrix
problems.space: O(N²) for the logits
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def log_softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))

def clip_loss(img, txt, tau=0.07):
    img = img / np.linalg.norm(img, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    txt = txt / np.linalg.norm(txt, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logits = img @ txt.T / tau
    idx = np.arange(len(logits))
    loss_i = -log_softmax(logits)[idx, idx].mean()     # image -> text
    loss_t = -log_softmax(logits.T)[idx, idx].mean()   # text -> image
    return (loss_i + loss_t) / 2
problems.description: Learning aligned image-text (or audio-text, video-text) embeddings from paired data, enabling zero-shot classification and retrieval.

examples.input: Why is the loss symmetric?
examples.output: Each direction is a separate $N$-way classification, image to text and text to image; averaging trains both encoders to retrieve in both directions.

examples.input: What does the temperature do?
examples.output: It scales the cosine similarities before the softmax; small $\tau$ makes the distribution sharper and weights hard negatives more.

examples.input: Where do the negatives come from?
examples.output: Every other pair in the batch, so batch size directly sets the number of negatives.

examples.input: How is zero-shot classification done with CLIP?
examples.output: Embed a text prompt per class, embed the image, and pick the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity.

constraints: Temperature $\tau$ (fixed or learned)
Batch size $N$ (number of negatives)
Embedding dimension $D$
Encoder architectures and projection heads
edgeCases: Forgetting to normalise embeddings changes the loss and can make training unstable
Duplicate or very similar captions in one batch act as false negatives
Here $\tau$ is a constant; CLIP learns it and clamps it to a maximum scale
Distributed training needs gathered embeddings from all devices to get the full negative set

problems.title: Data and Concept Drift Detection
problems.summary: Production data shifts away from the training data. Compare the live distribution of each feature with a reference window using PSI or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and track performance for changes in the input-to-label relationship.
problems.bruteForce: Drift in inputs is not the same as harm: a shifted feature may be irrelevant. And these tests cannot see changes in $P(y\,|\,x)$ with stable inputs; use labelled performance monitoring for that.
problems.intuition: A model is a snapshot of the world at training time. Inputs can move (covariate drift) or the rule linking inputs to labels can move (concept drift). Input drift is visible without labels by comparing distributions, but concept drift can leave the inputs unchanged, so it only shows up as delayed label feedback and falling performance.
problems.whyItWorks: PSI bins the reference by its own quantiles and sums (current − reference) times the log ratio of bin shares, which equals the symmetric KL divergence between the binned distributions, so it is zero only when they match. The KS statistic is the largest gap between two empirical CDFs, a distribution-free measure of how far two samples are apart.
approach: Freeze a reference sample, usually training data or a healthy recent window — drift is relative to something
Cut the reference into quantile bins, extending the outer edges to $\pm\infty$ — every new value falls in a bin
Compare bin shares of reference and current data with PSI — a single drift score per feature
Also compute the KS statistic between the raw samples — a bin-free cross-check
Alert on thresholds you calibrate to your own data, then check labelled performance — input drift is a warning, not proof of harm
problems.time: O(n log n) for the sorts and quantiles per feature
problems.space: O(n) for the sorted copies, O(bins) for histograms
dryRun: Shares clipped below by $\epsilon$ keep $\ln$ finite
problems.description: Monitoring deployed models: per-feature input checks, prediction-score drift, and scheduled comparison of recent data against the training or a recent reference window.

examples.input: Covariate drift versus concept drift?
examples.output: Covariate drift is a change in $P(x)$ and can be seen without labels; concept drift is a change in $P(y\,|\,x)$ and needs labels or proxy outcomes to detect.

examples.input: How does PSI work and what are its weaknesses?
examples.output: It sums bin-share differences times log ratios, equal to a symmetric KL divergence; it depends on the binning and has only conventional thresholds.

examples.input: What do you do when drift is detected?
examples.output: Check data pipelines first, assess impact on a labelled sample, then retrain on recent data, reweight, or roll back depending on the cause.

constraints: Bins for PSI — quantile bins from the reference
Reference window — training data or a rolling recent period
Alert thresholds — rules of thumb exist but should be tuned per feature
Window size — small windows are noisy, large ones are slow to react
edgeCases: Rule-of-thumb PSI cut-offs are conventions, not statistical tests
Many features and many windows give false alarms by chance
Large samples flag tiny, harmless shifts as significant with KS
Concept drift with unchanged inputs is invisible to these statistics

problems.title: Content Safety Classifiers and Thresholds
problems.summary: Moderate inputs and outputs with per-category classifier scores. Pick the threshold from the precision-recall trade-off, run a cheap filter first, escalate only the uncertain slice, and send the grey zone to humans.
problems.bruteForce: Do not use a recall target alone when the positive class is tiny, since the threshold then rests on a handful of examples. Do not treat raw scores as probabilities before checking calibration.
problems.intuition: A classifier gives a score, and the threshold turns it into an action by trading missed harm against false alarms. For a severe category you fix the recall you must reach and take the highest threshold that still meets it, which keeps precision as high as that recall allows. Most traffic is clearly fine, so an expensive model only needs to see the band of scores the cheap one is unsure about. Flow: text → cheap score → clear cases decided → uncertain band → big model or human.
problems.whyItWorks: Recall can only fall as the threshold rises, so the set of thresholds that reach a target is an interval and its top end is the $k$-th largest positive score with $k = \lceil r P \rceil$. A cascade pays $c_1$ for every item and $c_2$ only for the escalated fraction $p$, so it is cheaper than always using the large model exactly when $c_1 + p\,c_2 < c_2$, that is $p < 1 - c_1/c_2$.
approach: Score each item per category with a classifier — one threshold per category, not one global
Fix a target recall for severe categories — a miss costs more than a false alarm
Take the $k$-th highest positive score with $k = \lceil r P \rceil$ — the highest threshold that reaches the recall
Choose a band $[lo, hi)$ around the threshold for the second stage — only uncertain items pay the extra cost
Estimate cost as $c_1 + p\,c_2$ and route the grey zone to humans — keeps cost and review load predictable
problems.time: O(n log n) to sort the positive scores; O(n) per confusion count or band
problems.space: O(n) for the sorted positive scores
problems.solution:
import math

def confusion_at(scores, labels, thr):
    tp = fp = fn = tn = 0
    for s, y in zip(scores, labels):
        pred = s >= thr
        tp += pred and y == 1
        fp += pred and y == 0
        fn += (not pred) and y == 1
        tn += (not pred) and y == 0
    return tp, fp, fn, tn

def pick_threshold(scores, labels, target_recall):
    pos = sorted((s for s, y in zip(scores, labels) if y == 1),
                 reverse=True)
    k = math.ceil(target_recall * len(pos) - 1e-9)
    return pos[max(k, 1) - 1]

def cascade_cost(c1, c2, p_escalate):
    return c1 + p_escalate * c2

def escalate_band(scores, lo, hi):
    return [i for i, s in enumerate(scores) if lo <= s < hi]
dryRun: Rank: $k = \lceil r \cdot P \rceil$, thr = $k$-th top positive
problems.description: Gating prompts and responses with moderation scores, especially for severe categories where a target recall must be guaranteed on a labelled validation set, and where a cheap model can pre-screen traffic for a costly one.

examples.input: How do you choose a threshold for a severe category?
examples.output: Set the recall you must reach on a validation set and take the highest threshold that meets it. That keeps precision as high as the recall target permits.

examples.input: When does a two-stage cascade save money?
examples.output: When the expected cost $c_1 + p\,c_2$ is below $c_2$, which means the escalated fraction satisfies $p < 1 - c_1/c_2$. A very cheap first stage allows escalating a large share.

examples.input: Why are calibrated scores useful for moderation?
examples.output: A calibrated score of 0.8 means about 80 percent of such items are truly positive, so thresholds and review bands can be set from costs, and they stay stable when scores are compared across categories.

examples.input: What goes to human review?
examples.output: The grey zone around the threshold, plus a random sample of confident decisions to audit for drift and silent errors.

constraints: Target recall per category
Band edges $lo$ and $hi$ for escalation
Costs $c_1$ and $c_2$ of the two stages
Size and refresh rate of the labelled validation set
edgeCases: The threshold is tuned on one sample, so recall on new traffic can be lower; keep a margin and re-measure
Scores shift when the data or classifier changes, so a stored threshold can silently stop meeting the target
Ties in scores can push recall above the target or make the picked point jump; check the confusion counts
A rare positive class makes precision at high recall very unstable; report it with an interval

problems.title: Context Engineering and Token Budgeting
problems.summary: Treat the context window as a budget: reserve room for the output, spend the rest on the system prompt, recent history and the retrieved chunks with the best score per token, and place key facts at the ends.
problems.bruteForce: Short prompts that fit comfortably, or tasks where every source is essential, so nothing can be dropped. When exact optimality matters on a small set, solve the knapsack exactly instead of greedily.
problems.intuition: A context window is a fixed number of tokens shared by everything the model reads and writes, so every extra document displaces something else. Choosing what to include is a knapsack problem: take the chunks that give the most relevance per token, keep the most recent turns of history, and never spend the tokens reserved for the answer. Order matters too, since models use the start and end of a long prompt more reliably than the middle. Flow: window → reserve output → budget history → pack chunks by score per token → order.
problems.whyItWorks: Greedy by value density is optimal for the fractional knapsack, where a chunk may be split. For whole chunks it can be suboptimal, but the better of the greedy value and the best single chunk is at least half the optimum. Keeping the newest turns reflects that recent context is usually the most relevant, and reserving output tokens guarantees the model has room to answer.
approach: Subtract the output reserve and the system prompt from the window — what remains is the input budget
Give history a share of that budget and keep the newest turns that fit — recent turns matter most
Give the rest to retrieved chunks, sorted by value density $v_i / t_i$ — the greedy knapsack rule
Add a chunk only if it still fits, and keep scanning — a smaller later chunk may fit in the leftover space
Report tokens used per part and the slack — proves the total never exceeds the window minus the reserve
problems.time: O(n log n) to sort $n$ chunks, then O(n) to pack; O(m) for $m$ history turns
problems.space: O(n + m) for the kept lists
dryRun: Budget: $\sum_{i \in S} t_i \leq W - R - t_{sys}$
Maximise $\sum_{i \in S} v_i$ s.t. $\sum t_i \leq B$
problems.description: Any prompt assembled from several sources, such as RAG, chat with long history or tool outputs, where the total can exceed the window or where cost and latency grow with prompt length.

examples.input: Why reserve tokens for the output?
examples.output: Input and output share the window, so a prompt that fills it leaves no room to generate, which truncates or fails the answer.

examples.input: Why is greedy by score per token not always optimal?
examples.output: Chunks are indivisible. A dense chunk can use space that would have fit two slightly less dense ones with more total value.

examples.input: How do you decide what to drop from long chat history?
examples.output: Drop the oldest turns first, or replace them with a summary, and keep the system prompt and recent turns that the next reply depends on.

examples.input: Where should the most important facts go in a long prompt?
examples.output: Near the start or end, since models tend to use information in the middle of a long context less reliably.

constraints: Output reserve $R$ in tokens
History share of the input budget
Chunk scoring function (retrieval similarity, reranker score)
Summarise-or-drop policy for old turns
edgeCases: Token counts must come from the model's own tokenizer; counting words or characters undercounts
Greedy by density can be suboptimal for whole chunks, so compare against exact search on small cases
Stopping at the first chunk that does not fit leaves budget unused; keep scanning smaller ones
Dropping turns can remove the question a later turn refers to, so summarise or keep the pairs together

problems.title: Why Context Length Is Limited
problems.summary: Attention builds a $T \times T$ score matrix, so compute and score memory grow as $T^2$ while the KV cache grows linearly in $T$; sliding windows and RoPE position interpolation stretch the limit.
problems.bruteForce: Treating the quadratic score matrix as always materialised. Fused kernels avoid storing it, so the $T^2$ memory term then disappears even though the $T^2$ compute remains.
problems.intuition: Every token attends to every earlier token, so doubling the context quadruples the pairs to score. Separately, generation must keep keys and values for the whole context, which costs memory linearly. A model also only saw positions up to its training length, so longer inputs hit angles it never learned; squeezing positions back into the trained range is cheaper than retraining. Flow: longer context → more pairs → bigger scores and cache → limit.
problems.whyItWorks: Scores are one dot product per query-key pair, so there are $T^2$ of them. Linear interpolation works because RoPE angles are smooth in position: mapping position $p$ to $p \cdot L_{train}/L_{new}$ keeps every angle within the range seen in training, at the cost of packing nearby tokens closer together, so a short fine-tune helps.
approach: Model attention cost as $4 T^2 d_{head}$ FLOPs per head — $QK^\top$ and the weighted sum each cost $2T^2 d_{head}$
Score matrix holds $T^2$ values per head — memory grows quadratically unless fused or tiled
KV cache is $2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot T \cdot d_{head}$ values — linear in $T$ but large at long context
A sliding window of width $w$ keeps $T w$ scores — cost becomes linear in $T$
Position interpolation scales positions by $L_{train}/L_{new}$ — the angles stay inside the trained range
problems.time: O(T²·d) per head for full attention; O(T·w·d) with a window of width w
problems.space: O(T²) for materialised scores per head; O(T) for the KV cache per layer
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def attn_cost(T, d_head, bytes_per=4):
    flops = 4 * T * T * d_head        # QK^T and A V, 2*T*T*d each
    score_bytes = T * T * bytes_per   # the T x T score matrix
    return flops, score_bytes

def window_score_bytes(T, w, bytes_per=4):
    return T * min(T, w) * bytes_per  # sliding window: linear in T

def kv_bytes(T, layers, kv_heads, d_head, bytes_per=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * T * d_head * bytes_per

def rope_angles(positions, d_head, L_train=None, L_new=None,
                base=10000.0):
    s = 1.0 if L_new is None else L_train / L_new
    pos = np.asarray(positions, dtype=float) * s
    inv = base ** (-np.arange(0, d_head, 2) / d_head)
    return np.outer(pos, inv)         # angle = position * frequency
dryRun: Attention FLOPs $\approx 4 T^2 d_{head}$ per head
KV bytes $= 2 L h_{kv} T d_{head} \cdot \mathrm{bytes}$
RoPE angle $= p' \theta_i$, $p' = p L_{train} / L_{new}$
problems.description: Estimating whether a target context length fits in memory and time, and choosing between windowed attention, a bigger cache budget, or position interpolation to extend a pretrained model.

examples.input: Why does doubling the context quadruple attention cost?
examples.output: Each of the $T$ queries scores all $T$ keys, so there are $T^2$ scores. Doubling $T$ gives four times as many.

examples.input: Does the KV cache also grow quadratically?
examples.output: No. It stores one key and one value per token per layer and head, so it grows linearly in $T$, but it can still dominate memory in long-context serving.

examples.input: What does RoPE position interpolation do?
examples.output: It multiplies positions by $L_{train}/L_{new}$ so a longer input maps into the position range seen in training, then usually fine-tunes briefly.

examples.input: How does a sliding window help?
examples.output: Each token attends only to the last $w$ tokens, so scores and compute are linear in $T$, though information beyond the window must flow through the layers.

constraints: Context length $T$ (training and serving)
Window size $w$ for sliding-window attention
Interpolation factor $L_{train}/L_{new}$
Number of KV heads and cache precision
edgeCases: Fused attention kernels avoid storing the score matrix, so the quadratic memory figure is for the naive implementation; quadratic compute remains
A model accepting a long input does not mean it uses it well; quality over long contexts must be measured, not assumed
Interpolating positions without any fine-tuning degrades short-range resolution, since neighbouring tokens get closer angles

problems.title: Static vs Contextual Embeddings
problems.summary: A static table gives each word one vector whatever the sentence. A contextual model feeds the same table through attention, so each output vector is a mix of the word and its neighbours and changes with them.
problems.bruteForce: When a cheap, fixed vector per word is enough, such as for fast retrieval baselines or low-resource devices, where a static table such as word2vec is smaller and faster.
problems.intuition: A lookup table cannot tell "river bank" from "money bank" because the row for "bank" is fixed. Attention fixes this without changing the table: each token's output is a weighted average of value vectors over the whole sentence, with weights from query-key similarity, so the neighbours decide what the "bank" output contains. Stack such layers and the output becomes a representation of the word in its context, not of the word alone. Flow: tokens → static lookup → attention weights → mixed vectors.
problems.whyItWorks: The output for token $i$ is $\sum_j A_{ij} v_j$, a convex combination of value vectors. Since the weights $A_{ij}$ depend on the other tokens in the sentence, the output is a function of the whole input, so one word can map to different vectors. Without positional information the layer is permutation-equivariant: reordering the tokens just reorders the outputs.
approach: Look up each token id in the embedding table $E$ — this is the static vector, identical in every sentence
Project the rows to queries, keys and values with $W_q, W_k, W_v$ — three roles for the same token
Score all pairs with $QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d}$ — how relevant each token is to each other
Softmax each row — turns scores into mixing weights that sum to 1
Output $A V$ — each token becomes a context-weighted average, so the same word gets different vectors
problems.time: O(n²·d) for the attention scores over n tokens, O(n·d²) for the projections
problems.space: O(n²) for the attention matrix plus O(V·d) for the embedding table
dryRun: Static: $e_i = E[\mathrm{id}_i]$, same in every sentence
$Q = X W_q,\;\; K = X W_k,\;\; V = X W_v$
problems.description: Whenever meaning depends on context: word sense, coreference, any task where a word's role is set by its neighbours. Contextual outputs of a pretrained encoder are the standard input to downstream classifiers.

examples.input: Why can a static embedding not handle polysemy?
examples.output: It stores one vector per word type, so every sense of "bank" shares the same vector, and the model downstream sees no difference between them.

examples.input: How do contextual embeddings get different vectors for the same word?
examples.output: The output at a position is a weighted mix of all tokens in the sentence, and the weights depend on those tokens, so a different sentence gives a different mix.

examples.input: Why is attention without positions permutation-equivariant?
examples.output: Every token is treated with the same weights and the output depends on the set of other tokens, not their order, so permuting the inputs permutes the outputs. Positional encodings are added to break this.

examples.input: What do ELMo and BERT do differently from word2vec?
examples.output: word2vec learns a fixed table. ELMo uses the states of a bidirectional language model and BERT uses a transformer encoder, so their vectors depend on the sentence.

constraints: Embedding dimension $d$
Number of attention heads and layers
Projection (key) dimension $d_k$
Whether positional information is added
edgeCases: With no positional encoding the layer ignores word order; "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" give the same set of outputs
One attention layer on random weights only shows the mechanism; useful contextual vectors need trained weights and several layers
A word's contextual vector is not a single "meaning"; compare vectors in the same context, not across layers blindly

problems.title: Continuous Batching and Paged KV Cache
problems.summary: Keep every batch slot busy by admitting new requests and evicting finished ones at each decoding step, and store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks so memory is not wasted.
problems.bruteForce: Offline jobs with near-identical lengths, where static batching is as good and simpler. It also adds scheduler complexity and needs attention kernels that handle sequences at different positions.
problems.intuition: Generation lengths differ wildly, so a static batch runs as long as its longest sequence while finished slots sit idle. Scheduling at the granularity of one decoding step removes the wait: a slot freed this step is refilled the next. Paging the cache the same way, in small blocks looked up through a table, means no sequence reserves memory for tokens it may never produce. Flow: queue + free slots → admit each step → decode → evict finished → refill.
problems.whyItWorks: A static batch of $B$ takes $\max_i L_i$ steps but only uses $\sum_i L_i$ slot-steps, so the gap is idle capacity. A scheduler that refills slots every step never leaves a slot idle while requests wait, so its total steps are close to the lower bound $\sum_i L_i / B$. Fixed-size blocks bound the cache waste per sequence by one partial block.
approach: Keep a queue of waiting requests and a set of at most $B$ active ones — $B$ is the slot count
At each step, admit waiting requests into free slots — no slot idles while work waits
Decode one token for every active sequence — the whole batch moves one step together
Evict sequences that just finished — their slots and cache blocks are freed immediately
Allocate KV memory in blocks of $s$ tokens via a block table — a sequence wastes only its last partial block
problems.time: O(total steps · B) for the simulation
problems.space: O(n) for the queue
problems.description: Online serving of generation requests whose output lengths vary, where throughput and GPU utilisation matter more than strict batch alignment.

examples.input: Why is static batching inefficient for generation?
examples.output: Sequences stop at different lengths, but the batch runs until the longest one finishes, so finished slots do no useful work.

examples.input: What does iteration-level scheduling change?
examples.output: The scheduler runs at every decoding step, so finished sequences leave and waiting ones join immediately instead of at batch boundaries.

examples.input: What problem does a paged KV cache solve?
examples.output: Reserving contiguous space for the maximum length wastes memory through fragmentation, while fixed-size blocks with a block table allocate memory as tokens arrive and waste at most one partial block per sequence.

examples.input: Does continuous batching change the output of a request?
examples.output: No. Each sequence is decoded the same way; only when it runs, and with which neighbours, changes.

constraints: Maximum number of concurrent sequences $B$
KV block size $s$ in tokens
Admission policy and queue order
Total cache memory reserved for blocks
edgeCases: Prompt prefill is far more expensive than one decode step, so admitting a long prompt can stall the running sequences
Small blocks cut waste but enlarge the block table and slow attention lookups; large blocks do the reverse
Slot utilisation is not throughput: a full batch can still be memory-bound
This simulation assumes one token per step and known lengths; real lengths are unknown until generation ends

problems.title: Convex Optimisation and Lagrange Multipliers
problems.summary: For a convex objective every local minimum is global. Lagrange multipliers turn a constrained problem into stationarity of a Lagrangian, and the KKT conditions extend this to inequality constraints, as used in the SVM dual.
problems.bruteForce: Large sparse or inequality-constrained problems, where you would use an iterative or interior-point solver, and non-convex problems where a KKT point need not be a global minimum.
problems.intuition: At a constrained optimum you cannot slide along the constraint surface and improve, so the objective gradient has no component along the surface: it points straight along the constraint normals, and the multipliers are the weights. A multiplier is also a price: it says how much the optimal value changes when the constraint is relaxed. For an inequality constraint, either it is tight and has a price, or it is slack and its price is zero (complementary slackness). Flow: objective + constraints → Lagrangian → stationarity → solve → multipliers as prices.
problems.whyItWorks: If the Hessian $Q$ is positive semidefinite, the objective lies below every chord, so any stationary point on the feasible set is a global minimum. Stationarity says $\nabla f = -A^\top \lambda$ at the optimum. Perturbing $b$ to $b + \delta$ changes the optimal value by about $-\lambda^\top \delta$ with this sign convention, which makes $\lambda$ the shadow price. For inequalities, KKT adds $\lambda_i \geq 0$ and $\lambda_i g_i = 0$.
approach: Check convexity — a quadratic is convex when $Q$ has no negative eigenvalue, so a stationary point is the global minimum
Form the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}x^\top Q x + c^\top x + \lambda^\top (Ax - b)$ — folds constraints into the objective
Set the gradient in $x$ to zero and keep $Ax = b$ — stationarity plus feasibility
Stack both into one linear KKT system and solve — a quadratic program with equalities is just linear algebra
Check residuals and read $\lambda$ — a good solution makes both residuals near 0 and $\lambda$ is the price
problems.time: O((n+m)³) to solve the dense KKT system
problems.space: O((n+m)²) for the KKT matrix
dryRun: Convex iff Hessian $\nabla^2 f$ is PSD
Lagrangian: $\frac{1}{2}x^\top Q x + c^\top x + \lambda^\top (Ax - b)$
problems.description: Equality-constrained quadratic problems, understanding duals and support vectors in the SVM, and reading any constrained optimum as stationarity of a Lagrangian with multipliers as prices.

examples.input: Why do we care about convexity?
examples.output: In a convex problem every local minimum is a global minimum, so gradient methods and stationarity conditions are enough to find the best solution.

examples.input: What do Lagrange multipliers mean?
examples.output: They weight the constraint normals in the stationarity condition, and they are the sensitivity of the optimal value to the constraint level, a shadow price.

examples.input: What is complementary slackness?
examples.output: For each inequality constraint either the constraint is tight or its multiplier is zero. In the SVM this means only support vectors, which lie on the margin, have non-zero dual variables.

examples.input: How do you test whether a quadratic is convex?
examples.output: Its Hessian $Q$ must be positive semidefinite: all eigenvalues of the symmetrised matrix are at least 0.

constraints: Objective matrix $Q$ and vector $c$
Constraint matrix $A$ and level $b$
Tolerance for the eigenvalue convexity test
edgeCases: The KKT system is singular if the constraints in $A$ are linearly dependent; remove redundant rows
Sign conventions for $\lambda$ differ between texts, so the sign of the shadow price flips with them
For non-convex $Q$ a KKT point can be a saddle or a maximum, not the minimum

problems.title: 2D Convolution
problems.summary: Slide a small learned filter across an image and take a dot product with each local patch, producing a feature map per filter.
problems.bruteForce: Not when long-range or global relations dominate and there is little locality (consider attention), or for unordered tabular features.
problems.intuition: A filter is a tiny pattern detector reused at every location, so the network looks for the same edge or texture wherever it appears and needs far fewer weights than a dense layer. Stacking layers grows the receptive field, so later filters respond to larger shapes built from earlier ones.
problems.whyItWorks: Images have local structure and the same features matter at any position, so sharing weights across positions (translation equivariance) is a strong, correct prior. Local connectivity cuts parameters and computation, which lets models learn from limited data.
approach: Zero-pad the input by p on each side — controls the output size and keeps border pixels in play
Compute output height and width from kernel, stride and padding — fixes the loop bounds
For each output position take the matching input patch across all channels — that is the filter's receptive field
Multiply the patch with every filter and sum over channels and kernel — one dot product per filter
Add the bias and write the result at that position — builds the feature maps
problems.time: O(N·F·C·kH·kW·oH·oW)
problems.space: O(N·F·oH·oW) for the output; the filters hold F·C·kH·kW
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def conv2d(x, w, b, stride=1, pad=0):
    x = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    n, c, h, wd = x.shape
    f, _, kh, kw = w.shape
    oh = (h - kh) // stride + 1
    ow = (wd - kw) // stride + 1
    out = np.zeros((n, f, oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
            patch = x[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw]
            axes = ([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
            out[:, :, i, j] = np.tensordot(patch, w, axes) + b
    return out
dryRun: Cross-correlation: the filter is not flipped
problems.description: Images, spectrograms and other grid data where nearby values are related and patterns repeat across positions.

examples.input: Why use convolution instead of a dense layer on images?
examples.output: Local connectivity and shared weights cut parameters sharply and build in translation equivariance.

examples.input: How is the output size computed?
examples.output: ⌊(H + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1 along each spatial dimension, for padding p, kernel k and stride s.

examples.input: What is the receptive field?
examples.output: The region of the input that influences one output value; it grows with kernel size, stride and depth.

constraints: Kernel size (receptive field of one layer)
Stride (step between positions; larger downsamples)
Padding (zero border; same-size output needs p = (k − 1)/2 at stride 1)
Number of filters (output channels)
edgeCases: Deep learning libraries compute cross-correlation, not flipped convolution
Wrong padding or stride arithmetic gives off-by-one output sizes
Channel order (NCHW versus NHWC) differs between frameworks
Loops like this are slow; real implementations use im2col or FFT-style kernels

problems.title: Cosine Similarity for Embeddings
problems.summary: Compare two embedding vectors by the cosine of the angle between them, ignoring their lengths, and use it to rank nearest neighbours.
problems.bruteForce: When vector magnitude carries information you want to keep, for example confidence or popularity, or with sparse count data where other measures fit better. Zero vectors have no direction.
problems.intuition: Embedding length often reflects things like word frequency or text length rather than meaning, while direction carries the semantics. Dividing the dot product by both norms keeps only direction, and after normalising rows, a whole similarity matrix is a single matrix product.
problems.whyItWorks: The dot product equals the product of the norms times the cosine of the angle, so dividing by the norms leaves a pure angle between −1 and 1. For unit vectors the squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus twice the cosine, so ranking by cosine and by Euclidean distance agree once the vectors are normalised. Scaling either vector leaves the value unchanged.
approach: Compute each row's L2 norm — the length to be removed
Divide each row by its norm, with a small floor — unit vectors, safe for zero rows
Multiply normalised queries by normalised keys transposed — every dot product is now a cosine
Sort scores in descending order and take the top k — the nearest neighbours by angle
problems.time: O(m·n·d) for m queries, n items and width d
problems.space: O(m·n) for the similarity matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def cosine_matrix(A, B, eps=1e-12):
    na = np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    nb = np.linalg.norm(B, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    An = A / np.maximum(na, eps)
    Bn = B / np.maximum(nb, eps)
    return An @ Bn.T

def top_k_neighbors(q, E, k):
    s = cosine_matrix(q[None, :], E)[0]
    idx = np.argsort(-s)[:k]
    return idx, s[idx]
problems.description: Semantic search, retrieval for RAG, deduplication and clustering of text embeddings, and any model whose embeddings are trained with a cosine or contrastive objective.

examples.input: Why use cosine similarity instead of the raw dot product?
examples.output: The dot product grows with vector length, so long vectors look similar to everything. Cosine removes length and compares direction only.

examples.input: Is cosine distance a true metric?
examples.output: No. 1 − cos can violate the triangle inequality. The angle itself is a metric, and the Euclidean distance between normalised vectors is too.

examples.input: How do you speed up cosine search over millions of vectors?
examples.output: Normalise once, then maximum inner product search with an approximate index works directly, since cosine becomes a dot product.

constraints: Epsilon floor for zero-norm vectors
Number of neighbours k
Whether embeddings are pre-normalised
edgeCases: Zero vectors divide by zero without the epsilon floor, and then give similarity 0
A cosine score is not calibrated; thresholds depend on the embedding model
Full argsort is O(n log n); real systems use partial selection or an approximate index

problems.title: Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder)
problems.summary: Let each decoder position look up information in the encoder output: queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder.
problems.bruteForce: Decoder-only language models have no separate source, so they use self-attention over a concatenated prompt instead. Very long sources make the target-by-source score matrix expensive.
problems.intuition: Self-attention lets a sequence read itself; cross-attention lets one sequence read another. The decoder state asks "which source words do I need to produce the next word?", and the encoder outputs answer with keys to match and values to hand over. The source length and target length are independent, so the weight matrix is rectangular, one row per target position and one column per source position.
problems.whyItWorks: The encoder compresses the source once; the decoder can then consult any source position at every step with content-based weights instead of squeezing the source into one fixed vector. Keys and values are computed once per source and reused for every generated token. A padding mask sets the scores of padded source columns to $-\infty$ so they receive exactly zero weight.
approach: Project decoder states to queries — the decoder is the one asking
Project encoder outputs to keys and values — the source supplies what to match and what to give
Score every target-source pair with $QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k}$ — rectangular matrix, scaled to keep softmax healthy
Mask padded source columns with $-\infty$ — padding must receive zero weight
Softmax each row and multiply by $V$ — each target position gets a weighted average of source values
problems.time: O(T_dec·T_enc·d) for target length T_dec, source length T_enc and width d
problems.space: O(T_dec·T_enc) for the attention matrix; K and V (O(T_enc·d)) can be cached across decoding steps
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(s):
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_attention(Xd, Xe, Wq, Wk, Wv, src_mask=None):
    Q = Xd @ Wq                  # queries: decoder
    K, V = Xe @ Wk, Xe @ Wv      # keys, values: encoder
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
    if src_mask is not None:     # True = real token, False = pad
        scores = np.where(src_mask[None, :], scores, -np.inf)
    A = softmax(scores)
    return A @ V, A
dryRun: $K = X_{enc}\,W_k,\;\; V = X_{enc}\,W_v \qquad (T_{enc} \times d_k,\ T_{enc} \times d_v)$
Padding: $S[i, j] = -\infty$ if source $j$ is padding
$A = \mathrm{softmax}(S)$ row-wise, so each row sums to 1
problems.description: Translation, summarisation, speech recognition and any encoder-decoder model where the output must be conditioned on a separate input sequence, including image-to-text models whose encoder outputs are patches.

examples.input: Where do $Q$, $K$ and $V$ come from in cross-attention?
examples.output: Queries come from the decoder's current hidden states; keys and values come from the encoder's final outputs. The attention matrix is therefore target length by source length.

examples.input: Why can encoder keys and values be cached during generation?
examples.output: The source does not change while decoding, so its keys and values are computed once and reused at every step; only the new query is computed each step.

examples.input: Does cross-attention need a causal mask?
examples.output: No. The decoder may look at the whole source; causality applies only to the decoder's self-attention over its own previous outputs. A padding mask on the source is what it needs.

constraints: Key/query dimension $d_k$ (sets the scale $\sqrt{d_k}$)
Number of heads (this code is a single head)
Source padding mask (needed whenever sources in a batch differ in length)
Attention dropout
edgeCases: Forgetting the source padding mask lets the decoder attend to padding tokens
A source that is entirely padding gives a fully masked row and NaN; real batches contain at least one real token
Queries must come from the decoder; swapping the roles gives a source-by-target matrix instead
This is one head with no output projection, residual or layer norm, which a real decoder layer adds

problems.title: K-Fold Cross-Validation
problems.summary: Estimate generalisation by splitting the data into k folds, training on k − 1 of them and scoring on the held-out one, rotating through all k.
problems.bruteForce: Skip plain shuffled k-fold for time series (use forward chaining) and grouped data (use group k-fold), and avoid it when one fit is so expensive that k fits are impractical.
problems.intuition: A single train/validation split wastes data and its score depends on which rows landed where. Rotating the held-out fold means every row is used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times, so the averaged score is steadier and the spread shows how fragile it is.
problems.whyItWorks: Each fold's score is an unbiased-ish estimate of error on unseen data because the model never saw those rows. Averaging k such estimates reduces the variance caused by one lucky or unlucky split. It is slightly pessimistic because each model trains on only a fraction (k − 1)/k of the data.
approach: Shuffle the row indices with a fixed seed — so folds are not ordered by collection time and runs repeat
Split the indices into k nearly equal folds — each row lands in exactly one fold
For each fold, train on the other k − 1 — the model must never see its validation rows
Score the held-out fold — gives one honest estimate per fold
Report mean and spread — the spread shows how stable the estimate is
problems.time: k times the cost of one fit, plus O(n) for the splits
problems.space: O(n) for the index folds
dryRun: folds $F_1 \ldots F_k$ partition $\{1 \ldots n\}$, sizes differ $\leq 1$
spread = std of the $k$ fold scores
problems.description: Comparing models or hyperparameters on small to medium datasets when a single hold-out set would be too noisy or too costly in data.

examples.input: Why k = 5 or 10 and not leave-one-out?
examples.output: Leave-one-out has low bias but the n models are highly correlated, so the estimate has high variance and costs n fits; 5 or 10 folds is a good compromise.

examples.input: Why use stratified k-fold for classification?
examples.output: It keeps the class proportions in every fold, so rare classes do not vanish from some validation folds.

examples.input: How do you tune hyperparameters without fooling yourself?
examples.output: Use nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks hyperparameters and an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure.

constraints: Number of folds k (5 or 10 is typical; larger k means less bias and higher cost)
Shuffling and random seed
Stratification for classification (keeps class ratios per fold)
Scoring metric
edgeCases: Fitting preprocessing (scaler, imputer, feature selection) on all data before splitting leaks into the folds
Using the CV score to tune many hyperparameters and then reporting it as final performance overfits to the folds
Random folds on time-ordered or grouped data leak the future or the same entity

problems.title: Data Augmentation
problems.summary: Create new training examples on the fly by applying random, label-preserving transformations such as flips and crops to the existing images.
problems.bruteForce: Not on validation or test data (only deterministic preprocessing there), and not with transforms that change the label such as flipping text or digits.
problems.intuition: A flipped or slightly shifted cat is still a cat, so each random transform shows the model the same label under a new appearance. This teaches the invariances you care about without collecting more data, and it makes memorising exact pixel patterns much harder. Normalisation is applied last, with fixed statistics, so training and test inputs are on the same scale.
problems.whyItWorks: Augmentation enlarges the effective training distribution along directions where the true label does not change, which acts as a data-dependent regulariser and reduces variance. It only helps if the transform really preserves the label; a flipped digit or a crop that removes the object injects label noise.
approach: Draw the random decisions (flip or not, crop offsets) — each epoch sees a different version
Flip the width axis when the coin says so — mirror symmetry preserves most labels
Slice a random crop of the target size — shifts and rescales what the model sees
Subtract the channel mean and divide by the channel std — same scaling at train and test
problems.time: O(C·size²) per image
problems.space: O(C·size²) for the output; flips and crops are views
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def augment(x, rng, size, mean, std):
    # x: (C, H, W) image; returns (C, size, size)
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        x = x[:, :, ::-1]
    top = rng.integers(0, x.shape[1] - size + 1)
    left = rng.integers(0, x.shape[2] - size + 1)
    x = x[:, top:top + size, left:left + size]
    return (x - mean[:, None, None]) / std[:, None, None]
problems.description: Small or medium image datasets and any model prone to overfitting, with transforms matched to the task's real invariances.

examples.input: Why does augmentation reduce overfitting?
examples.output: It makes the model see many label-preserving variants of each image, so it cannot rely on exact pixels and learns the intended invariances.

examples.input: Should you augment at test time?
examples.output: Normally no, only deterministic preprocessing; test-time augmentation is a separate technique that averages predictions.

examples.input: How do you choose augmentations?
examples.output: Pick transforms the label is truly invariant to in your domain and validate that they help.

constraints: Flip probability
Crop size (and padding or scale range in practice)
Strength of colour or geometric jitter (not modelled here)
Normalisation mean and std
edgeCases: Augmenting validation or test data hides the true generalisation
Transforms that change the label (flipped digits, over-aggressive crops) add noise
Normalise with training statistics, not per-batch statistics
This sketch only flips, crops and normalises; real pipelines add scale, rotation and colour changes

problems.title: Data Leakage
problems.summary: Information from the validation or test data leaks into training, so the measured score looks better than real-world performance.
problems.bruteForce: Not a technique to apply but a failure to avoid. Statistics from the unlabelled target domain are legitimately used in transductive or domain-adaptation setups, if documented as such.
problems.intuition: Anything computed with the test rows, such as scaling statistics, imputation values, selected features or even a duplicated row, lets the model peek at the answer sheet. The rule is simple: every data-dependent step is part of the model, so fit it on the training fold only and merely apply it to held-out data.
problems.whyItWorks: A fair evaluation simulates deployment, where future data and labels are unseen when the model is built. Fitting a transform on the training split and reusing its parameters mimics that exactly, whereas fitting on all data lets validation rows influence the parameters they are scored with.
approach: Split first, before any data-dependent step — the test rows stay unseen
Fit scaler, imputer and feature selector on the training rows only — these are part of the model
Apply the fitted transform to validation and test rows — same parameters, no refitting
Do all of this inside each cross-validation fold — a pipeline object enforces it
Check for duplicates, group overlap and target-derived features — other common leaks
problems.time: O(n·d) for the scaling; the cost is a wrong estimate, not compute
problems.space: O(d) for the fitted statistics
dryRun: Leaky stats shrink the train/test shift: test looks easier
problems.description: Audit every pipeline before trusting a metric, especially when the score looks too good, or when preprocessing and feature selection precede the train-test split or cross-validation.

examples.input: Your model scores very well offline but poorly in production. What do you check first?
examples.output: Leakage: preprocessing or feature selection fit on all data, target-derived features, duplicates across splits, or a split that ignores time or groups.

examples.input: How do you prevent preprocessing leakage in cross-validation?
examples.output: Put the transforms and the model in one pipeline so each fold fits the transforms on its own training part only.

examples.input: Is scaling before the split really a problem?
examples.output: It is a mild leak since only means and variances cross over, but selection, imputation and target encoding can leak far more.

constraints: Split strategy (random, time-based or grouped) that matches deployment
Where preprocessing is fitted (inside each fold with a pipeline)
edgeCases: Selecting features with the labels on all data before cross-validation inflates scores even on pure noise
Random splits of time series let the model train on the future
Duplicate or near-duplicate rows (or the same user) in both train and test
Features computed after the outcome, such as a status flag set once the event happens

problems.title: DBSCAN
problems.summary: Grow clusters from dense regions: a point with enough neighbours inside radius eps is a core point, clusters are chains of overlapping core neighbourhoods, and points reachable from no core are noise.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when clusters have very different densities (one eps cannot fit both), in high dimensions where distances concentrate, or for big data without a spatial index (this code is quadratic).
problems.intuition: A cluster is a region where you can keep walking from point to point without ever stepping across a gap bigger than eps in a crowd of at least min_pts. This defines clusters by connectivity of density rather than by distance to a centre, so it finds crescents and rings and needs no cluster count, and it can say that a point belongs nowhere.
problems.whyItWorks: Core points that lie within eps of each other are density-connected, and connectivity among core points is an equivalence relation, so each connected component is one well-defined cluster. Border points (non-core, but within eps of a core) attach to a neighbouring cluster, and everything else is labelled noise.
approach: Compute all pairwise distances and eps-neighbourhoods — the definition of density is neighbour count
Mark points with at least min_pts neighbours as core — only these may grow clusters
Visit unlabelled core points in order and start a new cluster at each — one seed per connected component
Flood-fill from a core point through its neighbours, expanding only through other core points — border points join but do not spread the cluster
Leave unreached points as $-1$ — noise is a legitimate outcome
problems.time: O(n²) with the distance matrix here; O(n log n) with a KD/ball tree in low dimensions
problems.space: O(n²) for the distance matrix here; O(n) with a spatial index
dryRun: $j$ reachable from $i$ if $i$ core and $j \in N_{\epsilon}(i)$
Cluster = linked core points plus their borders
Noise = not reachable from any core, label $-1$
problems.description: Non-convex clusters, unknown number of clusters, data with outliers you want flagged, and low-dimensional spatial or geographic data.

examples.input: What are core, border and noise points?
examples.output: Core points have at least min_pts points within eps, border points are within eps of a core but not core themselves, and noise is everything else.

examples.input: How do you choose eps?
examples.output: Plot each point's distance to its $k$-th nearest neighbour sorted ascending and pick the knee, then sanity-check the clusters.

examples.input: Why can DBSCAN beat k-means?
examples.output: It needs no cluster count, finds arbitrary shapes, and marks outliers, whereas k-means assumes compact, similar-sized convex clusters and assigns every point.

constraints: eps — neighbourhood radius; read it off a k-distance plot
min_pts — density threshold; a common start is twice the dimension
metric — Euclidean by default, but any distance works
edgeCases: Features must be scaled first, otherwise eps means nothing
Border points touching two clusters go to whichever is reached first, so results depend on row order
Mixed-density data: a single eps merges the dense clusters or drops the sparse ones as noise
min_pts counts the point itself, so conventions differ between libraries

problems.title: Decision Tree
problems.summary: Predict by asking a chain of yes/no questions on single features. The tree is grown greedily, choosing at each node the split that makes the two child groups as pure as possible.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a single deep tree when you need stable predictions or smooth boundaries: small data changes flip splits, and axis-aligned cuts approximate diagonal boundaries badly.
problems.intuition: A tree carves feature space into axis-aligned boxes and predicts the majority class of each box. Growing it is just a repeated search: try every threshold on every feature and keep the one that most reduces impurity, then recurse on each side as if it were a new problem.
problems.whyItWorks: Each split can never increase the weighted impurity, because the parent is a mix of its children. So deeper trees fit the training data ever better, which is also the danger: with no depth limit the tree memorises noise. The greedy choice is not globally optimal, but it is cheap and works well in practice.
approach: Compute the Gini impurity of the node — it measures how mixed the classes are
Stop if depth is used up or the node is pure — this limits overfitting
Try midpoints between sorted values of each feature — these are all distinct splits
Score each split by weighted child impurity — pick the lowest cost
Recurse on left and right subsets — each child is a smaller copy of the problem
Predict by walking from the root to a leaf — each test sends the sample left or right
problems.time: O(d · n² ) naive per node as written; O(d · n log n) per level with sorting and running counts
problems.space: O(n) for the data plus O(nodes) for the tree
dryRun: $\mathrm{Gini}(S) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2,\;\; p_k$ = share of class $k$ in $S$
problems.description: Interpretable models on tabular data with mixed scales and non-linear interactions, and as the base learner for forests and boosting.

examples.input: Gini or entropy?
examples.output: Both measure impurity and usually pick near-identical splits; Gini avoids the logarithm so it is slightly faster.

examples.input: How do you stop a tree from overfitting?
examples.output: Limit depth, require a minimum leaf size, or grow fully and prune with cost-complexity; or average many trees in a forest.

examples.input: Do trees need feature scaling?
examples.output: No. Splits compare a feature to a threshold, so any monotonic rescaling gives the same tree.

constraints: max_depth — main control of over/underfitting
min_samples_leaf — forbids tiny, noisy leaves
criterion — Gini or entropy, rarely matters
ccp_alpha — cost-complexity pruning strength
edgeCases: Unlimited depth reaches 100% training accuracy and overfits
Split search favours features with many distinct values
Equal-gain splits are tied: sklearn breaks ties by a random feature order, so deep trees can differ from this code
Predictions are piecewise constant, so a tree cannot extrapolate

problems.title: Decoder-Only (GPT-Style) Transformer Block
problems.summary: A GPT-style layer with pre-LayerNorm: normalise, causal self-attention, add back, normalise, feed-forward, add back; stacked, it is the whole body of a decoder-only language model.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks that need bidirectional context over a fixed input, where an encoder is a better fit, or very long contexts where quadratic attention cost dominates.
problems.intuition: A decoder-only model has no encoder and no cross-attention; one stack of identical blocks reads the prefix and predicts the next token. Each block only adds corrections to a residual stream, and the causal mask guarantees that position $t$ never sees later tokens, so one parallel pass trains the prediction at every position at once. Flow: tokens → LayerNorm → causal attention → add → LayerNorm → FFN → add.
problems.whyItWorks: The causal mask makes the output at position $t$ a function of tokens up to $t$ only, which makes next-token training parallel and lets generation reuse cached keys and values. The pre-norm residual form $x + f(\mathrm{LN}(x))$ keeps an identity path through all layers, which keeps gradients healthy in deep stacks.
approach: Normalise each position with LayerNorm — a stable input scale for attention
Project to $Q$, $K$, $V$ and split into heads — each head attends in its own subspace
Mask scores above the diagonal with $-\infty$ — a token cannot see the future
Softmax, mix values, merge heads, project with $W_o$ and add to $x$ — first residual update
Normalise, apply the feed-forward network and add — second residual update; shape stays $(T, d)$
problems.time: O(T²·d + T·d²) per block
problems.space: O(h·T²) attention scores plus O(T·d) activations
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def layer_norm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    return g * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + b

def causal_attn(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h):
    T, d = x.shape
    q, k, v = (x @ W for W in (Wq, Wk, Wv))
    q, k, v = (m.reshape(T, h, d // h).transpose(1, 0, 2)
               for m in (q, k, v))
    s = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d // h)
    s = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((T, T), bool), 1), -np.inf, s)
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    a = (e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ v
    return a.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d) @ Wo

def ffn(x, W1, W2):
    t = x @ W1
    c = np.sqrt(2 / np.pi)
    g = 0.5 * t * (1 + np.tanh(c * (t + 0.044715 * t**3)))
    return g @ W2

def block(x, P, h):
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g1"], P["b1"])
    x = x + causal_attn(y, P["Wq"], P["Wk"], P["Wv"], P["Wo"], h)
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g2"], P["b2"])
    return x + ffn(y, P["W1"], P["W2"])
problems.description: Building or reading any GPT-style language model: embeddings, $N$ stacked blocks, a final LayerNorm and a projection to vocabulary logits.

examples.input: What makes a block decoder-only?
examples.output: It uses causal self-attention only, with no cross-attention to an encoder, so each position sees just the tokens before it and itself.

examples.input: Why pre-LayerNorm instead of post-LayerNorm?
examples.output: Normalising inside the residual branch leaves the skip path as a pure identity, so deep stacks train stably and need less learning-rate warmup.

examples.input: How would you test that the mask works?
examples.output: Change a later token's input and check that all earlier output positions are unchanged.

constraints: Model width $d$ and number of heads $h$ (with $d$ divisible by $h$)
FFN hidden size (about $4d$, or $\frac{8}{3}d$ when gated)
Number of stacked blocks
LayerNorm epsilon and the activation
edgeCases: Applying the mask after softmax instead of before it leaks the future and breaks the row sums
Forgetting the final LayerNorm after the last block when using pre-norm
Adding the residual to the normalised tensor instead of the raw stream destroys the identity path

problems.title: Depthwise Separable Convolution
problems.summary: Split a standard convolution into a per-channel spatial filter (depthwise) followed by a 1×1 convolution that mixes channels (pointwise).
problems.bruteForce: When compute is plentiful and accuracy matters most; the factorised layer is less expressive and depthwise operations can run inefficiently on some hardware despite fewer operations.
problems.intuition: A standard convolution does two jobs at once: it looks at spatial neighbourhoods and it mixes channels, with a separate weight for every pair. Factoring these apart gives each channel its own small spatial filter, then mixes channels per pixel. The product of two cheap steps approximates the expensive joint one, and the saving grows with the number of channels and the kernel area.
problems.whyItWorks: The factorised layer is a low-rank structure on the full kernel: the spatial pattern is shared across all output channels instead of being learned separately for each. Natural images often have features where spatial and cross-channel structure can be treated separately, so far fewer parameters and multiplications lose little accuracy.
approach: Pad the input like an ordinary convolution — same output-size rules apply
For each position, take the patch of every channel separately — channels are not mixed yet
Multiply each channel's patch by that channel's own $k \times k$ filter and sum — the depthwise step
Mix channels at each pixel with a $F \times C$ matrix — the pointwise 1×1 step produces $F$ maps
problems.time: O(N·oH·oW·C·(kH·kW + F))
problems.space: O(N·C·oH·oW) for the intermediate maps
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def depthwise_separable(x, dw, pw, stride=1, pad=0):
    # x: (N,C,H,W)  dw: (C,kh,kw)  pw: (F,C)
    x = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    _, kh, kw = dw.shape
    oh = (h - kh) // stride + 1
    ow = (w - kw) // stride + 1
    mid = np.zeros((n, c, oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
