            patch = x[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw]
            mid[:, :, i, j] = (patch * dw).sum((2, 3))
    return np.einsum("nchw,fc->nfhw", mid, pw)
dryRun: Params: standard $F C k^2$;  separable $C k^2 + F C$
problems.description: Mobile and edge models (MobileNet, Xception, EfficientNet) where parameters and compute are limited.

examples.input: How does a depthwise separable convolution save parameters?
examples.output: It uses $C \cdot k^2$ spatial weights plus $F \cdot C$ mixing weights instead of $F \cdot C \cdot k^2$ for the full kernel.

examples.input: What does the depthwise step do?
examples.output: It filters each input channel independently with its own spatial kernel, so it mixes no information across channels.

examples.input: What does the pointwise step do?
examples.output: A 1×1 convolution that linearly combines channels at every position, producing the output channels.

constraints: Kernel size of the depthwise filter
Stride and padding
Output channels $F$ of the pointwise layer
Depth multiplier (not modelled; this uses one filter per channel)
edgeCases: Fewer multiply-adds do not always mean faster inference; memory-bound depthwise kernels can be slow
Normalisation and a nonlinearity between the two steps matter in real blocks; this sketch has none
Biases are omitted in this sketch
Compare parameter counts with equal accuracy, not with equal width

problems.title: Derivatives, Chain Rule and Gradient Checking
problems.summary: The gradient collects the slope of a function in every input direction, the chain rule multiplies local slopes through a composition, and a finite-difference check tests a hand-derived gradient against a numerical one.
problems.bruteForce: As a training method, since it costs one or two function evaluations per parameter. Also unreliable near kinks such as ReLU at 0, and with very small $h$ where floating-point round-off dominates.
problems.intuition: A derivative is the local slope: how much the output moves per unit nudge of the input. For a composition, a nudge passes through each stage and the slopes multiply, which is all backpropagation does, stage by stage. Because a wrong gradient still looks plausible, you nudge each input by a small $h$ both ways and compare the measured slope with your formula. Symmetric nudges cancel the first-order error, so the central difference is far more accurate. Flow: function → nudge input ± h → numerical slope → compare with analytic.
problems.whyItWorks: Taylor expansion gives $f(x \pm h) = f(x) \pm h f' + \frac{h^2}{2} f'' \pm \frac{h^3}{6} f'''$. The forward difference leaves a $\frac{h}{2} f''$ error, while in the central difference the even terms cancel and the error is of order $h^2$. Round-off adds an error of order $\epsilon / h$, so there is a sweet spot for $h$, typically around $10^{-5}$ in double precision.
approach: Differentiate each stage locally — for $f(x) = \sum_i \tanh(Wx+b)_i^2$ the stages are affine, $\tanh$ and square-and-sum
Multiply local slopes from the output backwards — the chain rule, giving $\nabla f = W^\top(2 t (1 - t^2))$ with $t = \tanh(Wx+b)$
Nudge one coordinate at a time by $\pm h$ — the central difference $(f(x+h)-f(x-h))/(2h)$
Assemble the numerical gradient from all coordinates — same shape as $x$
Compare with $\|a-n\| / (\|a\|+\|n\|)$ — below about $10^{-6}$ is a pass; above $10^{-2}$ the gradient is wrong
problems.time: Analytic gradient costs about one extra forward pass; the numerical one needs 2n evaluations for n inputs
problems.space: O(n) for the gradient
dryRun: Gradient: $\nabla f = (\partial f/\partial x_1, \ldots, \partial f/\partial x_n)$
Jacobian: $J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j$, $J_{f \circ g} = J_f J_g$
problems.description: Debugging a hand-written backward pass or a custom autograd function: check the analytic gradient against finite differences on a tiny input before trusting it in training.

examples.input: What is the chain rule in terms of backpropagation?
examples.output: For a composition $y = f(u)$, $u = g(x)$, the slope is $\frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$: multiply the local slopes. Backpropagation applies this stage by stage from the loss back to the inputs, reusing the forward values.

examples.input: Why is the central difference better than the forward difference?
examples.output: The first-order error terms cancel, leaving an error of order $h^2$ instead of $h$, at the price of two function evaluations per coordinate.

examples.input: What relative error should a gradient check reach?
examples.output: Around $10^{-7}$ or smaller in double precision is excellent; above $10^{-2}$ the gradient is almost certainly wrong. Use float64 and a small input for the check.

examples.input: Why not train with numerical gradients?
examples.output: They need about $2n$ forward passes for $n$ parameters and are noisy, whereas backpropagation gives all $n$ partial derivatives for the cost of a few passes.

constraints: Step size $h$ (around $10^{-5}$ in float64)
Difference scheme (forward or central)
Pass threshold on the relative error
edgeCases: Too small an $h$ amplifies round-off; too large a bias. Do the check in float64, not float32
Non-differentiable points (ReLU at 0, max pooling ties) make a correct gradient look wrong
Turn off dropout and other randomness during the check, or the two evaluations differ

problems.title: Diffusion Forward (Noising) Process
problems.summary: Gradually turn data into Gaussian noise by adding a little noise at each step, and jump straight to any step $t$ with one closed-form sample.
problems.bruteForce: Sampling new data, which needs the learned reverse process. The forward process alone is fixed and has no parameters to learn.
problems.intuition: Each noising step shrinks the signal slightly and adds fresh Gaussian noise, and a chain of Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian. Their combined effect collapses into a single draw with a scaled copy of the data plus noise, so training can pick a random $t$ and corrupt $x_0$ in one shot instead of simulating $t$ steps.
problems.whyItWorks: Each step maps $x$ to a Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{1-\beta}\,x$ and variance $\beta$. A Gaussian pushed through a linear map plus independent Gaussian noise stays Gaussian, so the mean shrinks by $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ each step and the variance obeys $v \leftarrow (1-\beta_t)\,v + \beta_t$. Solving these recursions gives mean $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0$ and variance $1-\bar{\alpha}_t$, and variance one is preserved at the noise limit. This code uses a linear schedule; other schedules are common.
approach: Choose a noise schedule $\beta_1 \ldots \beta_T$ — how much noise each step adds
Form $\bar{\alpha}_t$ as the running product of $(1-\beta_t)$ — the fraction of signal variance that survives to step $t$
Draw $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ — the only randomness
Output $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\epsilon$ — a sample of $q(x_t\,|\,x_0)$ in one step
Optionally iterate $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon$ — the same distribution by single steps
problems.time: O(d) per sample at any t, versus O(t·d) by iterating
problems.space: O(T) for the schedule and O(d) per sample
problems.description: Building the training pairs for denoising diffusion models, where a random t and fresh noise corrupt each clean example, and analysing a noise schedule such as its signal-to-noise ratio.

examples.input: Why can we sample $x_t$ directly from $x_0$?
examples.output: Each step is Gaussian and linear in the previous state, so composing $t$ of them gives one Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0$ and variance $1-\bar{\alpha}_t$.

examples.input: Why scale the signal by $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ instead of only adding noise?
examples.output: The shrinkage keeps the total variance bounded, so the chain ends near a standard normal instead of growing without limit.

examples.input: What does the network learn in DDPM?
examples.output: It predicts the noise $\epsilon$ from $x_t$ and $t$, which is equivalent to estimating $x_0$ using the closed-form relation between the two.

constraints: Number of steps $T$
Schedule endpoints $\beta_1$ and $\beta_T$, or the schedule family (linear, cosine)
Data scaling, usually to $[-1, 1]$
edgeCases: Indexing off by one: array position $t$ here is step $t+1$ of the maths
The final $\bar{\alpha}_T$ must be near zero or the terminal distribution is not standard normal
The equivalence with iterating holds in distribution, not sample by sample for the same $\epsilon$

problems.title: Document Chunking Strategies
problems.summary: Cut documents into retrievable pieces: fixed windows with overlap (stride $\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}$), or recursive splitting that tries paragraph, line, sentence and word boundaries in turn until every piece fits the size limit.
problems.bruteForce: Short documents that already fit one chunk, or structured data such as tables and code, where the natural unit (a row, a function) should be the chunk instead of a character count.
problems.intuition: A chunk is the unit that gets embedded, retrieved and pasted into the prompt, so its size sets a trade-off. Small chunks match a query precisely but lose the context around the fact; large chunks keep the meaning but blur many topics into one vector and waste prompt space. A fact of length $L$ is guaranteed to sit whole inside some chunk only if $\mathrm{overlap} \geq L - 1$, which is why overlap exists. Cutting at natural boundaries (paragraphs before sentences before words) keeps each piece readable and self-contained. Flow: document → split at boundaries → overlapping chunks → embeddings.
problems.whyItWorks: Fixed windows advance by $\mathrm{size} - \mathrm{overlap}$, so the chunk count is a simple ceiling and every item is covered. Because consecutive windows share exactly the overlap, dropping the repeated prefix of each later chunk rebuilds the input. The recursive splitter tries the coarsest separator first and only falls back to a finer one for pieces that are still too long, so it cuts at the most meaningful boundary that satisfies the limit.
approach: Pick the stride as size minus overlap — each window starts one stride after the last
Slice tokens[i : i + size] for each start i below n − overlap — the final window then reaches the end
Pack whole sentences greedily up to the limit — keeps chunks readable instead of cutting mid-sentence
For text, split on the coarsest separator first — paragraphs are the most meaningful boundary
Recurse on any piece still too long with the next finer separator — falls back to lines, sentences, words, then characters
Merge small neighbouring pieces back up to the limit — avoids a flood of tiny chunks
problems.time: O(n) for one pass over the text; the recursion revisits each oversized piece at most once per separator level
problems.space: O(n + overlap · chunks) because overlapping chunks store boundary items twice
dryRun: Fact of length $L$ whole if $\mathrm{overlap} \geq L - 1$
problems.description: Preparing any corpus for embedding and retrieval, where documents are longer than the embedding model's input or than the useful retrieval unit. Use recursive splitting for prose and fixed windows when the text has no structure.

examples.input: How do chunk size and retrieval quality relate?
examples.output: Small chunks give precise matches but lack context, and large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and use more prompt tokens. The best size is found by measuring retrieval recall on a labelled set.

examples.input: Why use overlap, and what does it cost?
examples.output: A fact that straddles a boundary would be cut in two; overlap at least as long as the fact guarantees one chunk holds it whole. The cost is a larger index and duplicate-looking results.

examples.input: How many chunks does a document of n items produce?
examples.output: With window size s and overlap o the stride is $s - o$, so the count is $\lceil (n - o)/(s - o) \rceil$ for $n > s$, and one chunk otherwise.

examples.input: What does recursive splitting add over fixed windows?
examples.output: It prefers natural boundaries such as paragraphs and sentences and only cuts finer when a piece is too long, so chunks are more coherent.

constraints: Chunk size (tokens or characters)
Overlap, often 10 to 20 percent of the size
Separator hierarchy for recursive splitting
Unit of length (characters versus model tokens)
edgeCases: Measuring size in characters while the embedding model limit is in tokens; chunks can silently be truncated
Overlap multiplies index size by about $\frac{\mathrm{size}}{\mathrm{size}-\mathrm{overlap}}$ and returns near-duplicate hits
Splitting on a separator that is absent (a long line with no spaces) falls back to hard character cuts
Splitting tables, code or lists by length destroys their structure; chunk them by their own units

problems.title: Document Loading and Text Extraction
problems.summary: Turn raw documents into clean text plus metadata before chunking and embedding: strip HTML boilerplate, normalise Unicode and whitespace, drop header and footer lines that repeat across pages, and tag every chunk with its source and page.
problems.bruteForce: Do not rely on these rules for PDFs, scans and tables. Layout-aware parsers or OCR are needed there, and extraction errors in those formats are the main source of failures in retrieval pipelines.
problems.intuition: An embedding model sees only the text it is given, so navigation menus, scripts, page footers and broken hyphenation become part of the chunk vectors and pull unrelated chunks together. Boilerplate repeats on most pages while real content does not, so a line seen on a large fraction of pages is almost certainly not content. Cleaning is cheap next to bad retrieval, and metadata attached now is what later makes citations and filters possible. Flow: raw file → parse → clean text → chunks with metadata → embeddings.
problems.whyItWorks: Compatibility normalisation (NFKC) maps look-alike characters such as ligatures and full-width letters to one canonical form, so the same word always gets the same tokens. Counting each distinct line once per page and thresholding the fraction of pages separates repeated furniture from unique text without any layout model. Metadata carried on each chunk survives retrieval, so the answer can point back to the exact source.
approach: Parse the HTML and skip script, style and navigation subtrees — they carry no content
Keep block boundaries as blank lines — headings and paragraphs stay separable for chunking
Apply NFKC and rejoin words split by line-end hyphens — one canonical spelling per word
Collapse runs of spaces and blank lines — removes layout noise
Count each distinct line once per page and drop lines on at least min_frac of pages — removes repeated headers and footers
Attach source, page and section to every chunk — enables citations and metadata filters
problems.time: O(total characters) for parsing and cleaning; the repeated-line pass is one hash-table count over all lines
problems.space: O(distinct lines) for the repeat counter plus the cleaned text
problems.description: Any ingestion pipeline for web pages, reports or exports, as the first stage before chunking, where text quality directly limits retrieval quality.

examples.input: Why clean text before embedding?
examples.output: Boilerplate and broken text add shared noise to chunk vectors, which makes unrelated chunks look similar and lowers retrieval precision. Clean input also gives stable tokenisation.

examples.input: How do you detect repeated headers and footers without layout analysis?
examples.output: Count how many pages each distinct line appears on and drop lines whose page fraction passes a threshold, masking digits so page numbers still match.

examples.input: Why attach metadata to every chunk?
examples.output: After chunking, a chunk no longer knows where it came from. Source, page and section let the system cite answers and filter retrieval by document, date or access level.

examples.input: What is the hardest part of document loading in practice?
examples.output: Non-HTML formats. PDFs, scans and tables lose reading order and structure on extraction, so they need layout-aware parsers or OCR and careful checking.

constraints: min_frac, the page fraction above which a line counts as boilerplate
Set of tags to skip and tags that mark block boundaries
Unicode normalisation form (NFKC versus NFC)
Metadata fields to keep (source, page, section, date)
edgeCases: Digits are masked when counting so that Page 1, Page 2 match, which also merges unique lines that differ only by a number
A low min_frac on a short document deletes real content; a short repeated line is only boilerplate if it appears on most pages
NFKC changes meaning for some text, for example it turns superscript digits into ordinary ones, so keep the raw text if exact quotes matter
PDFs, scanned pages and tables need dedicated parsers or OCR; these rules do not fix reading order or merged columns

problems.title: Dot Product and Matrix Multiplication
problems.summary: A dot product is a weighted sum that measures how much two vectors agree; a matrix product is a table of dot products that composes two linear maps. The answer is independent of grouping, the cost is not.
problems.bruteForce: The chain DP only matters for long chains with unequal shapes. For square matrices of equal size every order costs the same, and real libraries call tuned BLAS kernels rather than this triple loop.
problems.intuition: Every neural-network layer is a bundle of dot products, so matrix multiplication is the unit of work. Multiplication is associative, so $(xW_1)W_2$ and $x(W_1W_2)$ give the same numbers, but with a skinny $x$ the first never builds a big matrix and costs thousands of times less. The same fact shapes batching, low-rank layers and the order in which frameworks fuse operations. Flow: vectors → dot products → matrix product → pick the grouping → cost.
problems.whyItWorks: Matrix multiplication corresponds to composing linear maps, and composition is associative, so every parenthesisation gives the same matrix up to floating-point rounding. The cost of a product depends on the shapes of its two operands, and the shape of an intermediate is fixed by which outer dimensions it keeps. The optimal split of a chain is built from optimal splits of its two halves, which gives the DP.
approach: Compute each entry as a dot product of a row of $A$ and a column of $B$ — $C_{ij} = \sum_{p} A_{ip} B_{pj}$
Count $2mkn$ FLOPs for $(m \times k)(k \times n)$ — $mkn$ multiplies and about as many adds
Cost a full parenthesisation by summing the cost of every pairwise product — shapes shrink to outer dimensions
Fill a table $M_{ij}$ of the cheapest cost for matrices $i$ to $j$, trying every split $s$ — subproblems overlap
Keep the best split per interval — lets you rebuild the optimal order
problems.time: O(mkn) per product; the chain DP is O(n³) for n matrices
problems.space: O(n²) for the DP tables; the product itself needs O(mn)
problems.description: Estimating the cost of a layer or a chain of projections, deciding whether to apply a low-rank factorisation as two thin matmuls, and choosing an evaluation order for a product with very different dimensions.

examples.input: Is matrix multiplication commutative or associative?
examples.output: It is associative, so grouping never changes the result, but it is not commutative in general: $AB \neq BA$, and the shapes may not even allow $BA$.

examples.input: Why does the order of multiplication matter for speed?
examples.output: The number of FLOPs depends on the shapes of the intermediates. With a short, wide chain, multiplying the thin matrix first keeps every intermediate thin.

examples.input: What does a dot product measure?
examples.output: The sum of elementwise products. For unit vectors it equals the cosine of the angle between them, so it is a similarity score and also the coefficient of a projection.

examples.input: How is matmul batched in a neural network?
examples.output: Inputs of shape $(B, T, d)$ are multiplied by one weight matrix of shape $(d, d')$, equivalent to flattening to $(BT, d)$, or by a stack of matrices with a batched matmul as in attention heads.

constraints: Matrix dimensions m, k, n (they set the cost)
Parenthesisation of a chain
Numeric precision (float32, float16, bfloat16)
edgeCases: Shapes (m, k) and (k, n) must share the inner dimension; swapping operands is a common bug
FLOPs are not wall time: memory traffic and kernel shape often dominate
The triple loop here is for clarity only; it is orders of magnitude slower than BLAS

problems.title: Direct Preference Optimisation Loss
problems.summary: Fine-tune a language model on pairs of preferred and rejected responses by pushing up the log-probability gap between them, measured relative to a frozen reference model, with no separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.
problems.bruteForce: When preferences must be gathered online from the current policy, when a reusable reward model is needed for ranking or filtering, or when the preference data is far from the reference model's distribution.
problems.intuition: DPO treats $\beta\cdot\log(\pi/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ as an implicit reward: how much more the tuned model likes a response than the reference does. The loss is a logistic loss on the difference of that implicit reward between the chosen and rejected response, so it raises the chosen response and lowers the rejected one relative to the reference. Anchoring to the reference is what keeps the model from drifting arbitrarily far.
problems.whyItWorks: The KL-regularised reward maximisation problem has a closed-form optimal policy, which can be inverted to express any reward as a log-ratio of policy to reference. Substituting that into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood cancels the intractable normaliser, leaving a loss that depends only on sequence log-probabilities. The gradient weights each pair by how wrongly the implicit reward currently orders it.
approach: Compute sequence log-probabilities of the chosen and rejected responses under the policy and the frozen reference — the four quantities the loss needs
Subtract reference from policy for each response — the log-ratio is the implicit reward up to $\beta$
Take the chosen-minus-rejected difference and scale by $\beta$ — the preference margin
Apply $-\log\sigma(\mathrm{margin})$ and average over pairs — the Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood
Backpropagate into the policy only — the reference stays frozen
problems.time: O(N) given the log-probabilities; the real cost is two forward passes (policy and reference) per response
problems.space: O(N) for the margins; the reference model's weights must also be held in memory
problems.description: Aligning an instruction-tuned model with a static dataset of preference pairs when a simple, stable supervised-style training loop is preferred over PPO.

examples.input: How does DPO avoid training a reward model?
examples.output: It reparameterises the reward as a log-ratio of policy to reference, so the preference likelihood can be written directly in terms of the policy. Training the policy on that likelihood implicitly fits the reward.

examples.input: What does $\beta$ control?
examples.output: It scales the log-ratio reward, so it sets how strongly the policy is tied to the reference. A larger $\beta$ penalises movement away from the reference more and gives smaller updates for a given log-ratio gap.

examples.input: How does DPO relate to RLHF with PPO?
examples.output: Both target the same KL-regularised reward objective. PPO learns an explicit reward and samples from the policy online; DPO optimises a closed-form loss on a fixed dataset of preference pairs.

constraints: $\beta$ (strength of the pull toward the reference; larger keeps the policy closer)
Learning rate (usually very small for fine-tuning)
Reference model (usually the supervised fine-tuned checkpoint)
Preference dataset quality and size
edgeCases: Inputs must be sequence-level log-probs (summed over response tokens), computed with the same prompt formatting
Reference log-probs are constants; backpropagating into the reference is a bug
Both chosen and rejected log-probs can fall during training; DPO constrains only their gap
This code returns gradients with respect to the log-probs; a real model backpropagates them into its parameters, and long sequences make the log-probs very negative

problems.title: Dropout
problems.summary: During training, randomly zero each activation with probability p and scale the survivors by 1 / (1 − p); at inference do nothing.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the model underfits or data is plentiful, and be careful alongside batch norm, where the two interact badly. Always disable it at evaluation.
problems.intuition: Randomly silencing units stops any neuron from relying on specific partners, so the network must spread useful information across many features. Scaling the survivors at training time keeps the expected activation unchanged, so no adjustment is needed at inference.
problems.whyItWorks: Each training step samples a different thinned sub-network, so the full network behaves like an average over exponentially many models that share weights, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. The 1 / (1 − p) factor (inverted dropout) makes the expected output equal the input.
approach: Sample a keep mask with probability 1 − p per element — decides which units survive this step
Divide the mask by 1 − p — keeps the expected activation equal to the input
Multiply input by the scaled mask — dropped units output zero
Reuse the same scaled mask in the backward pass — dropped units must receive zero gradient
Return the input unchanged in eval mode — inference is deterministic
problems.time: O(n) for n activations
problems.space: O(n) for the stored mask
problems.description: Large fully connected layers or models that overfit, and inside transformers on attention and feed-forward outputs.

examples.input: What is inverted dropout?
examples.output: Scaling surviving activations by 1 / (1 − p) at training time so the expected output equals the input and inference needs no change.

examples.input: Why does dropout regularise?
examples.output: It prevents co-adaptation of units and approximates averaging over many thinned networks.

examples.input: What happens to gradients of dropped units?
examples.output: They are zero for that step, because the same mask multiplies the upstream gradient.

constraints: Drop probability p (higher means stronger regularisation)
Where to place it (after which layers)
Variant (element-wise dropout, spatial dropout for channels)
edgeCases: Leaving dropout on at inference makes predictions random
Mixing up p (drop probability) with keep probability gives the wrong scale
The mask must be reused in backward, not resampled
The mask here comes from NumPy's generator, so it cannot match torch's random mask element for element

problems.title: Early Stopping
problems.summary: Watch the validation loss during training and stop when it has not improved for a set number of epochs, then keep the weights from the best epoch. Training length becomes a regularised hyperparameter chosen automatically.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the validation set is tiny or noisy (the stopping point becomes random), and note that the chosen epoch is tuned on validation data, so report results on a separate test set.
problems.intuition: Training loss usually keeps falling, but past some point the model starts fitting noise and validation loss turns upward. Number of epochs therefore acts as a capacity knob: early on the model is simple, later it is flexible. Stopping near the validation minimum buys a simple model for free, and patience stops a noisy blip from ending training too soon.
problems.whyItWorks: For gradient descent from small initial weights, the weights grow gradually away from zero, so fewer steps restrict the effective model size, similar in effect to an L2 penalty. The validation curve estimates generalisation error, and the rule picks the epoch where that estimate was lowest, with patience trading a small delay for robustness to noise.
approach: Hold out a validation set the model never trains on — it measures generalisation
After each epoch, evaluate validation loss — the signal for when overfitting begins
If it beats the best by more than min_delta, record it, save the weights and reset the counter — progress is real
Otherwise increment the patience counter — a few bad epochs may just be noise
Stop when the counter reaches patience and restore the saved weights — the last epochs were overfit
problems.time: O(1) per epoch for the check; the cost is the validation pass itself
problems.space: O(P) to keep a copy of the best weights (this snippet tracks indices only)
dryRun: Stop at the first epoch where $\mathrm{wait} \geq \mathrm{patience}$
Return the weights saved at the best epoch
problems.description: Neural networks and boosted ensembles trained iteratively, especially when you cannot afford to tune the epoch count by hand.

examples.input: Why is early stopping a regulariser?
examples.output: Fewer gradient steps keep weights near their small initial values, limiting effective capacity, much as a weight penalty does.

examples.input: What does patience do?
examples.output: It tolerates a few non-improving epochs so a noisy validation curve does not end training prematurely.

examples.input: Which data decides when to stop, and which reports the final score?
examples.output: Validation data decides the stopping epoch; a separate untouched test set gives the final unbiased estimate.

constraints: patience — epochs to wait without improvement
min_delta — smallest change that counts as improvement
monitor — the validation metric (loss or a score) and whether lower or higher is better
restore_best_weights — whether to roll back to the best epoch
edgeCases: Patience too small stops on noise; too large wastes compute and overfits
Stopping on training loss never triggers, since it keeps decreasing
The validation set is reused to choose the epoch, so it no longer gives an unbiased final score
Without restoring the best weights you keep the over-trained final model

problems.title: Eigen-Decomposition and Power Iteration
problems.summary: Eigenvectors are directions a matrix only stretches. Power iteration applies the matrix again and again and normalises, which converges to the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue in magnitude.
problems.bruteForce: When you need all eigenpairs of a small dense matrix (use a direct solver such as symmetric eigendecomposition), or when the top two eigenvalues have nearly equal magnitude and convergence is very slow.
problems.intuition: Write a start vector in the eigenbasis. Each multiplication by $A$ scales the component along eigenvector $i$ by $\lambda_i$, so the biggest eigenvalue gradually wins and the vector aligns with its eigenvector. Normalising only stops the numbers overflowing. A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, which is why PCA can read principal axes off the covariance matrix. Flow: matrix → apply repeatedly → normalise → dominant direction.
problems.whyItWorks: For a symmetric matrix, $A^k v = \sum_{i} c_i \lambda_i^k u_i$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_i$. Dividing by $\lambda_1^k$ shrinks every term except the first by $(\lambda_i/\lambda_1)^k$, so the direction converges to $u_1$ at rate $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$ per step, provided $c_1 \neq 0$ and $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2|$. The Rayleigh quotient of a vector lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalue.
approach: Start from a random unit vector $v$ — it almost surely has a component along the top eigenvector
Replace $v$ by $Av$ — each eigen-component is scaled by its eigenvalue
Divide by $\|v\|$ — keeps the length at 1 so nothing overflows
After enough steps read the eigenvalue as $v^\top A v$ — the Rayleigh quotient of a unit vector
Subtract $\lambda v v^\top$ to deflate and repeat — removes the found direction to expose the next
problems.time: O(n²) per iteration for a dense matrix, O(nnz) for a sparse one
problems.space: O(n) beyond the matrix itself
problems.description: Finding the top eigenpair of a huge or sparse matrix, as in PageRank or the first principal component, where a full decomposition is too costly and only a few eigenvectors are needed.

examples.input: Why does power iteration converge to the dominant eigenvector?
examples.output: Each step multiplies the component along eigenvector $i$ by $\lambda_i$, so the largest in magnitude dominates, and the error shrinks like $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k$.

examples.input: When does power iteration fail?
examples.output: If the start vector has no component along the top eigenvector, or if the top two eigenvalues have equal magnitude, such as $+1$ and $-1$: the vector then keeps oscillating instead of settling.

examples.input: What is the Rayleigh quotient used for?
examples.output: It estimates an eigenvalue from an approximate eigenvector, and for symmetric matrices it is always between the smallest and largest eigenvalue.

examples.input: How does this relate to PCA?
examples.output: The principal components are the eigenvectors of the symmetric covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue; power iteration with deflation finds them one at a time.

constraints: Number of iterations
Random seed for the start vector
Convergence tolerance on the change in $v$
edgeCases: Slow when $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|$ is close to 1; shifted or inverse iteration can help
Equal-magnitude top eigenvalues give no convergence; the vector flips between two directions
Deflation as written needs a symmetric matrix and accurate eigenvectors; errors accumulate with each deflation

problems.title: Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent
problems.summary: Linear regression with a mix of L1 and L2 penalties, solved by cycling through coordinates and updating one weight at a time with a soft-threshold. The L1 part zeroes weights; the L2 part stabilises groups of correlated features.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you want unbiased estimates of the large coefficients (the penalty shrinks them), when features are unscaled, or when you need coefficient standard errors and p-values.
problems.intuition: With all other weights held fixed, the objective in one weight is a one-dimensional problem whose answer is closed form: take the plain least-squares fit to the current residual, shrink it toward zero by the L1 amount (stopping at exactly zero) and divide by a factor that includes the L2 penalty. Cycling over coordinates repeats this until nothing moves.
problems.whyItWorks: The squared loss is smooth and convex and the penalty is convex and separable across coordinates, which is the case where coordinate descent provably converges to the global minimum. Each one-dimensional subproblem is solved exactly by soft-thresholding, so the objective never increases.
approach: Start at $w = 0$ with residual $r = y$ — the exact solution once α is large enough
For coordinate $j$ compute its correlation with the partial residual, adding back its own contribution — the least-squares target for $w_j$ alone
Soft-threshold by $\alpha\rho$ and divide by $z_j + \alpha(1-\rho)$ — the closed-form minimiser of the one-dimensional problem
Update the residual by the change in $w_j$ — keeps each step O(n) instead of recomputing $Xw$
Sweep all coordinates until the largest change is below tol — all coordinate steps are small only at the minimum
problems.time: O(iters·n·d) with the residual trick; each sweep costs O(n·d)
problems.space: O(n·d) for the data, O(n + d) extra
problems.description: Many correlated features where lasso picks one arbitrarily, $p$ larger than $n$, automatic feature selection with stable grouping, and large sparse problems where coordinate descent is fast.

examples.input: Why use elastic net instead of lasso?
examples.output: Among correlated features lasso tends to pick one at random, while the L2 term makes elastic net share weight across the group and also lets it keep more than $n$ features when $p$ is larger than $n$.

examples.input: What does the soft-threshold do?
examples.output: It shrinks the least-squares coordinate estimate toward zero by the L1 amount and sets it exactly to zero when it is smaller than that amount, which is how sparsity arises.

examples.input: Why does coordinate descent converge here?
examples.output: The loss is smooth and convex and the penalty is convex and separable by coordinate, so exact one-dimensional minimisation steps decrease the objective and reach the global minimum.

constraints: $\alpha$ — overall penalty strength, chosen by cross-validation along a path
l1_ratio $\rho$ in $[0, 1]$ — mix between L1 (sparse) and L2 (grouping)
tol and max iterations — stopping rule for the sweeps
Standardisation — features must be on the same scale for the penalty to be fair
edgeCases: Unscaled features are penalised unequally; standardise first
Intercept is not penalised, so centre $y$ and $X$ or fit it separately (this code has no intercept)
Convergence is slow for highly correlated features and small $\alpha$
Selected features can change across resamples; check stability, not just one fit

problems.title: Ranking Models from Pairwise Comparisons - Elo and Bradley-Terry
problems.summary: Turn many head-to-head votes between models into a leaderboard. Elo updates ratings game by game, while Bradley-Terry fits one strength per model by maximum likelihood over all games at once.
problems.bruteForce: When each model has an absolute score on a fixed test set, where averaging is simpler. Also when comparisons are not transitive, for example rock-paper-scissors style matchups, or when the match graph is disconnected so strengths cannot be compared.
problems.intuition: A vote only says which of two answers was better, so a ranking has to be inferred from who beats whom. Both methods assume the chance that $A$ wins depends on the rating gap alone. Elo nudges ratings after every game, so the final numbers depend on the order of the games, while Bradley-Terry looks at the whole win table and finds the strengths that make the observed wins most likely, with no order dependence. Elo is the same logistic model, just fitted by online stochastic updates. Flow: pairwise votes → win table → fit strengths → rating scale → leaderboard.
problems.whyItWorks: Under $P(A \succ B) = p_A/(p_A + p_B)$ the log-likelihood is $\sum_{ij} W_{ij}\left[\log p_i - \log(p_i + p_j)\right]$. Setting its gradient to zero gives the fixed point $p_i = W_i / \sum_j n_{ij}/(p_i + p_j)$, and iterating it is a minorisation-maximisation scheme that increases the likelihood monotonically. Elo is a stochastic gradient step on the same logistic likelihood with step size $K$, so it tracks a moving target and depends on the order of games.
approach: Collect votes as a win matrix $W_{ij}$, the times $i$ beat $j$ — the sufficient statistic for the model
For Elo, compute $E_A = 1/(1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400})$ — the predicted win probability from the rating gap
Update $R_A \leftarrow R_A + K(S_A - E_A)$ and subtract the same from $R_B$ — a surprise moves ratings, and total rating is conserved
For Bradley-Terry, start with all strengths equal — a neutral starting point
Set $p_i = W_i / \sum_j n_{ij}/(p_i + p_j)$, with $W_i$ total wins — the minorisation-maximisation step that never decreases the likelihood
Renormalise strengths to geometric mean $1$ — only ratios are identifiable
Convert with rating $= 400\log_{10} p + c$ — puts Bradley-Terry on the familiar Elo scale
problems.time: Elo is O(1) per game; each Bradley-Terry iteration is O(M²) for M models, with a few hundred iterations at most
problems.space: O(M) ratings for Elo, O(M²) for the win matrix
problems.description: Ranking systems from crowdsourced or LLM-judged head-to-head comparisons, where scores are relative and models are not all compared on a shared absolute metric.

examples.input: How do Elo and Bradley-Terry differ?
examples.output: Both use a logistic win probability from a strength gap. Elo updates online after each game, so results depend on game order and on $K$. Bradley-Terry fits all games jointly by maximum likelihood and is order independent.

examples.input: Why does the Elo update conserve total rating?
examples.output: The winner gains $K(S_A - E_A)$ and the loser loses exactly the same amount, so the sum of ratings never changes. A $400$ point gap means odds of $10$ to $1$.

examples.input: Why can strengths only be found up to scale?
examples.output: The probability $p_A/(p_A + p_B)$ is unchanged if every $p$ is multiplied by a constant. So the fit fixes the scale, for example geometric mean $1$, and only ratios matter.

examples.input: How is this related to a reward model?
examples.output: It is the same Bradley-Terry likelihood, but here each item has a free strength in a table rather than a score predicted from text features.

constraints: Elo step size $K$ and initial rating
Number of Bradley-Terry iterations or a convergence tolerance
Tie handling, for example counting a tie as half a win to each side
Which matchups to sample, since uneven coverage widens intervals
edgeCases: A model with no wins, or no losses, has an unbounded maximum-likelihood strength; add a small prior or pseudo-counts
Elo with a large $K$ is noisy and order dependent; shuffle games or prefer Bradley-Terry for a final leaderboard
Ratings are only meaningful relative to the compared set and prompt distribution, and a point estimate needs bootstrap intervals
The matchup graph must be connected, or models in separate groups cannot be compared

problems.title: Entropy, Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence
problems.summary: Entropy measures the uncertainty of a distribution, cross-entropy the cost of describing it with another one, and KL divergence the extra cost.
problems.bruteForce: KL is asymmetric and infinite when $q$ is zero where $p$ is not, so for a symmetric bounded measure use Jensen-Shannon or a Wasserstein distance.
problems.intuition: Entropy is the average surprise of samples from $p$ when you code them optimally. Cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ is the average surprise if you use $q$'s code instead, and the gap between the two is KL, a one-sided measure of how badly $q$ approximates $p$. Because $H(p)$ is fixed by the data, minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising KL.
problems.whyItWorks: KL is non-negative by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave log, and is zero only when $q$ equals $p$ almost everywhere. That makes cross-entropy minimised exactly when the model matches the data distribution, which is why it is the standard classification loss.
approach: Drop zero-probability terms of $p$ — $0 \cdot \log 0$ is defined as $0$
Entropy is the negative sum of $p \cdot \log p$ — average surprise under $p$
Cross-entropy swaps in $\log q$ — cost of coding $p$'s samples with $q$
KL is cross-entropy minus entropy — the pure mismatch term
Use natural log for nats, log base 2 for bits — only changes the scale
problems.time: O(k) for k outcomes
problems.space: O(k)
problems.description: Training and evaluating classifiers, comparing distributions, VAEs, distillation, and anywhere you need a divergence between probabilities.

examples.input: Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?
examples.output: With one-hot labels it is the negative log-likelihood of the true class, and its minimiser makes the model distribution match the data distribution.

examples.input: What is the difference between forward and reverse KL?
examples.output: Forward $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ is mass-covering, so $q$ spreads over all modes of $p$; reverse $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ is mode-seeking, so $q$ locks onto one mode.

examples.input: Is KL divergence a distance?
examples.output: No. It is asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

constraints: Log base (natural log for nats, base 2 for bits)
Direction of the KL (forward $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ or reverse $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$)
Smoothing epsilon added to $q$ to avoid log of zero
edgeCases: KL is not symmetric and is not a true distance
$q$ must be positive wherever $p$ is, otherwise KL is infinite
Framework kl_div functions expect log-probabilities as input and probabilities as target
Inputs must be normalised distributions

problems.title: Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt)
problems.summary: Forecast a series with a running level (and optionally a trend) that is nudged toward each new observation by a smoothing weight. Simple smoothing gives a flat forecast; Holt's method adds a linear trend.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the series has seasonality you have not modelled (use Holt-Winters), when you need prediction intervals from a fitted likelihood, or when external regressors drive the series.
problems.intuition: The newest observation is the best clue about where the series is now, but a single value is noisy. Blending it with the previous estimate gives weights on past values that decay geometrically, so recent data matters most and old data fades without being stored.
problems.whyItWorks: Unrolling the recursion $\ell = \alpha y + (1-\alpha)\ell$ shows the level is a weighted average of all past observations with weights $\alpha(1-\alpha)^k$ that sum to one. It is the optimal one-step predictor for a random walk plus noise, and Holt's method is the same idea applied to level and slope.
approach: Choose a start level $\ell_0$ (and slope $b_0$ for Holt) — the recursion needs a state before the first observation
For each point, record the one-step prediction from the current state — these are the fitted values used to score the model
Update the level as a blend of the observation and the predicted level — $\alpha$ sets how fast old data is forgotten
For Holt, update the slope from the change in level — $\beta$ sets how quickly the trend can change
Forecast ahead from the final state, flat for simple and linear for Holt — no further data is available to update it
problems.time: O(n) per pass; fitting α and β with a numerical optimiser multiplies this by the number of evaluations
problems.space: O(1) state for forecasting, O(n) if the fitted values are stored
problems.description: Short-horizon forecasts of many series, a cheap and strong baseline, demand or traffic with slowly drifting level, and online updating where only the last state is kept.

examples.input: Why is it called exponential smoothing?
examples.output: Unrolling the recursion gives each past observation a weight that shrinks by a constant factor $(1-\alpha)$ per step back, an exponential decay that sums to one.

examples.input: What do $\alpha$ near $0$ and $\alpha$ near $1$ mean?
examples.output: $\alpha$ near $1$ trusts the latest value and nearly copies it forward, a naive forecast; $\alpha$ near $0$ keeps the initial level almost unchanged, close to a long-run average.

examples.input: Why does simple smoothing fail on trending data?
examples.output: Its forecast is a weighted average of past values, so it always lags behind a rising or falling series; Holt's slope term removes that lag.

constraints: $\alpha$ level smoothing in $(0, 1)$ — large reacts fast, small averages more
$\beta$ trend smoothing in $(0, 1)$ — large lets the slope change quickly
Initial level and slope — first value or a regression on the first few points
Damping $\phi$ — optional factor that flattens a Holt trend over long horizons (not in this code)
edgeCases: Undamped Holt trends extrapolate forever and overshoot at long horizons
A high $\alpha$ on a noisy series chases noise; the fitted values lag turning points when $\alpha$ is small
The start state matters for short series, so conventions differ between libraries
Pick $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by one-step error on held-out data, not by eye

problems.title: Group Fairness Metrics and Counterfactual Tests
problems.summary: Compare a model's decisions across groups: selection rates, true and false positive rates, calibration, and for language models the change in output when only a group term in the prompt is swapped.
problems.bruteForce: As a proof that a system is fair. These are descriptive statistics on one dataset; they depend on label quality, group definitions and sample size, and small groups give noisy rates.
problems.intuition: Each criterion fixes a different quantity to be equal across groups: selection rate (demographic parity), true-positive rate (equal opportunity), both error rates (equalised odds), or calibration. They are different questions, and when base rates differ they cannot all hold at once, so the choice is a decision about the application. Flow: predictions + group → per-group rates → gaps → compare to a threshold.
problems.whyItWorks: Each metric reduces a group's confusion matrix to a rate and compares rates. Equal rates make the chosen criterion hold on that data. When base rates differ, a non-perfect classifier cannot satisfy calibration and equal error rates together, so one criterion has to give way. This is stated here, not proved.
approach: Split predictions by group — every metric is computed within a group
Compute selection rate, $\mathrm{TPR}$ and $\mathrm{FPR}$ per group — the building blocks of all the gaps
Take the spread across groups — demographic parity uses selection rates, equal opportunity uses $\mathrm{TPR}$
Combine for equalised odds and the ratio — the larger of the two gaps, and the lowest rate over the highest
For an LLM, fill one template with each group term and score it — a gap above zero means the term changes the output
problems.time: O(n) to compute all group rates over $n$ examples
problems.space: O(number of groups) beyond the input arrays
dryRun: Equal opportunity is the same gap on $y=1$
problems.description: Auditing a classifier or a model-assisted decision for gaps between groups, before and after changes, with the group label held out of the model's inputs but available for evaluation.

examples.input: How do demographic parity and equal opportunity differ?
examples.output: Demographic parity compares how often each group receives a positive prediction, ignoring the true label. Equal opportunity compares the true-positive rate, so it only looks at people who truly qualify.

examples.input: Why can't all fairness criteria hold together?
examples.output: When base rates differ between groups, a classifier that is not perfect cannot satisfy calibration and equal error rates at the same time. The result is known and is stated here without proof.

examples.input: How do you test an LLM for group differences?
examples.output: Build prompts that are identical except for a swapped group term, score each response with a fixed scorer, and report the spread. A scorer that ignores the term gives zero.

examples.input: What does the 80% rule measure?
examples.output: It is a rule of thumb on the ratio of the lowest to the highest selection rate; a ratio below 0.8 is treated as a flag for review, not a verdict.

constraints: Decision threshold applied to scores
Choice of criterion and the gap tolerance
Minimum group size for a stable estimate
edgeCases: Rates from very small groups are noisy; report counts or intervals
A group with no positive labels makes the true-positive rate undefined
Optimising one criterion can worsen another, so report several
A counterfactual swap can change more than the group, such as names that carry other signals

problems.title: Feature Encoding (One-Hot, Target, Cyclical, Binning)
problems.summary: Turn raw columns into numeric model inputs: one-hot for categories, leak-safe out-of-fold target encoding for high-cardinality ones, sine and cosine for periodic values, and equal-width bins.
problems.bruteForce: One-hot on very high-cardinality columns (huge sparse matrices), ordinal codes for unordered categories in linear models (they invent an order), and target encoding on tiny data where fold estimates are noisy. Tree ensembles often need no scaling or binning at all.
problems.intuition: An encoding is a claim about geometry. One-hot says categories are equally far apart. Sine and cosine say hour 23 sits next to hour 0, which a raw number gets wrong. Target encoding replaces a category by its average label, which is powerful for thousands of categories but dangerous: if a row's own label is inside its own encoding, the model is handed the answer. Computing each row's encoding from the other folds, and shrinking rare categories toward the global mean, keeps the signal and removes the leak. Flow: raw column → encode → leak-safe fit → model input.
problems.whyItWorks: Out-of-fold encoding makes the feature for row $i$ a function of rows that do not include row $i$, so the same statistic computed at test time (from training labels only) has the same distribution as the one seen in training. Smoothing $\frac{n\bar{y}_c + a\bar{y}}{n + a}$ is a weighted average of the category mean and the prior, trusting the category more as $n$ grows. The pair $(\sin, \cos)$ places a period on the unit circle, so values one step apart across the wrap-around are close.
approach: Fit the category list on training data only — the model never sees test categories
One-hot each category into its own indicator column — no false ordering between categories
For target encoding, split rows into $K$ folds and encode each fold from the other folds — a row never sees its own label
Shrink with $\frac{n\bar{y}_c + a\bar{y}}{n + a}$ — rare categories fall back to the global mean
Map a periodic feature to $(\sin, \cos)$ of $2\pi x / P$ — keeps the wrap-around neighbours close
Cut a numeric column into equal-width bins from the training min and max — captures step-like effects
problems.time: O(n·K) for one-hot with K categories, O(n) for target encoding, cyclical and binning
problems.space: O(n·K) for the one-hot matrix, O(K) for the category statistics
dryRun: Here $n$ counts rows in other folds, $a$ smooths
Bin id = floor of $(x - x_{min})/w$, max in last bin
problems.description: One-hot for low-cardinality categories and linear models, target or frequency encoding for high-cardinality ones with tree or linear models, cyclical encoding for hour, weekday or angle, binning when a nonlinear step-like effect is expected, a log transform for skewed positive values.

examples.input: Why does naive target encoding leak?
examples.output: Each row's encoding includes its own label, so the feature already contains the answer. The model looks accurate on training data and collapses on test data, where the label is not available.

examples.input: How does out-of-fold encoding fix it?
examples.output: Each row is encoded using only the other folds, so it never sees its own label, and the training feature has the same noise level as the feature at test time.

examples.input: Why encode hour with sine and cosine?
examples.output: Hour 23 and hour 0 are one step apart but numerically 23 apart. Placing hours on a circle with $(\sin, \cos)$ makes neighbours close, and both are needed to tell positions apart.

examples.input: When prefer one-hot over ordinal encoding?
examples.output: When the categories have no order, particularly with linear models, which would otherwise treat the codes as magnitudes. Trees can cope with ordinal codes more easily.

constraints: Smoothing strength $a$ — larger values pull rare categories toward the global mean
Number of folds for out-of-fold target encoding
Period $P$ of the cyclical feature (24 for hour, 7 for weekday)
Number of bins $k$ and the binning strategy (uniform or quantile)
edgeCases: Fitting target encoding on all rows and then training on it leaks each label into its own feature; the model overfits and fails on new data
Unseen categories at test time need a fallback, here the prior mean through $n=0$; one-hot needs an unknown-category rule
Encoding statistics (categories, bin edges, prior) must come from training data only, never from validation or test
A single raw number for a cyclical feature puts 23h and 0h far apart; $\sin$ alone is ambiguous, so use both $\sin$ and $\cos$

problems.title: Feature Scaling
problems.summary: Rescale each feature to a comparable range so distance-based and gradient-based models are not dominated by whichever feature has the largest units. Standard, min-max and robust scalers differ in what they subtract and divide by.
problems.bruteForce: Tree-based models (splits are invariant to monotone rescaling) and features already on a meaningful common scale. Do not fit the scaler on test data.
problems.intuition: Many models implicitly compare features with one shared yardstick: distances add squared differences, and a single learning rate steps every weight. A feature measured in thousands then drowns one measured in fractions. Scaling gives every feature the same units of spread, and the choice of centre and spread decides how outliers behave.
problems.whyItWorks: Each scaler is an affine map $z = (x-c)/s$ with a per-feature centre and scale. Standardisation uses mean and standard deviation, min-max uses the minimum and range, and the robust scaler uses median and interquartile range, which a few extreme values barely move. Affine maps keep order and shape, so only the geometry the model sees changes.
approach: Choose centre and scale statistics per feature — they define the scaler
Compute them on the training rows only — held-out rows must not influence them
Replace zero scales with 1 — a constant column would divide by zero
Apply $(x-\mathrm{centre})/\mathrm{scale}$ to train, validation and test — same parameters everywhere
Invert with $x = z\cdot\mathrm{scale}+\mathrm{centre}$ when you need original units — the map is affine
problems.time: O(n·d) to fit and to apply (percentiles need a partial sort)
problems.space: O(d) for the stored centre and scale
dryRun: Fit statistics on train only, then apply to val/test
problems.description: k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, regularised linear models and neural networks, and anything optimised with gradient descent.

examples.input: Which models need feature scaling?
examples.output: Distance-based (k-NN, k-means, SVM), regularised and gradient-trained models; trees do not, since splits depend only on feature order.

examples.input: Standardisation or min-max?
examples.output: Standardise by default; use min-max when a bounded range is required and outliers are absent, and robust scaling when outliers are present.

examples.input: How does scaling relate to data leakage?
examples.output: The scaler's statistics are learned parameters, so fit them on training data only; fitting on everything lets test rows shape the transform.

constraints: Which scaler — standard, min-max or robust
Quantile range for the robust scaler
Output range for min-max, such as $0$ to $1$ or $-1$ to $1$
edgeCases: Fitting on all data before splitting leaks test statistics
Min-max is dominated by a single outlier, squeezing everything else
Test values outside the train range land outside the target range
Scaling a one-hot or sparse matrix by its mean destroys sparsity

problems.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Network (GELU and SwiGLU)
problems.summary: The position-wise feed-forward network expands each token from $d$ to a wider hidden size, applies a nonlinearity and projects back; the gated SwiGLU variant multiplies a SiLU branch by a linear branch.
problems.bruteForce: When the model has no token-wise MLP at all, or on tiny models where the extra weight matrix and the hidden-size bookkeeping buy little.
problems.intuition: Attention only mixes tokens linearly, so the feed-forward network is where each token gets its nonlinear processing, and most of a block's parameters live there. A gated unit lets one linear branch decide, per hidden unit, how much of the other branch passes, which is a richer nonlinearity for the same parameter budget once the hidden size is shrunk to about $\frac{8}{3}d$. Flow: token vector → expand → gate or activate → project back.
problems.whyItWorks: GELU is a smooth version of ReLU, $x\,\Phi(x)$, so gradients do not die at zero. In the gated form, the product of two linear projections adds a multiplicative interaction between features, a second-order term a single activation cannot express, and the SiLU branch keeps it smooth. Shazeer found such gated variants improve quality over ReLU and GELU FFNs.
approach: Expand $x$ to a hidden size $h$ with $W_1$ — a wide space where features can be separated
Apply GELU, or compute a SiLU branch $\mathrm{silu}(xW_1)$ — the nonlinearity
For SwiGLU multiply elementwise by a linear branch $xW_3$ — a learned gate per hidden unit
Project back to $d$ with $W_2$ — so the output can join the residual stream
Set $h \approx \frac{8}{3}d$ for the gated form — keeps parameters equal to the $4d$ ungated FFN
problems.time: O(T·d·h) per layer, with h = 4d or about 8d/3
problems.space: $2dh$ weights for the plain FFN, $3dh$ for the gated one
problems.description: Inside every transformer block. Use GELU for the classic BERT or GPT-2 style FFN, and SwiGLU when following modern LLM designs that report better quality at matched parameters.

examples.input: Why is the gated hidden size about 8d/3 instead of 4d?
examples.output: The gated form has three weight matrices instead of two. Using $h = \frac{8}{3}d$ gives $3dh = 8d^2$, the same count as the $4d$ ungated FFN.

examples.input: What is the difference between exact GELU and the tanh approximation?
examples.output: Exact GELU uses the Gaussian CDF via erf; the tanh form is a cheap polynomial-inside-tanh fit that differs by about $10^{-3}$ at most.

examples.input: Why do gated FFNs help?
examples.output: The elementwise product of two projections gives each hidden unit a learned input-dependent gate, a multiplicative interaction that improves quality at matched parameters.

constraints: Hidden size $h$ ($4d$ plain, about $\frac{8}{3}d$ gated, often rounded to a multiple of 64)
Activation (ReLU, GELU exact or tanh, SiLU gate)
Whether to use biases (many LLMs drop them)
edgeCases: Comparing a gated and an ungated FFN at the same $h$ gives the gated one 50% more parameters
The tanh and erf GELU variants differ slightly, so match the variant a checkpoint was trained with
SwiGLU needs three matrices; loading weights with only $W_1$ and $W_2$ silently breaks the layer

problems.title: Few-Shot Prompting and Example Selection
problems.summary: Put $k$ worked input-output examples in the prompt before the real query so the model infers the task from context, with no weight updates; choose the examples by embedding similarity to the query.
problems.bruteForce: When examples would not fit in the context window, when the task is well served by an instruction alone, or when thousands of labelled cases justify fine-tuning a smaller, cheaper model.
problems.intuition: A language model continues text, so a prompt that already contains several solved instances makes "the next instance, solved" the most likely continuation. The examples specify format, label set and style better than an instruction can, and examples that resemble the query show the model a nearby solved case instead of a random one. Flow: query → embed → top-$k$ similar examples → prompt → completion.
problems.whyItWorks: Pretraining on text full of repeated patterns teaches a large model to continue a pattern it sees, so the examples act as a task specification read at inference time. Retrieval by cosine similarity chooses demonstrations whose inputs are close to the query, so the needed input-output mapping is shown locally. Why in-context learning works internally is still an open research question.
approach: Write a short instruction — states the task once in plain words
Embed the query and all candidate examples — puts them in one vector space
Rank candidates by cosine similarity and keep the top $k$ — nearby solved cases are the most informative
Break ties by index and put the closest example last — the output is deterministic and the most relevant case sits next to the query
Check label balance of the chosen set — a skewed set biases the model towards the majority label
Render $k$ example blocks and end with the query and an empty label — the model completes exactly the missing part
problems.time: O(N·d) to score $N$ candidates, plus sorting; the prompt costs $O(L^2)$ attention for length $L$
problems.space: O(N·d) for the example embeddings, and the $k$ examples add to the context length
problems.description: A new task with a handful of labelled cases and no budget for fine-tuning, when output format matters, or when a large labelled pool exists and similar cases can be retrieved per query.

examples.input: How is few-shot prompting different from fine-tuning?
examples.output: It changes only the input, not the weights, so it is instant and reversible, but the examples use context on every call and the gain is bounded by what fits.

examples.input: Why select examples by similarity instead of at random?
examples.output: Examples close to the query show the model a nearby solved case, which usually helps more than random ones, though it can overfit to surface similarity.

examples.input: Does the order of the examples matter?
examples.output: Yes. Models are often sensitive to order, with recent examples weighing more, so teams fix an order such as most similar last and test it.

examples.input: What goes wrong with an unbalanced example set?
examples.output: The model leans towards the majority label, so a set that is mostly one class inflates that prediction.

constraints: Number of examples $k$ (limited by the context window)
Selection rule: random, cosine top-$k$, or diverse (such as MMR)
Example order, for instance most similar last
Prompt template and separators between blocks
edgeCases: Choosing examples that all share one label biases the model towards that label
Retrieving near-duplicates of the query can leak the answer in evaluation, so exclude the query itself from the pool
A format that differs between examples and the query confuses the completion; use one template for all blocks

problems.title: Fine-Tuning Data Prep with MinHash Dedup and Group Splits
problems.summary: Clean fine-tuning data by removing exact duplicates through a normalised hash, near duplicates through MinHash signatures, splitting train and validation by group, and flagging eval text that overlaps the training set by n-grams.
problems.bruteForce: Tiny hand-curated sets where every example is deliberate, or tasks where repeated phrasing is the signal itself, such as templated classification. Aggressive thresholds can delete legitimate variants.
problems.intuition: Duplicates make validation scores optimistic and bias what the model memorises. Exact hashing misses lightly edited copies, and comparing every pair of documents is quadratic. MinHash fixes both: apply a random hash to every shingle and keep the minimum, and two sets agree on that minimum with probability equal to their Jaccard similarity, so a short signature estimates similarity. Random row splits still leak, since near copies from one source land on both sides, so split by group. Flow: texts → normalise → shingles → signatures → groups → split.
problems.whyItWorks: For a random hash function over the union of two sets, the element with the smallest hash lies in the intersection with probability $J(A,B)$, so the two minima are equal with exactly that probability. Averaging $k$ independent hash functions gives an unbiased estimate with standard deviation $\sqrt{J(1-J)/k}$. Splitting by group keeps correlated items on one side, so validation measures generalisation.
approach: Normalise text (lowercase, collapse punctuation and spaces) and hash it — identical items collapse to one key
Turn each text into a set of word shingles — similarity becomes set overlap
Hash every shingle with $k$ random hash functions and keep each minimum — the signature has $k$ numbers
Estimate Jaccard as the fraction of signature positions that match — an unbiased estimate with error about $1/\sqrt{k}$
Drop or cluster pairs above a similarity threshold — removes near duplicates
Split train and validation by group id such as source or conversation — near-identical items never straddle the split
Compare eval n-grams with training n-grams and drop or flag overlap — decontaminates the benchmark
problems.time: O(N·s·k) to sign N documents of s shingles with $k$ hashes; near-duplicate search needs bucketing to avoid $O(N^2)$ pair checks
problems.space: O(N·k) for signatures plus the n-gram set of the training text
problems.description: Any instruction or domain fine-tuning corpus scraped or merged from several sources, before training and before trusting a validation score or a benchmark number.

examples.input: Why does a MinHash match estimate Jaccard similarity?
examples.output: Under a random hash the smallest element of the union is equally likely to be any union member, and the two sets share the minimum exactly when it lies in the intersection, which has probability $J(A,B)$.

examples.input: Why split by group rather than at random?
examples.output: Items from one source or conversation are near duplicates of each other, so a random split puts copies on both sides and the validation loss measures memorisation.

examples.input: How many hash functions are needed?
examples.output: The error shrinks as $1/\sqrt{k}$, so $k = 128$ gives a standard deviation of at most about $0.044$, which is enough for coarse thresholds.

examples.input: Why remove eval overlap from training data?
examples.output: If eval text appears in training, the benchmark score reflects memorisation. N-gram overlap detects verbatim copies, though not paraphrases.

constraints: Number of hash functions $k$ (signature length)
Shingle size and unit (words or characters)
Similarity threshold for dropping near duplicates
N-gram length for decontamination and validation fraction
edgeCases: Python's built-in hash for strings changes between runs; use a stable hash for signatures
Group labels must follow the leak path: split by source or conversation, not by row, or copies still straddle the split
A very short n-gram length flags common phrases as contamination, a very long one misses lightly edited copies
Normalising too aggressively merges items that differ in numbers or code and are genuinely distinct

problems.title: Evaluating a Fine-Tune - Win Rate and Sign Test
problems.summary: Decide whether a fine-tune beat its baseline: compare held-out loss, count pairwise wins with ties handled explicitly, test the wins and losses with an exact sign test, size the eval, and report forgetting.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks with a deterministic metric and many examples, where a paired bootstrap on the score is simpler. A sign test also ignores the size of each win, so it is conservative when margins vary.
problems.intuition: A better loss number does not mean better answers, and a win rate of 55% on 40 prompts is mostly noise. Each prompt gives a paired verdict (win, loss or tie), and under "no difference" the non-tied pairs are fair coin flips, so the exact binomial answers how surprising the count is. Ties carry no direction, so report how you treated them. Flow: held-out loss → paired win/loss/tie → sign test → size → forgetting check.
problems.whyItWorks: If the two models are equally good, each non-tied comparison is a win with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, so the number of wins among $n$ non-tied pairs is $\mathrm{Binomial}(n, \frac{1}{2})$ and the sign test p-value is an exact tail probability with no distributional assumption. The sample-size rule comes from requiring a normal-approximation interval of half-width $m$ around $p$.
approach: Compare held-out loss or perplexity before and after — a cheap first signal, not a verdict
Judge each prompt as win, loss or tie against the baseline — paired data removes prompt difficulty
Compute win rate with ties counted half, and also the rate excluding ties — report both and say which
Run an exact sign test on wins and losses only — ties carry no direction
Add a confidence interval to the win rate — the point estimate alone hides the noise
Size the eval with $n \approx z^2 p(1-p)/m^2$ — decide the margin before collecting data
Measure a general benchmark before and after and report the change separately — fine-tuning can cause forgetting
problems.time: O(n) to tally, O(n) for the exact sign test over $n$ non-tied pairs
problems.space: O(n) outcomes, O(1) summary statistics
problems.description: Comparing a fine-tuned model with its base or a previous version on open-ended prompts judged pairwise, by humans or by an LLM judge.

examples.input: How should ties be handled in a win rate?
examples.output: Either count a tie as half a win, or drop ties and report how many there were. Whichever you pick, state it, because the two give different rates when ties are common.

examples.input: Why a sign test instead of a t-test here?
examples.output: The data are paired win, loss or tie verdicts, not numeric scores. Among non-tied pairs the null is a fair coin, so the exact binomial applies with no distributional assumption.

examples.input: How many prompts do I need to detect a small improvement?
examples.output: Use $n \approx z^2 p(1-p)/m^2$. For $p = 0.5$ and a margin of 0.05 at 95% confidence this is about 385 pairs, and halving the margin quadruples it.

examples.input: What is a forgetting check?
examples.output: Evaluate a general-capability benchmark before and after fine-tuning and report the change separately, since a gain on the target task can hide a loss elsewhere.

constraints: Significance level or confidence level ($z$)
Tie policy: half credit or excluded
Target margin $m$ for sample sizing
Which general benchmark to track for forgetting
edgeCases: Counting ties as losses, or silently dropping them, shifts the win rate; always report the tie count
Running many comparisons and reporting the best one inflates false positives; correct for multiple tests
A judge that prefers longer or first-listed answers biases wins; randomise order and check length
A significant win rate on a narrow prompt set says nothing about prompts outside it, or about forgetting

problems.title: FlashAttention and Online Softmax
problems.summary: Compute exact softmax attention one block of keys at a time, keeping a running maximum, denominator and output per query row, so the full $T \times T$ score matrix is never stored.
problems.bruteForce: Very short sequences where the score matrix is tiny, or when you need the full attention weights (for visualisation), since they are never materialised. Plain NumPy gains no speed; the benefit needs a fused GPU kernel.
problems.intuition: Softmax needs a global maximum and a global sum, which seems to force all scores to exist at once. But the sum can be corrected after the fact: when a new block raises the running maximum, multiply the old denominator and output by $\exp(m - m_{new})$ and carry on. The result is identical to standard attention, not an approximation. The gain is fewer slow GPU memory reads and writes, not fewer FLOPs. Flow: load block → scores → update max → rescale → accumulate → divide.
problems.whyItWorks: For one row with scores split into blocks, let $m$ be the max so far and $\ell = \sum_i e^{s_i - m}$. If the max changes to $m'$, then $\sum_i e^{s_i - m'} = e^{m - m'} \ell$ for the old terms, so rescaling is exact. The same factor applies to the weighted sum of values. After all blocks, $o/\ell$ equals the ordinary softmax-weighted average, with the usual max subtraction for stability built in.
approach: Keep per row a running max $m$, denominator $\ell$ and output $o$ — all of size $O(T)$, not $O(T^2)$
Compute the score tile for one key block — only a $T \times$ block tile exists at a time
Update $m_{new} = \max(m, \max s)$ — new scores may dominate
Rescale $\ell$ and $o$ by $\exp(m - m_{new})$ and add this block's terms — old terms re-expressed relative to the new max
After the last block return $o / \ell$ — the exact softmax-weighted average of $V$
problems.time: O(T^2 d) FLOPs, same as standard attention
problems.space: O(T d) plus one $T \times$ block score tile, instead of an $O(T^2)$ score matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def online_softmax_attention(Q, K, V, block, causal=False,
                             stats=None):
    T, d = Q.shape
    m = np.full(T, -np.inf)
    l = np.zeros(T)
    o = np.zeros((T, V.shape[1]))
    for j in range(0, K.shape[0], block):
        s = Q @ K[j:j + block].T / np.sqrt(d)
        if causal:
            cols = np.arange(j, j + s.shape[1])
            future = cols[None, :] > np.arange(T)[:, None]
            s = np.where(future, -np.inf, s)
        if stats is not None:
            stats.append(s.shape)
        m_new = np.maximum(m, s.max(axis=1))
        ms = np.where(np.isinf(m_new), 0.0, m_new)
        a = np.exp(m - ms)
        p = np.exp(s - ms[:, None])
        l = l * a + p.sum(axis=1)
        o = o * a[:, None] + p @ V[j:j + block]
        m = m_new
    return o / l[:, None]
problems.description: Long sequences in training or prefill, where the $T \times T$ score matrix is too large or its memory traffic dominates runtime, and an exact result is required.

examples.input: Is FlashAttention an approximation?
examples.output: No. It computes exactly the same $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})V$ as standard attention, up to floating-point rounding.

examples.input: Where does the speed-up come from if FLOPs are the same?
examples.output: Attention is limited by memory traffic. Tiling keeps blocks in fast on-chip memory and avoids writing and reading the $T \times T$ matrix in slow GPU memory.

examples.input: Why is the rescaling factor needed?
examples.output: The softmax terms were computed relative to an older maximum. Multiplying by $\exp(m - m_{new})$ re-expresses them relative to the new maximum so the sums stay consistent.

examples.input: What does it do to memory?
examples.output: The extra memory per row is a few scalars and one output vector, so it grows linearly in $T$ rather than quadratically.

constraints: Key/value block size (set by on-chip memory size)
Query block size in a real tiled kernel
Causal masking on or off
Accumulator precision (float32 or float64)
edgeCases: Initialising $m$ to $0$ instead of $-\infty$ gives wrong results when all scores are very negative
With a causal mask a block can be fully masked for a row, so $m_{new} = -\infty$ and $\exp(m - m_{new})$ is NaN unless handled
Forgetting to rescale $o$ as well as $\ell$ silently corrupts the output
This NumPy version shows the arithmetic only; it is not faster and still forms a $T \times$ block tile

problems.title: Focal Loss
problems.summary: Cross-entropy multiplied by $(1-p_t)^{\gamma}$, which down-weights examples the model already classifies confidently so training focuses on hard ones.
problems.bruteForce: Balanced problems where plain cross-entropy works, or when labels are noisy: the loss up-weights hard examples, which may be the mislabelled ones. Probabilities from a focal-trained model are also usually less calibrated.
problems.intuition: With extreme imbalance, such as thousands of easy background boxes per object, the many easy examples each contribute a tiny loss but their sum swamps the few hard ones. The modulating factor $(1-p_t)^{\gamma}$ is near zero when the model is right and confident, and near one when it is wrong, so easy examples fade out of the gradient. Setting $\gamma$ to zero recovers ordinary weighted cross-entropy.
