examples.output: Layer-wise pruning removes the same fraction in every layer, while global pruning uses one threshold, so layers with smaller weights end up sparser.

examples.input: Why prune iteratively?
examples.output: Removing a few weights and fine-tuning in between keeps the network near a good solution, while removing most weights at once can cause damage that fine-tuning cannot repair.

examples.input: When is structured pruning preferred?
examples.output: When you want real speed-ups on dense hardware, because removing whole rows, channels or heads produces smaller dense matrices.

constraints: Target sparsity $s$ and its schedule across rounds
Global or per-layer thresholding
Norm used to score channels ($L_1$ or $L_2$)
Fine-tuning steps between pruning rounds
edgeCases: Counting zeros as saved compute or memory when the model is still stored and multiplied densely
Pruning the weights but letting fine-tuning regrow them; the mask must be applied after every update
Global pruning can wipe out an entire layer whose weights are small in scale
Removing a channel also requires removing the matching input columns of the next layer

problems.title: Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS)
problems.summary: Approximate a sparse user-by-item rating matrix by a product of two low-rank factor matrices, fitted only on the observed entries by alternating least squares.
problems.bruteForce: Cold start (new users or items with no ratings have no data to learn from), when side features matter more than interactions, or when a very large sparse matrix needs SGD or distributed ALS.
problems.intuition: Tastes are not random: a few hidden factors (genre, mood, level) explain most ratings. Give each user and item a short vector and predict a rating as their dot product. With one side held fixed, finding the best vectors for the other side is an ordinary ridge regression for each user or item, so alternating the two solves a hard non-convex problem with easy convex steps.
problems.whyItWorks: The joint objective is non-convex in $(U, V)$ but convex in each factor with the other fixed. Each ALS half-step solves its subproblem exactly, so the regularised loss can never increase and the iterates converge to a stationary point. Observed entries only are used, so missing ratings are not treated as zeros.
approach: Initialise small random user and item factors — breaks symmetry without large values
For each user, gather the item vectors they rated and solve the ridge normal equations — the exact best user vector given the items
Swap roles and repeat per item using the transposed matrix and mask — the exact best item vector given the users
Evaluate the masked, regularised loss after each sweep — it must be non-increasing
Predict missing ratings with U @ V.T — the low-rank reconstruction fills the gaps
problems.time: O(iters·(|Ω|·k² + (n+m)·k³)) for n users, m items, |Ω| ratings
problems.space: O((n+m)·k) for the factors plus the rating matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def solve_side(R, M, V, lam):
    k = V.shape[1]
    U = np.zeros((R.shape[0], k))
    for i in range(R.shape[0]):
        Vi = V[M[i] > 0]
        A = Vi.T @ Vi + lam * np.eye(k)
        U[i] = np.linalg.solve(A, Vi.T @ R[i, M[i] > 0])
    return U

def als(R, M, k=3, lam=0.1, iters=20, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    U = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (R.shape[0], k))
    V = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (R.shape[1], k))
    loss = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        U = solve_side(R, M, V, lam)
        V = solve_side(R.T, M.T, U, lam)
        E = M * (R - U @ V.T)
        reg = lam * ((U ** 2).sum() + (V ** 2).sum())
        loss.append((E ** 2).sum() + reg)
    return U, V, loss
dryRun: User step: $(V_u^{\top} V_u + \lambda I)\,u_u = V_u^{\top} r_u$
$V_u$ = rows of $V$ for items rated by user $u$
Item step: $(U_i^{\top} U_i + \lambda I)\,v_i = U_i^{\top} r_i$
Each half-step is an exact ridge regression
problems.description: Collaborative filtering with explicit ratings or implicit feedback, filling in missing entries of a low-rank matrix, and learning embeddings that feed other models.

examples.input: Why alternate instead of optimising $U$ and $V$ jointly?
examples.output: The joint problem is non-convex, but with one factor fixed it is a set of independent ridge regressions with exact closed-form solutions.

examples.input: How does ALS handle missing entries?
examples.output: It only sums over observed ratings, using the mask to select each user's rated items, so missing values are ignored rather than treated as zero.

examples.input: ALS versus SGD for matrix factorisation?
examples.output: ALS parallelises easily across users or items and each step is exact; SGD is cheaper per update and handles streaming or very large data.

examples.input: How do you evaluate a recommender factorisation?
examples.output: Hold out some observed ratings and compare RMSE against simple baselines like the global or per-item mean; also use ranking metrics when top-N matters.

constraints: Rank $k$ — number of latent factors
Regularisation $\lambda$ — controls overfitting, tuned on held-out ratings
Number of ALS sweeps
Implicit versus explicit feedback — implicit uses confidence weights (not shown)
edgeCases: $R$ is a dense array with a 0/1 mask $M$ here; real systems use sparse formats
A user or item with no ratings gets a zero vector, so cold start needs other signals
Plain $\lambda$ is not scaled by the number of ratings per user (the weighted-$\lambda$ variant does); a simplification
No user or item bias terms, so subtract the global mean or add biases for better accuracy

problems.title: Max Pooling
problems.summary: Slide a small window over a feature map and keep only the maximum in each window, shrinking the map while keeping the strongest responses.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks needing precise positions, such as segmentation or keypoints, where strided convolutions or learned upsampling retain more. Many modern networks replace pooling with strided convolution.
problems.intuition: A feature detector fires strongly where its pattern appears. Taking the maximum over a neighbourhood keeps that "it is here somewhere" signal while discarding the exact position, which gives a little tolerance to small shifts and cuts the size of later layers.
problems.whyItWorks: The max is a cheap, parameter-free summary that keeps the strongest evidence in each region, so a feature shifted slightly within its window gives the same output. During backpropagation the gradient is routed only to the position that held the maximum, which acts like a sparse selection of the most responsive units.
approach: Choose a window size $k$ and stride — together they set the output size
Compute the output size as $\lfloor (H-k)/\mathrm{stride} \rfloor + 1$ — only full windows are used
For each output cell, slice the matching $k \times k$ window — each window is independent
Take the maximum of the window — keeps the strongest activation
problems.time: O(H·W) when windows do not overlap; O(oh·ow·k²) in general
problems.space: O(oh·ow) for the output
dryRun: $\mathrm{out}[i,j] = \max_{(u,v) \in \mathrm{window}} x[i\cdot s + u,\; j\cdot s + v]$
$u, v$ range over $0 \ldots k-1,\;\; s$ = stride
Backward: gradient only to each window's arg-max
problems.description: Downsampling feature maps in convolutional networks when you want small shift tolerance and a cheaper next layer, especially with detection-like features where a strong response matters.

examples.input: What invariance does max pooling give?
examples.output: Small local translations leave the output unchanged as long as the maximum stays inside the window; it is only approximate, not full invariance.

examples.input: How is the gradient computed through max pooling?
examples.output: Each output's gradient flows to the input position that held the maximum and is zero for the rest of the window.

examples.input: Max pooling versus average pooling?
examples.output: Max keeps the strongest activation and suits sparse feature detectors; average keeps the overall level and smooths.

constraints: Window size $k$
Stride
Padding
Dilation
edgeCases: This code handles one channel, no padding and no dilation; real layers apply it per channel and batch item
Leftover rows or columns that do not fill a window are dropped (floor mode)
Ties in the maximum need a rule for gradient routing in backward

problems.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
problems.summary: Choose the parameters under which the observed data would have been most probable, usually by minimising the negative log-likelihood.
problems.bruteForce: With very little data it overfits (the Gaussian variance estimate is biased low), and with a strong prior you should use MAP or full Bayesian inference instead.
problems.intuition: Instead of asking how likely a parameter is, ask how likely the data are under each parameter and pick the winner. Taking logs turns the product over independent samples into a sum, which is why familiar losses fall out: Gaussian noise gives squared error and Bernoulli labels give cross-entropy.
problems.whyItWorks: Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent (it converges to the true parameter) and asymptotically efficient. Setting the derivative of the log-likelihood to zero gives closed forms for simple families; for the Gaussian they are the sample mean and the biased, divide-by-n sample variance.
approach: Write the likelihood of independent samples — a product of densities
Take the log — turns the product into a sum and is monotonic
Differentiate with respect to each parameter — stationary points are candidates
Set to zero and solve — closed form for the Gaussian mean and variance
Check the NLL at the solution against nearby values — confirms a minimum
problems.time: O(n) for the closed form; iterative solvers cost O(n) per step
problems.space: O(1) beyond the data
problems.description: Fitting any probabilistic model with a tractable likelihood: regression noise models, classifiers, language models and mixture models.

examples.input: Why maximise the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?
examples.output: The log is monotonic so the argmax is the same, and it turns products into sums, which is numerically stable and easy to differentiate.

examples.input: Which losses are MLE in disguise?
examples.output: Squared error is Gaussian MLE, binary cross-entropy is Bernoulli MLE and categorical cross-entropy is multinomial MLE.

examples.input: How does MAP differ from MLE?
examples.output: MAP maximises likelihood times a prior, which adds a regulariser; with a flat prior they coincide.

constraints: Choice of distribution family (Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson)
Optimiser and tolerance when no closed form exists
Regularisation or prior, which turns MLE into MAP
edgeCases: The Gaussian MLE variance divides by n and is biased low; the unbiased version divides by n − 1
Multiplying many small probabilities underflows, so always work with log-likelihood
Likelihood can be unbounded (a mixture component collapsing on one point)

problems.title: Detection Mean Average Precision
problems.summary: Rank detections by confidence, mark each as a true or false positive by IoU matching, and take the area under the precision-recall curve per class, then average over classes.
problems.bruteForce: Deployment decisions at one fixed operating point (use precision, recall or F1 at that threshold), or tasks without boxes, and when localisation quality at strict IoU matters more than one threshold shows.
problems.intuition: A detector must both find objects and rank its confident boxes above its doubtful ones, so a single threshold hides too much. Sweeping the confidence threshold traces a precision-recall curve, and its area (AP) rewards detectors that keep precision high as recall grows. Matching uses IoU, so a box counts only if it overlaps a ground-truth box enough, and each ground-truth box can be claimed only once.
problems.whyItWorks: AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, so it summarises ranking quality over all thresholds instead of one. The monotone precision envelope removes the jitter from individual false positives, and the one-match-per-ground-truth rule stops duplicate boxes from inflating recall. Averaging over classes weights rare classes equally.
approach: Sort one class's detections by descending score — simulates lowering the confidence threshold
Match each detection to its best still-unmatched ground-truth box in the same image — $\mathrm{IoU}\geq\mathrm{threshold}$ makes it a TP, otherwise FP
Take cumulative TP and FP counts — precision and recall at every threshold
Make precision monotone: replace it by the maximum precision at any higher recall — removes zig-zags
Sum precision $\times$ recall increments, then average AP over classes — all-point interpolated AP, then mAP
problems.time: O(D log D + D·G_img) per class for D detections
problems.space: O(D + G) for the TP flags and matched marks
dryRun: $\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) = \frac{|a \cap b|}{|a \cup b|}$;  TP if $\mathrm{IoU} \geq t$ and GT unmatched
Sort by score; $TP_k, FP_k$ = cumulative counts at $k$
problems.description: Comparing object detectors and instance segmenters on a labelled benchmark (VOC, COCO), tuning NMS or score thresholds, and tracking detection quality across releases.

examples.input: What does a detection need to count as a true positive?
examples.output: Same class, IoU with an unmatched ground-truth box at or above the threshold; extra boxes on an already matched object are false positives.

examples.input: Why take the monotone envelope of precision?
examples.output: It replaces each precision with the best precision at that recall or higher, removing the zig-zag so AP is the area under a non-increasing curve.

examples.input: How does AP50 differ from COCO mAP?
examples.output: AP50 uses a single IoU threshold of $0.5$; COCO mAP averages over IoU thresholds $0.50$ to $0.95$ and also uses 101-point recall interpolation.

examples.input: Why must you sort detections by score first?
examples.output: The curve is built by lowering the confidence threshold, so confident detections must be matched first and claim ground truths before weaker ones.

constraints: IoU threshold(s) for matching
Interpolation scheme (all-point or 101-point)
Max detections per image
Object size ranges for small, medium, large breakdowns
edgeCases: Conventions differ: VOC07 uses 11 points, VOC10+ all points, COCO 101 points and averaged IoUs
Detections must be matched within the same image and class only
Unsorted detections, or unfiltered duplicates, change the result
No crowd or ignore regions, area ranges or maximum-detection caps in this sketch

problems.title: Metadata Filtering in Vector Search
problems.summary: Restrict nearest-neighbour search to rows whose metadata matches a condition (date, tenant, source, access level), either before the search (pre-filter) or after it (post-filter with oversampling).
problems.bruteForce: Do not post-filter for access control, since a shortfall or a bug leaks or loses documents. Do not oversample blindly when the filter is correlated with the query, because the formula assumes survivors are spread evenly among the candidates.
problems.intuition: Pre-filtering searches only the allowed rows, so the answer is exact but the index cannot use its usual shortcuts. Post-filtering searches everything and then discards, which is fast but wasteful: if only a fraction $s$ of rows pass the filter, only about $s$ of the returned hits survive, so asking for $k$ results gives far fewer. The fix is to fetch about $k/s$ candidates first. Because oversampling is only probabilistic, a filter that enforces access control must be applied as a hard pre-filter, never as a best-effort clean-up. Flow: query + filter → candidate rows → top-k scores → allowed results.
problems.whyItWorks: A candidate list of $c$ items contains a hit that passes the filter with probability $s$, independently if the filter is unrelated to the query, so the number of survivors is Binomial$(c, s)$ with mean $cs$. Setting $c = k/s$ makes the mean equal to $k$, and a larger factor makes a shortfall unlikely. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set itself, so it returns exactly the best $k$ allowed rows.
approach: Build a boolean mask for the filter — one flag per stored vector
Pre-filter: score only masked rows and take the top k among them — exact, respects the filter by construction
Post-filter: score all rows and keep the top c = k · oversample — candidates before filtering
Drop candidates whose mask is false and return at most k — the filter applied after the search
Estimate the selectivity s and set the oversample from k / s — compensates for rows the filter removes
Use the pre-filter path for access control — a hard guarantee instead of a probability
problems.time: pre-filter O(m·d) over the m matching rows by brute force; post-filter O(N·d) to score all rows plus a sort, or a fast ANN query for the candidates
problems.space: O(N) for the boolean mask beside the O(N·d) vectors
problems.solution:
import math
import numpy as np

def prefilter_topk(q, X, mask, k):
    idx = np.flatnonzero(mask)
    scores = X[idx] @ q
    order = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")[:k]
    return idx[order]

def postfilter_topk(q, X, mask, k, oversample=1):
    c = min(k * oversample, len(X))
    scores = X @ q
    top = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")[:c]
    return top[mask[top]][:k]

def needed_candidates(k, s):
    return math.ceil(k / s)
problems.description: Pre-filter whenever correctness or security matters (tenant, access level) or the filter is very selective. Post-filter with oversampling when the filter is loose and the index is much faster without it.

examples.input: What is the difference between pre-filtering and post-filtering?
examples.output: Pre-filtering restricts the candidate rows and then searches them, which is exact but may be slow. Post-filtering searches all rows and then drops hits that fail the filter, which is fast but can return fewer than k.

examples.input: How many candidates does post-filtering need to return k results?
examples.output: About $k/s$ for selectivity $s$, since only a fraction $s$ of candidates survive. A safety factor above 1 is needed because survivors are random.

examples.input: How should access control be enforced in retrieval?
examples.output: As a hard pre-filter on every query, using the user's permissions, so documents the user cannot see are never scored or returned.

examples.input: Why can filtered approximate search lose recall?
examples.output: A graph or cluster index is built over all vectors. A selective filter removes most nodes, so the remaining ones may not be reachable from the entry point and true neighbours are missed.

constraints: Candidate count c (or the oversample factor)
Estimated selectivity s of the filter
Pre-filter versus post-filter, chosen per query
Number of results k
edgeCases: With oversample $= 1$ and a selective filter, post-filtering can return zero results, not just a few fewer
Setting $c = k/s$ only gives $k$ survivors on average; about half of queries still fall short, so use a safety factor such as 2
Access control applied after the search is unsafe; enforce it as a pre-filter or inside the index
Filtering inside an approximate graph index can disconnect the graph and lower recall, so a very selective filter may need brute force over the subset

problems.title: Metropolis-Hastings Sampling
problems.summary: Draw samples from a distribution known only up to a constant by running a Markov chain that proposes random moves and accepts them with a probability that favours higher density.
problems.bruteForce: High dimensions or strongly correlated, multimodal targets, where random walks mix very slowly (use HMC/NUTS or variational inference), or when a direct sampler or a deterministic integrator is available.
problems.intuition: You can evaluate how probable a point is relative to another, but you cannot sample from the distribution directly. Wander randomly: propose a nearby point, always move uphill in density, and move downhill only with probability equal to the density ratio. Time spent at each place then ends up proportional to its probability, and the unknown normalising constant cancels because only ratios appear.
problems.whyItWorks: The acceptance rule is chosen so the chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to the target: probability flow from $x$ to $y$ equals flow from $y$ to $x$ at stationarity. Detailed balance implies the target is the stationary distribution, and with an irreducible aperiodic chain the samples converge to it. Consecutive samples are correlated, so the effective sample size is smaller than the number of draws.
approach: Start at an initial point and evaluate its log density — logs avoid underflow
Propose a Gaussian step from the current point — a symmetric random-walk move
Compute the log density ratio of proposal to current — the normaliser cancels
Accept if $\log u$ is below the ratio, otherwise stay — uphill is always taken, downhill sometimes
Record the current state every iteration, including repeats — rejected moves must be counted
Discard a burn-in and check the acceptance rate — too high means tiny steps, too low means huge ones
problems.time: O(n) target evaluations for n iterations
problems.space: O(n) for stored samples (O(1) if only running statistics are kept)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def metropolis(logp, x0, n, step, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x, lp = x0, logp(x0)
    out, acc = np.empty(n), 0
    for i in range(n):
        y = x + step * rng.normal()
        lq = logp(y)
        if np.log(rng.random()) < lq - lp:
            x, lp = y, lq
            acc += 1
        out[i] = x
    return out, acc / n
dryRun: Log: accept if $\log u < \log p(y) - \log p(x),\ u \sim U(0,1)$
problems.description: Bayesian posteriors with unnormalised densities, low-dimensional problems with no conjugate form, and as the base for HMC and Gibbs-style samplers.

examples.input: Why does the normalising constant not matter?
examples.output: The acceptance probability depends only on the ratio $p(y)/p(x)$, in which the unknown constant cancels.

examples.input: What is detailed balance and why does it matter?
examples.output: It says stationary probability flow $x$ to $y$ equals $y$ to $x$; any chain satisfying it with respect to $\pi$ has $\pi$ as a stationary distribution, which is the correctness condition.

examples.input: How do you choose the proposal step size?
examples.output: Tune it so the acceptance rate is moderate, neither near zero nor near one; both extremes give highly autocorrelated samples.

examples.input: How does Metropolis-Hastings differ from Gibbs sampling?
examples.output: Gibbs draws each variable from its exact conditional and always accepts; Metropolis-Hastings proposes from any distribution and corrects with an accept-reject step, so it needs no conditionals.

constraints: Proposal step size $\sigma$ — tune for a moderate acceptance rate
Burn-in length — samples discarded before the chain is near stationary
Number of iterations $n$ and thinning — set by effective sample size
Starting point and number of chains — several chains diagnose non-convergence
edgeCases: This is a 1-D random walk with a symmetric proposal; asymmetric proposals need the Hastings correction
Tiny steps accept almost everything but explore slowly; huge steps are mostly rejected
Samples are autocorrelated, so naive standard errors are too small
A single chain can look converged while stuck in one mode; run several and compare

problems.title: Reverse-Mode Autograd Engine (Micrograd)
problems.summary: Each scalar Value remembers its parents and a tiny local backward rule. The forward pass builds the graph, and backward sorts it topologically and sweeps it in reverse, accumulating gradients with addition.
problems.bruteForce: Anything real-sized: scalar Python objects are thousands of times slower than tensor kernels, and the engine has no broadcasting, no in-place checks and no memory-saving tricks.
problems.intuition: The chain rule needs no symbolic algebra: every operation only has to know its own local derivative, and the graph glues them together. A node that feeds two later operations receives two gradient contributions, one per use, so they must be added with $+=$, never assigned. Visiting nodes in reverse topological order guarantees that a node's gradient is complete before it passes anything to its parents. Flow: forward builds graph → sort → reverse sweep → accumulate grads.
problems.whyItWorks: For $y = f(g(x))$ the chain rule gives $\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial y}{\partial g}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}$, and for a node used several times the total derivative is the sum over its consumers. Reverse order guarantees that when a node is processed its gradient already contains every consumer's contribution, so one sweep gives all $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i}$ at about the cost of a forward pass, however many inputs there are.
approach: Wrap each number in a Value with data, grad = 0, its parents and a no-op backward — the graph is built as a side effect of the arithmetic
Each operation creates the output Value and stores a closure that adds local derivative times the output gradient to every parent — the local chain rule
Sort the graph topologically from the output with a depth-first visit — every node comes after its parents
Set the output gradient to $1$ and call the stored closures in reverse order — a node is processed after all of its consumers
Read the gradients from the leaves and zero them before the next call — accumulation means a second call adds on top
problems.time: O(nodes) forward and O(nodes) backward, each about the cost of the forward pass
problems.space: O(nodes), since every intermediate value and closure is kept for the sweep
dryRun: Total: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial x_i}$
Mul: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = y$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = x$
problems.description: Understanding how a deep learning framework computes gradients, and checking hand-derived gradients on small graphs. The same mechanism, on tensors and with fused kernels, is what runs under every training loop.

examples.input: Why does backward use += and not =?
examples.output: A node used in several places receives a gradient from each use, and the total derivative is their sum. Assignment would keep only the last one.

examples.input: Why is a topological order needed?
examples.output: A node may only pass gradient to its parents after all its consumers have added theirs. Reverse topological order ensures that.

examples.input: Why do we zero gradients between steps?
examples.output: Gradients accumulate across backward calls. Without zeroing, stale values are added to the new ones, so leaf gradients come out wrong (exactly doubled for a single operation, more in deeper graphs). Training loops zero them before each step.

examples.input: Why is reverse mode used for neural networks and not forward mode?
examples.output: Training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters. Reverse mode gets all parameter gradients in one sweep, while forward mode needs one pass per input.

constraints: Which operations are supported and their local rules
Initial seed gradient of the output (1 for a scalar loss)
When to zero gradients (before each backward call)
Whether intermediate values are kept or recomputed (checkpointing)
edgeCases: Using = instead of += in a local backward breaks any graph where a node is reused
Not zeroing gradients between backward calls adds stale values to the new ones; leaves double for one operation and inflate further in deeper graphs
Recursive graph traversal hits Python's recursion limit on very deep graphs; use an explicit stack
The ReLU derivative at $0$ is a convention (here $0$); frameworks may differ in edge cases

problems.title: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing
problems.summary: A router scores $E$ expert networks per token, keeps the top $k$, softmax-normalises their gates and sums the chosen experts' outputs, so parameters scale with $E$ while compute scales with $k$.
problems.bruteForce: Memory-bound or on-device deployment, where holding $E$ experts costs more than the saved compute, and small-batch serving where few tokens reach each expert and hardware sits idle.
problems.intuition: Capacity and per-token cost need not grow together. Store many feed-forward experts, but let each token wake up only the few the router likes: the model has the parameters of $E$ experts and the compute of about $k$. The catch is that a greedy router collapses onto a few favourites, so an auxiliary loss pushes the load flat. Flow: token → router scores → top-$k$ → softmax gates → weighted expert sum.
problems.whyItWorks: Different experts can specialise on different token types, so the model uses a large parameter pool while each token pays for only $k$ experts. Softmax over the kept logits makes the gates a convex combination, and with $k=E$ the layer reduces to a dense weighted sum. The balance loss $E\sum_i f_i P_i$ is minimised, at the value $1$, when both $f$ and $P$ are uniform, and its gradient flows through the differentiable $P_i$.
approach: Score the token with the router, $z = xW_r$ — one logit per expert
Keep the $k$ largest logits — only those experts will run
Softmax over just the kept logits — the gates sum to $1$ for the token
Run each chosen expert and sum $g_i\,e_i(x)$ — the other $E-k$ experts cost nothing
Measure load: $f_i$ is the share of assignments to expert $i$, $P_i$ the mean router probability — add $\alpha E\sum_i f_i P_i$ to the loss
problems.time: O(k·d·h) FFN compute per token (plus O(E·d) for the router), independent of E
problems.space: O(E·d·h) expert parameters, all of which must be held in memory
dryRun: Gates on kept set: $g_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j \in S} e^{z_j}}$
problems.description: Scaling model capacity under a fixed per-token compute budget, where memory for all experts is available and the batch is large enough to keep every expert busy.

examples.input: Why does a mixture-of-experts layer add parameters without adding much compute?
examples.output: Each token runs only $k$ of the $E$ experts, so FLOPs scale with $k$ while the parameter count scales with $E$.

examples.input: What is expert collapse and how is it prevented?
examples.output: The router sends most tokens to a few experts, which then train more and win more. An auxiliary loss $E\sum_i f_i P_i$ penalises uneven load, and capacity limits cap each expert.

examples.input: What happens to tokens that exceed an expert's capacity?
examples.output: They are dropped from that expert and typically pass through the residual connection unchanged, so a too-small capacity factor hurts quality.

examples.input: Why is the balance loss differentiable although $f_i$ is not?
examples.output: $f_i$ comes from a hard top-$k$ count and carries no gradient, but $P_i$ is the mean softmax probability, so gradients flow through $P_i$.

constraints: Number of experts $E$
Experts per token $k$
Capacity factor $c$ for each expert's token buffer
Balance-loss weight $\alpha$
edgeCases: Too small a balance weight lets experts collapse; too large forces uniform routing that ignores token content
All $E$ experts must sit in memory even though only $k$ run, so serving cost is memory-bound
The Python loop here is for clarity; real layers group tokens by expert and run batched matrix products
Taking the softmax over all $E$ logits and then keeping $k$ gives gates that do not sum to $1$

problems.title: MLP Forward Pass
problems.summary: Push a batch of inputs through a stack of affine layers with a non-linearity between them, ending in raw scores (logits).
problems.bruteForce: Not ideal for images or sequences where structure matters (use convolution or attention), since an MLP ignores locality and order and needs many more parameters.
problems.intuition: Each layer is one matrix multiply plus a bias that re-describes the data in a new feature space, and the activation bends that space so the next layer can separate what the last one could not. Handling the whole batch as a matrix turns many small dot products into a single fast operation.
problems.whyItWorks: A hidden layer with enough units and a non-linearity can approximate any continuous function, and extra layers build features from features. He initialisation sets the weight variance from the fan-in so activations keep a stable scale as they pass through ReLU layers.
approach: Initialise each weight matrix with std $\sqrt{2 / \mathrm{fan\_in}}$ and zero biases — keeps activation scale stable through ReLU
Set $a = X$ with one row per sample — the whole batch moves together
Compute $z = aW + b$ for each layer — a learned affine re-mapping
Apply ReLU on hidden layers but not the last — the output stays as unbounded logits
Apply softmax to logits only when probabilities are needed — losses usually take logits directly
problems.time: O(batch · Σ mₗ·nₗ) multiply-adds
problems.space: O(Σ mₗ·nₗ) for weights plus O(batch · widest layer) for activations
problems.description: Tabular data and as the building block inside larger models such as transformer feed-forward blocks and classifier heads.

examples.input: What happens if you remove all activations?
examples.output: The network collapses to a single linear map, whatever the depth.

examples.input: Why initialise weights randomly rather than at zero?
examples.output: Zero weights give every unit in a layer the same output and gradient, so they never differentiate.

examples.input: Why scale init by fan-in?
examples.output: It keeps the variance of activations and gradients roughly constant across layers, avoiding vanishing or exploding signals.

constraints: Layer sizes (depth and width)
Activation function (ReLU, GELU, tanh)
Weight initialisation scheme (He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh)
edgeCases: Using a weight layout of (out, in) in one place and (in, out) in another gives silent shape bugs
Zero or all-equal weight init makes every unit in a layer identical
Adding an activation after the final layer distorts logits for most losses
Without biases the layer cannot shift its output

problems.title: Choosing Among LLM Families (Decision Rule)
problems.summary: Pick a model by constraints, not by name: filter out candidates that break a must-have, rank the survivors by a weighted utility, and price the workload as cost per request.
problems.bruteForce: As a replacement for evaluating candidates on your own task data. The utility only orders profiles you filled in; it does not measure quality, which you must test.
problems.intuition: Model names and leaderboards go stale within months, but the trade-offs between hosted-large, open-medium, open-small, mixture and reasoning-tuned families stay put. Requirements such as privacy or on-device execution are not preferences you can trade away, so they are hard filters; only the soft goals (quality, cost, speed) enter a weighted score. This card teaches that method, with made-up profiles. Flow: requirements → hard filter → normalise scores → weighted utility → rank.
problems.whyItWorks: A hard filter encodes constraints that no amount of quality can offset, which a plain weighted sum would wrongly allow. Normalising against the best survivor makes scores comparable across units, and dividing by the weight total means $U$ and its ranking are unchanged if every weight is multiplied by the same positive constant.
approach: Write requirements as must-haves (privacy, on-device, licence) and limits (context, memory) — these are pass or fail
Drop every candidate that fails any must-have — a failed constraint cannot be bought back with quality
Compute cost per request $= (n_{in} p_{in} + n_{out} p_{out}) / 10^6$ — turns price per million tokens into a workload cost
Normalise each soft criterion to $(0, 1]$ against the best survivor — puts quality, cost and speed on one scale
Rank by $U = \sum_c w_c s_c / \sum_c w_c$ — dividing by the weight total makes the weights relative, not absolute
problems.time: O(n·m) for n candidates and m criteria
problems.space: O(n) for the filtered set and scores
dryRun: Feasible: all must-haves hold, ctx $\geq$ need
problems.description: Choosing between model families for a product, or justifying a choice to a team, when requirements such as privacy, latency, budget and context length are known and written down.

examples.input: Why treat privacy or on-device execution as a filter instead of a weight?
examples.output: A model that violates it is unusable however good it scores. A weighted sum could let high quality compensate, which is wrong for a hard requirement.

examples.input: Why price input and output tokens separately?
examples.output: Providers usually charge different rates for each, and output tokens are typically more expensive, so cost depends on the prompt-to-completion ratio of your workload.

examples.input: Why not just rank models by a public leaderboard?
examples.output: Leaderboards go stale, may not match your task or data, and ignore cost, privacy and latency. Evaluate the shortlist on your own examples.

examples.input: When does a larger weight on quality change the winner?
examples.output: When the quality gap between candidates outweighs their cost and speed ratios, as the weight on quality grows the best model moves toward the highest-quality family.

constraints: Criterion weights $w_c$ (only their ratios matter)
Request mix: input and output tokens per request
Hard limits: context length, memory budget
Normalisation scheme (ratio to best, or min-max)
edgeCases: Model names, versions, prices and scores go stale quickly; use this as a method and refill the profiles from current data
The quality field in a profile is a placeholder; replace it with scores from your own evaluation set
Ratio-to-best normalisation depends on which candidates survive the filter, so adding a model can reorder the rest
Self-hosting cost is hardware and operations, not a clean price per million tokens; the profile values are an estimate

problems.title: SGD with Momentum
problems.summary: Gradient descent that adds a velocity: a running sum of past gradients, so the update keeps moving in directions where gradients consistently agree.
problems.bruteForce: When you want little tuning on sparse or badly scaled gradients, an adaptive method such as Adam is often easier. Too high a momentum with a large learning rate can oscillate or diverge.
problems.intuition: Think of a ball rolling down the loss surface rather than a walker taking independent steps. Gradients that point the same way accumulate into fast progress along narrow valleys, while components that flip sign from step to step cancel out. Nesterov momentum looks ahead by applying the gradient at the position momentum is about to reach, which corrects overshoot a little earlier.
problems.whyItWorks: The velocity is an exponentially weighted sum of past gradients, so consistent directions are amplified and oscillating ones are damped. On ill-conditioned quadratics this allows a larger effective step along the shallow direction without diverging along the steep one.
approach: Start the velocity buffer at zero — no history yet
Update $v \leftarrow \mu \cdot v + g$ — accumulates gradients with exponential decay
Pick the step direction: $v$ for classical, $g + \mu \cdot v$ for Nesterov — Nesterov peeks ahead
Move the weights by $-\eta$ times that direction — the usual descent step
problems.time: O(d) per step for d parameters
problems.space: O(d) extra for the velocity buffer
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def sgd_step(w, g, buf, lr=0.1, mu=0.9, nesterov=False):
    buf = mu * buf + g
    step = g + mu * buf if nesterov else buf
    return w - lr * step, buf
problems.description: Training CNNs and other deep nets with SGD, especially with a tuned learning-rate schedule, where it often generalises well.

examples.input: What problem does momentum solve?
examples.output: It speeds progress along consistent gradient directions and damps oscillation across steep, narrow valleys.

examples.input: How does Nesterov differ from classical momentum?
examples.output: It uses a lookahead gradient direction, $g + \mu \cdot v$ after updating $v$, which reacts sooner when momentum overshoots.

examples.input: How does momentum change the effective learning rate?
examples.output: For a steady gradient the velocity approaches a geometric series in $\mu$, so the effective step is larger by $1 / (1 - \mu)$.

constraints: Learning rate $\eta$
Momentum $\mu$
Nesterov on or off
Dampening (not modelled here)
edgeCases: Libraries differ in where the learning rate multiplies the velocity; this follows PyTorch's convention
The effective step grows with momentum, so lower the learning rate when raising $\mu$
Weight decay and dampening are omitted here
Reset the buffer when you restart or change the optimiser

problems.title: Multi-Head Attention
problems.summary: Run several attention operations in parallel on lower-dimensional slices of the projections, then concatenate and mix their outputs.
problems.bruteForce: Very long sequences where quadratic cost dominates, or tiny models where extra heads add little. Heads can also be redundant, so more is not always better.
problems.intuition: One attention head produces a single weighting over tokens, so it must pick one notion of relevance. Splitting the width into several heads lets each attend with its own pattern, for example nearby words in one and a matching subject in another, at about the same total cost as one full-width head.
problems.whyItWorks: Each head projects into a lower-dimensional subspace, so different heads can learn different query-key similarities and attend to different positions at once. The output projection then recombines them, giving a richer function than a single softmax average while the total parameter count stays comparable to a single full-width head.
approach: Project X with Wq, Wk, Wv at full width — one matmul serves all heads
Reshape the width into h heads of size d/h — each head works in its own subspace
Compute scaled dot-product attention per head — separate attention patterns
Concatenate head outputs back to width d — gathers what each head found
Apply the output projection Wo — mixes information across heads
problems.time: O(T²·d + T·d²) for length T and width d
problems.space: O(h·T²) for the attention maps
dryRun: $Q = XW_q,\;\; K = XW_k,\;\; V = XW_v \qquad (T \times d)$
problems.description: Transformer encoders and decoders, and whenever one attention pattern is too limiting, such as language, vision transformers and multimodal models.

examples.input: Why use multiple heads instead of one large head?
examples.output: Each head can learn a different attention pattern in its own subspace, which a single softmax over all positions cannot express.

examples.input: How does the cost compare with single-head attention?
examples.output: Per-head width shrinks as d/h, so the total score computation is about the same as one full-width head; extra cost is the output projection.

examples.input: Why is the output projection needed?
examples.output: Concatenated heads are just side by side; Wo mixes information across heads and maps back to the model width.

constraints: Number of heads h (must divide d here)
Model width d
Attention dropout
Causal masking on or off
edgeCases: d must be divisible by h, otherwise the reshape fails
This code has no biases, masking or dropout; PyTorch adds biases by default
Reshape and transpose order matters; a wrong order still runs but mixes heads

problems.title: Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1)
problems.summary: Reduce a $K$-class confusion matrix to per-class precision, recall and F1, then average them three ways. The choice of averaging decides whether rare classes count.
problems.bruteForce: When costs differ strongly between error types (use a cost matrix or per-class thresholds), for multilabel problems without adapting the counts, or when probability quality matters (use log loss or calibration instead of a hard-label metric).
problems.intuition: A single accuracy number hides which classes fail. Per-class F1 exposes that, but you still need one headline score. Macro averaging gives every class equal say, so a failing rare class drags it down; micro averaging pools all decisions, so frequent classes dominate; weighted averaging sits between by weighting each class by its support.
problems.whyItWorks: Everything derives from the confusion matrix: the diagonal holds true positives, column sums are predicted counts and row sums are true counts. Micro averaging pools true positives, false positives and false negatives across classes; for single-label problems every error is one false positive and one false negative, so micro precision, recall and F1 all equal accuracy. Macro and weighted differ only in the weights on the per-class F1 values.
approach: Build the confusion matrix by counting (true, predicted) pairs — the single object all metrics come from
Take true positives from the diagonal and divide by column and row sums — per-class precision and recall
Guard the divisions with a floor — a class that is never predicted or absent should score zero, not NaN
Combine into per-class F1 — the harmonic mean punishes a gap between precision and recall
Average unweighted for macro and by support for weighted — rare classes count fully versus in proportion
Divide total true positives by $n$ for micro — pooled counts reduce to accuracy
problems.time: O(n + K²) to count pairs and aggregate
problems.space: O(K²) for the confusion matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def confusion(y, p, K):
    C = np.zeros((K, K), dtype=int)
    np.add.at(C, (y, p), 1)
    return C

def f1_report(C):
    tp = np.diag(C).astype(float)
    prec = tp / np.maximum(C.sum(0), 1)
    rec = tp / np.maximum(C.sum(1), 1)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / np.maximum(prec + rec, 1e-12)
    sup = C.sum(1)
    macro = f1.mean()
    weighted = (f1 * sup).sum() / sup.sum()
    micro = tp.sum() / C.sum()
    return f1, macro, weighted, micro
problems.description: Reporting multiclass classifiers, choosing the average to match the business goal (macro when every class matters, micro or accuracy when overall hit rate matters, weighted for a support-aware compromise), and diagnosing which class pairs get confused.

examples.input: When use macro over micro F1?
examples.output: When all classes matter equally, especially with imbalance: macro exposes poor performance on rare classes that micro or accuracy would hide.

examples.input: Why does micro F1 equal accuracy in multiclass?
examples.output: Each misclassification is exactly one false positive for the predicted class and one false negative for the true class, so pooled precision and recall both equal the fraction correct.

examples.input: What does weighted F1 do?
examples.output: It averages per-class F1 with weights proportional to class support, so it tracks frequent classes but still reflects per-class balance of precision and recall.

examples.input: How do you handle a class that is never predicted?
examples.output: Its precision is undefined; set it to zero (zero_division) so its F1 is zero, and flag it explicitly in the report.

constraints: average — macro, micro or weighted
zero_division — value used when a class has no predictions or no samples
Class labels and order — fix them so the matrix aligns across runs
edgeCases: Labels must be integers 0 to $K-1$ here; map strings first
Micro F1 equals accuracy for single-label problems, so it adds nothing beyond accuracy
Macro F1 swings on tiny classes with few support samples, so report supports too
A class missing from the true labels gives a zero F1 that still enters the macro mean in this code (sklearn behaves the same only if its labels are listed)

problems.title: Gaussian Naive Bayes
problems.summary: Classify with Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class. With Gaussian features, training is just a per-class mean, variance and prior.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when strongly correlated features carry the signal, when you need trustworthy probabilities, or when class-conditional features are far from Gaussian.
problems.intuition: The independence assumption is wrong almost always, but it turns an impossible joint density into a product of one-dimensional densities, each estimated from a few numbers. Each feature then casts an independent vote, in log space, for every class, and the largest total wins.
problems.whyItWorks: The classifier only needs the ranking of $P(c\,|\,x)$, not calibrated probabilities. Even when correlated features double-count evidence and push the probabilities toward $0$ or $1$, the argmax is often still right. The model has so few parameters that it has very low variance, so it works well on small data.
approach: Estimate the class priors from label frequencies — the $P(c)$ term
Estimate a mean and variance per class and feature — this fully defines each Gaussian
Add a tiny variance floor — avoids division by zero
Compute $\log P(c)$ plus the sum of per-feature log-densities — logs avoid underflow
Subtract the max and exponentiate to normalise — a stable softmax gives probabilities
problems.time: O(n·d) to fit, O(k·d) per prediction for k classes
problems.space: O(k·d) for the means and variances
problems.description: A fast baseline for small datasets, high-dimensional data and text (multinomial variant), and when you need training and prediction in a single cheap pass.

examples.input: Why is it called naive?
examples.output: It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which lets the likelihood factorise into per-feature terms.

examples.input: Why does it work despite the false assumption?
examples.output: Classification needs only the argmax over classes; correlated evidence distorts the probabilities more than it changes which class is largest.

examples.input: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?
examples.output: Naive Bayes is generative, fits fast and does well on little data; logistic regression is discriminative, handles correlated features better and wins with more data.

constraints: var_smoothing — variance floor that stabilises tiny-variance features
Priors — learned from data or set manually for imbalanced costs
Variant — Gaussian, Multinomial (counts) or Bernoulli (binary)
edgeCases: Probabilities are over-confident when features are correlated
A feature with zero variance in a class needs the smoothing floor
Multiplying raw probabilities underflows; always sum logs
Discrete variants need Laplace smoothing so unseen values do not zero a class

problems.title: Next-Token Prediction Loss and Perplexity
problems.summary: Shift the sequence by one so position $t$ predicts token $t+1$, average the cross-entropy over all unmasked positions, and report perplexity as the exponential of that loss.
problems.bruteForce: Comparing perplexity across models with different tokenizers, since the per-token loss is not on the same scale. Use bits per byte or character instead.
problems.intuition: A single sentence gives one training example per position: the input is the prefix and the label is simply the next token, so no human labels are needed. Perplexity turns the average loss into an effective branching factor, the number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing between, which is why uniform logits over $V$ tokens score exactly $V$. Flow: tokens → shift by one → log-probs → masked mean → exp.
problems.whyItWorks: Minimising the average negative log-likelihood of each next token maximises the likelihood of the sequence under the chain rule, $p(x) = \prod_t p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$. The causal mask lets one forward pass produce all $T-1$ predictions, and dividing by the count of unmasked tokens keeps the loss independent of padding.
approach: Split tokens into inputs $x_{1:T-1}$ and targets $x_{2:T}$ — position $t$ must predict token $t+1$
Run the model to get logits of shape $(T-1, V)$ — one distribution per position
Take the log-softmax and pick the target's log-probability — the negative is the token loss
Mask positions equal to the ignore index — padding and prompt tokens carry no loss
Average over unmasked tokens, then $\exp$ for perplexity — comparable across lengths
problems.time: O(T·V) for the softmax over the vocabulary at every position
problems.space: O(T·V) for the logits, often the largest tensor in training
problems.description: Pretraining and supervised fine-tuning of any autoregressive language model, and evaluating one on held-out text; use the ignore index to train only on response tokens.

examples.input: Why shift the targets by one?
examples.output: The model output at position $t$ is its prediction for the next token, so the label for position $t$ is token $t+1$; the last position has no label.

examples.input: Why mask prompt and padding tokens?
examples.output: Padding is not real text, and in fine-tuning the prompt is given rather than predicted. Masked positions are excluded from both the sum and the divisor.

examples.input: What does perplexity of 20 mean?
examples.output: The model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 20 tokens at each step, on average in the geometric sense.

examples.input: Why is perplexity not comparable across tokenizers?
examples.output: A tokenizer with longer tokens makes each prediction harder and the sequence shorter, so per-token loss changes without a real quality difference.

constraints: Ignore index for padding and prompt tokens (commonly $-100$)
Reduction: mean over tokens versus mean over sequences
Label smoothing, if any
edgeCases: Dividing by the total number of positions instead of the unmasked count biases the loss low
Forgetting to shift makes the model copy its input, giving a near-zero loss that means nothing
Masked targets must still be a valid index when gathering, or the lookup fails

problems.title: Non-negative Matrix Factorisation
problems.summary: Factor a non-negative matrix X into W H with both factors non-negative and a small inner rank. Multiplicative updates rescale each entry by a ratio of positive terms, so non-negativity is kept without any projection step.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when data has negative values, when you need a unique answer (the factorisation is not unique and depends on initialisation), or when plain SVD's optimality and speed are enough.
problems.intuition: Forbidding negative entries means each row of X can only be built by adding parts, never subtracting them, so the learned factors tend to be parts such as topics, strokes or sources. The update multiplies each entry by how much the data wants it, over how much the model already uses it, which grows an entry when it is too small and shrinks it when too large.
problems.whyItWorks: The Frobenius error is not jointly convex, but it is convex in W for a fixed H and the other way round. The multiplicative step is a majorise-minimise update, built from an auxiliary function that touches the loss at the current point, so each update cannot increase the loss. It converges to a stationary point, not necessarily the best one.
approach: Start from non-negative W and H — updates only rescale, so a zero entry stays zero and a positive one stays positive
Multiply W by the data-to-model ratio computed with H fixed — the W step cannot raise the loss
Multiply H by the same kind of ratio using the new W — the H step cannot raise it either
Floor the denominator with a tiny constant — avoids dividing by zero for entries that become zero
Track the loss each sweep and stop when it stops falling — it is monotone, so flatness means a stationary point
problems.time: O(iters·n·m·r) for an n×m matrix with rank r
problems.space: O((n + m)·r) for factors plus the n×m data
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def nmf(X, W, H, iters=200, eps=1e-10):
    loss = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        W = W * (X @ H.T) / np.maximum(W @ H @ H.T, eps)
        H = H * (W.T @ X) / np.maximum(W.T @ W @ H, eps)
        loss.append(0.5 * ((X - W @ H) ** 2).sum())
    return W, H, loss
dryRun: $\nabla_W = W H H^{\top} - X H^{\top}$ (positive $-$ negative part)
Loss is non-increasing under the updates
problems.description: Parts-based features from non-negative data such as word counts, images and spectra, topic modelling, and interpretable low-rank structure where signs would be confusing.

examples.input: How is NMF different from PCA or SVD?
examples.output: NMF forces non-negative factors and gives additive, parts-based components that are not orthogonal and not unique; SVD allows signs, is orthogonal and gives the best rank-r approximation.

examples.input: Why do multiplicative updates preserve non-negativity?
examples.output: Each update multiplies an entry by a ratio of non-negative quantities, so entries stay non-negative if they start that way.

examples.input: Does NMF find the global optimum?
examples.output: No. The problem is non-convex in W and H jointly, so the updates reach a stationary point that depends on initialisation.

constraints: Rank r — number of parts; chosen by reconstruction error or interpretability
Initialisation — random or SVD-based (NNDSVD) and it changes the result
Loss — Frobenius here; KL divergence suits counts, with different updates
Regularisation — L1 or L2 on W and H for sparser or smaller factors
edgeCases: Entries that reach exactly zero can never recover under multiplicative updates
Different initialisations converge to different local solutions, so use restarts
Convergence is slow compared with alternating least squares or coordinate descent
Scale ambiguity: W and H can trade a scale factor, so normalise before comparing factors

problems.title: NumPy Broadcasting and Vectorisation
problems.summary: Broadcasting stretches arrays of different shapes to a common shape without copying, so one array expression replaces a Python loop over rows, pairs or batches.
problems.bruteForce: When the temporary is too large for memory (chunk the work or use the dot identity), or when each step depends on the previous result, as in a recurrence, which cannot be vectorised along that axis.
problems.intuition: Align the shapes from the right. An axis of size 1 (or a missing leading axis) is repeated virtually to match the other operand, so inserting a size-1 axis with `None` decides which pairs are formed: $A[:,\mathrm{None}]-B[\mathrm{None}]$ subtracts every row of $B$ from every row of $A$. The loop then runs in compiled code, not in Python. Flow: shapes → align from right → stretch size-1 axes → one array op.
problems.whyItWorks: Broadcasting is only an indexing rule: a size-1 axis uses stride 0, so the same element is read again for every position. No data is copied, and the elementwise loop runs in optimised compiled code. The distance identity follows from expanding the square and is exact in real arithmetic, though it can lose precision when two points are nearly equal.
approach: Write both shapes right-aligned, padding the shorter with leading 1s — missing axes count as size 1
For each axis require equal sizes or a 1 — otherwise raise ValueError
Take the larger size per axis as the output shape — size-1 axes are stretched virtually
Use None or reshape to add size-1 axes — this chooses which axes pair up
Prefer the identity $\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2-2a\cdot b$ for distances — it avoids the $n \cdot m \cdot d$ temporary
problems.time: O(output size) per operation; pairwise distances cost O(n·m·d)
problems.space: Broadcast view is free, but the diff temporary is O(n·m·d); the dot identity needs only O(n·m)
dryRun: Broadcast temp: $n \cdot m \cdot d$ floats; identity: $n \cdot m$
problems.description: Any elementwise or reduction work over rows, pairs or batches: normalising features, distance matrices, attention scores, masks and softmax. If you write a Python loop over array rows, look for the broadcast form first.

examples.input: What are the broadcasting rules?
examples.output: Align shapes from the trailing axis, pad the shorter shape with leading 1s, and require each pair of sizes to be equal or one of them 1. The result takes the larger size on each axis.

examples.input: Why is a vectorised expression faster than a Python loop?
examples.output: The loop runs in compiled code over contiguous memory instead of the interpreter, and there is no per-element Python overhead. Broadcasting does it without copying the smaller operand.

examples.input: How do you get all pairwise differences between two sets of vectors?
examples.output: Add a size-1 axis to each, A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :], giving shape (n, m, d), then reduce over the last axis. The dot identity gives the squared distances without the (n, m, d) temporary.

examples.input: Why subtract the row maximum in softmax?
examples.output: Softmax is unchanged by a constant shift, and subtracting the maximum keeps every exponent at most zero, which avoids overflow.

constraints: Axis chosen for each reduction
keepdims, so the reduced result still broadcasts back
Chunk size when the temporary does not fit in memory
dtype (float32 or float64), which sets accuracy of the dot identity
edgeCases: A shape $(n,)$ against $(n,1)$ broadcasts to $(n,n)$, silently producing a matrix instead of an elementwise result
Forgetting keepdims=True in a reduction makes the result broadcast along the wrong axis
The dot identity can give tiny negative squared distances from rounding; clip at zero before a square root
In-place ops such as a += b cannot change the shape of a, so broadcasting only works toward a's shape

problems.title: Output Validation and Guardrails
problems.summary: Run model output through layered checks before it reaches a user or a tool, report every failure, retry with feedback or fall back, and decide whether a broken check blocks or lets the output through.
problems.bruteForce: Do not treat validators as a replacement for least-privilege tools and human approval of dangerous actions. Regex rules are brittle against paraphrase, and extra layers also add latency and false rejections.
problems.intuition: Treat the model as an untrusted producer: whatever it writes will be rendered, executed or acted on, so each destination deserves its own checks. Cheap checks (length, patterns, PII) run first and catch different failures than slow ones (grounding), so stacking them in series trades more false rejections for fewer misses. Each check also needs a policy for when it crashes: fail closed blocks safely, fail open keeps the product up. Flow: model output → validators → pass, retry with feedback or fallback.
problems.whyItWorks: A bad output has to get past every checker in series. If the checkers fail independently, the chance that all of them miss is the product of the miss rates, so each added layer multiplies the miss rate down. The price is that a good output must also pass every checker, so the false-reject rate climbs as $1-\prod_i(1-f_i)$. Independence is an assumption: checkers built on similar rules tend to miss the same outputs, so the real miss rate is higher.
approach: Write each checker as a function returning ok and a reason — checkers stay small, testable and composable
Run all checkers and collect every failing reason — one pass tells the retry everything that was wrong
Treat a checker exception by the policy, closed blocks and open skips — a crash must not silently decide the outcome
On failure, retry with the reasons added to the prompt, up to a limit — the model can fix specific problems
After the retries use a safe fallback response — the user never sees the rejected output
Estimate series rates as $1-\prod_i(1-f_i)$ false rejects and $\prod_i m_i$ misses — shows what each extra layer costs and buys
problems.time: O(sum of checker costs) per attempt, times at most retries + 1 attempts
problems.space: O(1) beyond the output and the collected reasons
dryRun: False reject of good output $F = 1 - \prod_i (1 - f_i)$
problems.description: Whenever model text is shown to users, parsed by code, or turned into a tool call, especially in regulated or customer-facing settings where a bad output has a real cost.

examples.input: When would you fail open instead of fail closed?
examples.output: Fail closed when a bad output is costly, such as a tool call or a regulated answer. Fail open when availability matters more and the check is advisory, but log every skipped check so the gap is visible.

examples.input: How is this different from schema validation or injection defence?
examples.output: Schema validation checks only shape, and injection defence protects the input side and the tools. Output guardrails add content policy, privacy and grounding checks on whatever the model produced, whatever the cause.

examples.input: Why does adding more validators not always help?
examples.output: Each one raises the false-reject rate and latency. If validators share blind spots they miss the same outputs, so the gain is smaller than the independent product suggests.

constraints: Fail-closed or fail-open per checker
Maximum number of retries
Grounding threshold and minimum word length
Order of checkers, cheap ones first
edgeCases: Rates multiply only under independence; measure the combined rates on labelled data instead of trusting the formula
Retry feedback that quotes the offending text can leak it back into the prompt; give reasons, not content
Word-overlap grounding passes fluent but unsupported claims; use entailment checks for high stakes
Validate for the destination, for example escape text before putting it in HTML or SQL, not only for content

problems.title: Pandas Groupby, Merge and Window Features
problems.summary: Groupby aggregates rows per key, merge joins tables on a key, and rolling or shift builds features from earlier rows. Together they produce most tabular features.
problems.bruteForce: Data too large for memory (use a database or a distributed engine), or when order does not exist: rolling and lag features only make sense on data sorted by time within each group.
problems.intuition: All three are index operations on a table. Groupby splits rows by key, applies a function per group and combines the results; a join looks up each left row's key in the right table, so a duplicated right key multiplies the left row; a window or lag reads earlier rows. The danger is time: a feature for time $t$ may only use data up to $t-1$, otherwise the model sees the answer. Flow: table → group keys → aggregate → join back → lag features.
problems.whyItWorks: Hashing the key turns matching into a lookup, so no pairwise comparison of rows is needed. The rolling mean averages each length-$w$ window, and a NaN poisons only the windows containing it. Shifting the feature by one step guarantees that row $t$ was computed only from rows before it.
approach: Split rows by key into groups — every row lands in exactly one group
Apply the aggregate to each group and combine into one value per key — a single pass, $O(N)$
Index the right table by key, then look up each left row — a dict makes the join $O(N+M)$
Emit one output row per matching right row, or one row of NaN if none — this is a left join
Build rolling and lag features, then shift by at least 1 — the feature at $t$ must not contain $x_t$
problems.time: groupby and join O(N+M) with hashing; rolling mean O(N·w) as written, O(N) with cumulative sums
problems.space: O(N) for the groups or the join index and the output
dryRun: One pass over rows: $\sum_k n_k = N$, cost O(N)
problems.description: Turning raw event or transaction tables into model features: per-user statistics, enriching rows with a lookup table, and lagged or rolling features for time series and forecasting.

examples.input: What happens to row counts when the right table has duplicate keys?
examples.output: Each left row is repeated once per matching right row, so a join can grow the table. Check key uniqueness on the side that should be unique.

examples.input: Difference between inner and left join?
examples.output: An inner join keeps only keys present on both sides. A left join keeps every left row and fills right columns with missing values when no match exists.

examples.input: How does a rolling feature leak the future?
examples.output: A window ending at $t$ includes $x_t$, which is the value being predicted at $t$. Shift the feature by at least one step before using it.

examples.input: How do you compute group statistics without leaking across a train/test split?
examples.output: Compute them on the training rows only and join them onto both sets, or use out-of-fold statistics for target-based aggregates.

constraints: Window size $w$ for rolling features
Lag $k$ (at least 1 when predicting the current step)
Join type (inner, left) and the key columns
Aggregate function (mean, sum, count, std)
edgeCases: Computing the rolling mean on $x$ and aligning it to the same row leaks $x_t$ into the feature for $t$
Rolling or lag across several entities without grouping first mixes the end of one series with the start of the next
Joining on a key with duplicates silently multiplies rows and inflates later sums
Target-based group means computed on all data leak labels; compute them within training folds

problems.title: Parameter Count, FLOPs and Memory of a Transformer
problems.summary: A decoder-only transformer has about $12 L d^2$ parameters plus $V d$ for embeddings, costs about $6 N D$ FLOPs to train and $2 N$ FLOPs per generated token, and needs bytes proportional to $N$.
problems.bruteForce: Precise accounting. The rules ignore attention over the context (matters for long sequences), activations, the KV cache, and sparse or mixture-of-experts models where only some parameters are active.
problems.intuition: Almost all parameters live in a few square-ish matrices per layer, so the count is set by depth and width: $4 d^2$ for attention and $8 d^2$ for a $4\times$ FFN. Compute follows the same count, because each parameter is used in one multiply-add per token on the forward pass and about twice that on the backward pass. Memory is the count times bytes per value, plus gradients and optimizer state when training. Flow: layers and width → parameters → FLOPs per token → bytes.
problems.whyItWorks: Each weight matrix of shape $a \times b$ applied to a token costs $a b$ multiply-adds, which is $2ab$ FLOPs, so forward compute per token is about twice the parameter count. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights, about two more forward passes, giving $6N$ per token in total.
approach: Count one block: $4 d^2$ attention plus $2 d\, d_{ff}$ FFN (biases and norms are lower order) — this is the per-layer cost
Multiply by $L$ and add the embedding $V d$ (once if tied, twice if not) — the table is shared or separate
Training FLOPs $\approx 6 N D$ for $D$ tokens — $2N$ forward and $4N$ backward per token
Inference FLOPs $\approx 2 N$ per token — forward pass only, ignoring attention over the context
Weights take $N \cdot$ bytes per value; training adds gradients and Adam states, about $16 N$ bytes in mixed precision — a stated rule of thumb
problems.time: O(1) arithmetic once the shape is known; training compute scales as $6ND$
problems.space: O(N) bytes for weights, about 16 bytes per parameter to train with Adam
dryRun: Attention per layer: $4 d^2$ (Q, K, V, O)
FFN per layer: $2 d\, d_{ff} = 8 d^2$
problems.description: Budgeting a training run, sizing a GPU for serving, or checking that a quoted model size matches its architecture before running anything.

examples.input: Why is training about $6ND$ FLOPs?
examples.output: The forward pass is about $2N$ per token (a multiply-add per weight) and the backward pass is about twice that, so $6N$ per token and $6ND$ for $D$ tokens.

examples.input: How much memory does training need beyond the weights?
examples.output: Gradients and optimizer state. With mixed precision and Adam a common estimate is 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for fp16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for fp32 master weights, 8 for the two Adam moments. Activations come on top.

examples.input: Where are most parameters in a transformer?
examples.output: In the per-layer matrices, about $12 d^2$ each layer, so they grow with depth and the square of width. The embedding adds $V d$, which matters for small models with large vocabularies.

examples.input: Does weight tying change the count?
examples.output: Yes. Sharing the input embedding with the output projection saves $V d$ parameters.

constraints: Number of layers $L$ and model width $d$
FFN width $d_{ff}$ (often $4d$)
Vocabulary size $V$ and whether embeddings are tied
Precision (fp32, fp16/bf16, int8) and optimizer
edgeCases: The $6ND$ and $2N$ rules drop attention over the context, which adds real cost at long sequence lengths
The 16 bytes per parameter figure assumes mixed-precision Adam with fp32 master weights; other setups differ, and activations are extra
Biases are counted here; many modern models drop them, and gated FFNs use three matrices, so recount for the actual architecture

problems.title: Principal Component Analysis
problems.summary: Rotate centred data onto orthogonal directions ordered by how much variance they capture, then keep only the first $k$. It is computed directly from the SVD of the centred data matrix.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when features have very different scales and you have not standardised, when the structure is non-linear (use kernel PCA or t-SNE/UMAP), or when high-variance directions are noise rather than signal.
problems.intuition: Real data often lives near a low-dimensional slab inside a high dimensional space. The direction along which the points spread most is the first component, the next most-spread direction at right angles is the second, and dropping the low-spread directions loses the least information.
problems.whyItWorks: The variance along a unit direction $v$ is $v^{\top}\Sigma v$, which is maximised by the top eigenvector of the covariance $\Sigma$, and the next one under the orthogonality constraint, and so on. The SVD of the centred data gives those eigenvectors directly, without forming $\Sigma$, and the discarded variance is exactly the squared reconstruction error.
approach: Subtract the column means — PCA is about spread around the mean
Take the SVD of the centred matrix — its right vectors are the principal axes
Square the singular values and divide by $n-1$ — these are the variances per axis
Keep the top $k$ rows of $V^{\top}$ — the k directions with most variance
Project centred data onto them — gives the $k$-dimensional representation
problems.time: O(n·d·min(n, d)) for a full SVD; randomised SVD gives O(n·d·k)
problems.space: O(n·d) for the data, O(d·k) for the components
problems.description: Compressing correlated features, denoising, visualising in 2-D or 3-D, and decorrelating inputs before a model that dislikes collinearity.

examples.input: How does PCA relate to SVD?
examples.output: The right singular vectors of the centred data are the eigenvectors of the covariance, and the squared singular values divided by $n-1$ are its eigenvalues.

examples.input: How many components do I keep?
examples.output: Enough to reach a target share of explained variance, or at the elbow of the scree plot; validate against the downstream task.

examples.input: Why centre the data?
examples.output: Without centring, the first component mostly points at the mean instead of the direction of maximum spread.

constraints: n_components $k$ — chosen by explained-variance ratio or a scree plot
whiten — rescale components to unit variance
svd_solver — full, randomized or arpack for large data
edgeCases: Unscaled features: PCA follows the feature with the largest units
Components are only defined up to sign, so compare projections carefully
High variance does not mean predictive; the label may live in a low-variance direction
Fit PCA on training data only, then reuse it on validation/test data

problems.title: Perceptron Learning Rule
problems.summary: Predict $\mathrm{sign}(w \cdot x + b)$ and, only on a mistake, nudge the weights towards the misclassified point. On linearly separable data it stops after a bounded number of mistakes; on XOR it never settles.
problems.bruteForce: Non-separable problems (it oscillates forever), when calibrated probabilities are needed, or when a good margin matters; use logistic regression or a maximum-margin SVM instead.
problems.intuition: A mistake means the current hyperplane is on the wrong side of $x$, and adding $y\,x$ to $w$ rotates it towards the correct side of that point. Correct points cause no change at all, so the learner is purely mistake driven. Each update also increases the alignment with any true separator by at least the margin $\gamma$, while the weight norm grows only like $R\sqrt{k}$, which squeezes the number of mistakes $k$ below $(R/\gamma)^2$. Flow: predict → mistake? → add $y\,x$ → repeat until a clean pass.
problems.whyItWorks: Suppose a unit vector $w^*$ separates the data with margin $\gamma$, that is $y\,(w^* \cdot x) \geq \gamma$, and $\|x\| \leq R$. Each mistake raises $w \cdot w^*$ by at least $\eta\gamma$, so after $k$ mistakes it is at least $k\eta\gamma$. On a mistake $y\,(w \cdot x) \leq 0$, so $\|w\|^2$ grows by at most $\eta^2 R^2$, giving $\|w\| \leq \eta R\sqrt{k}$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $k\eta\gamma \leq \eta R\sqrt{k}$, hence $k \leq (R/\gamma)^2$. The bias is covered by appending a constant $1$ to $x$.
approach: Start from $w = 0$, $b = 0$ — no prior preference between classes
For each example compute the score $w \cdot x + b$ — its sign is the prediction
If $y\,(w \cdot x + b) \leq 0$ it is a mistake — correct points leave the model untouched
On a mistake do $w \leftarrow w + \eta\,y\,x$ and $b \leftarrow b + \eta\,y$ — pushes the score of this point in the right direction
Stop after a pass with no mistakes — on separable data this is guaranteed to happen, otherwise cap the epochs
problems.time: O(n·d) per epoch; at most $(R/\gamma)^2$ updates in total when separable
problems.space: O(d) for the weights
problems.description: Teaching the mistake-driven update, quick online baselines on data that is close to linearly separable, and as the unit that a neural network stacks: one neuron with a step activation.

examples.input: What is Novikoff's theorem?
examples.output: If the data is linearly separable with margin gamma and every point has norm at most R, the perceptron makes at most (R/gamma)^2 mistakes, regardless of the order and of the learning rate when starting from zero.

examples.input: What happens on XOR?
examples.output: No line separates XOR, so every pass contains a mistake and the weights cycle forever. A hidden layer or a feature such as the product of the inputs fixes it.

examples.input: How does the perceptron relate to logistic regression and the SVM?
examples.output: Logistic regression replaces the hard mistake test by a smooth loss and gives probabilities. The SVM also seeks a separator but picks the maximum-margin one, while the perceptron returns any separator.

examples.input: Does the learning rate matter?
examples.output: Starting from zero, scaling the rate only rescales $w$ and $b$, so the predictions and mistake count do not change.

constraints: Learning rate $\eta$ (irrelevant for the decisions when starting from zero)
Maximum number of epochs, as a guard on non-separable data
Order of the examples, which changes which separator is found
Whether to include a bias term
