edgeCases: Never converges when the data is not separable; always cap the epochs and track the training error
The result depends on the example order and is not the maximum-margin separator, so it can generalise worse than an SVM
Zero scores count as mistakes; using a strict test instead keeps the all-zero start from ever updating
The bound uses the norm of the input including the constant bias feature

problems.title: Perplexity of a Language Model
problems.summary: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; how many equally likely choices the model is effectively hesitating between at each step.
problems.bruteForce: Comparing models with different tokenizers or vocabularies, where values are not comparable, or judging quality of generated text, since low perplexity does not guarantee helpful or factual output.
problems.intuition: Cross-entropy in nats is hard to feel, but its exponential has a concrete reading: a model that spreads probability uniformly over V tokens has perplexity V. A lower value therefore means the model is effectively choosing among fewer candidates, so it assigns higher probability to the text it actually sees.
problems.whyItWorks: Perplexity is exp of the empirical cross-entropy between the data and the model, so minimising training loss is the same as minimising perplexity. The exponential of an entropy is the effective number of equally likely outcomes, and the geometric mean of inverse token probabilities has the same value, which explains the branching-factor reading.
approach: Turn logits into log-probabilities with a stable log-softmax — avoids overflow and log of zero
Pick the log-probability of each true next token — the model's probability for the actual data
Negate and average over all tokens — this is the cross-entropy in nats
Exponentiate the mean — converts nats into an effective branching factor
problems.time: O(N·V) for N tokens and vocabulary size V
problems.space: O(N·V) for the log-probabilities
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def perplexity(logits, targets):
    z = logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    lse = np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    logp = z - lse
    nll = -logp[np.arange(len(targets)), targets]
    return np.exp(nll.mean())
problems.description: Comparing language models on the same text and tokenizer, tracking validation loss during pretraining, and detecting distribution shift.

examples.input: What does a perplexity of V mean?
examples.output: On average the model is as uncertain as if it picked uniformly among V tokens at each step.

examples.input: Why must the tokenizer be the same when comparing perplexities?
examples.output: Perplexity is per token. A tokenizer that splits text into more tokens spreads the same information over more steps, so per-token numbers are not comparable.

examples.input: How is perplexity related to bits per token?
examples.output: Bits per token is the cross-entropy in base 2, and perplexity equals 2 raised to that value, the same quantity as the natural-log version.

constraints: Context window used to condition each token
Stride when evaluating with a sliding window
Tokenizer and vocabulary
edgeCases: Average over all tokens, not per sequence, or short sequences are over-weighted
Evaluate with enough context; truncated windows inflate perplexity
Mask padding tokens in real code; this version assumes every target is a real token

problems.title: PII Detection and Redaction
problems.summary: Find personal data with pattern detectors, validate card numbers with a checksum, replace each value with a typed, consistent placeholder, and measure the detector with precision and recall.
problems.bruteForce: Do not rely on patterns alone for names, addresses or identifiers that depend on context; those need a named-entity model and human review. Redaction is also not anonymisation, since remaining text can still identify a person.
problems.intuition: Text sent to a model, a log or a training set can carry identifiers that should not travel with it. Fixed formats such as emails and card numbers are easy to match, and a checksum rejects most random digit runs. A typed placeholder keeps the sentence useful, and giving the same value the same placeholder keeps references intact. Names and context-dependent facts have no fixed format, so patterns miss them. Flow: raw text → detect spans → drop overlaps → placeholders → redacted text.
problems.whyItWorks: Emails, phones and IPs have regular structure that regexes capture, and a payment-card number carries a check digit, so about one random digit run in ten passes the Luhn test, which removes most false matches. Keying placeholders on the normalised value makes the map a function from value to token, so repeats stay linked without revealing the value. Precision $TP/(TP+FP)$ and recall $TP/(TP+FN)$ expose both over-redaction and leaks.
approach: Run one regex per type (email, phone, IPv4, card) — each format has a recognisable shape
Validate candidates, Luhn for cards and range for IP octets — cuts false positives from random digits
Resolve overlaps by priority — one character must belong to at most one span
Map each distinct value to <TYPE_n> in order of first appearance — the same value gets the same placeholder
Score detectors on labelled text with $P = TP/(TP+FP)$ and $R = TP/(TP+FN)$ — recall is the privacy risk
problems.time: O(L) per pattern over L characters, plus O(m log m) to sort m matches
problems.space: O(m) for spans and the placeholder map
problems.description: Cleaning text before logging, analytics, fine-tuning data or calls to an external model, where structured identifiers such as emails, phone numbers, IP addresses and card numbers must not leave the system.

examples.input: Why use a Luhn check on card numbers?
examples.output: Any long digit run matches a card regex, but real card numbers satisfy a checksum. About nine in ten random runs fail it, so false positives drop sharply.

examples.input: Why map the same value to the same placeholder?
examples.output: It keeps references and counts intact, so a model can still tell that two mentions are one person or address, without seeing the value.

examples.input: Which metric matters more for a redactor, precision or recall?
examples.output: Usually recall, because a missed identifier is a leak, while a false positive only removes some context. Track both and choose the trade-off per data type.

examples.input: Is redacted text anonymous?
examples.output: No. Names, rare facts or combinations of details can still re-identify someone, and the placeholder map is itself sensitive. Redaction lowers risk but does not guarantee anonymity.

constraints: Set of entity types and their regexes
Overlap priority between types
Placeholder format and whether values are normalised before keying
Minimum digit count for the card detector
edgeCases: Regexes miss names, street addresses and free-form identifiers, so recall on the unchecked classes is unknown
A phone or ID number can pass the card regex, so run the checksum and resolve overlaps
Keeping the value-to-placeholder map next to the redacted text defeats the purpose; store it separately or drop it
Evaluate on labelled synthetic or consented text, never on real people's data, and re-check when formats change

problems.title: Pipeline Parallelism (GPipe Bubble and 1F1B)
problems.summary: Cut the model into $p$ stages of consecutive layers and stream $m$ microbatches through them; the idle warm-up and cool-down form a bubble of fraction $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$, and 1F1B bounds activation memory.
problems.bruteForce: When $m$ is small compared with $p$ (the bubble is large), when stages cannot be balanced, or when the model already fits in memory.
problems.intuition: With one batch, stage $s$ must wait for stage $s-1$, so only one stage works at a time. Splitting the batch into microbatches lets stage $s$ start microbatch 0 while stage $s-1$ moves to microbatch 1. The pipeline still fills and drains, which costs $p-1$ idle steps per stage. 1F1B starts backward passes early so activations are freed sooner. Flow: split layers → feed microbatches → fill, steady state, drain → flush.
problems.whyItWorks: Stage $s$ can process microbatch $j$ once stage $s-1$ has finished it, giving start time $j+s$ and a total of $m+p-1$ steps. Each stage works on $m$ of them, so it idles $p-1$ steps, and the idle fraction is $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$, which shrinks as $m$ grows.
approach: Assign consecutive layers to $p$ stages — each device holds only its slice
Split the batch into $m$ microbatches — creates work that can overlap across stages
Run microbatch $j$ on stage $s$ at step $j+s$ — respects the dependency on stage $s-1$
Count the idle slots — each stage idles $p-1$ of $m+p-1$ steps, the bubble
Reorder with 1F1B: warm-up forwards, alternate forward and backward, cool-down — frees activations early
problems.time: $m+p-1$ steps for $m$ microbatches instead of $m \cdot p$ if run one stage at a time
problems.space: GPipe stores activations for up to $m$ microbatches per stage; 1F1B for about $p$
dryRun: Microbatch $j$ on stage $s$ at step $t = j + s$
problems.description: Models too deep for one device, where layers can be cut into balanced stages and the link between stages only carries activations, which is cheap compared with a per-layer all-reduce.

examples.input: Why does a pipeline have a bubble?
examples.output: The first microbatch must traverse the earlier stages before later stages can start, and the last stages sit idle while the pipeline drains. That is $p-1$ idle steps per stage.

examples.input: How do you shrink the bubble?
examples.output: Use more microbatches, since the fraction is $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$, at the price of smaller microbatches and lower per-step efficiency.

examples.input: What does 1F1B improve over GPipe?
examples.output: The bubble is the same, but backward passes start early, so a stage holds activations for at most about $p$ microbatches instead of all $m$.

constraints: Number of pipeline stages $p$
Number of microbatches $m$
Layer-to-stage assignment (balance of compute per stage)
edgeCases: Unbalanced stages make the slowest stage set the pace for the whole pipeline
Batch normalisation statistics change when the batch is split into microbatches
Gradients from all microbatches must be accumulated before one optimiser step

problems.title: Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
problems.summary: Add a fixed vector of sines and cosines at many frequencies to each token embedding so an order-blind attention layer can tell positions apart.
problems.bruteForce: When learned, relative or rotary position schemes fit better: they are often preferred in modern language models, especially for long contexts. This code also assumes an even dimension $d$.
problems.intuition: Attention treats its input as a set, so something must say where each token sits. Using sinusoids of geometrically spaced wavelengths gives every position a unique code, like the digits of a clock with fast and slow hands, and shifting by a fixed offset becomes a simple rotation of each sin-cos pair.
problems.whyItWorks: Each sin-cos pair at frequency $\omega$ is a point on a circle, and moving $k$ positions rotates that point by angle $\omega k$, which is the same linear map for every starting position. A model can therefore compute relative offsets from the encodings with linear operations, and the many wavelengths make every position's overall code distinct.
approach: Make a column of positions and a row of even dimension indices — one grid covers every (position, dimension) pair
Compute $\mathrm{angle} = \mathrm{pos} / 10000^{i/d}$ — each pair gets its own wavelength, from short to long
Put $\sin(\mathrm{angle})$ in the even columns and $\cos(\mathrm{angle})$ in the odd ones — a pair encodes position on a circle
Add the result to the token embeddings — the model sees content and position together
problems.time: O(T·d) to build the table
problems.space: O(T·d); it can be precomputed once and reused
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def sinusoidal_pe(T, d):
    pos = np.arange(T)[:, None]
    i = np.arange(0, d, 2)[None, :]
    angle = pos / 10000 ** (i / d)
    pe = np.zeros((T, d))
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angle)
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angle)
    return pe
problems.description: Transformers that need order information with no extra parameters and possible use on sequences somewhat longer than seen in training.

examples.input: Why does a transformer need positional encoding?
examples.output: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without position information it cannot distinguish word order.

examples.input: Why sines and cosines of many frequencies?
examples.output: They give each position a unique code, are bounded, and make relative shifts a linear rotation within each pair.

examples.input: Fixed sinusoids versus learned position embeddings?
examples.output: Sinusoids add no parameters and can extrapolate in form, while learned embeddings are flexible but limited to trained positions.

constraints: Model dimension $d$
Base constant (10000 in the original)
Maximum sequence length $T$
edgeCases: The code assumes $d$ is even; odd $d$ needs special handling for the last column
Interleaved sin and cos columns versus concatenated halves are both used; the choice must match the rest of the model
Adding to embeddings without matching scale can drown the content signal

problems.title: PPO Clipped Objective
problems.summary: Improve a policy with several gradient steps on one batch of experience, while clipping the probability ratio so a step cannot move the new policy too far from the one that collected the data.
problems.bruteForce: When sample efficiency from off-policy replay is critical, or in settings with deterministic policies and continuous control tasks where off-policy methods such as SAC are preferred.
problems.intuition: Reusing a batch of data is efficient but dangerous: the further the policy moves from the one that generated the data, the less the advantages mean. PPO measures movement by the ratio of new to old action probability and stops rewarding progress once that ratio leaves a small band around one, in the direction the advantage wants. Taking the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms makes the objective a pessimistic bound, so there is no incentive to push further, but a harmful move is still fully penalised.
problems.whyItWorks: The ratio-weighted advantage is a first-order surrogate for the true improvement that is only valid near the sampling policy. Clipping removes the gradient where the ratio has already moved beyond the band in the favourable direction, which acts as a cheap trust region without the second-order machinery of TRPO. Where the policy moved the wrong way, the unclipped term is the smaller one and keeps its gradient, so mistakes can be corrected.
approach: Store log-probabilities of the sampled actions under the old policy — the fixed reference for the ratio
Compute the ratio exp(logp_new − logp_old) — how much the policy has moved on each sample
Form the unclipped term $\rho \cdot \hat{A}$ and the clipped term $\mathrm{clip}(\rho) \cdot \hat{A}$ — the plain surrogate and its limited version
Take the elementwise minimum and average — a pessimistic bound with no reward for moving too far
Maximise it for a few epochs of minibatch gradient steps — reuse the batch safely
problems.time: O(N) per evaluation for N samples (the policy network dominates the real cost)
problems.space: O(N) for the ratios and advantages
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def ppo_clip_loss(logp_new, logp_old, adv, eps=0.2):
    ratio = np.exp(logp_new - logp_old)
    unclipped = ratio * adv
    clipped = np.clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv
    obj = np.minimum(unclipped, clipped)
    # gradient flows only where the unclipped term is the minimum
    active = unclipped <= clipped
    grad = np.where(active, ratio * adv, 0.0) / len(adv)
    return -obj.mean(), -grad     # loss, dloss/dlogp_new
dryRun: $\frac{\partial L_{CLIP}}{\partial\,\mathrm{logp}_{new}} = \rho\hat{A}$ if unclipped is the min, else 0
problems.description: On-policy deep RL and RLHF fine-tuning of language models, where stable updates with minimal tuning matter and rollouts are expensive to collect.

examples.input: Why take the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms?
examples.output: It makes the objective a lower bound on the unclipped surrogate. Improvements beyond the clip band are not rewarded, while moves in the harmful direction keep their full gradient.

examples.input: When is the gradient zero?
examples.output: For a positive advantage when the ratio is above 1 plus $\epsilon$, and for a negative advantage when the ratio is below 1 minus $\epsilon$. In those regions the clipped term is a constant.

examples.input: How does PPO relate to TRPO?
examples.output: Both limit how far the policy moves per update. TRPO enforces a KL constraint with second-order optimisation, while PPO uses a first-order clipped objective that is simpler to implement.

constraints: Clip range $\epsilon$ (smaller is more conservative)
Number of epochs and minibatches per batch of data
Advantage estimator settings ($\gamma$ and $\lambda$) and normalisation
Value-loss and entropy coefficients when added to the objective
edgeCases: Clipping bounds the gradient incentive, not the actual policy change; large steps can still overshoot the band
Advantages are usually normalised per batch; the sign of $\hat{A}$ decides which side of the band is clipped
Log-probs must be from the policy that sampled the actions and be stored detached
This is only the policy term; real PPO adds a value-function loss and an entropy bonus, and usually early-stops on KL

problems.title: Precision, Recall and F1
problems.summary: Score a binary classifier by how clean its positive predictions are (precision), how many real positives it finds (recall), and their harmonic mean (F1).
problems.bruteForce: Avoid F1 alone when the two error types have very different costs (use an F-beta or a cost-based metric), or when true negatives matter, or for threshold-free comparison (use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC).
problems.intuition: Accuracy hides the cost of rare positives, because predicting "negative" everywhere looks great. Precision asks "when I raise an alarm, how often am I right?" and recall asks "of the real events, how many did I catch?". The harmonic mean punishes a lopsided pair, so F1 is high only when both are.
problems.whyItWorks: All three are ratios of counts from the confusion matrix, and none uses true negatives, so a flood of easy negatives cannot inflate them. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller of the two numbers, which is why you cannot buy a good F1 by maximising just one side.
approach: Count TP, FP and FN from predictions and labels — every metric is built from these
Precision is TP over predicted positives — it measures false alarms
Recall is TP over actual positives — it measures misses
Guard zero denominators — a model with no positives would divide by zero
F1 is the harmonic mean of the two — it needs both to be good
problems.time: O(n) to count the confusion matrix
problems.space: O(1) beyond the inputs
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def confusion(y, pred):
    tp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 1))
    fp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 0))
    fn = np.sum((pred == 0) & (y == 1))
    return tp, fp, fn

def prf1(y, pred):
    tp, fp, fn = confusion(y, pred)
    p = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    r = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r) if p + r else 0.0
    return p, r, f1
problems.description: Imbalanced problems such as fraud, defect or disease detection, and any time false positives and false negatives have different costs.

examples.input: Why the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
examples.output: The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide a very low recall behind a high precision.

examples.input: How does raising the threshold move precision and recall?
examples.output: Fewer samples are called positive, so precision usually rises and recall falls.

examples.input: When prefer recall over precision?
examples.output: When misses are costlier than false alarms, such as screening for a serious disease.

examples.input: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
examples.output: A classifier that always predicts the majority class scores high accuracy while finding no positives.

constraints: Decision threshold on the predicted probability (moves the precision-recall trade-off)
Averaging for multiclass (macro, micro, weighted)
$\beta$ in F-beta (weights recall over precision when above one)
edgeCases: Precision and recall are undefined with no predicted or no actual positives; pick an explicit convention
Micro, macro and weighted averages tell different stories on imbalanced classes
F1 depends on the threshold, so compare models at tuned thresholds
Ignores true negatives, which can hide poor performance on the majority class

problems.title: Probability Calibration
problems.summary: A model is calibrated when, among predictions of probability $p$, about a fraction $p$ are actually positive. Measure it with a reliability diagram, expected calibration error and the Brier score.
problems.bruteForce: If only the ranking matters (AUC), calibration adds nothing. Binned ECE is noisy with few samples, so do not over-read a single number.
problems.intuition: Ranking quality and honesty of probabilities are different things: a model can order examples perfectly yet say 99% for things that happen far less often. Bin the predictions, and in each bin compare the average predicted probability with the observed frequency of positives; the gap is the miscalibration, and decisions based on expected cost depend on it.
problems.whyItWorks: If predictions are calibrated, $E[y\,|\,\hat{p}=p]=p$, so every bin's observed rate matches its mean prediction. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probabilities and is a proper scoring rule, so it is minimised only by the true probabilities and rewards both calibration and sharpness. ECE summarises the bin gaps, weighted by bin size.
approach: Hold out data the model never trained on — in-sample probabilities are too confident
Cut $[0,1]$ into equal-width bins and assign each prediction — groups predictions of similar confidence
Per bin, compute the observed positive rate and the mean predicted probability — the two sides of the reliability diagram
Weight the absolute gaps by bin size to get ECE — one summary number
Compute the Brier score too — it needs no binning and is a proper scoring rule
If miscalibrated, fit a monotone map (Platt, isotonic or temperature) on separate data — it fixes probabilities without changing the ranking
problems.time: O(n) for binning, Brier and ECE
problems.space: O(n_bins) beyond the input arrays
problems.description: Whenever probabilities feed decisions (thresholds, costs, risk scores, ensembles), after training boosted trees, SVMs or networks that tend to be over- or under-confident.

examples.input: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated?
examples.output: Among all cases given probability $p$, the observed positive rate is $p$; the reliability diagram then lies on the diagonal.

examples.input: How is the Brier score related to calibration?
examples.output: It is the squared error of the probabilities and a proper scoring rule, so it improves with better calibration and with sharper, more discriminative predictions.

examples.input: How do you fix a miscalibrated model?
examples.output: Fit a monotone post-hoc map such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling on held-out data; ranking and AUC stay the same.

constraints: n_bins — fewer bins are stable but coarse, more bins are noisy
Binning strategy — equal-width (this code) or equal-frequency quantiles
Calibrator — Platt (sigmoid), isotonic or temperature scaling
edgeCases: Calibrating on the training data, or on the same data used to evaluate it
ECE depends on the bin count and is noisy in sparsely populated bins
Isotonic regression can overfit when the calibration set is small
A calibrated model can still be a poor classifier; check discrimination as well

problems.title: Probability Distributions and Sampling
problems.summary: The handful of distributions ML leans on (Bernoulli, Binomial, Categorical, Gaussian, Poisson, Exponential) and how to draw samples from them using only uniform random numbers.
problems.bruteForce: Inverse transform needs a CDF you can invert; for awkward densities use rejection sampling or MCMC. In practice call the library sampler (it is faster and well tested) and keep these versions for understanding.
problems.intuition: Each distribution is a model of one kind of randomness: a coin flip, a count of flips, a choice among classes, a sum of many small effects, rare events in a window, a waiting time. Sampling reduces them all to the uniform draw $u$: push $u$ through the inverse CDF, $x = F^{-1}(u)$, and $x$ has CDF $F$, because $F^{-1}$ just reshuffles probability mass. Box-Muller is the same idea in two dimensions, because the Gaussian CDF has no closed-form inverse. Flow: uniform $u$ → inverse CDF or transform → sample from the target.
problems.whyItWorks: If $U$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ then $P(F^{-1}(U) \leq x) = F(x)$, because the event is $U \leq F(x)$. So the transformed variable has CDF $F$. For a categorical the CDF is the cumulative sum of the probabilities, and the sample is the first index whose cumulative sum exceeds $u$. For Box-Muller, the squared radius of a 2-D standard normal is exponential with rate $1/2$ and the angle is uniform, so $r=\sqrt{-2\ln u_1}$ and $\theta=2\pi u_2$ reproduce a standard normal pair.
approach: Draw uniform numbers $u$ on $(0,1)$ — the only randomness the sampler needs
For a categorical, build the cumulative sum of the probabilities — it is the discrete CDF
Find where $u$ lands in that cumulative sum with a binary search — the landing index is the class
For an exponential, invert the CDF to get $-\ln(1-u)/\lambda$ — closed-form inverse transform
For a Gaussian, turn two uniforms into a radius and an angle and take the cosine — Box-Muller, since no closed-form inverse exists
Check samples against the theory, via mean, variance or a KS test — catches a wrong transform
problems.time: O(n) for n samples; categorical adds O(n log K) for the binary search over K classes
problems.space: O(n) for the samples, O(K) for the cumulative sum
problems.description: Simulating data, Monte Carlo estimates, sampling from a softmax or a noise model, and understanding which likelihood matches which kind of data: Bernoulli for binary labels, Categorical for classes, Gaussian for real values, Poisson for counts, Exponential for waiting times.

examples.input: How do you sample from any distribution given only uniform numbers?
examples.output: Apply the inverse CDF: if $U$ is uniform then $F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$. It works whenever the CDF can be inverted, numerically if not in closed form.

examples.input: How do you sample from a categorical distribution?
examples.output: Take the cumulative sum of the probabilities, draw $u$ uniform, and return the first index whose cumulative value exceeds $u$.

examples.input: Why is Box-Muller needed for the Gaussian?
examples.output: The Gaussian CDF has no closed-form inverse. Box-Muller uses the fact that a 2-D standard normal has an exponential squared radius and a uniform angle.

examples.input: How are the Bernoulli, Binomial and Poisson related?
examples.output: A Binomial is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli draws, and with $n$ large and $p$ small, Binomial$(n,p)$ approaches Poisson with $\lambda = np$.

constraints: Binomial and Poisson parameters $n$, $p$, $\lambda$ (the rate)
Gaussian mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ (scale the standard normal as $\mu + \sigma z$)
Number of samples $n$ (error of a sample mean shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$)
Random seed or generator for reproducibility
edgeCases: rng.random() can return exactly $0$, so use $1-u$ inside the logarithm to avoid $\ln 0$
A cumulative sum of probabilities can end at $0.9999999$ instead of $1$; clip the index so a draw near $1$ stays in range
Box-Muller gives a pair per two uniforms; this version uses only the cosine, which is correct but wastes half the work
The exponential is parameterised by rate $\lambda$ here; many libraries use scale $1/\lambda$

problems.title: Prompt Injection Defence in Depth
problems.summary: Untrusted text can carry instructions the model may follow. Defend with layers: delimit untrusted data, screen it, restrict tools, ask for confirmation on risky actions, and check outputs.
problems.bruteForce: Do not rely on these steps alone: delimiters and regex screening do not stop a determined attacker. They are cheap layers to combine with tool restrictions, not a replacement for them.
problems.intuition: A language model reads instructions and data as one stream of tokens, so nothing in the model itself marks a sentence in a web page as data rather than a command. Prompt wording can lower the risk but cannot enforce a boundary, so the strong controls live outside the model: what the tools are allowed to do and who confirms. Assume some injection succeeds and limit the damage. Flow: untrusted text → wrap → detect → gate tools → confirm → validate output.
problems.whyItWorks: A random nonce delimiter cannot be forged by text written before the nonce exists, and removing it from the data guarantees the wrapper has exactly one closing marker. The tool gate works because it is ordinary code that the model cannot talk its way past. If layer $i$ blocks an attack with probability $q_i$ and layers fail independently, the attack passes all of them with probability $\prod_i (1 - q_i)$, so each added layer multiplies the risk down.
approach: Wrap untrusted text in delimiters with a random nonce — the attacker cannot guess the closing marker
Strip the nonce and fake markers from the text — the data cannot close its own wrapper
Scan for known injection phrasing and log matches — a weak signal for review, not a boundary
Gate every tool call against an allow-list policy — least privilege limits what a hijacked model can do
Require human confirmation for dangerous actions and validate outputs — the last layers before real effects
problems.time: O(L) for wrapping and regex screening of L characters; O(1) per gate check
problems.space: O(L) for the wrapped copy of the text
problems.description: Any application that feeds web pages, emails, documents, tool results or user uploads into a model, especially when the model can call tools that read private data or change something.

examples.input: Why can't a system prompt alone prevent injection?
examples.output: The model processes instructions and data as one token stream, so a system prompt is only a strong hint. It is not an access control, and a crafted input can still override it.

examples.input: What is the single most effective control?
examples.output: Least privilege on tools: if the model cannot send email or read secrets, a successful injection has little to abuse. Confirmation by a human for risky actions adds a hard stop.

examples.input: Why use a random nonce in the delimiter?
examples.output: A fixed delimiter can be copied into the untrusted text to close the data block early. A random one is unknown to the attacker, and any copy that appears is removed anyway.

constraints: Which tools and actions the policy allows
Which actions require human confirmation
Detector pattern list and how matches are used (log, block, or review)
Number and independence of defence layers
edgeCases: Regex detection is trivially bypassed by rephrasing, translation or encoding; treat a match as a signal, never as a guarantee
The product formula assumes independent layers; layers that share a weakness, such as the same model, block less than it predicts
Model output is untrusted too: rendering it as HTML or running it as a command reopens the hole
No prompt-only defence is complete, so design the system to stay safe when an injection succeeds

problems.title: Systematic Prompt Optimisation
problems.summary: Improve a prompt by search instead of by feel: fix a metric and a dev set, propose candidate prompts, score each, keep the best, and report the uncertainty of every score.
problems.bruteForce: No reliable metric exists, or the dev set is tiny, where the search mostly fits noise. A one-off prompt used once is not worth a search.
problems.intuition: A prompt is a discrete parameter and the dev-set accuracy is a noisy objective, so tuning it is hyperparameter search. With $n$ examples a score has a standard error near $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, so a gain of two points on 100 examples is usually noise. Pair the candidates on the same examples, measure the gap with a bootstrap, and keep a final test set that the search never touched. Flow: metric → candidates → score on dev → keep best → confirm on test.
problems.whyItWorks: Scoring candidates on the same examples makes the comparison paired, which cancels example difficulty and shrinks the variance of the gap. The Wilson interval stays inside $[0, 1]$ and behaves well for small $n$ or extreme $p$, unlike the normal approximation. The hill climb only accepts strict improvements, so the dev score cannot fall.
approach: Define the metric and split the data into dev and test — the test set is touched once, at the end
Score the start prompt on dev with $\hat{p} = k/n$ — a baseline to beat
Apply each mutation to the current best prompt — candidates come from edits, not guesses
Keep a candidate only if its dev score is higher — greedy, so the history never decreases
Compare finalists with a paired bootstrap and Wilson intervals — shows whether the gap is real
problems.time: O(m·n) model calls for m candidates on n dev examples; bootstrap adds O(B·n)
problems.space: O(n) per-example correctness vector for each candidate
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def wilson_interval(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    d = 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d
    h = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return c - h, c + h

def evaluate(prompt, dataset, model_fn):
    return np.array([model_fn(prompt, x) == y
                     for x, y in dataset], float)

def hill_climb(start, mutations, dataset, model_fn):
    best = start
    best_s = evaluate(best, dataset, model_fn).mean()
    history = [best_s]
    for mutate in mutations:
        cand = mutate(best)
        s = evaluate(cand, dataset, model_fn).mean()
        if s > best_s:
            best, best_s = cand, s
        history.append(best_s)
    return best, history

def paired_bootstrap_prob(a, b, n_boot=2000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(a)
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(n_boot, n))
    gap = (np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b))[idx].mean(axis=1)
    return (gap > 0).mean() + 0.5 * (gap == 0).mean()
dryRun: P(A beats B) = share of resamples, $\bar{d} > 0$
problems.description: A prompt is going into a product and you can write a metric and collect a few hundred labelled examples. Also for choosing between a handful of hand-written variants.

examples.input: Why report an interval and not just the accuracy?
examples.output: On a small dev set the standard error is several points, so two prompts that differ by one or two points are statistically indistinguishable.

examples.input: Why a paired bootstrap?
examples.output: Both prompts are scored on the same examples, so resampling examples and comparing the difference removes the shared example difficulty and gives a tighter estimate of the gap.

examples.input: How do you avoid overfitting the dev set?
examples.output: Every comparison made against the dev set leaks a little of it into the prompt, so keep a separate test set, score only the final prompt on it, and limit the number of candidates tried.

constraints: Dev and test set sizes
Number of candidates and mutation operators
Confidence level $z$ (1.96 for 95 percent)
Bootstrap resamples $B$ and seed
edgeCases: Selecting the best of many candidates on the dev set inflates its score, so the winner's dev accuracy overstates its real accuracy
A model sampled at nonzero temperature makes scores noisy; fix the seed, or average several runs
Greedy hill-climbing stops at the first local optimum; it does not explore edits that only help in combination

problems.title: Prompt Templates and Safe Variable Filling
problems.summary: A prompt template has named placeholders filled from variables, with strict checks for missing or extra values, delimiters around untrusted text, a token budget, and a version label.
problems.bruteForce: One-off exploratory prompts. Delimiters reduce but do not remove prompt injection, so they are not a substitute for permission checks on tools and outputs.
problems.intuition: A template separates fixed instructions from variable data, and that boundary is a security boundary. If user text is pasted in raw, it can contain placeholders, braces or a closing tag and rewrite the prompt. Filling in a single pass, wrapping untrusted values in delimiters, and removing the delimiter from the value keeps data as data. Flow: template → check variables → wrap untrusted → fill → fit budget.
problems.whyItWorks: A single left-to-right substitution pass never re-reads inserted text, so a value like "{secret}" stays literal and cannot pull in another variable. Removing the delimiter from the value until none remains guarantees the block ends only where the template ends it. Whitespace tokens are only an approximation, so real systems count with the model's own tokenizer.
approach: Parse $\{name\}$ placeholders and treat doubled braces as literals — the template declares exactly what it needs
Raise on missing or extra variables — a typo fails loudly instead of leaking a raw placeholder
Fill in one regex pass over the template — braces inside values are never re-expanded
Wrap untrusted values in delimiters and strip the delimiter from the value — user text cannot close the block
Truncate the long variable to the token budget left after the fixed text — the prompt always fits
problems.time: O(L) per render for template plus values of total length L
problems.space: O(L) for the rendered prompt
problems.description: Any application that builds prompts from variables: chat apps, RAG prompts with retrieved passages, extraction jobs, evaluation harnesses where the same instructions run over many inputs.

examples.input: How can a user value break a naive template?
examples.output: If values are substituted repeatedly or the delimiter is not stripped, user text can add placeholders or close the data block and inject its own instructions.

examples.input: Why raise on extra variables as well as missing ones?
examples.output: An extra variable usually means a renamed or misspelled placeholder, so the intended data silently never reaches the prompt.

examples.input: Why version templates?
examples.output: Prompt wording changes model behaviour, so pinning a version lets you reproduce results, compare changes and roll back.

examples.input: Do delimiters stop prompt injection?
examples.output: No. They help the model see where data starts and ends, but the model can still follow instructions inside the data, so other defences are needed.

constraints: Delimiter strings (tags that cannot occur in normal data)
Token limit $L$ and which variable absorbs truncation
Strict or lenient handling of missing and extra variables
Template version pinned per deployment
edgeCases: Using str.format on user-controlled templates lets values reach attributes; use a fixed regex filler
Stripping the delimiter once can leave a rebuilt delimiter such as </da</data>ta>; strip until stable
Whitespace tokens undercount for real tokenizers, so leave a safety margin below the true context limit
Truncating the middle or end of a variable may drop the part that matters; choose what to cut deliberately

problems.title: Prompt Versioning, Regression Gates and Canary Rollout
problems.summary: Treat prompts like code: store immutable content-hashed versions in a registry, gate each release on a paired comparison against the old prompt, and roll out to a small hashed slice of users first.
problems.bruteForce: One-off scripts or notebooks. A significance gate on a tiny eval set has almost no power, so with few examples rely on review of the failures instead of a p-value.
problems.intuition: A prompt edit changes behaviour as surely as a code edit, but it is easy to tweak in place and lose track of what is live. Hashing the normalised text gives every version an identity that cannot drift, so a log line names exactly what ran. To release, run old and new on the same fixed examples and look only at the examples where they disagree: if the new prompt loses far more of those than it wins, the sign test says the drop is not luck. Canary routing by user hash then limits the damage of anything the eval set missed. Flow: edit → hash → register → eval gate → canary → full rollout.
problems.whyItWorks: A cryptographic hash makes accidental collisions between different texts negligible, so the id identifies the text. For the gate, under the null hypothesis that old and new are equally good, each disagreement is equally likely to favour either prompt, so the number favouring old is $\mathrm{Binomial}(b+c, 1/2)$ and the exact tail gives a valid p-value without a normal approximation. A uniform hash sends each user to the canary independently with probability close to the chosen fraction, and always to the same side.
approach: Normalise the template and hash it — the same text always gets the same id, any edit changes it
Register name, version label and note; refuse to overwrite a label — versions stay immutable and the changelog is the notes
Score old and new prompts on the same fixed eval set — paired results remove example difficulty from the comparison
Count $b$ examples only new gets right and $c$ only old gets right, drop ties — only disagreements carry information
Fail the gate if the one-sided sign test on $c$ out of $b+c$ gives $p < \alpha$ — blocks a prompt that is significantly worse
Route a user to the new prompt if a hash of the user id mapped to $[0,1)$ is below the fraction — each user sees one version consistently
problems.time: O(len(prompt)) to hash; O(n) pairs plus an exact binomial tail for the gate
problems.space: O(number of versions) in the registry; O(n) for the eval results
dryRun: $b$ = new right only, $c$ = old right only
problems.description: Any product where prompts change over time and several people edit them, so you need to know which text produced which answer, to roll back quickly, and to stop a change that quietly lowers quality.

examples.input: Why use a paired test instead of comparing the two accuracies?
examples.output: Both prompts see the same examples, so most of the variation comes from example difficulty. Pairing cancels it, and only the examples where the prompts disagree decide the result.

examples.input: Why hash the user id for canary routing instead of random choice per request?
examples.output: Hashing keeps each user on one version across requests, so their experience is consistent and results are comparable, and the assignment can be reproduced from logs.

examples.input: Is a passing gate proof that the new prompt is as good?
examples.output: No. Failing to detect a drop is not evidence of no drop, especially with a small eval set. Use a tolerance or confidence bound, keep the eval set representative, and still monitor the canary.

constraints: Significance level $\alpha$ of the gate
Size and coverage of the fixed eval set
Canary fraction and the ramp schedule
Normalisation rules applied before hashing
edgeCases: Reusing the eval set while tuning the prompt overfits it; keep a held-out set for the gate
Many releases each tested at $\alpha$ will sometimes pass a worse prompt by chance, so track results over time
Changing the salt reshuffles every user between old and new, which breaks comparisons
Versioning the template alone misses model, temperature and tool changes that also alter behaviour

problems.title: Generators and Functional Python for Data Pipelines
problems.summary: Generators produce items one at a time on demand, so a pipeline of small generator stages streams data of any size in constant memory. Closures, partial, caching and decorators compose the stages.
problems.bruteForce: When you need random access, the length, or several passes over the same data: a generator is one-shot, so materialise it as a list. Memoising impure functions or unhashable arguments is also wrong.
problems.intuition: A generator function is a paused computation: each `next` runs it to the next `yield` and freezes its state. Chaining generators makes every item flow through all stages before the next item is read, so nothing is materialised. The price is that a generator is one-shot: once consumed it is empty. Flow: source → clean (lazy) → batch (lazy) → consumer pulls.
problems.whyItWorks: Calling a generator function returns an iterator that holds only its frame, not the results. Each `next` resumes the frame, so work happens when a value is demanded. `islice` on a shared iterator advances it, which is why consecutive batches do not overlap. `reduce` threads one value through the list of functions in order.
approach: Write each stage as a generator that takes an iterable and yields items — stages stay small and testable
Chain stages by passing one generator into the next — nothing runs until a consumer pulls
Group items with batched using islice on one shared iterator — each batch continues where the last stopped
Combine functions with compose or functools.partial — fixes arguments and builds a pipeline from parts
Wrap pure, expensive functions with a memoize decorator — repeated arguments return the stored result
problems.time: O(1) per item pulled; whole pipeline O(N) time
problems.space: O(1) for the stages plus O(n) for one batch, instead of O(N) for the full list
dryRun: List of $n$ items of size $s$: $n \cdot s$ bytes
problems.description: Reading files, streams or database cursors too large for memory, feeding mini-batches to training, and any multi-stage transform where you want one pass and early exit.

examples.input: Difference between an iterator and a generator?
examples.output: An iterator is any object with __next__ and __iter__. A generator is an iterator created by a function with yield or a generator expression, which keeps its local state between calls.

examples.input: Why does a generator give nothing the second time?
examples.output: It is a one-shot iterator: after StopIteration its frame is finished. Re-create it or store the items in a list if you need another pass.

examples.input: What does yield from do?
examples.output: It delegates to a sub-iterator, yielding each of its items, and returns the sub-generator's return value. It replaces a for loop with yield.

examples.input: When is lru_cache or a memoize decorator safe?
examples.output: For pure functions with hashable arguments. A cache of an impure function returns stale results and an unbounded cache grows without limit.

constraints: Batch size $n$ for batched
maxsize of lru_cache (None means unbounded)
Order of stages in compose
Prefetch or buffer size when overlapping reading with compute
edgeCases: Iterating a generator twice silently yields nothing the second time, for example calling len or sum then looping
Late binding in closures: lambdas created in a loop all see the final loop variable unless it is bound as a default argument
Memoizing with unhashable arguments such as lists raises TypeError, and unbounded caches leak memory
An exception inside a stage surfaces only when the consumer pulls, which can hide the real source of the bug

problems.title: Dataclasses, Protocols and Pipelines for ML Code
problems.summary: Frozen dataclasses hold validated configs, a Protocol states which methods a component must have, and a Pipeline composes components that follow the fit, transform and predict convention.
problems.bruteForce: Tiny one-off scripts where a function is enough, or deep inheritance hierarchies to share a few lines; prefer composition and plain functions there.
problems.intuition: Structure ML code around data and small interfaces, not deep class trees. A config is a value, so make it immutable and check it once at construction. A component is anything with the right methods, so a Protocol accepts it by shape, with no common base class. A pipeline holds its steps instead of inheriting from them, which keeps each piece testable and swappable. Flow: config → validate → steps fit/transform → model fit/predict.
problems.whyItWorks: A frozen dataclass makes assignment raise, so a config cannot drift after validation, and `__post_init__` runs on every construction path. A Protocol checks structure instead of ancestry, so independent classes interoperate. Fitting each step on the previous step's output is exactly manual chaining, and keeping fitted state on the object lets the same transform be applied to new data.
approach: Declare the config as a frozen dataclass with defaults — immutable values cannot change mid-run
Use field(default_factory=...) for mutable defaults and check ranges in __post_init__ — bad configs fail at creation
Define a Protocol with the methods a step needs — any class with them qualifies, no inheritance
Write steps as fit returning self plus transform or predict — chaining and uniform handling follow
Compose steps in a Pipeline that fits each on the output of the previous — mirrors manual chaining
problems.time: Pipeline fit and predict cost the sum of the step costs; validation is O(1)
problems.space: O(d) per fitted scaler (mean and scale) plus the model state
problems.description: Experiment configs, reusable preprocessing and model components, and any code that swaps parts (scalers, models, metrics) behind a common method set so that training and serving share one code path.

examples.input: Protocol versus abc.ABC?
examples.output: ABC is nominal: a class must inherit from it. A Protocol is structural: any class with the right methods matches, and runtime_checkable allows isinstance, which only checks method names exist.

examples.input: Why a frozen dataclass for configs?
examples.output: Assignment raises FrozenInstanceError, so a config cannot be changed after validation, and with immutable fields it is hashable and safe to log and compare.

examples.input: Why default_factory instead of a default list?
examples.output: A literal mutable default would be shared by all instances, and dataclasses reject it with a ValueError. default_factory builds a fresh object per instance.

examples.input: Why must a scaler be fitted on training data only?
examples.output: Fitting on test data leaks its statistics into training. The pipeline fits the scaler on the training set and reuses its stored mean and scale for new data.

constraints: Config fields with sensible defaults (learning rate, epochs)
Validation bounds enforced in __post_init__
Order of pipeline steps
Zero-variance handling in the scaler (scale set to 1)
edgeCases: frozen=True blocks rebinding only; a list or dict field can still be mutated in place
isinstance against a runtime_checkable Protocol checks that methods exist, not their signatures or behaviour
Fitting a scaler on all data before the split leaks test statistics; fit inside the training fold
A fit that returns None instead of self breaks chaining such as scaler.fit(X).transform(X)

problems.title: PyTorch Training Loop Anatomy
problems.summary: One training step is zero the gradients, forward, loss, backward, optionally clip, then step. Evaluation switches to eval mode and turns off gradient tracking.
problems.bruteForce: Accumulation does not reproduce batch statistics for batch norm, and with a sum-reduced or uneven microbatch loss the $1/k$ scaling must be adjusted. Clipping hides problems if gradients are constantly clipped.
problems.intuition: PyTorch accumulates into .grad on every backward call instead of overwriting it, so the order of the steps carries the meaning. Clear first, or old gradients leak into the new step. Clip after backward (the gradient must exist) and before step (it must be used). The same accumulation lets $k$ microbatches imitate one large batch: scale each loss by $1/k$ and the summed gradient is the mean over all of the data. Dropout and batch norm act differently in train and eval mode, so evaluation also needs the mode switch. Flow: zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → clip → step.
problems.whyItWorks: Gradients are linear in the loss, so the sum of gradients of $L_i/k$ over $k$ equal microbatches equals the gradient of their mean loss, which is the gradient of the large batch. Calling $\mathrm{zero\_grad}$ before backward makes each step start from zero, and no_grad prevents building a graph that evaluation does not need.
approach: Call $\mathrm{zero\_grad}$ — backward adds to existing gradients
Run the forward pass in train mode and compute the loss — builds the graph
Call backward — fills .grad for every parameter
Clip the global gradient norm if wanted — after backward, before step
Call the optimiser step — updates parameters from the gradients
problems.time: One forward and backward pass per microbatch plus one optimiser step
problems.space: Activations of one microbatch; accumulation avoids holding the full batch
problems.solution:
import torch

def train_step(model, xb, yb, loss_fn, opt, clip=None):
    model.train()
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
    loss.backward()
    if clip is not None:
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), clip)
    opt.step()
    return loss.item()

def accumulate_step(model, microbatches, loss_fn, opt):
    model.train()
    opt.zero_grad()
    k = len(microbatches)
    for xb, yb in microbatches:
        (loss_fn(model(xb), yb) / k).backward()
    opt.step()

def evaluate(model, loader, loss_fn):
    model.eval()
    total, n = 0.0, 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for xb, yb in loader:
            total += loss_fn(model(xb), yb).item() * len(xb)
            n += len(xb)
    return total / n
problems.description: Every PyTorch training job; gradient accumulation when the desired batch does not fit in memory, clipping when loss spikes appear.

examples.input: Why must zero_grad be called every step?
examples.output: Backward adds into the existing gradients rather than replacing them, so without clearing, the gradient is the sum over steps.

examples.input: How does gradient accumulation match a large batch?
examples.output: Scale each microbatch mean loss by $1/k$, call backward on each, and step once; the summed gradient equals the gradient of the mean over all samples.

examples.input: What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() each do?
examples.output: eval switches layers such as dropout and batch norm to inference behaviour; no_grad stops graph construction. They are independent, so evaluation needs both.

examples.input: Where does gradient clipping go?
examples.output: After backward, so gradients exist, and before the optimiser step, so the step uses the clipped values.

constraints: Batch size and number of accumulation steps $k$
Learning rate
Clipping threshold $\tau$
edgeCases: Forgetting zero_grad, so each step uses the sum of all past gradients
Forgetting model.eval() or no_grad, which keeps dropout active and wastes memory in evaluation
Not dividing each microbatch loss by $k$, which makes the update $k$ times too large
Clipping before backward or after step, which has no effect on the update

problems.title: Tabular Q-Learning
problems.summary: Learn the value of every state-action pair from experience by nudging each estimate toward the reward plus the discounted best value of the next state.
problems.bruteForce: Large or continuous state spaces, where a table is infeasible and function approximation can make updates unstable. Also not when transitions are costly to sample and a model is available.
problems.intuition: $Q(s, a)$ should equal the reward you get now plus the value of playing optimally afterwards. Each step turns that definition into an update: compare the current estimate with reward plus discounted best next value, and move a little toward it. Because the target uses the max, the agent learns the optimal policy even while it explores randomly.
problems.whyItWorks: The optimal Q-function is the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, which is a contraction for discount below one. Q-learning applies that operator to sampled transitions, so with every pair visited often enough and suitable step sizes the estimates converge to the optimum. Using the max makes it off-policy.
approach: Initialise the $Q$ table to zeros — a neutral starting estimate
Pick an action $\epsilon$-greedily in the current state — mostly exploit, sometimes explore
Step the environment to get reward and next state — one real transition
Form the target $r + \gamma \max Q(\mathrm{next})$ and move $Q(s,a)$ toward it by $\alpha$ — the temporal-difference update
Repeat over many episodes and read the policy as argmax over actions — the learned behaviour
problems.time: O(episodes · steps · |A|) for the max over actions
problems.space: O(|S|·|A|) for the Q table
problems.description: Small discrete state and action spaces, such as grids and toy control tasks, or as the conceptual base of DQN.

examples.input: Why is Q-learning off-policy?
examples.output: The target uses the max over next actions, the greedy policy, no matter which action the exploring behaviour policy actually took.

examples.input: How does Q-learning differ from SARSA?
examples.output: SARSA bootstraps from the action actually taken next, so it learns the value of the exploring policy. Q-learning bootstraps from the max, learning the optimal value.

examples.input: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
examples.output: The agent must try uncertain actions to find better ones but also use what it knows. $\epsilon$-greedy mixes the two with a random-action probability.

constraints: Learning rate $\alpha$ (use a smaller $\alpha$ or decay it in stochastic environments)
Discount $\gamma$
Exploration rate $\epsilon$ (often decayed over training)
Number of episodes
Initial $Q$ values (optimistic values encourage exploration)
edgeCases: Terminal states must have value zero; here their rows stay zero because they are never updated
The environment is deterministic here; stochastic transitions need decaying step sizes
Starting each episode from a random state is a simplification that aids exploration of all pairs
Max over noisy estimates is biased upward (overestimation); Double Q-learning corrects it

problems.title: QLoRA and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)
problems.summary: Store a frozen base model in 4 bits using 16 levels placed at normal quantiles, quantised in blocks, and train only 16-bit LoRA adapters on top.
problems.bruteForce: Weights that are far from normal, very small models where memory is not the constraint, or deployments needing the fastest possible matmul, since 4-bit weights must be dequantised before use.
problems.intuition: Trained weights are roughly bell shaped, so evenly spaced 4-bit levels waste codes in the sparse tails while crowding too few near zero. Placing the 16 levels at quantiles of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ gives each level about equal probability mass, and splitting the weights into small blocks with their own scale keeps the normal assumption true locally and contains outliers to one block. Flow: weights → scale per block → round to levels → dequantise.
problems.whyItWorks: If weights follow $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, then after dividing by the block maximum they sit in $[-1,1]$ with a roughly normal shape. Levels at equal-probability quantiles make the expected rounding error small for that shape. Including $0$ exactly matters because padding and many weights are exactly zero. Blocking limits each scale to 64 weights, so the scale overhead of $32/64 = 0.5$ bits per weight is cut by quantising the scales to 8 bits (double quantisation). Gradients flow through the dequantised weights to the 16-bit LoRA adapters while the 4-bit base is never updated.
approach: Build 16 levels from normal quantiles, normalised to $[-1,1]$ with $0$ included — a level for exact zeros and both extremes
Split weights into blocks of 64 — one outlier then only affects its own block
Scale each block by its $\max|w|$ — maps the block into $[-1,1]$ where the levels live
Store the index of the nearest level plus the block scale — 4 bits per weight
Dequantise by level times scale in the forward pass — the base stays frozen while 16-bit LoRA adapters train
problems.time: O(n·16) to quantise n weights by nearest-level search, O(n) to dequantise
problems.space: About 0.5 byte per parameter plus 0.127 bits per parameter for double-quantised scales
dryRun: levels $=$ quantiles of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, divided by max
problems.description: Fine-tuning a large model on a GPU too small to hold it in 16 bits: the frozen base sits in 4 bits and only small adapters and their optimiser state use higher precision.

examples.input: Why 4-bit NormalFloat instead of uniform 4-bit integers?
examples.output: Weights are close to normal, so quantile-spaced levels give each code about equal probability and lower average error than evenly spaced levels, which waste codes in the tails.

examples.input: Why must zero be an exact level?
examples.output: Zeros and near-zero weights are common, and representing them exactly avoids adding noise. The construction uses 8 positive, 7 negative levels and an explicit zero for this reason.

examples.input: What does double quantisation save?
examples.output: The per-block scales cost $32/64 = 0.5$ bits per parameter in fp32. Quantising the scales to 8 bits shrinks that to about $0.127$ bits per parameter.

examples.input: What is trained in QLoRA?
examples.output: Only the 16-bit LoRA adapters. The 4-bit base is frozen, dequantised on the fly for forward and backward passes, and gradients reach the adapters through it.

constraints: Block size $B$ (64 in the paper)
Whether to use double quantisation
LoRA rank and scaling $\alpha$ for the adapters
Compute dtype used after dequantisation (bfloat16, float16)
edgeCases: The exact level values come from the paper's specific construction (the asymmetric split and the offset); this card reproduces that construction, so treat small differences from a library's table as construction details, not bugs
Smaller blocks cut error but raise scale overhead; $B = 64$ is a trade-off
This code stores indices as uint8 for clarity; real storage packs two 4-bit codes per byte
Dequantisation happens on every forward pass, so 4-bit saves memory, not necessarily time

problems.title: Query Transformation and HyDE
problems.summary: Fix the mismatch between a short question and answer-like documents before searching: embed a hypothetical answer (HyDE), search with several paraphrases and fuse the ranks, or rewrite the query using the chat history.
problems.bruteForce: Latency- or cost-sensitive paths, queries that are exact identifiers or keywords, and topics the generator knows nothing about, where its hypothetical text can point the wrong way.
problems.intuition: A question and its answer rarely look alike, and an embedding of a short question can land far from the passage that answers it. HyDE has the language model write a plausible answer first and embeds that instead: it is document-shaped, so it lands in the right neighbourhood even if its facts are wrong, because only the neighbourhood is used and the results are real documents. Multi-query search hedges by asking several ways and fusing the rankings. Flow: question → hypothetical answer → embedding → nearest real documents.
problems.whyItWorks: The encoder compresses text into a vector that keeps topic and style but discards much exact detail, so an invented answer on the right topic is close to real answers on that topic. The score used here for fusion, $\sum_{r} \frac{1}{k+\mathrm{rank}_r(d)}$, rewards documents ranked high by any list and still favours those found by several, with $k$ damping the lead of a single top rank.
approach: Pick the transformation — rewrite from chat history, paraphrase several ways, or generate a hypothetical answer
For HyDE, have the generator write a document-like answer to the query — it looks like what we want to find
Embed that text with the same encoder as the corpus — query and corpus must share a space
Search the corpus vectors with it and take the top k — real documents, not the generated text
For multi-query, retrieve a ranked list per paraphrase — each wording finds different documents
Fuse the lists with reciprocal rank fusion — ranks are comparable across lists, raw scores are not
problems.time: HyDE adds one LLM generation plus one embedding per query; multi-query costs one search per paraphrase
problems.space: O(N·d) for the corpus vectors; fusion keeps only a score per seen document
dryRun: Retrieve top-$k$ of $\cos(v, e(d_i))$ over the corpus
Typical $k = 60$; a document missing from $R_j$ adds 0
problems.description: Zero-shot retrieval over a new domain with no relevance labels, short or vague user questions, and chat settings where the latest message depends on earlier turns.

examples.input: Why embed a fake answer instead of the question?
examples.output: Documents look like answers, not questions. The hypothetical text is document-shaped, so its embedding falls near real relevant documents even when its facts are wrong.

examples.input: Why use ranks instead of scores when fusing multi-query results?
examples.output: Scores from different queries are not on a common scale. Ranks are, and reciprocal rank fusion needs no tuning beyond the constant $k$.

examples.input: What does query rewriting from chat history fix?
examples.output: A follow-up such as 'how much does it cost?' has no standalone meaning. Rewriting resolves pronouns and context into a self-contained query before retrieval.

examples.input: When does HyDE hurt?
examples.output: When the generator is wrong about the topic, the hypothetical text points to the wrong neighbourhood. It also adds latency and cost.

constraints: Number of paraphrases or hypothetical documents
Generator prompt and sampling temperature
RRF constant $k$ (60 is common)
Number of results k per list
edgeCases: A hallucinated hypothetical document can pull retrieval to the wrong place, so check it against the original query or fuse it with plain query results
HyDE adds an LLM call of latency and cost before every search
The generator here is a stub; a real one makes results vary run to run unless temperature is zero
Rewriting from chat history must keep the user's intent; an over-eager rewrite can drop a constraint

problems.title: RAG Retrieval (Chunk, Embed, Top-k)
problems.summary: Split documents into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk and the query as vectors, and return the k chunks whose vectors are most similar to the query to put in the language model's prompt.
problems.bruteForce: When the whole corpus fits in the prompt, when queries need exact keyword or ID matching that embeddings blur, or when the answer requires reasoning across many scattered passages that top-k cannot gather.
problems.intuition: A language model cannot read a whole corpus, so retrieval chooses the few passages worth reading. Chunking sets the unit of retrieval: too large and the relevant sentence is diluted, too small and it loses its context, and overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary from being cut in half. Normalising embeddings turns cosine similarity into a plain dot product, so search is one matrix-vector product.
problems.whyItWorks: If the embedding places related texts near each other, nearest neighbours of the query vector are likely relevant passages, and the generator can then ground its answer in text it was never trained on. With unit-length vectors, ranking by dot product is identical to ranking by cosine similarity, which is why indexes normalise once at build time and search with a single product.
approach: Split each document into word chunks of fixed size with overlap — sets the unit of retrieval and protects boundary sentences
Embed every chunk once and normalise to unit length — an offline index; unit length makes dot product equal cosine
Embed the query the same way — query and chunks must live in the same space
Score all chunks with one matrix-vector product — cosine similarity for every chunk
Take the k highest scores — the passages to place in the prompt
problems.time: O(N·d) to score N chunks of dimension d by brute force; approximate indexes reduce this at some recall cost
problems.space: O(N·d) for the chunk embedding matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np, zlib

def chunk(words, size=8, overlap=2):
    step = size - overlap
    stop = max(len(words) - overlap, 1)
    return [words[i:i + size] for i in range(0, stop, step)]

def embed(words, dim=256):
    v = np.zeros(dim)
    for w in words:
        h = zlib.crc32(w.encode())
        v[h % dim] += 1 if (h >> 16) & 1 else -1
    n = np.linalg.norm(v)
    return v / n if n else v

def retrieve(query, chunks, k=3):
    E = np.stack([embed(c) for c in chunks])
    sims = E @ embed(query)
    top = np.argsort(-sims)[:k]
    return top, sims[top]
dryRun: Chunks: words$[i : i + size]$ for $i = 0, step, 2\cdot step, \ldots$
Top-$k$: indices of the $k$ largest $\cos(q, c_i)$
problems.description: Question answering over private or fresh documents, where the model needs facts that are not in its weights and answers should cite sources.

examples.input: Why use overlapping chunks?
examples.output: Information near a chunk boundary would be split across two chunks and could be missed by both. Overlap repeats boundary text so at least one chunk contains the whole passage, at the cost of a larger index.

examples.input: Why normalise embeddings before search?
examples.output: For unit vectors the dot product equals cosine similarity, so exact search is a single matrix product and magnitude differences cannot affect the ranking.

examples.input: What are the trade-offs of exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour search?
examples.output: Exact search is simple and gives the true top-k but scales linearly with corpus size. Approximate indexes such as graph or clustering based ones are much faster on large corpora but can miss true neighbours.

constraints: Chunk size and overlap
Number of retrieved chunks k
Embedding model and dimension (a hashing stand-in here)
Similarity (cosine on normalised vectors, or dot product)
Exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour index
edgeCases: The embedding here is a signed hashing bag of words, so it only matches shared words; it has no semantic understanding, unlike a trained embedding model
Embedding the chunks inside retrieve is for brevity; real systems embed once and store the matrix
Chunk by words here for simplicity; production systems chunk by tokens or sentences and keep metadata
Query and chunks must use the same embedding model and normalisation

problems.title: RAG Evaluation - Retrieval, Faithfulness, Relevance
problems.summary: Score a retrieval-augmented system in parts: did retrieval rank the relevant chunks high and cover the needed facts, is the answer supported by the retrieved text, and does it address the question.
problems.bruteForce: As a measure of factual truth: faithfulness only checks agreement with the retrieved text. Without relevance labels or reference facts the retrieval metrics cannot be computed.
problems.intuition: A single end-to-end score cannot tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure. Splitting the pipeline localises the fault: poor context precision or recall means fix the retriever, while good context but unsupported claims means fix the generator. Faithfulness asks only whether the answer follows from the context, not whether the context is true. Flow: query → retrieve → score contexts → split answer into claims → check support.
problems.whyItWorks: Context precision is average precision: the mean of precision at each relevant rank, divided by the number of relevant items, so it rewards placing relevant chunks first and penalises missing ones. Recall and faithfulness are simple proportions over facts and claims, so each metric isolates one stage and is easy to interpret and track.
approach: Label each ranked context as relevant or not — precision needs the ranking, not just the set
Context precision is average precision over the ranking — relevant chunks ranked early score higher
Context recall is the share of needed facts found in the retrieved text — missing facts cap the answer
Split the answer into atomic claims — support is judged per claim, not per answer
Faithfulness is the fraction of claims supported by the context — a support function stands in for an entailment judge
Answer relevance checks the answer addresses the question — a faithful answer can still be off topic
problems.time: O(k) for ranking metrics over $k$ contexts; judging claims costs one judge call per claim
problems.space: O(k + c) for $k$ contexts and $c$ claims
problems.description: Diagnosing a RAG pipeline, comparing retrievers or chunking choices, and regression-testing a pipeline when prompts or indexes change.

examples.input: How do you tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure?
examples.output: Look at the parts separately. Low context recall or precision points at the retriever. Good context with unsupported claims points at the generator.

examples.input: Why is context precision computed like average precision?
examples.output: Order matters, since models attend more to early chunks and context is limited. Average precision rewards ranking relevant chunks first, and dividing by the number of relevant items makes a missed relevant chunk cost score.

examples.input: Does high faithfulness mean the answer is correct?
examples.output: No. It only means the claims follow from the retrieved text. If the context is wrong or incomplete, a faithful answer can still be wrong.

examples.input: How reliable are LLM judges for claim support?
examples.output: They are useful but imperfect, with their own biases and errors, so validate them against a human-labelled sample and track agreement.

constraints: Support threshold $\theta$ for the overlap check, or the judge prompt
Claim splitting method (granularity of atomic claims)
Number of retrieved contexts $k$
edgeCases: Token overlap is a crude proxy: it passes paraphrased contradictions that share words and fails correct paraphrases that do not
An LLM or NLI judge for support has its own errors and biases; treat its scores as estimates and spot-check them against humans
Retrieval labels depend on the annotator, so precision and recall are only as good as those labels
Faithfulness ignores truth of the context and whether the answer leaves out needed facts

problems.title: Random Forest
problems.summary: Train many decision trees on bootstrap resamples, letting each split see only a random subset of features, then average their votes. The code is a simplified binary-class version, with no out-of-bag scoring or parallelism.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you need a tiny fast model, extrapolation beyond the training range, or the last bit of accuracy (boosting usually wins), or with very sparse high-dimensional text.
problems.intuition: One deep tree has low bias but high variance, so its errors are largely random noise. Averaging many trees cancels that noise, but only if the trees disagree, which is why each gets a different bootstrap sample and a different random feature subset at every split.
problems.whyItWorks: The variance of an average of $B$ models with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$ is $\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$. More trees kill the second term, and random feature subsets shrink $\rho$, the part more trees cannot fix. Bias stays about that of one deep tree, so the average is better.
approach: Draw $n$ rows with replacement — each tree sees a different dataset
At each node pick $m$ random features — decorrelates the trees
Grow a tree to the depth limit using Gini — low-bias, high-variance learner
Repeat for $B$ trees — more trees only reduce variance, never overfit
Average the votes (probabilities) — cancels the trees' independent errors
problems.time: O(B · m · n² ) as written (naive scan); O(B · m · n log n · depth) with sorted splits; trees are independent so training parallelises
problems.space: O(B · nodes) for the stored trees
dryRun: Classification: $\hat{y}$ = majority vote of the $B$ trees
problems.description: A strong default for tabular data: little tuning, handles non-linear interactions, mixed scales and noisy features, and gives feature importances.

examples.input: Why does bagging help but not hurt by adding more trees?
examples.output: Averaging reduces variance and leaves bias unchanged; extra trees only shrink the $(1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$ term, so the error plateaus rather than rises.

examples.input: What is the role of max_features?
examples.output: Fewer candidate features per split decorrelates trees, which lowers ensemble variance at the cost of weaker individual trees.

examples.input: What is out-of-bag error?
examples.output: Each tree misses about a third of the rows, so scoring each row only with trees that did not see it gives a free validation estimate.

constraints: n_estimators $B$ — more is better, with diminishing returns
max_features $m$ — smaller means more diverse trees but weaker ones
max_depth / min_samples_leaf — control each tree's variance
bootstrap — sample with replacement (default) or use all rows
edgeCases: Highly correlated trees give little gain, so keep $m$ below $d$
Impurity-based feature importance favours high-cardinality features; use permutation importance
Trees cannot extrapolate outside the training range
This card's code simplifies sklearn: no out-of-bag scoring, binary labels only

problems.title: Receptive Field
problems.summary: The receptive field of a unit is the patch of the input that can influence its value. It grows layer by layer, and strides make it grow faster.
problems.bruteForce: This theoretical field ignores how much each pixel actually matters. Actual influence is concentrated near the centre, so for what the network uses, measure gradients instead. It also does not describe attention layers, whose field is global.
problems.intuition: Each layer looks at a $k$-wide window of the previous layer, but one step in a deeper layer already spans several input pixels. Every new kernel therefore adds $(k - 1)$ steps of the current spacing between neighbouring units, and strides multiply that spacing. This is why a stack of small kernels can see a large region, and why a unit can only reason about context inside its own receptive field.
problems.whyItWorks: Unrolling the dependency of an output on its inputs layer by layer gives a simple recurrence: the field is the previous field plus $(k - 1)$ times the product of all earlier strides (the jump). The recurrence is exact for a plain stack of convolutions or pooling layers, because each layer's window is a contiguous block of the layer below.
approach: Start with field 1 and jump 1 at the input — a single pixel sees only itself
For each layer add $(k - 1) \cdot \mathrm{jump}$ to the field — a wider window over spaced-out units
