Temperature (divides logits; higher is flatter, lower is sharper)
Class weights (rescale the loss for imbalanced classes)
edgeCases: Naive exp overflows for large logits; always subtract the row max
Taking log of softmax in two steps loses precision; use log-sum-exp
Applying softmax then a framework CrossEntropyLoss applies it twice
Outputs are confident but not necessarily calibrated

problems.title: Speculative Decoding
problems.summary: A small draft model proposes $\gamma$ tokens, the large target model scores them in one parallel pass, and a rejection rule keeps the output distribution exactly the target's while emitting several tokens per target pass.
problems.bruteForce: Large-batch throughput serving where the target is already compute-bound, or when no draft model tracks the target well, since a low acceptance rate $\alpha$ makes the draft overhead a net loss.
problems.intuition: Generation is slow because each target pass yields one token, yet checking many proposed tokens costs about the same as one step, since the pass is memory-bound. The rejection rule fixes any draft error: a draft token $x$ survives with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$, and a rejection is replaced by a draw from the leftover mass, so the output is distributed as the target alone. A bad draft only costs speed, never correctness. Flow: draft proposes → target verifies → accept or resample → emit.
problems.whyItWorks: A token $x$ is emitted either by acceptance, with probability $\min(p(x), q(x))$, or after a rejection by a residual draw. The residual draw contributes exactly $\max(0, p(x)-q(x))$, because the rejection probability $1-\sum_y \min(p(y), q(y))$ cancels with the residual normaliser. Adding them gives $p(x)$. Each position is therefore exact, and by induction so is the whole sequence.
approach: Sample $\gamma$ tokens from the draft $q$ autoregressively — cheap because the draft is small
Run the target once over the prefix plus drafts to get $p$ at every position — one parallel pass
Accept draft token $x$ with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$ — keeps tokens the target likes at least as much
On the first rejection, resample from $\mathrm{norm}(\max(0, p-q))$ and stop — restores exactly the target distribution
If all are accepted, draw one bonus token from the target — the pass already computed it
problems.time: One target pass plus $\gamma$ draft passes per step; about $\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$ tokens emitted
problems.space: Both models weights and two KV caches, plus $O(\gamma)$ extra positions per step
problems.description: Latency-bound generation where a much cheaper draft model agrees with the target on many tokens, and exact sampling from the target distribution must be preserved.

examples.input: Why is the output distribution unchanged?
examples.output: The accept-or-resample rule emits $x$ with total probability $\min(p,q) + \max(0,p-q) = p(x)$, so each token is an exact draw from the target.

examples.input: What does the acceptance rate depend on?
examples.output: On how close the draft is to the target, $\alpha = \sum_x \min(p(x), q(x))$, under an i.i.d. assumption across positions. Real acceptance varies by context.

examples.input: Why does it speed up decoding at all?
examples.output: Autoregressive decoding is memory-bound, so scoring $\gamma+1$ positions in one pass costs about the same as one position, and each pass yields more than one token on average.

examples.input: What happens with a terrible draft?
examples.output: Most tokens are rejected, so each step emits about one token and the draft work is wasted, but the output is still exactly the target's.

constraints: Speculation length $\gamma$ (drafted tokens per step)
Choice and size of the draft model
Sampling temperature, applied identically to target and draft
Cost ratio of a draft pass to a target pass
edgeCases: Rejection sampling compares $p$ and $q$ after the same temperature and truncation; mismatched processing breaks exactness
Larger $\gamma$ is not always better: gains saturate as $\alpha^{\gamma}$ shrinks while draft cost grows linearly
The formula $\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$ assumes the same $\alpha$ at every position, which real text violates
Both models need their KV caches rolled back to the last accepted position after a rejection

problems.title: Hypothesis Testing, Welch's t-Test, Bootstrap and FDR
problems.summary: Test whether two samples differ with Welch's t-test, put an interval on any statistic with the bootstrap, and control false positives when running many tests with Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg.
problems.bruteForce: Binary outcomes (see the A/B test card, a two-proportion $z$-test), tiny or heavy-tailed samples where the $t$ approximation fails, dependent observations, and the bootstrap for extreme order statistics such as the maximum. A small $p$-value says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter.
problems.intuition: A test asks how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on. The $p$-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as the one seen. It is not the probability that the null is true. The catch with many tests is arithmetic: run 100 true nulls at $\alpha = 0.05$ and about 5 will look significant, so the threshold must tighten, either to protect against any false positive (Bonferroni) or to cap the fraction of false discoveries among the rejections (Benjamini-Hochberg). Flow: data → statistic under the null → $p$-value → corrected decision.
problems.whyItWorks: Under the null the Welch statistic is approximately $t$-distributed, with the Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom matching its variance when the group variances differ. Under a true null a continuous $p$-value is uniform, so rejecting at $p \leq \alpha$ errs with probability $\alpha$. Bonferroni follows from the union bound. Benjamini-Hochberg compares the sorted $p$-values to a rising line and, for independent tests, keeps the expected false discovery proportion at most $\alpha$. The bootstrap resamples the data with replacement to imitate drawing new samples, so the spread of the statistic over resamples estimates its sampling spread.
approach: Compute the two sample means and variances — the statistic compares means in units of their noise
Divide the mean gap by $\sqrt{s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y}$ — Welch does not assume equal variances
Estimate the degrees of freedom with Welch-Satterthwaite — gives the right $t$ tail when variances differ
Take the two-sided tail probability as the $p$-value — how extreme the data is under the null
For an interval, resample with replacement $B$ times and take quantiles of the statistic — no formula needed
For many tests, compare against $\alpha/m$ (Bonferroni) or the BH step-up line — controls false positives across the family
problems.time: O(n) for the t-test, O(B·n) for the bootstrap, O(m log m) for BH (sort), O(m) for Bonferroni
problems.space: O(B·n) for the resampled indices, O(m) for the p-values
problems.solution:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import t as t_dist

def welch_t(x, y):
    nx, ny = len(x), len(y)
    a, b = x.var(ddof=1) / nx, y.var(ddof=1) / ny
    t = (x.mean() - y.mean()) / np.sqrt(a + b)
    df = (a + b) ** 2 / (a**2 / (nx - 1) + b**2 / (ny - 1))
    return t, df, 2 * t_dist.sf(abs(t), df)

def bootstrap_ci(x, stat, B, alpha, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(x), size=(B, len(x)))
    s = np.array([stat(x[i]) for i in idx])
    return tuple(np.quantile(s, [alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2]))

def bonferroni(pvals, alpha):
    return np.asarray(pvals) <= alpha / len(pvals)

def bh_fdr(pvals, alpha):
    p = np.asarray(pvals)
    m = len(p)
    order = np.argsort(p)
    ok = p[order] <= alpha * np.arange(1, m + 1) / m
    k = np.nonzero(ok)[0].max() + 1 if ok.any() else 0
    reject = np.zeros(m, bool)
    reject[order[:k]] = True
    return reject
problems.description: Comparing two group means with unequal variances or sizes (Welch's test is a safe default), getting a confidence interval for a median or other awkward statistic (bootstrap), and screening many features, genes or metrics at once (Bonferroni or BH).

examples.input: What does a p-value mean?
examples.output: The probability, under the null hypothesis, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null is true or that the result is a fluke.

examples.input: What are Type I and Type II errors, and power?
examples.output: Type I is rejecting a true null, with probability $\alpha$. Type II is missing a real effect, with probability $\beta$. Power is $1-\beta$, the chance of detecting a real effect, and it grows with sample size and effect size.

examples.input: Why use Welch over the pooled t-test?
examples.output: It does not assume equal variances and loses little when they are equal, so it is a safe default with unequal group sizes or spreads.

examples.input: Bonferroni versus Benjamini-Hochberg?
examples.output: Bonferroni controls the probability of any false positive by testing each at $\alpha/m$. BH controls the expected fraction of false discoveries among rejections, which is less strict and has more power when many effects are real.

constraints: Significance level $\alpha$ — tolerated false-positive rate (or FDR for BH)
Number of bootstrap resamples $B$ — more resamples give smoother interval ends
Number of tests $m$ — sets the Bonferroni threshold and the BH line
Two-sided or one-sided alternative — fixed before looking at the data
edgeCases: A $p$-value is not the probability that the null is true, and "not significant" is not evidence that there is no effect (low power looks the same)
Testing many hypotheses and reporting only the significant ones inflates false positives; correct across the whole family
BH guarantees hold for independent or positively dependent tests; Bonferroni controls the chance of any false rejection and is more conservative
The percentile bootstrap undercovers for small samples and for statistics that depend on the extremes

problems.title: Stratified Train/Test Split
problems.summary: Split data by shuffling and sampling each class separately so train and test keep (almost) the same class proportions as the full dataset.
problems.bruteForce: Time series or grouped data, where the split must respect time order or keep groups together instead (use a temporal or group split); also regression targets unless you bin them first.
problems.intuition: A purely random split of an imbalanced dataset can, by bad luck, put too few or even zero minority samples in the test set, making the metric noisy or undefined. Sampling the same fraction from each class removes that source of variance: every class appears in test in proportion to its overall share, up to rounding.
problems.whyItWorks: Random sampling gives test class counts that vary like a hypergeometric draw, which is noisy for small classes. Stratifying fixes each class's test count by design, so only rounding remains and the class proportions in train and test differ from the population by at most a single sample per class. This lowers the variance of the evaluation without introducing bias for the overall population.
approach: Seed a random generator — makes the split reproducible
For each class, shuffle the indices of that class — random choice within the class
Take the first $\mathrm{round}(f \cdot n_c)$ shuffled indices for test — same fraction from every class
Collect test indices, then train is the complement — a clean partition with no overlap
Check proportions in both parts — confirms the stratification worked
problems.time: O(n) plus shuffling each class
problems.space: O(n) for the index arrays
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def stratified_split(y, test_frac=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    test = []
    for c in np.unique(y):
        idx = rng.permutation(np.flatnonzero(y == c))
        k = int(round(test_frac * len(idx)))
        test.extend(idx[:k])
    test = np.array(sorted(test))
    train = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), test)
    return train, test
dryRun: Test $T = \bigcup_c$ ($k_c$ random of class $c$), train = rest
problems.description: Classification with imbalanced or small classes, small datasets where one rare sample matters, and cross-validation folds (stratified k-fold).

examples.input: Why stratify?
examples.output: It keeps class proportions the same in train and test, so rare classes are represented in evaluation and metrics have lower variance.

examples.input: Does stratifying introduce bias?
examples.output: No for population-level estimates: each sample still has the same inclusion probability within its class, and the only change is removing class-count variance.

examples.input: When is stratifying the wrong tool?
examples.output: For temporal or grouped data, where you must split by time or by group to avoid leakage, and for continuous targets unless they are binned.

examples.input: How do you stratify on several columns?
examples.output: Combine them into one composite label (for example class and region) and stratify on that, making sure each combination has enough samples.

constraints: test_frac — fraction held out
seed — fixes the shuffle for reproducibility
stratify target — the label (or a combined label or binned target)
edgeCases: Per-class rounding can make the total test size differ slightly from $f \cdot n$; sklearn allocates counts to hit it exactly, so splits are close but not identical
A class with a single sample cannot appear in both parts; sklearn raises an error here, this code silently keeps it in train
Stratifying does not fix leakage: duplicates or related rows can still straddle the split
Split before preprocessing or feature selection, otherwise test statistics leak into training

problems.title: Structured Outputs with JSON Schema
problems.summary: Ask the model for JSON in a fixed schema, extract it from the reply, validate it, and retry with the errors fed back; constrained decoding makes the output valid by construction instead.
problems.bruteForce: Free-form prose where no downstream parser exists. Constrained decoding is unavailable on hosted models that expose no logits, and a schema valid in shape can still hold wrong values.
problems.intuition: A program downstream cannot parse "Sure, here you go!". Prompting only makes valid JSON likely, so you wrap it in a check: extract, validate, and on failure retry with the error message. Constrained decoding goes further and removes the failure mode: at each step it zeroes the probability of tokens the grammar forbids, so every sampled sequence is valid and no retry is needed. Flow: prompt → reply → extract JSON → validate → retry or accept.
problems.whyItWorks: If one attempt is valid with probability $p$ and attempts are independent, the number of tries is geometric with mean $1/p$ and $P(\text{at least one valid in } n) = 1 - (1-p)^n$, which approaches 1 quickly. Masking sets forbidden logits to $-\infty$, so their softmax weight is exactly 0 and the rest renormalise; any sampled sequence stays inside the grammar.
approach: Put the schema and an instruction to reply with JSON only in the prompt — raises the chance of valid output
Extract the first balanced $\{\dots\}$ from the reply, ignoring fences and prose — models wrap JSON in chatter
Validate the parsed object against the JSON Schema — types, required keys and enums are checked, not trusted
On failure append the validator errors to the prompt and retry up to $n$ times — the model can repair a specific error
Optionally mask logits of grammar-forbidden tokens before softmax — valid by construction, no retries
problems.time: O(L) to extract and validate a reply of length L; the retry loop costs up to $n$ generations
problems.space: O(L) for the reply plus O(V) for one step's mask over vocabulary size V
problems.description: Any pipeline where code consumes model output: tool calls, data extraction, classification labels, form filling. Validation plus retry works with any model; constrained decoding when you control the sampler and need a hard guarantee.

examples.input: Why is validating the output not enough on its own?
examples.output: Each retry costs a full generation and independence is optimistic, so with a low $p$ you pay roughly $1/p$ calls and still have no guarantee.

examples.input: How does constrained decoding guarantee valid JSON?
examples.output: A grammar or state machine tracks which tokens may come next; logits of all other tokens are set to $-\infty$ before softmax, so they can never be sampled.

examples.input: Does a schema-valid reply mean a correct reply?
examples.output: No. The schema checks shape, types and enums, not truth; the model can still fill valid fields with wrong values.

examples.input: Why feed the validation errors back on retry?
examples.output: The specific message, such as a missing key, lets the model fix that error instead of resampling blindly, which raises the success probability on later attempts.

constraints: Maximum number of retries $n$ (bounds cost and latency)
Sampling temperature (lower raises $p$ for strict formats)
Schema strictness: required keys, enums, additional properties
Whether to use constrained decoding or validate-and-retry
edgeCases: Taking the first brace to the last brace breaks when prose contains braces; track depth and string state
Retrying at the same temperature with the same prompt repeats the same mistake; add the error text
Masking tokens can force a valid but wrong answer when the model wanted a forbidden token; the content may degrade
Treating $1-(1-p)^n$ as exact: failures are often correlated across attempts, so real success is lower

problems.title: Singular Value Decomposition
problems.summary: Every matrix factors as $A = USV^{\top}$ with orthonormal $U$ and $V$ and non-negative singular values in $S$. Keeping only the largest few gives the best low-rank approximation of $A$.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a full SVD for huge sparse matrices (use truncated or randomised methods) and when missing entries need handling, since SVD needs a fully observed matrix. The eigen-route in the code squares the condition number, so use a library SVD in production.
problems.intuition: A matrix maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid. The SVD names the ellipsoid's axes: $V$ gives the input directions, the singular values give how much each is stretched, and $U$ gives the output directions. Directions with tiny stretch contribute almost nothing, so you can drop them and keep a compact matrix that behaves nearly the same.
problems.whyItWorks: $A^{\top}A = VS^2V^{\top}$, so the right singular vectors are eigenvectors of $A^{\top}A$ and the singular values are the square roots of its eigenvalues. The Eckart-Young theorem says that, in both the Frobenius and spectral norms, no rank-$k$ matrix is closer to $A$ than the truncation that keeps the top $k$ singular triplets, and the error is set by the discarded singular values.
approach: Form $A^{\top}A$ — its eigenvectors are the right singular vectors
Eigendecompose it and sort eigenvalues in decreasing order — singular values are conventionally ordered
Take square roots (clipping tiny negatives from rounding) — gives the singular values
Compute $U = AV/s$ column by column — the left vectors follow from the right ones
Truncate to the top $k$ triplets for a low-rank approximation — Eckart-Young says this is optimal
problems.time: O(m·n²) for AᵀA plus O(n³) for the eigen step (m ≥ n); library SVD is similar but more stable
problems.space: O(m·n) for the matrices and O(n²) for AᵀA
dryRun: $A = U S V^{\top},\;\; U^{\top}U = I,\;\; V^{\top}V = I,\;\; s_1 \geq s_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$
problems.description: PCA, low-rank compression, denoising, latent semantic analysis, recommender factorisation, pseudo-inverses and least squares on ill-conditioned problems.

examples.input: How does SVD relate to eigendecomposition?
examples.output: The right singular vectors are the eigenvectors of $A^{\top}A$ and the left ones those of $AA^{\top}$, with singular values the square roots of the shared non-zero eigenvalues.

examples.input: What does the Eckart-Young theorem say?
examples.output: Truncating the SVD to rank $k$ gives the closest rank-$k$ matrix to $A$ in the spectral and Frobenius norms.

examples.input: How is SVD used in PCA?
examples.output: Centre the data, take its SVD, and the right singular vectors are the principal axes while squared singular values over $n-1$ are the variances.

examples.input: Why is SVD better than the normal equations for least squares?
examples.output: It works with $A$ directly, avoiding the squared condition number of $A^{\top}A$, and gives a stable pseudo-inverse for rank-deficient problems.

constraints: Rank $k$ — chosen from the singular-value spectrum or an energy target
Full or thin (economy) factorisation
Solver — full, truncated or randomised
edgeCases: This code assumes $m\geq n$ and nonzero singular values; zero ones leave zero columns in $U$
Forming $A^{\top}A$ squares the condition number and loses accuracy for small singular values
Singular vectors are only defined up to a joint sign flip, and are unstable when singular values are close
SVD of uncentred data is not PCA; centre the columns first

problems.title: Support Vector Machine
problems.summary: Find the separating hyperplane with the widest margin. The code is a simplified linear soft-margin SVM trained by full-batch sub-gradient descent on the hinge loss; kernels and the dual solver (SMO) are not implemented.
problems.bruteForce: Skip kernel SVMs on very large datasets (training scales badly with $n$), when you need probabilities directly, or when classes overlap heavily and features are unscaled.
problems.intuition: Many hyperplanes separate two classes, but the one farthest from both is least likely to be thrown off by new points. Only the points on or inside the margin matter for the solution (the support vectors), so confidently classified points are simply ignored.
problems.whyItWorks: The hinge loss $\max(0, 1 - y\cdot f)$ is zero for points beyond the margin, so they give no gradient, and the $\|w\|^2$ term maximises the margin $2/\|w\|$. The objective is convex, so sub-gradient descent with a decaying step converges to the global optimum, the same one the dual quadratic program finds.
approach: Encode labels as $-1$/$+1$ — so $y\cdot f > 0$ means correct
Find points with $y\cdot f(x) < 1$ — only margin violators contribute to the gradient
Sum their $yx$ terms and add $\lambda w$ — hinge sub-gradient plus margin regulariser
Take a step with size $1/(\lambda(t + 10))$ — a decaying step gives convergence
Repeat for many iterations — then classify with $\mathrm{sign}(w^{\top}x + b)$
problems.time: O(iters · n · d) here; kernel SVM solvers are between O(n²) and O(n³)
problems.space: O(n · d) for the data; kernel SVMs also store the support vectors
problems.description: Medium-sized, high-dimensional problems (text, genomics) with a clear margin, and with a kernel when the boundary is curved.

examples.input: What are support vectors?
examples.output: The training points on or inside the margin; they alone determine the hyperplane and removing any other point leaves it unchanged.

examples.input: What does $C$ control?
examples.output: The penalty on margin violations: large $C$ tolerates few violations (narrow margin, low bias), small $C$ allows more (wide margin, more regularisation).

examples.input: What is the kernel trick?
examples.output: The dual problem uses only dot products $x_i\cdot x_j$, so replacing them with a kernel $k(x_i, x_j)$ gives a linear margin in an implicit high-dimensional space without computing it.

constraints: $C$ (or $\lambda = 1/(C\cdot n)$) — large $C$ fits training data harder, small $C$ widens the margin
kernel — linear, RBF, polynomial
gamma — RBF width; large values overfit
Feature scaling — required, since the margin is distance-based
edgeCases: Unscaled features let one large feature dominate the margin
Scores are not probabilities; Platt scaling is needed
RBF with a large gamma memorises the training set
This card's code is linear only and uses sub-gradient descent instead of the dual solver

problems.title: T5 Span Corruption Pretraining Objective
problems.summary: Replace random spans of the input with numbered sentinel tokens and train an encoder-decoder to output the dropped spans, each preceded by its sentinel, followed by an end-of-sequence token.
problems.bruteForce: Decoder-only language models, which use the plain next-token loss, or encoder-only models where per-token masked prediction in place is enough and no generation is needed.
problems.intuition: BERT predicts masked tokens independently in place, and GPT predicts the next token left to right. Span corruption turns denoising into a text-to-text task: the encoder reads the corrupted text once and the decoder writes out only what is missing. The target is short (about the corrupted fraction of the input), so pretraining is cheap, and the decoder must model whole spans jointly, not token by token. Flow: text → drop spans → sentinels → encoder → decoder writes spans.
problems.whyItWorks: The sentinel marks each gap, so the corrupted input plus the target carries exactly the information of the original text, and reconstruction is a lossless inverse. Predicting a whole span from its two sides forces the model to use context on both sides, while the target stays much shorter than the input.
approach: Choose non-overlapping spans $(s_i, n_i)$ — each one is dropped as a block
Replace span $i$ in the input with sentinel $i$ — the encoder sees where text is missing
Build the target as sentinel $i$ then the dropped tokens, for every span — sentinels keep the spans ordered
Append an end-of-sequence token to the target — the decoder learns when to stop
Train with cross-entropy on the target only — the input is never a prediction target
problems.time: O(n) to build one corrupted example; the loss covers only the short target
problems.space: O(n) for the input and target token lists
problems.description: Pretraining a text-to-text encoder-decoder, or any model that should learn to fill in missing spans, where the output is far shorter than the input.

examples.input: How does span corruption differ from BERT masking?
examples.output: BERT replaces tokens in place and predicts each masked token independently from the encoder output. Span corruption drops whole spans, collapses each to one sentinel, and a decoder generates the spans autoregressively.

examples.input: Why are the sentinels numbered?
examples.output: The number lets the decoder tie each output span to its gap in the input and keeps the spans in order, so the original text can be rebuilt exactly.

examples.input: Why is the target shorter than the input?
examples.output: Only the dropped tokens are emitted, plus one sentinel per span and an end token, so the target length is $m + k + 1$ for $m$ dropped tokens in $k$ spans.

constraints: Corruption rate $r$, the fraction of tokens dropped
Mean span length $\bar{\ell}$ (longer spans mean fewer sentinels)
Number of available sentinel tokens in the vocabulary
edgeCases: Overlapping or unsorted spans break the sentinel order and the inverse; sort and merge spans first
Computing the loss on the corrupted input as well as the target wastes capacity on copying
A real tokenizer uses reserved sentinel ids; a literal text token that looks like a sentinel would be ambiguous

problems.title: Temperature Sampling
problems.summary: Divide the logits by a temperature $T$ before the softmax. Low $T$ sharpens the distribution towards greedy, high $T$ flattens it towards uniform.
problems.bruteForce: When you need a deterministic answer: use greedy decoding, not a tiny $T$ with a random draw. $T=0$ is also undefined as a division, so implementations special-case it as argmax.
problems.intuition: Dividing logits by $T$ changes the gaps between them while keeping their order. Small $T$ stretches the gaps, so the top token takes almost all the probability. Large $T$ shrinks them, so every token becomes about equally likely. One scalar therefore slides between deterministic and random, and the entropy rises as it grows. Flow: logits → divide by T → softmax → sample a token.
problems.whyItWorks: The scaled softmax is $p_i \propto \exp(z_i/T)$. As $T \to 0^+$ the largest logit dominates, so the mass concentrates on the argmax. At $T=1$ the model's own distribution is unchanged. As $T \to \infty$ all $z_i/T \to 0$, so $p_i \to 1/V$ and the entropy approaches $\log V$. The entropy grows monotonically with $T$.
approach: Divide the logits by $T$ — scales all gaps between logits
Subtract the max before exponentiating — keeps $\exp$ from overflowing
Normalise to get probabilities — a valid distribution over the vocabulary
Draw one token from it with a seeded generator — reproducible randomness
Compute the entropy if needed — shows how spread out the choice is
problems.time: O(V) per token for a vocabulary of size V
problems.space: O(V) for the probability vector
problems.description: Creative or varied text generation, where you want to control how adventurous the model is with a single knob. Use a low $T$ for factual or code answers and a higher one for brainstorming.

examples.input: What does temperature do to the logits?
examples.output: It divides them by $T$ before the softmax. Their order stays the same, only the spread between them changes.

examples.input: What happens at $T \to 0$ and $T \to \infty$?
examples.output: At $T \to 0$ decoding becomes greedy argmax. At $T \to \infty$ the distribution becomes uniform over the vocabulary.

examples.input: Does temperature change which token is most likely?
examples.output: No. The ranking is unchanged, so the argmax is the same for any $T>0$. It only changes how much probability the others get.

examples.input: How does temperature combine with top-$k$ or top-$p$?
examples.output: They are usually applied together: scale the logits by $T$, then truncate the distribution, then renormalise and sample.

constraints: Temperature $T$ (often between 0.2 and 1.5 in practice)
Random seed for reproducible sampling
Truncation such as top-$k$ or top-$p$ applied alongside
edgeCases: $T=0$ divides by zero; handle it as argmax rather than passing it to the formula
Skipping the max subtraction overflows $\exp$ for large logits at small $T$
High $T$ gives the long tail of junk tokens real probability; truncate with top-$p$ if quality drops

problems.title: Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style Sharded MLP)
problems.summary: Split one layer's weight matrices across devices: the first linear by columns, the second by rows, so the whole MLP needs a single all-reduce (sum) of the partial outputs.
problems.bruteForce: Across slow links, where the per-layer all-reduce dominates, or when the model fits on one device and data parallelism is enough.
problems.intuition: A nonlinearity cannot be applied to partial sums, so the split must not cut the contraction of the first matrix. Splitting $W_1$ by columns gives each device complete hidden units, so the activation is local. Splitting $W_2$ by rows then turns the output into a sum of per-device terms, and one all-reduce adds them. Attention does the same with heads. Flow: split weights → local compute → all-reduce → next layer.
problems.whyItWorks: Column blocks of $W_1$ give $xW_1 = [xW_1^{(1)}, \dots, xW_1^{(n)}]$, and an elementwise activation acts on each block independently. Row blocks of $W_2$ give $hW_2 = \sum_i h^{(i)} W_2^{(i)}$, a sum of local terms. So the sharded computation equals the unsplit one, up to summation order.
approach: Split $W_1$ into column blocks, one per device — each device owns a slice of the hidden units
Compute $x W_1^{(i)}$ on each device with the full input $x$ — needs no communication
Apply the activation locally — each hidden unit is complete, so it is exact
Multiply by the matching row block $W_2^{(i)}$ — gives a partial output of full width
All-reduce (sum) the partial outputs — equals the unsplit result; one collective per MLP
problems.time: Same total FLOPs as the unsplit MLP, divided over $n$ devices, plus one all-reduce
problems.space: Weights and hidden activations per device shrink by about $1/n$; the output stays $B \times T \times d$
problems.description: A layer or model too large for one accelerator, on devices joined by a fast interconnect, since the all-reduce sits on the critical path of every layer.

examples.input: Why split the first linear by columns and the second by rows?
examples.output: Column blocks give each device whole hidden units, so the nonlinearity needs no communication. Row blocks of the second matrix make the output a sum of partials, which one all-reduce combines.

examples.input: How is attention split?
examples.output: Heads are divided across devices; each device holds its heads' $Q$, $K$, $V$ slices and the matching rows of the output projection, then one all-reduce sums the partial outputs.

examples.input: What does tensor parallelism cost in communication?
examples.output: One all-reduce of a $B \times T \times d$ activation per sharded block in the forward pass, and another in the backward pass, so it needs a fast interconnect.

constraints: Tensor-parallel degree $n$ (must divide the hidden width and the head count)
Interconnect bandwidth between the devices
Activation precision, which sets bytes per all-reduce
edgeCases: Row-splitting the first matrix puts the activation on partial sums, which is wrong
The degree must divide the number of heads and the hidden width evenly
Tensor parallelism beyond one fast node usually loses to the communication cost

problems.title: Text Preprocessing, Stemming and Lemmatisation
problems.summary: Turn raw text into clean tokens: lowercase, strip punctuation, split, drop stop words, then collapse word variants with a suffix-stripping stemmer or a dictionary lemmatiser.
problems.bruteForce: Pretrained subword or transformer models, which expect raw text and its own tokenizer. Stripping stop words or suffixes also destroys negation and tense ("not good", "was") that some tasks need.
problems.intuition: A model that counts words sees "run", "runs" and "running" as three unrelated symbols, which splits the evidence for one idea. A stemmer merges them cheaply by chopping suffixes with rules, so its output may not be a real word ("ponies" becomes "poni"). A lemmatiser looks each word up in a dictionary and returns the true base form, so it maps "ran" to "run" and "mice" to "mouse", at the cost of needing a lexicon. Flow: raw text → lowercase → tokens → stop words out → stems.
problems.whyItWorks: English inflection is mostly regular, so a short ordered list of suffix rules maps most variants to one key without any dictionary. Merging variants raises each key's count, which reduces sparsity and vocabulary size. A stem only has to be consistent, not a real word, because it is used as a lookup key and never shown to a reader.
approach: Lowercase and keep only letters and digits — removes case and punctuation variants
Split into tokens — gives the units that will be counted
Drop stop words — removes very frequent words that carry little topic signal
Apply plural rules ($\mathrm{sses}\rightarrow\mathrm{ss}$, $\mathrm{ies}\rightarrow\mathrm{i}$, drop a final s) — merges singular and plural
Strip ing or ed only if a vowel remains, then tidy the ending — avoids turning sing into s
Optionally map irregular words with a dictionary lemmatiser — fixes forms no suffix rule can reach
problems.time: O(n·L) for n tokens of length L; each token is a few suffix checks
problems.space: O(n) for the token list, plus the stop-word set and lemma dictionary
dryRun: Tokens: lowercase, keep letter and digit runs
Drop ing or ed if a vowel is left
problems.description: Bag-of-words, TF-IDF and search pipelines where vocabulary size and sparsity matter, and classical models that cannot share statistics between word forms on their own.

examples.input: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
examples.output: A stemmer chops suffixes with rules and may output a non-word such as poni. A lemmatiser uses a dictionary and part of speech to return a real base form, so it handles ran to run and mice to mouse but is slower.

examples.input: Why remove stop words, and when is it harmful?
examples.output: They are very frequent and add little topic signal to counts. They matter for negation, phrases and language models, so removing them hurts sentiment and generation tasks.

examples.input: What is over-stemming and under-stemming?
examples.output: Over-stemming merges unrelated words into one stem; under-stemming leaves related words apart, such as ran and running. Aggressive rules trade one error for the other.

constraints: Stop-word list (language and domain specific)
Stemmer or lemmatiser choice, and how aggressive its rules are
Whether to lowercase and how to treat digits and hyphens
Minimum token length
edgeCases: Apply the same preprocessing at training and inference time, or the vocabulary will not match
This simplified stemmer covers only a few rules; words like branches or hoped need later Porter steps and come out differently
Stemming ignores meaning, so unrelated words can collide and irregular forms such as ran stay apart

problems.title: TF-IDF
problems.summary: Represent each document as a vector of word counts, rescaled so that words found in few documents count more than words found everywhere.
problems.bruteForce: It ignores word order and meaning, so synonyms look unrelated. Prefer learned embeddings or transformers when semantics matter, and note that idf must be fitted on training data only.
problems.intuition: A word that appears in nearly every document says little about any one of them, while a word concentrated in a few documents is a strong signature. Multiplying the term count by the log of inverse document frequency keeps the frequent-here, rare-elsewhere words and mutes filler such as "the".
problems.whyItWorks: The idf term is the log of how surprising it is to find a word in a random document, so it is a cheap information weight. Smoothing adds one to the counts so unseen words never divide by zero, and L2 normalisation makes the dot product of two rows their cosine similarity, independent of document length.
approach: Build a vocabulary and count terms per document — gives the raw tf matrix
Count in how many documents each term occurs — this is $\mathrm{df}$
Compute idf with add-one smoothing — rare terms get larger weights, no division by zero
Multiply tf by idf column-wise — reweights each term by informativeness
Normalise each row to unit L2 length — removes the effect of document length
problems.time: O(total tokens) to count, O(N·V) for the dense weighting
problems.space: O(N·V) dense here; real systems use sparse matrices
dryRun: Cosine of two rows = dot product after L2 norm
problems.description: Strong, fast baseline features for text classification, search ranking and document similarity, especially with linear models and small datasets.

examples.input: Why take the log in idf?
examples.output: It damps the ratio $N/\mathrm{df}$ so that a very rare word does not dominate, and it makes the weight behave like an information measure.

examples.input: Why normalise rows?
examples.output: Long documents have larger counts. L2 normalisation makes rows comparable and turns the dot product into cosine similarity.

examples.input: How does TF-IDF differ from word embeddings?
examples.output: TF-IDF vectors are sparse, one dimension per word, and carry no notion of meaning. Embeddings are dense and learned so similar words lie close together.

constraints: smooth_idf (add one to document counts, as here)
sublinear_tf (use $1 + \ln(\mathrm{tf})$ so repeats saturate)
norm (l2 for cosine similarity, l1, or none)
min_df / max_df (drop very rare or very common terms)
n-gram range (include word pairs to recover some order)
edgeCases: Fitting idf on the full dataset leaks test statistics into training
This sketch splits on spaces only; real tokenisation handles case and punctuation
The dense matrix is huge for real vocabularies; use sparse storage
Variants differ (log base, smoothing, norm), so scores are not portable between libraries

problems.title: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
problems.summary: Truncate the next-token distribution to the $k$ most likely tokens, or to the smallest set whose probability reaches $p$, then renormalise and sample from what is left.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks with one right answer, such as translation or code, where greedy or beam search is better, and likelihood evaluation, where the full distribution must be used.
problems.intuition: Sampling from the full distribution occasionally picks a token from the long, unreliable tail and derails the text, while greedy decoding is repetitive. Cutting the tail removes the junk and keeps real randomness among plausible tokens; top-p adapts the cut to the model's confidence, keeping few tokens when it is sure and many when it is not.
problems.whyItWorks: Truncation sets the probability of unreliable tail tokens to exactly zero while keeping the relative odds among the survivors after renormalising. Top-p measures the cut in probability mass rather than token count, so the candidate set shrinks when the distribution is peaked and grows when it is flat. The token that crosses the threshold is kept, so the nucleus is never empty.
approach: Sort tokens by logit, highest first — fixes the order used for both cuts
Top-k: set every logit beyond the $k$-th to $-\infty$ — keeps a fixed number of candidates
Softmax the survivors and take cumulative sums — the mass collected so far
Top-p: drop a token once the mass before it is at least $p$ — keeps the smallest nucleus reaching $p$
Sample from the renormalised survivors — the softmax gives zero weight to $-\infty$
problems.time: O(V log V) for the sort over vocabulary size V
problems.space: O(V) for the filtered logits
problems.description: Open-ended generation such as chat, stories and brainstorming, where diversity is wanted but low-probability tokens cause incoherence.

examples.input: How does top-p differ from top-k?
examples.output: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the distribution looks like. Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching probability mass $p$, so its size adapts to how confident the model is.

examples.input: Why renormalise after truncating?
examples.output: The kept probabilities no longer sum to one. The softmax over the remaining logits rescales them so the sample is drawn from a valid distribution.

examples.input: What does temperature do and in what order is it applied?
examples.output: It divides the logits before the softmax; low values sharpen and high values flatten the distribution. It is normally applied first, then the truncation.

constraints: Top-k (0 disables)
Top-p threshold in $(0, 1]$
Temperature $\tau$
Order of temperature, top-k and top-p
edgeCases: Libraries differ on whether top-p uses the distribution before or after top-k; here top-p sees the renormalised top-k survivors
top_p = 0 would drop every token; use a value above zero
Ties at the cut are broken by sort order, so which tied token is kept is arbitrary

problems.title: Tracing, Logging and Cost Accounting for LLM Apps
problems.summary: Record each request as a tree of timed spans carrying model, token and cost attributes, emit structured logs with sensitive fields redacted, and summarise latency with percentiles.
problems.bruteForce: A single-call prototype where a plain log line is enough. Do not log raw prompts and outputs by default when they hold personal data; log sizes, hashes or redacted fields instead.
problems.intuition: One user request fans out into retrieval, several model calls and tool calls, so a single log line cannot say which step was slow or expensive. A span records one step with its start, end, parent and attributes; linking spans by parent id turns a request into a tree where the time and the tokens add up. Averages hide the slow requests users notice, so report percentiles such as $p_{95}$, and because full volume is costly, sample traces and redact secrets before anything is written. Flow: request → spans → timings and tokens → logs → alerts.
problems.whyItWorks: Because a child span starts after and ends before its parent, the tree structure and the timestamps are consistent, so the time spent inside any subtree can be read off directly. Cost is linear in token counts, so summing per-span costs gives the cost of the whole trace. A percentile is a sample estimate of the quantile of the latency distribution, which stays informative when the mean is dominated by a few outliers.
approach: Open a span per step with a context manager, using the current top of a stack as parent — nesting in code becomes nesting in the tree
Read an injected clock at enter and exit — tests can use a fake clock and stay deterministic
Attach attributes such as model name and input and output token counts — latency and cost can then be sliced by model
Compute cost as $\sum_k n_k c_k$ over token kinds with per-token prices — spend is derived from counts, not guessed
Redact configured keys recursively, then emit one JSON record per span — logs stay structured and safe to store
Summarise durations with $p_{50}$, $p_{95}$, $p_{99}$ and keep only a sampled fraction of traces — tail latency is visible and volume stays bounded
problems.time: O(1) per span; O(n log n) to sort $n$ durations for a percentile
problems.space: O(spans) per trace, plus the attributes stored on each span
dryRun: Child inside parent: $s_p \leq s_c$ and $e_c \leq e_p$
problems.description: Any LLM application with more than one model or tool call per request, where you need to explain latency and spend, debug a bad answer by replaying its steps, and alert on tail latency or cost.

examples.input: Why report p95 and p99 instead of the mean latency?
examples.output: LLM latency has a long tail from long outputs, retries and tool calls. The mean hides it, while the tail percentiles show what the slowest users experience.

examples.input: What is the relation between a trace and a span?
examples.output: A trace is the whole request, identified by one trace id. It is a tree of spans, each with its own span id, a parent id (none for the root), start and end times and attributes.

examples.input: How do you control tracing cost and privacy?
examples.output: Sample a fraction of traces, deterministically from the trace id so a trace is kept or dropped as a whole. Redact or hash sensitive fields before writing, and keep token counts rather than raw text where possible.

constraints: Sampling rate, possibly higher for errors and slow requests
Percentiles to report (p50, p95, p99)
Set of redacted keys
Price per token for each token kind and model
edgeCases: Percentiles of per-request latency cannot be averaged across machines; merge the raw values or histograms instead
Sampling each span independently breaks trees; decide once per trace from the trace id
Streaming responses need both time to first token and total time, or the span hides the wait users feel
A redact list misses new field names; prefer logging an allow-list of fields for sensitive paths

problems.title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
problems.summary: Start from a network pretrained on a large dataset, freeze some of its layers and train the rest, usually a new output head, on your small task.
problems.bruteForce: When the target domain is very different from the pretraining data and you have lots of data, training from scratch or unfreezing most layers may fit better. Frozen features also carry the pretraining biases.
problems.intuition: Early layers of a network trained on a big dataset learn generic features such as edges and textures that are useful for many tasks. Keeping them frozen reuses that knowledge and leaves very few parameters to fit on your small dataset, so the model overfits less and trains faster. Unfreezing more layers with a small learning rate lets the features adapt when the new task differs more.
problems.whyItWorks: A pretrained network is a strong prior in weight space, far better than random initialisation when data is scarce. Freezing means no gradient flows into those weights, so they stay at the prior, and only the head has to learn the task-specific mapping on top of fixed features.
approach: Run the forward pass through backbone and head — gives logits and the activations needed later
Compute the output error p − y — the starting signal for backpropagation
Always compute the head gradient — the head is the part being trained
Compute the backbone gradient only if it is not frozen — skipping it saves compute and keeps weights fixed
Update only parameters that received a gradient — frozen weights never change
problems.time: O(N·(D·H + H·K)) forward; the backbone backward is skipped when frozen
problems.space: O(N·H) activations plus gradients only for trainable weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def finetune_step(params, x, y, lr, frozen=()):
    W1, W2 = params["W1"], params["W2"]
    h = np.maximum(x @ W1, 0)
    z = h @ W2
    p = np.exp(z - z.max(1, keepdims=True))
    p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    p[np.arange(len(y)), y] -= 1
    dz = p / len(y)
    grads = {}
    if "W2" not in frozen:
        grads["W2"] = h.T @ dz
    if "W1" not in frozen:
        grads["W1"] = x.T @ ((dz @ W2.T) * (h > 0))
    new = dict(params)
    for k, g in grads.items():
        new[k] = params[k] - lr * g
    return new, grads
dryRun: Head gradient: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2} = h^{\top}(p - y)/N$
Frozen set $F$: update $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$ only for $w \notin F$
problems.description: Small labelled datasets in a domain related to a large pretraining set, such as images, text or audio with a public pretrained model.

examples.input: What is the difference between feature extraction and fine-tuning?
examples.output: Feature extraction freezes the whole backbone and trains only a new head; fine-tuning also updates some or all backbone weights.

examples.input: Why use a smaller learning rate for pretrained layers?
examples.output: Their weights are already good, so small steps adapt them without erasing the pretrained features.

examples.input: When does freezing help most?
examples.output: When the target dataset is small and similar to the pretraining data, so fixed features are good and few parameters need fitting.

constraints: Which layers to freeze (and when to unfreeze)
Learning rate (smaller for pretrained layers than for the new head)
Head architecture
Number of fine-tuning epochs
edgeCases: Frozen batch-norm layers still update running statistics unless put in eval mode
A large learning rate on pretrained layers destroys the features it should keep
Input preprocessing must match what the pretrained model expects
This toy has two layers and no biases; real fine-tuning uses deep pretrained backbones loaded from a model zoo

problems.title: Pre-Norm Transformer Block
problems.summary: One decoder layer: layer-normalise, apply causal multi-head attention, add the result back, then layer-normalise and apply a feed-forward network with a second residual connection.
problems.bruteForce: Very long inputs where quadratic attention is too costly, or small tabular and low-data problems where a simpler network suffices.
problems.intuition: Attention moves information between tokens, and the feed-forward network transforms each token on its own; stacking the two gives a layer that both gathers context and processes it. Keeping a clean residual path $x + f(\mathrm{norm}(x))$ lets each layer make a small correction to the stream, so gradients reach early layers and deep stacks train.
problems.whyItWorks: Residual connections give an identity path through the layer, so the signal and its gradient pass unchanged through any depth. Placing the norm inside each branch (pre-norm) keeps that path free of normalisation and is easier to optimise than post-norm, at some cost in final quality. Attention handles cross-token interaction while the MLP, which holds most of the parameters, handles per-token features.
approach: Normalise $x$ with LayerNorm — keeps the attention input at a stable scale
Project to $Q$, $K$, $V$ and split into heads — each head attends in its own subspace
Apply causal softmax attention per head — mixes past tokens into each position
Merge heads, project with $W_o$ and add to $x$ — the first residual update
Normalise, then apply Linear → GELU → Linear and add — position-wise processing with the second residual update
problems.time: O(T²·d + T·d²) per layer
problems.space: O(h·T²) for attention plus O(T·d) activations
problems.solution:
import numpy as np
from math import erf

def layer_norm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    return g * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + b

def gelu(x):
    return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.vectorize(erf)(x / np.sqrt(2)))

def transformer_block(x, P, h):
    T, d = x.shape
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g1"], P["b1"])
    q, k, v = (y @ P[w] for w in ("Wq", "Wk", "Wv"))
    q, k, v = (m.reshape(T, h, d // h).transpose(1, 0, 2)
               for m in (q, k, v))
    s = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d // h)
    s = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((T, T), bool), 1), -np.inf, s)
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    a = (e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ v
    x = x + a.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d) @ P["Wo"]
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g2"], P["b2"])
    return x + gelu(y @ P["W1"] + P["c1"]) @ P["W2"] + P["c2"]
problems.description: The building block of GPT-style decoder language models and of most modern transformer variants; stack it N times with embeddings in front and an output projection behind.

examples.input: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm?
examples.output: Pre-norm normalises the input of each sublayer and keeps the residual path clean, which trains stably in deep stacks. Post-norm normalises after the addition, as in the original Transformer, and usually needs warmup.

examples.input: Why does the block have a feed-forward network after attention?
examples.output: Attention only takes weighted averages of values, which is linear in $V$. The MLP adds a non-linearity and most of the capacity, applied to each position independently.

examples.input: Where are most of the parameters in a block?
examples.output: In the MLP, whose hidden width is usually a few times $d$, so its two matrices outweigh the four attention projections.

constraints: Model width $d$ and number of heads $h$
MLP hidden width (commonly a small multiple of $d$)
Pre-norm or post-norm placement
Number of stacked blocks and dropout rate
edgeCases: This code has no dropout, attention biases or weight tying; real models add some of these
It uses exact erf GELU; some libraries use the tanh approximation, which differs slightly
A final LayerNorm after the last block is still needed in pre-norm models

problems.title: Transposed Convolution
problems.summary: A learned upsampling layer: each input value paints a scaled copy of the kernel onto a larger output, and overlapping copies add up.
problems.bruteForce: When checkerboard artefacts matter, resize with fixed interpolation and then apply a normal convolution, or choose a kernel size divisible by the stride.
problems.intuition: A normal strided convolution shrinks a map by reading windows; the transposed one runs the same wiring backwards, so a small map grows. Instead of gathering a patch into one number, every input pixel scatters its value times the kernel into the output at stride spacing. Where those stamps overlap they sum, which is why mismatched kernel and stride produce a checkerboard pattern.
problems.whyItWorks: The layer is the transpose of the matrix that implements a convolution, so it maps gradients of a convolution's output back to its input shape. Because the kernel is learned, the network can learn a good interpolation rather than using a fixed one like bilinear upsampling.
approach: Allocate the full output of size $(H-1)\cdot s+k$ — large enough for every stamp
For each input position, multiply its channel vector with the kernel — one $k\times k$ stamp per output channel
Add the stamp into the output at offset $(s\cdot i,\, s\cdot j)$ — overlapping stamps accumulate
Crop $p$ rows and columns from each border — padding shrinks the output instead of growing it
problems.time: O(N·C·F·H·W·kH·kW)
problems.space: O(N·F·oH·oW) for the output
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def conv_transpose2d(x, w, stride=1, pad=0):
    # x: (N,C,H,W)  w: (C,F,kh,kw)
    n, c, h, wd = x.shape
    _, f, kh, kw = w.shape
    oh = (h - 1) * stride + kh
    ow = (wd - 1) * stride + kw
    full = np.zeros((n, f, oh, ow))
    for i in range(h):
        for j in range(wd):
            stamp = np.tensordot(x[:, :, i, j], w, axes=([1], [0]))
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
            full[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw] += stamp
    return full[:, :, pad:oh - pad, pad:ow - pad]
dryRun: Input $x$: $(N, C, H, W)$; kernel $w$: $(C, F, kH, kW)$
Full size: $(H - 1)\cdot s + kH$ (same for width)
Padding $p$ crops $p$ entries per border of full map
problems.description: Decoders of segmentation networks, autoencoders and GAN generators that must produce a higher resolution map from a coarse one.

examples.input: What is the output size of a transposed convolution?
examples.output: $(H-1)\cdot s-2p+k$ along each spatial dimension, plus any output padding.

examples.input: Why is it called transposed?
examples.output: Its forward pass multiplies by the transpose of the matrix that represents the corresponding convolution.

examples.input: Why do checkerboard artefacts appear?
examples.output: Stamps from neighbouring inputs overlap unevenly when the kernel size is not a multiple of the stride.

constraints: Kernel size
Stride (upsampling factor)
Padding (crops the output)
Output padding (not modelled here; it resolves size ambiguity)
edgeCases: Kernel size not divisible by stride gives uneven overlap and checkerboard artefacts
Called deconvolution, but it does not invert a convolution's values, only its shape
Dilation and output padding are not modelled in this sketch
The same output size can come from several input sizes of a strided convolution

problems.title: VAE and the Reparameterisation Trick
problems.summary: A variational autoencoder encodes each input as a Gaussian over latent codes, samples a code, decodes it, and trains on reconstruction error plus a KL penalty toward a standard normal prior.
problems.bruteForce: Discrete latent variables cannot be reparameterised this way, and samples are often blurrier than those of GANs or diffusion models. Watch for posterior collapse, where the decoder ignores $z$.
problems.intuition: Sampling is not differentiable, so gradients cannot flow back to the encoder. Writing the sample as $z = \mu + \sigma\cdot\epsilon$, with all the randomness moved into a parameter-free $\epsilon$, makes $z$ a smooth function of $\mu$ and $\sigma$. The KL term keeps codes near a common prior so that sampling from the prior later yields sensible outputs.
problems.whyItWorks: The loss is the negative evidence lower bound: expected reconstruction likelihood minus the KL between the encoder's posterior and the prior. Reparameterising turns the expectation over $z$ into one over $\epsilon$, whose distribution does not depend on the parameters, so the gradient can be moved inside the expectation and estimated with a single sample.
approach: Encode $x$ to a mean and a log-variance — the parameters of $q(z|x)$
Draw $\epsilon$ from a standard normal and form $z = \mu + \sigma\cdot\epsilon$ — the sample is now differentiable in $\mu$ and $\sigma$
Decode $z$ into a reconstruction and score it against $x$ — the likelihood term
Add the closed-form KL to the standard normal prior — regularises the latent space
Backpropagate through $z$ into both encoder heads — $dz$ flows to $\mu$ directly and to $\log\sigma^2$ via $\frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon$
problems.time: O(n·d·k) per step for input size d and latent size k
problems.space: O(n·(d+k)) for activations and O(d·k) for weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def vae_loss_grads(x, P, eps):
    Wm, bm, Ws, bs, Wd, bd = P
    n = len(x)
    mu = x @ Wm + bm
    lv = x @ Ws + bs
    sig = np.exp(0.5 * lv)
    z = mu + sig * eps
    xh = z @ Wd + bd
    rec = 0.5 * ((xh - x) ** 2).sum()
    kl = -0.5 * (1 + lv - mu ** 2 - np.exp(lv)).sum()
    dxh = (xh - x) / n
    dz = dxh @ Wd.T
    dmu = dz + mu / n
    dlv = dz * eps * 0.5 * sig + 0.5 * (np.exp(lv) - 1) / n
    g = [x.T @ dmu, dmu.sum(0), x.T @ dlv, dlv.sum(0),
         z.T @ dxh, dxh.sum(0)]
    return (rec + kl) / n, g
dryRun: Loss = mean over the batch of (Recon + KL)
problems.description: Learning a smooth latent space for generation, interpolation and representation learning, and as the basis for latent diffusion autoencoders.

examples.input: Why do we need the reparameterisation trick?
examples.output: Sampling $z$ from $q(z|x)$ blocks gradients to the encoder. Writing $z = \mu + \sigma\epsilon$ makes the randomness external and the path differentiable.

examples.input: What does the KL term do?
examples.output: It pulls each posterior toward the prior, which keeps the latent space smooth and lets us generate by sampling $z$ from the prior.

examples.input: What is posterior collapse?
examples.output: The KL term goes to zero because a strong decoder ignores $z$, so the latent code carries no information. KL annealing or a weaker decoder helps.

constraints: Latent dimension $k$
KL weight $\beta$ ($\beta > 1$ gives $\beta$-VAE with a more disentangled, blurrier model)
Decoder likelihood and its variance (Gaussian or Bernoulli)
KL annealing schedule to avoid posterior collapse
edgeCases: Predict log-variance, not variance or $\sigma$, so the value is unconstrained and stable
Use one fresh $\epsilon$ per sample per step; reusing $\epsilon$ removes the noise
Reconstruction and KL must be on the same scale (sum over features, mean over batch)
The linear encoder and decoder here are only for checking gradients; real VAEs use deep nonlinear networks

problems.title: Value Iteration
problems.summary: Compute the optimal state values of a known MDP by repeatedly applying the Bellman optimality backup until the values stop changing, then read off the greedy policy.
problems.bruteForce: When the model is unknown (use Q-learning or policy gradients), when the state space is huge or continuous (the sweep touches every state), or when $\gamma$ is close to one and convergence becomes slow.
problems.intuition: If you knew the best achievable future value of every state, the best action in a state would be the one maximising reward now plus discounted value of where it lands. Start with a guess of zero and apply that one-step lookahead everywhere over and over: information about rewards spreads outward one step per sweep until the guess is self-consistent.
problems.whyItWorks: The Bellman optimality operator is a contraction in the sup norm with factor equal to the discount $\gamma < 1$, so by the Banach fixed-point theorem repeated application converges to its unique fixed point, the optimal value function, from any start. The error shrinks at least geometrically, and a policy greedy with respect to the converged values is optimal.
approach: Initialise $V$ to zeros — any start converges, zero is neutral
Compute $Q = r + \gamma V[\mathrm{next}]$ for every state and action at once — a one-step lookahead using the current values
Take the max over actions and force terminal states to zero — the Bellman optimality backup, with no future after a terminal
Stop when the largest change is below a tolerance — contraction guarantees a small change means a small error
Recompute $Q$ from the final $V$ and take argmax per state — the greedy policy
problems.time: O(sweeps·|S|·|A|) for deterministic transitions (O(|S|²|A|) per sweep if stochastic)
problems.space: O(|S|·|A|) for Q and the reward and next-state tables
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def value_iteration(nxt, rew, done, gamma=0.9, tol=1e-10):
    V = np.zeros(len(done))
    for _ in range(10000):
        Q = rew + gamma * V[nxt]
        V2 = np.where(done, 0.0, Q.max(1))
        if np.abs(V2 - V).max() < tol:
            break
        V = V2
    Q = rew + gamma * V2[nxt]
    return V2, Q
problems.description: Small known MDPs (gridworlds, inventory, scheduling) where the transition model is available, as the exact reference to check model-free methods like Q-learning, and to teach dynamic programming in RL.

examples.input: Why does value iteration converge?
examples.output: The Bellman optimality backup is a $\gamma$-contraction in the max norm, so repeated application converges geometrically to the unique optimal value function.

examples.input: Value iteration versus policy iteration?
examples.output: Policy iteration alternates full policy evaluation with greedy improvement and often needs few outer iterations; value iteration folds one evaluation step and improvement into a single max backup per sweep.

examples.input: How does value iteration relate to Q-learning?
examples.output: Both aim at the fixed point of the Bellman optimality equation; value iteration applies the exact backup with a known model, Q-learning applies it to sampled transitions.

examples.input: How do you get a policy from $V^*$?
examples.output: Pick in each state the action maximising reward plus discounted value of the next state, which is the greedy policy and is optimal.

constraints: Discount $\gamma$ — closer to one looks further ahead but converges more slowly
Tolerance — stopping threshold on the largest value change
Maximum sweeps — a safeguard against slow convergence
edgeCases: Needs the full model (next state and reward for every state-action pair); Q-learning does not
Deterministic transitions only here; a stochastic MDP needs an expectation over next states
Rows of $Q$ for terminal states are not meaningful; their value is fixed at zero
The conventions (reward on the transition, terminal value zero) must match the environment, or comparisons with other methods will disagree

problems.title: Vectors, Norms and Distances
problems.summary: A vector is a point with a length and a direction. Norms measure length, the dot product measures alignment, and distances compare two points, each with different assumptions about the data.
problems.bruteForce: Distances on unscaled mixed-unit features without normalising, and Mahalanobis when the covariance is singular or estimated from too few samples. In very high dimension any distance carries less contrast, so reduce dimension first.
problems.intuition: Every distance answers a different question: $L_1$ adds up coordinate gaps, $L_2$ is straight-line length, $L_\infty$ is the single worst coordinate, cosine ignores length and keeps direction, and Mahalanobis rescales by the data's covariance so correlated or large-scale directions count less. After scaling vectors to length 1, $\|u - v\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos(u, v)$, so Euclidean and cosine rank neighbours identically. In very high dimension the nearest and farthest points end up almost equally far away. Flow: vectors → norm and dot product → unit vectors → angle → distance → ranking.
problems.whyItWorks: Expanding the squared difference gives $\|u - v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2\,u^{\top}v$, so with unit vectors it equals $2 - 2\cos$, a decreasing function of cosine, and rankings agree. Mahalanobis is Euclidean distance after whitening by $\Sigma^{-1/2}$. In high dimension squared distance is a sum of many independent terms, so it concentrates around its mean and the spread relative to the mean shrinks.
approach: Compute $\|x\|_p = (\sum_i |x_i|^p)^{1/p}$, with a max for $p = \infty$ — the length under the chosen geometry
Divide a vector by its $L_2$ norm — a unit vector keeps direction only
Take the dot product of two unit vectors — this is the cosine of their angle
Use $1 - \cos$ as the cosine distance — zero for equal directions, 2 for opposite ones
Solve with the covariance instead of inverting it — Mahalanobis whitens the difference stably
problems.time: O(d) per norm or distance; O(d³) once to factor the covariance, O(d²) per query
problems.space: O(d) for vectors, O(d²) for the covariance matrix
problems.description: Choosing a similarity for nearest-neighbour search, clustering or anomaly detection: $L_2$ for raw geometry, cosine for embeddings, $L_1$ for robustness to a few large coordinates, and Mahalanobis for correlated features with a known covariance.

examples.input: When do Euclidean and cosine give the same neighbours?
examples.output: When the vectors are normalised to unit length. Then the squared Euclidean distance equals 2 minus 2 times the cosine, so the ordering is identical.

examples.input: How is Mahalanobis different from Euclidean distance?
examples.output: It uses the inverse covariance, so directions with large variance or strong correlation count less. With an identity covariance it reduces to Euclidean distance.

examples.input: Why do distances lose meaning in high dimension?
examples.output: Distances to a query concentrate: the farthest point is barely farther than the nearest, so nearest-neighbour contrast fades and k-NN gets unreliable.

examples.input: Why use $L_1$ instead of $L_2$?
examples.output: $L_1$ grows linearly with each coordinate gap, so a few large deviations dominate less than under the squared $L_2$, and it can be more robust to outliers.

constraints: Norm order $p$ (1, 2, $\infty$)
Whether to normalise vectors to unit length first
Covariance estimate and its regularisation for Mahalanobis
edgeCases: Cosine distance is undefined for a zero vector; guard against dividing by zero
Cosine distance is not a true metric; the triangle inequality can fail
Invert-free solve is safer than inv(cov), and a singular covariance needs a small ridge
Unscaled features let the largest-range coordinate decide every $L_p$ distance

problems.title: ViT Patch Embedding and CLS Token
problems.summary: Cut an image into non-overlapping patches, project each flattened patch to a token, prepend a learnable CLS token and add position embeddings.
problems.bruteForce: Small datasets where a convolutional prior helps more, or tasks needing fine detail at pixel level, where large patches lose information before attention starts.
problems.intuition: A transformer expects a sequence of vectors, so ViT turns the image into one by treating every $P \times P$ patch as a "word". The patch projection is exactly a convolution whose stride equals its kernel size. Because attention ignores order, learned position embeddings tell the model where each patch came from, and the CLS token is an extra slot that can gather a global summary for classification.
problems.whyItWorks: Non-overlapping patches keep local pixel structure inside each token while shrinking the sequence from $H \cdot W$ to $HW/P^2$, which makes global self-attention affordable. A shared linear projection is a convolution with kernel and stride $P$, so the same filters are applied at every location. Position embeddings put back the order that attention itself discards.
approach: Split the image into a grid of $P \times P$ patches — turns $H \times W$ pixels into $N = HW/P^2$ tokens
Flatten each patch to a vector of length $C \cdot P^2$ — makes every patch a plain feature vector
Multiply by a shared matrix $W$ and add a bias — linear projection to model width $D$
Prepend a learnable CLS vector — an extra token whose final state represents the whole image
Add a learned position embedding to every token — restores the spatial order attention cannot see
problems.time: O(N·C·P²·D) for the projection, N = HW/P²
problems.space: O((N + 1)·D) for the token sequence plus C·P²·D weights
dryRun: $z_i = x_p^{(i)} W + b,\;\; W \in \mathbb{R}^{C P^2 \times D}$
Head reads final CLS token: $\hat{y} = \mathrm{softmax}(W_h z_L^0)$
problems.description: The input stage of vision transformers (ViT, DeiT, CLIP image encoders) and any model that turns a grid of pixels or a spectrogram into a token sequence.

examples.input: Why is patch embedding the same as a strided convolution?
examples.output: Each output token is a dot product of one $P \times P \times C$ block with the same filters, with the stride $P$ making blocks non-overlapping, which is exactly what flatten-and-project does.

examples.input: What does the CLS token do?
examples.output: It is a learned extra token that attends to all patches through the layers, so its final state is used as the image representation for the classifier.

examples.input: Why does ViT need position embeddings?
examples.output: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without them the model would not know which patch is where.

examples.input: What happens to compute when the patch size is halved?
examples.output: The token count $N$ grows 4×, and attention cost grows roughly 16×.

constraints: Patch size $P$
Embedding width $D$
Position embedding type (learned, sinusoidal, 2D-aware)
Use of a CLS token versus average pooling
edgeCases: $H$ and $W$ must be divisible by $P$ here; real code pads or resizes
Flatten order must match the weights you load ($C, P, P$ versus $P, P, C$)
Learned position embeddings are tied to one grid size; other resolutions need interpolation
This sketch has no dropout, layer norm or transformer blocks after the embedding

problems.title: Weight Initialization (Xavier and He)
problems.summary: Choose the starting weight scale from the layer's fan-in and fan-out so that signals and gradients neither shrink nor blow up with depth.
problems.bruteForce: Less critical when normalisation layers or residual connections keep activations in range, and it does not replace tuning the learning rate. Pretrained weights should be kept, not re-initialised.
problems.intuition: Each layer multiplies the signal by a random matrix, so the signal's variance gets multiplied by a factor set by the weight variance and the layer width. Stack many layers and any factor away from one compounds exponentially, so initialisation picks the weight variance that makes the factor about one for the activation in use.
problems.whyItWorks: For $y = \sum_i w_i x_i$ with independent zero-mean terms, Var(y) = fan_in · Var(w) · Var(x). Setting Var(w) near 1/fan_in keeps the forward variance stable, and the same argument backwards uses fan_out. Xavier compromises between the two, and He adds a factor of two to compensate for ReLU discarding the negative half of its input.
approach: Look up fan_in and fan_out of the layer — the scale depends on how many terms are summed
Xavier: variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out) — balances forward and backward signal for tanh-like units
He: variance 2/fan_in — ReLU zeroes half the signal, so the weights are doubled in variance
Draw from a uniform or normal with that variance — both give the same second moment
Check the signal scale through a deep stack — a quick sanity test for vanishing or exploding activations
problems.time: O(fan_in·fan_out) to draw one weight matrix
problems.space: O(fan_in·fan_out) for the matrix itself
problems.description: Every time you build a network from scratch. Use He for ReLU-family activations and Xavier for tanh, sigmoid or linear layers; frameworks already apply a sensible default per layer type.

examples.input: Why not initialise all weights to zero?
examples.output: Every unit in a layer would compute the same output and receive the same gradient, so they would never differentiate; random values break the symmetry.

examples.input: Why does He use a factor of two compared with plain fan-in scaling?
examples.output: ReLU zeroes about half of the pre-activations, which halves the second moment of the output, so the weight variance is doubled to compensate.

examples.input: What happens with too large or too small a scale?
examples.output: Activations and gradients grow or shrink exponentially with depth, causing exploding values or vanishing learning signals.

constraints: Gain (depends on the activation)
Fan mode: fan_in, fan_out or their average
Uniform or normal sampling
edgeCases: Weights here are shaped (fan_out, fan_in) like PyTorch Linear; swapping the order changes which fan is used
Convolution fans include the kernel area, not just channel counts
The derivation assumes independent, zero-mean inputs, so it is a heuristic, not a guarantee

problems.title: Word2Vec Skip-gram
problems.summary: Learn a dense vector for every word by training it to predict the words that appear in a small window around it.
problems.bruteForce: Each word has one vector regardless of context, so polysemy is lost. Use contextual encoders for that. The full softmax here is too slow for large vocabularies.
problems.intuition: Words used in similar contexts must give similar predictions about their neighbours, so the training signal forces them toward similar vectors. No labels are needed: the text supplies its own targets, and the vectors are the by-product of solving the prediction task.
problems.whyItWorks: Each pair is a softmax classification over the vocabulary, so the gradient is the familiar p − onehot. The centre vector moves toward the output vectors of words that really occur nearby and away from those the model over-predicts. Co-occurrence statistics end up encoded in the dot products of the two embedding tables.
approach: Slide a window over the token ids and emit (centre, context) pairs — the self-made training set
Look up the centre vector and score it against all output vectors — one logit per word
Softmax and take the negative log-probability of the true context word — the loss for the pair
Backpropagate p − onehot into both embedding tables — the exact gradient
Take SGD steps over many pairs and keep the input table as the embeddings — nearby words end up close
problems.time: O(V·d) per pair with the full softmax
problems.space: O(V·d) for the two embedding tables
dryRun: Pair $(c, o)$: predict context $o$ from centre $c$
$s = U v_c$ (one score per vocabulary word)
Negative sampling: a few sigmoid terms, not softmax
problems.description: Cheap unsupervised word features from a large unlabelled corpus, or to understand how embeddings are trained before moving to contextual models.

examples.input: How does skip-gram differ from CBOW?
examples.output: Skip-gram predicts each context word from the centre word, while CBOW predicts the centre word from the averaged context. Skip-gram handles rare words better.

examples.input: Why is negative sampling used?
examples.output: The softmax normalises over the whole vocabulary on every pair. Negative sampling contrasts the true pair with a few random words, making each step cheap.

examples.input: Why are there two embedding matrices?
examples.output: A word plays two roles, centre and context. Separate tables keep the scores asymmetric, and the input table is usually kept as the final embedding.

constraints: Embedding dimension d
Window size (small windows capture syntax, large ones topic)
Number of negative samples when using negative sampling
Learning rate and number of epochs
Subsampling of very frequent words
edgeCases: The full softmax costs O(V) per pair; real implementations use negative sampling or hierarchical softmax
The returned centre gradient applies to row c of W only; the rest of W has zero gradient
Very frequent words dominate the pairs unless subsampled
