Two tables are learned; using only the input table is the usual convention

problems.title: WordPiece Subword Tokenisation
problems.summary: Split a word greedily into the longest vocabulary pieces, marking every non-initial piece with $\#\#$. Training merges the pair with the highest $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$, not the most frequent pair.
problems.bruteForce: When you need byte-level coverage with no unknown tokens at all, where byte-level BPE is the usual choice. WordPiece also replaces a whole word by [UNK] if any part cannot be matched.
problems.intuition: BPE merges whatever pair is most common, which favours pairs made of very frequent pieces that would often appear together anyway. WordPiece divides by the frequencies of the two parts, so it prefers pairs that occur together far more often than chance, which is close to the likelihood gain of adding the merged token. At inference only the final vocabulary is kept and the word is cut by longest match, with $\#\#$ marking a piece that continues a word. Flow: characters → pair scores → best merge → vocabulary → longest match.
problems.whyItWorks: Choosing the pair with the highest $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$ approximates the merge that most increases the training-corpus likelihood under a unigram model, because it measures how much more often $a$ and $b$ co-occur than independence predicts. Longest-match inference is a cheap greedy cut using only the final vocabulary.
approach: Start from single characters, with $\#\#$ on every non-initial one — the base alphabet can spell any known word
Count each token and each adjacent pair, weighted by word frequency — the score needs both
Score each pair as $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$ — rewards association, not raw popularity
Merge the best pair into one token in every word — the merged token joins the vocabulary
Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size — only the vocabulary is kept
Tokenise by taking the longest matching prefix, then continuing with $\#\#$ — if no piece matches, the whole word is [UNK]
problems.time: O(L²) substring lookups per word of length L at inference; O(pairs) per merge in training
problems.space: O(V) for the vocabulary, plus the split corpus during training
dryRun: Token = longest prefix in $V$; rest gets $\#\#$
No prefix of the rest in $V$: word $\rightarrow$ [UNK]
problems.description: Building a subword vocabulary for BERT-style encoders, where an open vocabulary with a small table is needed and rare words should break into known pieces instead of one unknown token.

examples.input: How does WordPiece differ from BPE?
examples.output: BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece merges the pair with the highest $\mathrm{freq}(ab)/(\mathrm{freq}(a)\,\mathrm{freq}(b))$, so pieces that are individually common are not merged just because they are common. At inference WordPiece uses longest match, not the learned merge order.

examples.input: What does the $\#\#$ prefix mean?
examples.output: It marks a piece that continues the previous one inside a word, so the original words can be rebuilt by joining pieces and stripping $\#\#$.

examples.input: What happens to a word that cannot be segmented?
examples.output: If at some position no prefix of the remainder is in the vocabulary, the whole word becomes [UNK], not just the unmatched part.

examples.input: Is greedy longest match always the best segmentation?
examples.output: No. It is fast and deterministic but can choose a worse split than a search over all segmentations, as a unigram model with Viterbi would.

constraints: Target vocabulary size
Base alphabet and normalisation (lower-casing, accent stripping)
Continuation prefix (## in BERT)
Maximum characters per word before falling back to [UNK]
edgeCases: Training needs the splits to start as characters with $\#\#$; plain characters give a different vocabulary
The merged token drops the $\#\#$ of its second part, and keeps the $\#\#$ of its first part
Inference ignores merge order, so it can differ from how the vocabulary was built

sheets.description: Neural network foundations, training tricks and the first architectures.

sheets.name: LLM Engineer
sheets.description: The LLM engineer roadmap: language, transformers, how LLMs work and tokenisation.

sheets.description: Core classical machine learning, evaluation and the math behind them.

sheets.name: NLP, Vision and RL
sheets.description: Text, image and reinforcement-learning building blocks.

patterns.name: Linear models
patterns.summary: Predict with a weighted sum of features, then fit the weights by minimising a convex loss.
whenToUse: You need a fast, interpretable baseline.
Features are roughly linearly related to the target or a link of it.
Data is small or wide and a simple model should not overfit.
patterns.keyIdea: The model is one dot product, so the loss surface is a smooth bowl and the weights can be read as feature effects. Changing the loss (squared, log, hinge) changes the model but not the shape of the idea.
patterns.complexity: Fit O(n·d) per gradient step or O(n·d² + d³) closed form; predict O(d).
pitfalls: Collinear features make the weights unstable.
Unscaled features slow gradient descent and skew regularisation.

patterns.name: Regularisation
patterns.summary: Constrain or perturb a model during training so it cannot memorise the training set.
whenToUse: Training error is far below validation error.
You have many features or parameters relative to the data.
You want sparse weights (L1) or small stable weights (L2).
patterns.keyIdea: Every regulariser trades a little training fit for lower variance: penalties shrink weights, dropout and noise stop co-adaptation, early stopping limits how far optimisation goes. Pick the one whose bias you can live with.
patterns.complexity: Negligible extra cost per step; the tuning cost is choosing the strength.
pitfalls: Too much regularisation underfits.
Penalties assume scaled features; scale first.

patterns.name: Gradient-based optimisation
patterns.summary: Improve parameters by following the gradient of a loss, with tricks for speed and stability.
whenToUse: The loss is differentiable in the parameters.
There is no closed form or it is too expensive.
You train a neural network end to end.
patterns.keyIdea: The gradient says which way is downhill; the learning rate says how far to step. Momentum, adaptive scaling and schedules are all ways of choosing a better step from the same gradient history.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def sgd(w, g, lr):
    return w - lr * g

def adam(w, g, m, v, t, lr=1e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g
    mh, vh = m / (1 - b1 ** t), v / (1 - b2 ** t)
    return w - lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + eps), m, v
patterns.complexity: O(parameters) per step; memory doubles for Adam's two moments.
pitfalls: A learning rate that is too high diverges.
Adaptive methods can generalise slightly worse than tuned SGD.

patterns.name: Tree ensembles
patterns.summary: Combine many shallow or randomised decision trees by averaging (bagging) or by fitting residuals (boosting).
whenToUse: Tabular data with mixed feature types and interactions.
You want strong accuracy with little preprocessing.
Features are on different scales or have outliers.
patterns.keyIdea: One tree is high variance, so average many decorrelated trees (random forest) or add small trees that each correct the previous errors (boosting). Bagging cuts variance, boosting cuts bias.
patterns.complexity: Fit O(T·n·d·log n); predict O(T·depth).
pitfalls: Boosting overfits noisy labels without early stopping.
Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the training range.

patterns.name: Probabilistic models
patterns.summary: Model the data distribution explicitly and reason with Bayes rule and likelihoods.
whenToUse: You need calibrated uncertainty, not only a label.
Data is scarce and a sensible prior helps.
A latent structure (clusters, classes) generates the data.
patterns.keyIdea: Write down how the data could have been generated, then fit parameters by maximising likelihood or computing a posterior. Naive Bayes, Gaussian mixtures and logistic regression are all this idea with different assumptions.
patterns.complexity: Usually O(n·d·k) for k components or classes.
pitfalls: Wrong independence assumptions give overconfident probabilities.
Work in log space to avoid underflow.

patterns.name: Distance and clustering
patterns.summary: Group or classify points by how close they are in feature space.
whenToUse: You have no labels and want structure (clustering).
Similar examples should share a label (nearest neighbours).
A meaningful distance between examples exists.
patterns.keyIdea: Everything depends on the distance and the scale of the features. K-means uses centres, DBSCAN uses density, kNN uses the nearest labelled points; all fail if distances are meaningless.
patterns.complexity: O(n·k·d) per assignment pass; kNN prediction O(n·d) without an index.
pitfalls: Distances break down in very high dimensions.
Unscaled features let one column dominate.

patterns.name: Classification metrics
patterns.summary: Summarise a classifier's errors with numbers chosen for the cost of each mistake.
whenToUse: Classes are imbalanced and accuracy hides failures.
Missing a positive costs more than a false alarm, or the reverse.
You must compare models independent of a threshold.
patterns.keyIdea: Accuracy counts all errors equally. Precision, recall and F1 expose the trade-off at one threshold, ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds, and calibration asks whether the probabilities mean what they say.
patterns.complexity: O(n) per threshold; AUC needs a sort, O(n log n).
pitfalls: ROC-AUC looks optimistic on heavily imbalanced data.
Picking the threshold on the test set leaks information.

patterns.name: Validation hygiene
patterns.summary: Evaluate a model so the number you report is an honest estimate of future performance.
whenToUse: You tune hyperparameters or choose between models.
The dataset is small and one split is noisy.
Preprocessing uses statistics of the data.
patterns.keyIdea: Anything that sees the test data, even through a scaler or feature selection, inflates the score. Fit every preprocessing step inside the training fold only, and keep one untouched final test set.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def kfold(n, k, rng):
    idx = rng.permutation(n)
    folds = np.array_split(idx, k)
    for i in range(k):
        val = folds[i]
        train = np.concatenate(folds[:i] + folds[i + 1:])
        yield train, val
patterns.complexity: k times the cost of one fit.
pitfalls: Time series need forward-chaining splits, not shuffled folds.
Repeated tuning on one validation set overfits it.

patterns.name: Normalisation
patterns.summary: Rescale features or activations to a stable range so optimisation and distances behave.
whenToUse: Features have very different scales.
Deep network training is unstable or slow.
Distance-based or penalised models are used.
patterns.keyIdea: Subtract a mean and divide by a spread. Feature scaling does it once on the inputs; batch norm and layer norm do it on hidden activations, differing only in which axis the statistics are taken over.
patterns.complexity: O(n·d); batch norm also stores running statistics.
pitfalls: Compute scaling statistics on training data only.
Batch norm behaves differently in train and eval mode.

patterns.name: Attention and sequences
patterns.summary: Model ordered data by carrying state through time or by letting every position look at every other.
whenToUse: Inputs are sequences such as text, audio or time series.
Long-range dependencies matter.
You want parallel training over positions.
patterns.keyIdea: Recurrent cells compress the past into one state, which is sequential and forgets. Attention scores every pair of positions directly, so it is parallel and long-range, at the price of quadratic cost and the need for positional information.
patterns.complexity: Attention O(n²·d) in sequence length n; an RNN is O(n·d²) but sequential.
pitfalls: Without positional encoding attention ignores order.
Plain RNNs suffer vanishing gradients on long sequences.

patterns.name: Dimensionality reduction
patterns.summary: Compress features into fewer coordinates that keep most of the structure.
whenToUse: There are many correlated features.
You want to visualise or denoise data.
Downstream models are slow or overfit in high dimensions.
patterns.keyIdea: Find the directions that carry the most variance (PCA, via SVD) or learn a compressed code that reconstructs the input (autoencoder). A linear autoencoder spans the same subspace as PCA.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def pca(X, k):
    Xc = X - X.mean(0)
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
    return Xc @ Vt[:k].T, Vt[:k]       # scores, components
patterns.complexity: SVD O(min(n,d)·n·d).
pitfalls: Variance is not the same as usefulness for the label.
Scale features before PCA.

patterns.name: Information-theoretic losses
patterns.summary: Train by minimising the gap between the model's distribution and the data's, measured with entropy.
whenToUse: The model outputs a probability distribution.
You classify with softmax or sigmoid outputs.
You compare or regularise distributions (VAEs, distillation).
patterns.keyIdea: Cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL divergence, and the entropy of the data is fixed, so minimising cross-entropy minimises KL and maximises likelihood. Those three views are one idea.
patterns.complexity: O(n·classes).
pitfalls: Compute log-softmax with log-sum-exp, not log(softmax).
KL is asymmetric; the direction changes the behaviour.

patterns.name: Network building blocks
patterns.summary: The small differentiable pieces every neural network is assembled from.
whenToUse: You are designing or debugging a feed-forward network.
Gradients vanish or explode as depth grows.
You need non-linearity between linear layers.
patterns.keyIdea: A network is linear maps separated by non-linearities. Activations decide what gradients survive, and residual connections give the gradient a shortcut so depth stops hurting.
patterns.complexity: O(width²) per dense layer.
pitfalls: Without a non-linearity stacked layers collapse to one linear map.
Saturating activations such as sigmoid kill gradients in deep stacks.

patterns.name: Convolution and vision
patterns.summary: Process images with weights shared across positions, then pool and score regions.
whenToUse: Inputs have a grid structure such as images.
The same pattern can appear anywhere in the input.
You detect objects and must merge overlapping boxes.
patterns.keyIdea: Sliding one small kernel over the image reuses its weights everywhere, which gives translation equivariance with few parameters. Pooling then shrinks the map, and IoU with non-maximum suppression cleans up detections.
patterns.complexity: O(H·W·kh·kw) per channel pair.
pitfalls: Strided pooling throws away fine position information.
Plain NMS removes overlapping true objects of different classes.

patterns.name: Text processing
patterns.summary: Turn raw text into numbers: tokens, weights, embeddings and search over outputs.
whenToUse: Inputs are words or sentences.
You need a vocabulary that handles rare and unseen words.
You generate sequences and must choose among many continuations.
patterns.keyIdea: Models need numbers, so text is split into tokens. Tokens are then weighted by how informative they are (TF-IDF), mapped to vectors (word2vec), and generated by searching for the most likely sequence (beam search).
patterns.complexity: TF-IDF O(documents·vocabulary); beam search O(width·vocabulary·length).
pitfalls: Word-level vocabularies fail on unseen words; subword tokenisation helps.
Greedy decoding misses sequences whose early tokens look unlikely.

patterns.name: Reinforcement learning
patterns.summary: Learn to act by trial and error from rewards, by estimating values or improving a policy directly.
whenToUse: There is no labelled answer, only a delayed reward.
Actions change the situation you see next.
You can simulate the environment cheaply.
patterns.keyIdea: Value methods such as Q-learning learn how good each action is and act greedily on it. Policy-gradient methods such as REINFORCE nudge the policy toward actions that led to high return. Both trade exploration against exploitation.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99):
    target = r + gamma * Q[s2].max()
    Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
    return Q
patterns.complexity: O(1) per Q-learning update; table size O(states·actions).
pitfalls: Too little exploration locks in a poor policy.
Policy-gradient estimates have high variance; use a baseline.

patterns.name: Generative models
patterns.summary: Learn the data distribution well enough to sample new examples from it.
whenToUse: You need to create new images, text or other data.
You want a compact latent representation you can sample from.
Labels are scarce but raw data is plentiful.
patterns.keyIdea: Every generative model turns simple noise into data. VAEs do it with an encoder and a decoder trained on a likelihood bound, GANs with a generator trained against a critic, and diffusion models by learning to undo gradual noising.
patterns.complexity: Training is usually the expensive part; diffusion sampling needs many network passes.
pitfalls: GAN training can oscillate or collapse to few modes.
VAE samples tend to be blurry compared with GANs and diffusion.

patterns.name: Transfer and adaptation
patterns.summary: Reuse a trained model by fine-tuning it cheaply or compressing it into a smaller one.
whenToUse: You have little data for the target task.
A large pretrained model exists for a related domain.
You must fit a model into a small memory or latency budget.
patterns.keyIdea: Pretrained weights already encode useful features, so train only a small part (a head or low-rank update) or let a small student imitate the big teacher's outputs. You keep most of the accuracy for a fraction of the cost.
patterns.complexity: LoRA trains O(r·(d_in + d_out)) parameters per layer instead of O(d_in·d_out).
pitfalls: Fine-tuning with too large a learning rate destroys pretrained features.
A student cannot exceed what the teacher's outputs reveal.

patterns.name: Time series
patterns.summary: Forecast ordered data by smoothing the past, measuring how it correlates with itself, and modelling it autoregressively.
whenToUse: Observations are ordered in time and neighbours are related.
You need a quick baseline forecast before anything complex.
You want to know how many past steps still carry information.
patterns.keyIdea: Time series break the independence assumption, so we model the memory directly. Exponential smoothing keeps a decaying average, autocorrelation measures how far back the memory reaches, and ARIMA turns that memory into a regression on past values after differencing away trends.
patterns.complexity: O(n) per pass for smoothing and per lag for autocorrelation.
pitfalls: Shuffled train and test splits leak the future; split by time.
Trends and seasonality must be removed or modelled before assuming stationarity.

patterns.name: Graph neural networks
patterns.summary: Learn on graphs by letting every node repeatedly combine its neighbours' features.
whenToUse: Data is a graph such as molecules, social networks or citations.
A node's label depends on its neighbourhood.
The number of neighbours varies from node to node.
patterns.keyIdea: One layer aggregates each node's neighbours (a normalised sum, or an attention-weighted sum) and then transforms the result with shared weights. Stacking k layers lets information travel k hops, but too many layers blur all nodes together.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def gcn_layer(A, X, W):
    A = A + np.eye(len(A))               # add self-loops
    d = A.sum(1) ** -0.5
    A_hat = d[:, None] * A * d[None]       # D^-1/2 A D^-1/2
    return np.maximum(A_hat @ X @ W, 0)    # aggregate, then transform
patterns.complexity: O(edges·d) with a sparse adjacency; the dense version here is O(n²·d).
pitfalls: Deep stacks over-smooth: node features become nearly identical.
A dense adjacency does not scale to large graphs.

patterns.name: Preference alignment and policy gradients
patterns.summary: Steer a model with comparisons or rewards: learn a reward from preferences, or optimise the policy directly.
whenToUse: Quality is easier to compare than to label.
You fine-tune a language model toward human preferences.
An agent must improve a stochastic policy from rewards.
patterns.keyIdea: A pairwise Bradley-Terry loss turns preferences into a reward score. DPO folds that reward into the policy's own log-ratios, so no separate reward model or sampling loop is needed. PPO and advantage estimation do the reinforcement-learning version, clipping how far each update can move the policy.
patterns.complexity: O(batch) once log-probabilities are computed; the cost is in running the language model.
pitfalls: Preference data is noisy and can encode annotator bias.
Pushing the policy far from the reference can hurt fluency.

patterns.name: Text evaluation and retrieval
patterns.summary: Score generated text against references and measure how well search puts relevant documents first.
whenToUse: You compare machine translation or summaries with references.
You build search or retrieval-augmented generation.
You need to rank documents and report a single quality number.
patterns.keyIdea: Overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE count shared n-grams, so they are cheap but blind to meaning. Retrieval metrics judge the ranked list: recall at k asks whether the answer was found, MRR rewards finding it early, and nDCG also values graded relevance.
patterns.complexity: O(k) per query for recall and O(n) for MRR.
pitfalls: High n-gram overlap does not guarantee a correct or fluent answer.
Retrieval scores depend on the quality of the relevance labels.

patterns.name: Compare: Ridge vs Lasso
patterns.summary: Both shrink weights to fight overfitting; ridge shrinks smoothly, lasso can set weights exactly to zero.
whenToUse: Pick ridge when most features carry some signal or are correlated.
Pick lasso when you expect only a few features to matter and want a sparse model.
Use elastic net when features are correlated and you still want sparsity.
patterns.keyIdea: The L2 penalty has a gradient that shrinks as a weight shrinks, so weights get small but rarely reach zero. The L1 penalty pulls with constant strength, so small weights are driven all the way to zero. That is why lasso selects features and ridge does not.
patterns.complexity: Ridge has a closed form, O(n·d² + d³); lasso needs an iterative solver such as coordinate descent.
pitfalls: Both need scaled features, or the penalty treats columns unequally.
Lasso picks one of a group of correlated features more or less arbitrarily.

patterns.name: Compare: Random forest vs Gradient boosting
patterns.summary: Both combine many trees; a forest averages independent deep trees, boosting adds shallow trees one after another.
whenToUse: Pick a random forest for a strong, low-tuning baseline that is hard to overfit.
Pick gradient boosting when you can tune carefully and want the best accuracy on tabular data.
Prefer the forest when training must parallelise easily, because boosting is sequential.
patterns.keyIdea: A forest reduces variance by averaging trees trained on different samples. Boosting reduces bias by letting each new tree fix what the ensemble still gets wrong. So forests use deep trees and boosting uses shallow ones.
patterns.complexity: A forest trains its trees in parallel; boosting trains them in sequence.
pitfalls: Boosting overfits noisy labels without early stopping.
A forest with too few trees gives noisy predictions.
aliases: Compare: Random forest vs Gradient boosting

patterns.name: Compare: Batch norm vs Layer norm
patterns.summary: Both normalise activations; batch norm uses statistics across the batch, layer norm across the features of one example.
whenToUse: Pick batch norm for convolutional networks with reasonably large batches.
Pick layer norm for transformers and recurrent models, or when batches are tiny or vary.
Pick layer norm when training and evaluation behaviour must be identical.
patterns.keyIdea: The only difference is the axis the mean and variance are taken over. Batch norm needs the other examples in the batch, so it keeps running averages for evaluation. Layer norm looks at a single example, so it behaves the same in training and evaluation.
patterns.complexity: Both are O(n·d); batch norm also stores running statistics.
pitfalls: Batch norm degrades with very small batches.
In evaluation mode batch norm must use running statistics, not the batch's.
aliases: Compare: Batch norm vs Layer norm

patterns.name: Compare: Precision-recall vs ROC
patterns.summary: Both summarise a classifier across thresholds; precision-recall focuses on the positive class, ROC compares true and false positive rates.
whenToUse: Pick precision-recall when positives are rare and false alarms matter.
Pick ROC-AUC when classes are fairly balanced or both error types matter equally.
Report both when stakeholders care about different parts of the trade-off.
patterns.keyIdea: ROC uses the false positive rate, whose denominator is the large pool of negatives, so many false alarms barely move it. Precision divides by the predicted positives, so the same false alarms hurt it a lot. That is why ROC can look optimistic on imbalanced data.
patterns.complexity: O(n) per threshold; the full curves need a sort, O(n log n).
pitfalls: A random classifier has AUC 0.5 in ROC, but its precision-recall baseline equals the positive rate.
Both curves depend on the ordering of scores, not on whether probabilities are calibrated.

patterns.name: Compare: SGD with momentum vs Adam
patterns.summary: Both speed up gradient descent; momentum smooths the direction, Adam also rescales each parameter by its gradient history.
whenToUse: Pick SGD with momentum for well-tuned vision training where the best final accuracy matters.
Pick Adam for fast progress with little tuning, especially for transformers and sparse gradients.
Pick Adam when parameters have very different gradient scales.
patterns.keyIdea: Momentum averages past gradients to keep moving through noise and narrow valleys. Adam adds a second average of squared gradients and divides by it, giving every parameter its own step size. That makes it robust to scale but a little less predictable in how well the result generalises.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def momentum_step(w, g, v, lr=0.1, mu=0.9):
    v = mu * v + g
    return w - lr * v, v

def adam_step(w, g, m, s, t, lr=1e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.999):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    s = b2 * s + (1 - b2) * g * g
    mh, sh = m / (1 - b1 ** t), s / (1 - b2 ** t)
    return w - lr * mh / (np.sqrt(sh) + 1e-8), m, s
patterns.complexity: Momentum stores one extra vector per parameter; Adam stores two.
pitfalls: Adam needs about twice the optimiser memory of plain SGD.
Weight decay behaves differently in Adam; use the decoupled form (AdamW).
aliases: Compare: SGD with momentum vs Adam

patterns.name: Compare: PCA vs Autoencoder
patterns.summary: Both compress data into fewer dimensions; PCA is linear and has a closed form, an autoencoder can be non-linear and is trained.
whenToUse: Pick PCA for a fast, deterministic, interpretable linear projection.
Pick an autoencoder when the structure is curved and you have enough data to train one.
Start with PCA as a baseline; an autoencoder must beat it to be worth the effort.
patterns.keyIdea: A linear autoencoder trained with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA. Adding non-linear layers lets the encoder bend to curved structure, at the cost of training, tuning and a result that is not unique.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def pca_encode(X, k):
    Xc = X - X.mean(0)
    _, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
    return Xc @ Vt[:k].T                 # closed form

def ae_encode(X, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    return np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2   # learned by training
patterns.complexity: PCA is one SVD; an autoencoder needs many gradient steps.
pitfalls: PCA directions follow variance, which is not always what matters for the task.
An autoencoder with a large hidden layer can simply copy its input.

patterns.name: Compare: k-means vs Gaussian mixture
patterns.summary: Both group points around centres; k-means makes hard round clusters, a Gaussian mixture gives soft, shaped clusters.
whenToUse: Pick k-means for fast, simple clustering of roughly round, equal-sized groups.
Pick a Gaussian mixture when clusters differ in size or are elliptical.
Pick the mixture when you need membership probabilities.
patterns.keyIdea: K-means is the limit of a Gaussian mixture where every cluster is a sphere of equal size and each point belongs fully to one. The mixture keeps covariances and weights and shares points between clusters through responsibilities. Both are fit by alternating two steps and can end in local optima.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def kmeans_assign(X, C):
    d = ((X[:, None] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    return d.argmin(1)                      # hard labels

def gmm_responsibilities(logp):             # logp: (n, k)
    z = logp - logp.max(1, keepdims=True)
    r = np.exp(z)
    return r / r.sum(1, keepdims=True)      # soft labels
patterns.complexity: Both cost O(n·k·d) per iteration; the mixture adds covariance work.
pitfalls: Both depend on the starting centres, so restart several times.
You must choose the number of clusters in advance.

patterns.name: Compare: k-means vs DBSCAN
patterns.summary: K-means needs the number of clusters and finds round groups; DBSCAN finds dense regions of any shape and marks outliers as noise.
whenToUse: Pick k-means when you know roughly how many clusters there are and they are compact.
Pick DBSCAN when clusters have odd shapes or the data has outliers.
Avoid DBSCAN when the density varies a lot between clusters.
patterns.keyIdea: K-means assigns every point to the nearest centre, so it must place outliers somewhere and cuts curved shapes into round pieces. DBSCAN grows clusters from points that have enough neighbours within a radius, so shape is free and sparse points become noise. The radius and neighbour count replace the cluster count as the settings to tune.
patterns.complexity: K-means is O(n·k·d) per pass; plain DBSCAN is O(n²) without an index.
pitfalls: DBSCAN's radius is hard to choose when features are not scaled.
K-means is distorted by outliers because centres are means.

patterns.name: Compare: LSTM vs Attention
patterns.summary: Both model sequences; a recurrent cell passes one state step by step, attention lets every position read every other directly.
whenToUse: Pick attention for long-range dependencies and parallel training on modern hardware.
Pick a recurrent cell for streaming input with small, constant memory per step.
Pick attention-based models when you have enough data and compute.
patterns.keyIdea: A recurrent cell must squeeze everything it has seen into a fixed-size state and process steps in order. Attention compares each position with all the others, so information travels in one hop, but the cost grows with the square of the length. Attention also needs positional information because it ignores order by itself.
patterns.template:
import numpy as np

def rnn_step(h, x, Wh, Wx, b):
    return np.tanh(h @ Wh + x @ Wx + b)     # one state, in order

def attend(Q, K, V):
    s = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])      # all pairs at once
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    return (e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ V
patterns.complexity: A recurrent pass is O(n·d²) but sequential; attention is O(n²·d) but parallel.
pitfalls: Plain RNNs lose gradients over long sequences, and LSTMs only soften this.
Attention memory grows with the square of the sequence length.

patterns.name: Compare: VAE vs GAN
patterns.summary: Both generate data from noise; a VAE trains with a likelihood bound, a GAN trains a generator against a discriminator.
whenToUse: Pick a VAE when you need a smooth latent space and stable training.
Pick a GAN when sharp, realistic samples matter more than stability.
Pick a VAE when you also need to encode real data into latents.
patterns.keyIdea: A VAE is trained by reconstruction plus a KL term, so it has a clear loss to minimise but tends to give blurry samples. A GAN has no likelihood; the generator improves only by fooling a discriminator, which gives sharp samples but an unstable two-player game.
patterns.complexity: Both need many training steps; GANs also need careful balancing of two networks.
pitfalls: GANs can collapse to a few modes.
VAE samples blur when the decoder noise model is too simple.

patterns.name: Compare: Naive Bayes vs Logistic regression
patterns.summary: Both give a simple classifier; naive Bayes models how each class generates the features, logistic regression models the class probability directly.
whenToUse: Pick naive Bayes when data is tiny or very high-dimensional, such as text.
Pick logistic regression when you have enough data and correlated features.
Pick naive Bayes for a very fast baseline that trains in one pass.
patterns.keyIdea: Naive Bayes is generative: it learns each feature's distribution per class and assumes the features are independent given the class. Logistic regression is discriminative: it fits the decision boundary directly, so it copes with correlated features. With lots of data the discriminative model usually wins; with little data the generative one can win.
patterns.complexity: Naive Bayes fits in one pass over the data; logistic regression needs an iterative solver.
pitfalls: Naive Bayes probabilities are often overconfident.
Logistic regression needs scaling and regularisation for stable fits.
aliases: Compare: Naive Bayes vs Logistic regression

patterns.name: Compare: Squared error vs Cross-entropy
patterns.summary: Both are losses; squared error suits real-valued targets, cross-entropy suits class probabilities.
whenToUse: Pick squared error for regression with roughly Gaussian noise.
Pick cross-entropy for classification with softmax or sigmoid outputs.
Avoid squared error on probabilities, because its gradient vanishes when the output saturates.
patterns.keyIdea: Squared error is the negative log-likelihood of Gaussian noise, and cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical label. With a sigmoid or softmax output, the gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is simply prediction minus target, while squared error's gradient is damped by the saturating output.
patterns.complexity: Both are O(n) in the number of examples (times classes for cross-entropy).
pitfalls: Compute log-softmax with log-sum-exp, not log(softmax).
Class imbalance may call for class weights or focal loss on top of cross-entropy.
